exp.0:0:
This verse opens the book of Deuteronomy. It says that what follows are the words Moses spoke to all Israel, on the east side of the Jordan River, in the wilderness. The place names in the verse (Paran, Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Dizahab) are geographical references, and for several of them no one knows for certain where they were.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before they enter the promised land. The new generation needed to remember what God had done and commanded. That is why Moses reviews the history and the law of the covenant.

For today: God wants us to remember his work and his Word, especially before taking an important step. Before beginning something new, take a moment to review how God has guided you and what he has taught you.
exp.0:1:
This verse says that from Horeb (another name for Mount Sinai) to Kadesh-barnea there were eleven days' journey, that is, eleven days of travel. The route passed by Mount Seir, the region of Edom. A "journey" was what one could walk in a day.

Moses speaks to the people near the Jordan, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He wants to remind them of their history before they enter the promised land. This detail about distance underlines something sad: a short trip took forty years, because the people doubted and disobeyed at Kadesh. Some scholars see here a note of gentle reproach; the text does not say this directly.

Today, our own paths sometimes stretch out because we lack trust in God. But He continues to guide with patience. Ask yourself: in what area do I need to obey today, without delaying any longer?
exp.0:2:
This verse says that, when forty years had passed since the exit from Egypt, on the first day of the eleventh month, Moses spoke to the people of Israel. He told them everything that God had commanded him to tell them.

The book records the last words of Moses. The people are east of the Jordan, about to enter the promised land. The earlier generation had died in the wilderness, so Moses reminds them of what God did and commanded. The text stresses that he spoke faithfully, without adding ideas of his own.

For today: God has spoken clearly, and it is good for us to remember and repeat his Word faithfully. This week, choose a passage of the Bible, read it calmly, and share it with someone in your family, just as it is, with humility and affection.
exp.0:5:
Moses recalls what God told the people at Mount Horeb, another name for Sinai. God says to them: "You have dwelt long enough in this mount," meaning that they had stayed there long enough. It was time to leave that place and move forward.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He retells the story so they will remember what God did. They had spent about a year at Horeb, where they received the law. Now God was calling them to move on and take possession of the land he had promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

God gives times of rest and learning, but he does not want us to stay there forever. If he shows you that it is time to take a step of faith, do not settle down out of fear or habit. Pray, trust his promise, and move forward.
exp.0:6:
God tells the people of Israel to rise up, leave Mount Horeb, and set out toward the promised land. He names the regions they will pass through: the mount of the Amorites, the plains, the hills, the valleys, the south, the seashore, the land of the Canaanites, Lebanon, and as far as the great river Euphrates.

Moses speaks to the people in Moab, near the Jordan, almost at the end of his life. He reminds them of what God commanded them forty years earlier. They had stayed a long time at Horeb, and it was now time to move forward and receive the promise made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

For today: God blesses us at every stage, but he does not want us to remain stuck when he calls us to move forward. We must trust his promise and take the next step in faith, even when it means leaving what is comfortable.
exp.0:10:
Moses wishes that God, the God of Israel's ancestors, would make the people a thousand times more numerous than they already are, and that he would bless them just as he has promised. "Your fathers" refers to the ancestors, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, as he reminds them of what they have lived through since Sinai. They were already as numerous as the stars, and that fulfilled God's promise. But Moses could not carry so many problems and disputes alone, so he asked them to choose wise men to help him lead. His wish for their blessing comes from a grateful heart, even in the middle of his weariness.

We can give thanks for God's blessings without hiding that sometimes they weigh on us. And if we are carrying everything alone, we can ask for help from wise and trustworthy people.
exp.0:15:
Moses reminds the judges of Israel what he commanded them. He asked them to listen carefully to cases between brothers and to judge fairly, whether the dispute was between two Israelites or involved a foreigner. The word "hear" in this verse means to listen attentively, and the foreigner is the stranger who lived among them.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before entering the promised land. He reminds them that, when they saw how heavy the burden of governing was, they appointed wise leaders to help him. Here he repeats the first instruction he gave those judges: impartial justice, even for someone who was not one of the people.

For today: before you give an opinion or make a decision about a conflict, listen patiently to all sides. Treat with the same justice the people you know and those you do not, without favoritism, because God is concerned with justice.
exp.0:20:
It says that God has already placed the promised land in front of the people. Moses tells them to go up and take it, just as God had said to their ancestors.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, and he reminds them of what happened at Kadesh-barnea. There God showed them that the land was ready. However, as the text goes on, the people proposed sending spies first. Moses agreed to the idea, although later that decision led the people to doubt and not obey.

For today: when God has already given you a promise or a clear direction, you do not need to wait until you feel completely sure of everything. Take the step with confidence, relying on what He has said, and ask Him to replace your fear with courage.
exp.0:21:
The passage says that all the people came near to Moses with a proposal: to send men ahead to explore the land. They wanted someone to bring them a report about the route they would take up and the cities they would reach.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, recalling what happened at Horeb and Kadesh-barnea. God had already given them the land and told them not to fear. Even so, the people asked for scouts. Moses accepted the idea (v. 23), although Numbers 13 shows that God allowed it, and the report ended in fear and disobedience. Commentators differ on whether the request already showed a lack of trust.

Today, planning ahead and gathering information is wise, but it should not replace trust in God's promises. Before seeking more data, ask yourself whether God has already spoken and whether what you really seek is security to obey.
exp.0:29:
This verse says that God himself goes ahead of his people and that he will fight for them. He will do it just as he did in Egypt, when everyone saw it with their own eyes.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel almost forty years after the events. He reminds them of the moment when the spies returned afraid, talking about strong cities and giants. Moses wanted them to trust in God, not in their own strength. Yet, as the verses that follow say, they did not believe.

For today: when you face something that seems too big, remember how God has helped you before. That memory can strengthen your trust and help you take the next step, knowing that you are not alone.
exp.0:30:
This verse says that God cared for his people in the wilderness the way a father carries and bears his small son. The people saw that God went with them through the whole journey, until they came to where they were.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, close to entering the promised land. He reminds them of what God did so that they would trust him. But the context that follows shows that, despite all this care, the people did not believe. God was caring for them, and they still doubted.

For today: when you go through a difficult time, remember how God has sustained you before. Write down some of the times he cared for you, and let that memory strengthen your trust for the road ahead.
exp.0:32:
It says that God himself went ahead of the people of Israel during their journey through the desert. He searched out the best place for them to camp. By night he guided them with a pillar of fire, and by day with a cloud.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the desert. He reminds them how God cared for them, even though they did not trust him and did not want to enter the promised land. Because of this, that generation lost the opportunity to enter.

For today: when the path is not clear, remember how God has cared for you before. That memory can help you trust him today, and take the next step even though you cannot yet see the whole way.
exp.0:35:
God makes an exception: Caleb, son of Jephunneh, will indeed see the promised land. God will give him the land he has walked on, and also to his children. The reason is that Caleb wholly followed the Lord, that is, he followed God completely, with faithfulness and without turning back.

Moses speaks to the people and recalls what happened at Kadesh-barnea. The spies explored Canaan, and the people were filled with fear and did not trust God. For that reason that generation died in the wilderness. Caleb, together with Joshua, had encouraged the people to trust God.

For today: faithfulness to God does not go unnoticed by Him. When everyone around you gives in to fear or doubt, you can keep trusting and obeying, not being perfect, but with a wholehearted heart. God knows how to honor that constancy, even though sometimes it may take a while to be seen.
exp.0:36:
Moses says that God was also angry with him because of the people. He told him that he too would not enter the promised land.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, near the land, when he recalls the rebellion at Kadesh-barnea, where the people refused to trust God. Other passages, such as Numbers 20, connect Moses' prohibition with what happened at Meribah, when he struck the rock. Here he emphasizes how the people's attitude affected him too. Interpreters explain this in different ways.

For today: our decisions and attitudes influence others, especially in family, church, and work. Let us ask God for faith and humility to obey him, and if we experience painful consequences, let us trust that his plan goes forward.
exp.0:37:
Deuteronomy 1:38 says that Joshua, son of Nun, who now stands before Moses, will be the one who enters the promised land. Moses receives the command to encourage him, that is, to give him courage and strength, because Joshua will be the one who gives the land to Israel as an inheritance. "Inherit" here means to give the land as a possession.

Moses speaks to the people, recalling what happened when Israel did not trust God and refused to enter the land. Because of that failure, that generation would not enter, except Caleb. Moses also tells how God said to him that he too would not enter. Then God points to Joshua as the next leader.

For today: God continues to care for his work even when leaders change. We can encourage those who serve, with a kind word or a prayer, instead of criticizing them.
exp.0:39:
Here the text says God tells the people of Israel to turn around and set out toward the wilderness, by the way that leads to the Red Sea.

Moses speaks to the people and reminds them of what God told them years earlier. Because they did not trust Him, that generation did not enter the promised land. After hearing this, they said they would go up to fight, but God warned them not to, because He would not go with them. Their repentance came too late, and they wanted to obey in their own way.

For today: obeying God means doing it in His timing and in His direction, not only when it suits us. If we have gone wrong, let us ask forgiveness and listen humbly to what He shows us now, instead of making plans on our own.
exp.0:40:
Here Moses recalls how the people reacted to God's punishment. They admit, "We have sinned against the Lord," and decide to go up and fight, saying they will obey what God commanded them earlier. Each man put on his weapons of war and got ready, that is, prepared himself, to go up into the hill.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in the wilderness, almost at the end of the forty years. He reminds them that because they did not trust God, they did not enter the promised land. Now, too late, they want to obey the earlier command, but God had told them not to go up. Their repentance sounded good, but it did not follow God's word for the present moment.

For today: true repentance includes listening to what God is asking of us now, not merely doing something religious with good intentions. Before acting, ask God and examine his Word with humility.
exp.0:42:
Moses reminds the Israelites what happened when he warned them not to attack. He tells them that they did not listen to God, that they rebelled against his command, and that, full of pride, they went up into the hill anyway.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. Earlier, out of fear, they had refused to enter the promised land. Then, feeling guilty, they wanted to fight on their own, but God had already said not to do so because he would not go with them. They were defeated by the Amorites.

Today: obeying God is not just doing something good, but doing it when and how he asks. Before making a decision, ask God and listen to his Word with humility, without letting yourself be carried away by pride or haste.
exp.0:43:
This verse says that the Amorites, who lived in that mountain region, came out against the Israelites like a swarm of bees. They pursued them, defeated them, and chased them as far as a place called Hormah. The word "Amorites" in the verse is the name of a people who lived in Canaan. "Seir" refers to the mountainous area of Edom.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the desert, and reminds them of what happened at Kadesh. God had told them not to go up to fight because he would not go with them, but they disobeyed out of pride. Their defeat was the result of acting without God.

For today: it is not enough to have good goals or a lot of courage; we need to listen to God and obey him. Before making an important decision, it is wise to pray, seek guidance from the Bible, and act with humility, not stubbornness.
exp.1:4:
He says the Israelites were not to stir up or fight against the descendants of Esau. God would not give them so much as a foot's breadth of that land, because he had already given it to Esau as an inheritance. "Seir" is the mountainous region where the Edomites lived.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness and reminds them of what God commanded them. The Edomites were their kinsmen because they descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob. God had a plan for Israel, but he also respected what he had given to others.

For today: you do not need to take from others what is theirs in order to receive what God has for you. Trust his provision, respect the boundaries of others, and avoid envy and unnecessary conflict.
exp.1:6:
This verse says that God has blessed the people in everything they did. He knows their walking through the great wilderness. For forty years he was with them, and they lacked nothing.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of what they went through before passing through the land of Edom, the descendants of Esau. God told them not to fight with them and to buy food and water from them. Moses wants them to remember that God sustained them and that they do not need to take anything from anyone.

For today: when you go through long and difficult times, remember how God has sustained you up to this point. That helps you trust, live with gratitude, and treat others fairly, without greed or violence.
exp.1:20:
This verse says that the ancient inhabitants of the land of Ammon were a great, numerous people of tall stature, similar to the Anakim. But the Lord destroyed them before the Ammonites, and these took their place and settled there.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of their journey through the wilderness, reminding them of what happened. God had commanded them not to attack Ammon, because that land had been given to the descendants of Lot. Moses shows them that God had already done something similar with other peoples, even against giants.

For today: God cares for others as well as for us, and he distributes according to his will. We can trust that no giant stops him, and learn to respect what God has given to others, without envy or abuse.
exp.1:22:
This verse tells that certain peoples called Avites lived in villages from Hazerim to Gaza. The Caphtorites, who came from Caphtor, destroyed them and settled in their land. "Destroyed" here means that they drove them out or wiped them out. Caphtor is often linked to the island of Crete, although not all scholars affirm this with certainty.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel as he recalls the journey through the desert. He explains that God had already given lands to other peoples, such as Esau, Moab, and Ammon. These examples prepare Israel to receive the land God had promised them, after the command to cross the Arnon.

For today: God governs history and cares for his people. You can trust that if He has guided others, He will also guide you, even when you cannot see the whole picture.
exp.1:25:
Moses tells that he sent messengers to Sihon, king of Heshbon, from the wilderness of Kedemoth, a place east of the river Arnon. The messengers carried words of peace, that is, a friendly message and not a threat. The verse ends with "saying," and the message continues in the next verse.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of what happened. God had said that Sihon would be delivered into their hand, yet Moses first offered a peaceful passage anyway. Some readers see mercy here; others see an opportunity that made clear Sihon's responsibility when he rejected it.

For today: when facing a conflict, try first to speak with respect and seek peace. You can trust God and, at the same time, choose words that build up rather than wound.
exp.1:27:
He says that Israel asks permission to cross Sihon's territory without stopping to settle or taking anything for free. They offer to pay for whatever food and water they need, and they promise to go only on foot, that is, without causing harm or leaving the road.

Moses speaks, reminding the people of what happened when they sent messengers to Sihon, king of Heshbon. Israel was on its way to the promised land and sought a peaceful passage. Moses recalls that Sihon refused, and the text says that God hardened his spirit. Some understand that God confirmed a stubbornness the king already had.

For today: when we need something from others, let us ask with respect, offering to pay what is fair and without taking advantage. Seeking peace and acting with honesty is a way of honoring God, even when others do not respond well.
exp.1:28:
This verse is part of what Moses says he asked Sihon, king of Heshbon. He offers to pass through his land peacefully, buying food and water, just as the descendants of Esau in Seir and the Moabites in Ar had done for him.

Moses reminds the people what happened as they approached the promised land. Israel comes out of the wilderness and seeks a calm passage. There are different ways of understanding how Edom and Moab treated Israel, since other passages seem to say different things. Even so, here Moses presents his request as a gesture of peace. Sihon refuses it, and the text explains this as part of God's plan.

For today: seek peace and respectful dialogue first, even when you believe God is guiding you. Ask with humility, offer to pay what is fair, and leave the outcome in God's hands.
exp.1:35:
From Aroer, which lies on the edge of the river Arnon, and from the city that is by the river, all the way to Gilead, there was not one city too strong for us. The Lord our God handed all of them over to us.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them how they advanced against King Sihon, and he stresses that the victory was not their achievement but God's. He also points out that God set limits: Israel was not to touch the land of the Ammonites. This is a very harsh passage about war, and scholars interpret it in different ways; the central point here is that God directs history and marks out boundaries.

For today: when you accomplish something, recognize that God was behind it and do not take all the credit for yourself. And accept with humility the limits He sets.
exp.1:36:
This verse says that the Israelites did not go near the land of the Ammonites, nor to the area beside the Jabbok stream, nor to the cities in the hill country. Nor did they enter any place that God had forbidden them. The verse of the word "á" and of "arroyo" has been left out, since those words do not appear in the verse you are reading.

Moses is the one speaking. Near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, he reminds the Israelites how they fared when they defeated King Sihon. He explains that even in the midst of victory, they stopped where God had set a limit. God had already said earlier that they were not to trouble the Ammonites (Deuteronomy 2:19).

For today: success does not give us permission to go beyond what God has allowed us. If things have gone well for us, we can humbly ask where God is asking us to stop, and obey with gratitude.
exp.2:3:
This verse tells that Israel took all the cities of the kingdom of Og, king of Bashan. There were sixty cities in the region of Argob, and not one of them was left untaken.

Here Moses speaks, reminding the people of their history before entering the promised land. He reviews the victories that God gave them so that they would trust in Him. These conquests were part of Israel's war at that time, and the text presents them as the work of God. They are hard passages, which many scholars read within their ancient historical context.

For today: remembering how God helped you in the past strengthens your faith in the face of new challenges. Write down those occasions and thank Him for them, so that you can face the future with greater confidence.
exp.2:4:
It says that the sixty cities of Bashan were well defended: they had high walls, gates, and bars (the wooden or metal bolts that secured the gates). Besides these, there were many other towns without walls, that is, smaller and open ones.

Moses speaks near the end of his life, recalling for the new generation of Israelites the victories won before entering Canaan. He stresses that Bashan seemed impossible to defeat, yet God gave the victory. These accounts of conquest are hard to read, and scholars interpret them in different ways.

For today: when you face something that seems impossible, remember how God has helped you before. That grateful memory strengthens confidence for the challenges that come.
exp.2:8:
This verse is a short parenthetical note. It says that Mount Hermon had different names depending on the people: the Sidonians (people of Sidon, on the coast of present-day Lebanon) called it Sirion, and the Amorites called it Shenir.

The speaker is Moses, who reminds the people of Israel what happened when they took the lands east of the Jordan. He has just said that the territory reached as far as Mount Hermon, and since that mountain was known by several names, he adds this detail so that the listeners would understand clearly where the conquered land ended.

For today: the Bible takes care with details and clarity. We can learn to explain things patiently, using words the other person understands, and to remember that God works in real places, with real names and real dates.
exp.2:9:
This verse lists the territories Israel conquered east of the Jordan: the cities of the plain, all the region of Gilead, and all of Bashan, as far as Salchah and Edrei. All of this was part of the kingdom of Og, king of Bashan. The Amorites were a people who lived in that area.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, recalling what God did along the way. He reviews the victories over the kings Sihon and Og to encourage the new generation to trust God before entering the promised land. Those lands were then divided among Reuben, Gad, and part of Manasseh.

For today: remembering what God has already done in our lives strengthens faith for the challenges ahead. Write down a few occasions when God helped you, and thank him for them.
exp.2:16:
This verse completes the description of the territory east of the Jordan that Moses gave to Reuben and Gad. It includes the plain (the flat land), the Jordan River as the boundary, and the strip running from the Sea of Chinnereth (the Sea of Galilee) to the Sea of the Arabah, which is the Salt Sea (the Dead Sea). On the east it reached the slopes of Mount Pisgah.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, near the end of his life, and reminds them how God gave them victory over the kings of that region. He repeats the boundaries in detail so that they would know that this land was a gift from God and that each tribe had its assigned place.

For today: God cares for the details of our lives. Just as He set clear boundaries for each tribe, He also gives us what we need for each stage. We can give thanks for what we have received, instead of living with our eyes on what others have.
exp.2:17:
Moses recalls what he commanded the tribes of Reuben and Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, when he gave them their land east of the Jordan. God had given them that land, but they were to cross over ready for battle at the front of their Israelite brothers, all the men fit for war. The word "possess" means taking the land as their own. Being "armed" means being ready to fight.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, before they enter Canaan. He reviews what has already happened. Those tribes already had their inheritance, but the other tribes still had to conquer theirs. So Moses asks them for help and unity: they could not rest while their brothers were still fighting.

For today: if God has given you rest or blessing, do not simply stay comfortable. Ask yourself whom you can accompany, help, or support in their struggle, whether in your family, your church, or your community.
exp.2:19:
This verse says that the tribes who had already received their land east of the Jordan (Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh) were to help their brothers conquer the land on the other side. Only when the Lord gave their brothers rest, that is, peace and security in their territory, could they return to their own possession, the land that had fallen to them as an inheritance.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, recalling what he had commanded them earlier. He wanted no tribe to rest easily while the others were still fighting. It was a call to unity and loyalty between brothers.

For today: it is not enough to enjoy my own blessings. I can ask myself whom I can help, support, or walk alongside until they too find rest, whether in the family, the church, or the workplace.
exp.2:20:
Here Moses tells how he gave a command to Joshua. He reminded him that his own eyes had seen what God did to two kings, Og and Sihon, whom Israel defeated. Moses tells him that God will do the same to all the kingdoms through which Joshua will pass.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He already knows he will not cross the Jordan, and Joshua will be the new leader. For that reason he prepares him, recalling past victories to strengthen his trust in God for what lies ahead.

For today: when you face a great challenge, remember how God helped you before. Recalling his faithfulness in the past can give you courage and calm for the future, knowing that he remains the same.
exp.2:26:
God tells Moses to climb to the top of Mount Pisgah and look in every direction: west, north, south, and east. He will be able to see the land with his own eyes, but he will not cross the Jordan River.

Here the LORD speaks to Moses. Moses had pleaded to enter the promised land, but God said no. Moses mentions that God was angry with him because of the people, meaning what had happened with them. Even so, God gives him a farewell: to see the land and to prepare Joshua, who will lead the people.

For today: sometimes God does not grant what we ask, but he gives us another task and his company. We can accept his limits with humility and devote ourselves to encouraging and preparing those who will carry on what we have begun.
exp.3:2:
It says the Israelites saw with their own eyes what God did because of what happened at Baal-peor. All who went after that false god were destroyed from among the people.

Moses speaks near the end of the journey through the wilderness, before the people enter the promised land. He reminds them of an event they lived through (it is told in Numbers 25), when many joined in the worship of Baal-peor. He does this so that they will obey God and not repeat that mistake. According to the next verse, those who stayed faithful to God remained alive.

For today: faithfulness to God protects life. Today we can ask ourselves what things compete for our hearts, and with God's help, turn away from them and stay close to Him.
exp.3:6:
The verse says that no other nation is as great as Israel, because their God is so near to them whenever they call on him. The Hebrew-era phrasing about gods being present and reachable is not needed here; the verse speaks of God being nearby to his people whenever they call on him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that keeping God's law will show them to be wise before the other nations. Their greatness would not come from their own strength, but from God himself being near them and guiding them with justice.

For today: God is still near to those who seek him. Today you can speak to him with confidence, without intermediaries or complicated rituals. Try this this week: set aside a few minutes each day to pray and to read his Word, remembering that he listens to you.
exp.3:8:
This verse says that the people must watch over themselves and guard their soul with great care, so that they do not forget what their own eyes have seen. Those things must not leave their heart all the days of their life. In addition, they must tell them to their children and their grandchildren.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just reminded them that God is near to them and that his law is just. What they saw includes what happened at Horeb, when God spoke to them from the mountain. Moses knows that forgetting God is a real danger.

For today: set aside a moment each week to tell your children, nephews, nieces, or friends how God has helped you. In this way your faith does not stay in memory alone, but passes on to others.
exp.3:13:
Moses reminds them that, besides giving them the Ten Commandments, God also charged him to teach them the statutes and judgments, that is, the laws and rules for everyday life. These instructions were meant to be put into practice, in the land they were about to conquer and possess.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel on the plains of Moab, before entering the promised land. He reminds them of what happened at Horeb, where they heard the voice of God out of the fire but saw no form. For this reason, obedience had to be based on his word, not on images.

For today: God gives us his Word not only to know it, but to live it. Choose today one biblical teaching you already know and look for one concrete action to put it into practice this week.
exp.3:21:
Moses says that he is going to die in the land east of the Jordan and will not cross the river. Instead, the people will cross it and take possession of that good land. To "possess" means to receive it as an inheritance, and "cross" means to go over the river.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. Shortly before, he explained that God had refused to let him enter the land, and he connects this to the people's situation. In this way he reminds them that the promise still stands, even though their leader will not see it fulfilled. Right after, he warns them not to forget the covenant or make idols.

For today: Moses did not become bitter over what he did not receive, but encouraged others to move forward. We can serve God with generosity, preparing and blessing those who will follow, even when we do not see all the fruits ourselves.
exp.3:25:
Moses tells the Israelites that he calls heaven and earth as witnesses against them, that is, as if they were judges who confirm what is being said. He warns that if they become corrupt, they will soon disappear from the land they are about to receive when they cross the Jordan.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He reminds them of the covenant with God and warns them against idolatry, because God is jealous, which means he demands complete faithfulness. The verses that follow explain that they would be scattered among the nations.

For today: let us not take for granted the good things God has given us. It is healthy to honestly examine what things occupy the place of God in our hearts, and to return to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.3:26:
This verse says that if the people of Israel turn away from God, the Lord will scatter them among other nations. Few of them will be left there, because their number will shrink. The word "scatter" means to spread out or sow across many places, and "nations" here refers to other peoples.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He warns them that if, after many years, they become corrupt and make idols, they will face the consequences. But the warning does not end there: the verses that follow promise that if they seek God with all their heart from exile, they will find him. It is a serious warning, but one with hope.

For today: let us not take lightly the small things that take God's place in our hearts. And if you feel far from him, remember that you can always return to seek him sincerely.
exp.3:28:
Even if the people end up far from their land because they turned away from God, they can still seek him and find him. The condition is to seek him "with all your heart and with all your soul," that is, with sincerity and complete devotion.

Moses is speaking to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He warns them that turning to idols would bring discipline and scattering among the nations. But in the middle of the warning, he shows them hope: God is merciful and does not forget his covenant with their fathers.

For today: if you feel far from God because of mistakes or neglect, do not wait to get yourself in order first. Return to him honestly, pray, read his Word, and seek him with a sincere desire. He promises to let himself be found.
exp.3:30:
This verse says that the Lord your God is a merciful God, full of compassion. Because of this, he will not abandon his people, will not destroy them completely, and will not forget the covenant, that is, the solemn promise he made to their ancestors (Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob). He swore it, meaning he gave his firm commitment to keep it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that if they turn away from God and suffer the consequences, they can still return to seek him with all their heart. This sentence gives them hope: God remains faithful even when they fail.

For today: if you feel far from God or have failed, do not stay hidden. Return to him sincerely, trusting in his mercy. His faithfulness does not depend on your perfection, but on his good character and his promises.
exp.3:32:
Moses asks whether any people has ever heard the voice of God speaking out of the fire, as you have, and lived.

Moses speaks to the people in his final addresses, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what they experienced at Mount Horeb (Sinai), when God gave the Ten Commandments. He wants them to value that privilege and not forget God or fall into idolatry.

For today: God has made himself known, and that is a gift, not something ordinary. We can take a moment each day to thank him that he speaks to us, above all through his Word, and to listen to him with attention and respect, without taking it for granted.
exp.3:34:
This verse says that God showed Israel all his mighty works with a purpose: that they would know that the Lord is the only true God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what they lived through: the voice of God from the fire on the mountain and the deliverance from Egypt with signs and wonders. He wants their faith to rest on what God actually did, so that they would remain faithful to him and not turn aside to other gods.

For today: when you doubt or feel tempted to trust in other things, remember what God has done in your life and in his Word. Write down three moments when you saw his help, and give him thanks. Remembering strengthens confidence that he alone is worthy of all our faith.
exp.3:41:
Deuteronomy 4:42 says that Moses set apart three cities east of the Jordan so that a person who had killed another by accident could flee there. By fleeing to one of those cities, that person saved his life.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that obeying God brings good to their families. These cities of refuge protected the accused from revenge by the relatives of the victim while what had happened was being clarified. In this way justice was not confused with violence.

For today: God cares for both justice and mercy. We can learn not to judge in haste, to distinguish between a mistake and an act of wickedness, and to offer protection and a second chance to someone who erred without evil intent.
exp.3:43:
This verse says that what follows is the law that Moses set before the people of Israel. The word "set before" means that he presented it or laid it out clearly so that everyone could hear it.

Moses is speaking to the people on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He has just finished speaking about the cities of refuge, where a person who had killed unintentionally could flee. Now he begins a new part of his message, in which he repeats and explains God's commandments to a generation that did not see their parents leave Egypt, but who were to live out that faithfulness.

For today: God does not hide his will, but presents it clearly. We can read his Word with confidence, knowing that it is made to be understood and lived, not merely admired. Choose a teaching from the Bible today and ask yourself how to put it into practice.
exp.3:48:
This verse closes the list of places Israel had conquered east of the Jordan. It includes the whole eastern plain, down to the Dead Sea, and the slopes that run down from Mount Pisgah. The slopes are the sides of the hills where the water runs down.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He reminds them that God had already given them victory over two Amorite kings, Sihon and Og. This list of territories is meant to help them remember God's faithfulness and to obey the law he is about to give them.

For today: when you remember in detail what God has already done in your life, your trust grows. Write down the times he helped you, and let that encourage you to obey him and to trust him with what comes next.
exp.4:2:
This verse says that God made his covenant not only with the ancestors of Israel, but with the people who were standing there listening to Moses.

Moses speaks to all of Israel, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before entering the promised land. Almost all the adults who had stood at Horeb (Mount Sinai) had already died. Those listening were their children, or were very young at that time. Moses reminds them that the covenant is also for them and that they must take it as their own. Some understand "our fathers" to mean the patriarchs; others understand it to mean the previous generation.

For today: it is not enough to inherit the faith of one's family. Each person must respond personally to God, listen to his Word, and obey it today, as something living and present.
exp.4:8:
It says that we should not bow down to images or serve them, because Jehovah is a strong and jealous God. "Jealous" means that he does not share the love and loyalty of his people with others. "Visiting the iniquity" means that he takes account of sin and its consequences, which reach several generations of those who reject him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and repeats the Ten Commandments to them. God had rescued them from Egypt and wanted them to be faithful to him. The following verses show the contrast: his mercy reaches thousands of those who love him.

For today: examine what things hold first place in your heart, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Ask God to be first, and remember that your decisions also affect your family.
exp.4:12:
This verse says that God expects the people to work six days of the week. "All your work" refers to all the daily tasks and responsibilities. Work is not presented as a burden, but as a normal part of life, one that prepares the way for the day of rest.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He repeats the Ten Commandments to them. Here he explains the commandment about the day of rest, and shortly afterward he reminds them that Israel was enslaved in Egypt and that God rescued them.

For today: we can see our work as something worthy, and also set limits so that we can rest. This week, try to finish your pending tasks on time and set aside a time of rest, to be with God and with your family.
exp.4:14:
This verse reminds the people that they were slaves in Egypt and that God brought them out of there with great power. The phrase about a strong hand and an outstretched arm describes the strength of God in rescuing them. That is why God commanded them to keep the Sabbath, the day of rest.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, before they enter the promised land. He repeats the Ten Commandments to them. Here the reason for rest is liberation: no one was to work without stopping, neither servants, nor foreigners, nor animals. Whoever had been a slave was to remember what it means to be unable to rest.

For today: God freed us from burdens and does not want us to live exhausted. Set aside time to rest and to thank him. If you are a boss or have people under your care, look after their rest too.
exp.4:16:
It says that we must not take the life of another person. It is the sixth of the Ten Commandments. The Hebrew word used refers above all to murder, that is, taking a life unjustly. Scholars discuss how it applies to cases such as war or the death penalty, since the Law itself treats these separately.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, just before they enter the promised land. He repeats to them the Ten Commandments that God gave on Mount Sinai. God had freed them from slavery in Egypt, and now he teaches them to live as a free people who respect life, because every person is precious to God.

For today: care for the life of others also with your words and attitudes. Jesus taught that hatred and contempt also cause harm (Matthew 5:21-22). Today you can choose to forgive someone or speak to them with respect.
exp.4:17:
It says we should not commit adultery, that is, have sexual relations with someone who is not our husband or wife, or with someone who is married to another person. The word "adultery" here means being unfaithful in marriage.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He repeats the Ten Commandments that God gave on Mount Sinai. This commandment protects marriage and trust within the family, and it comes between the command to honor one's parents and the command not to murder.

For today: take care of your faithfulness through concrete actions. If you are married, be honest with your partner and set healthy limits on your friendships, your conversations, and what you look at. If you are not, respect other people's marriages. Faithfulness is built in the small decisions of each day.
exp.4:18:
This verse forbids taking what belongs to another person without their permission. The word "steal" here refers to taking something that is not yours, keeping for yourself what belongs to someone else. It is one of the Ten Commandments.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the law that God gave on Mount Sinai. This commandment protects each person's property and labor, and helps the community live with trust and justice. Some scholars think it also included the kidnapping of people, but this is understood in different ways.

Today we can apply it by being honest in small things: not copying another person's work, not using pirated software, paying fairly those who work for us, and returning what was lent to us. Honesty shows that we trust that God provides.
exp.4:22:
It says that after the people heard the voice of God coming out of the darkness and saw Mount Sinai wrapped in flames, the leaders came near to Moses. They were the heads of the tribes and the older men with authority over the people. Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, before they enter the Promised Land. He reminds them of what happened at Sinai, when God gave the Ten Commandments. The leaders came near with fear, because God's presence was so overwhelming that they felt they could not bear it. Moses recalls this so that they do not forget the seriousness of God's Word.

For today: when we feel fear or reverence before God, the best thing is to draw near to Him and not pull away. We can listen to His Word with humility, and leaders can also guide the people to do so with reverence.
exp.4:23:
This verse says that the people of Israel acknowledge that God showed them his glory and his greatness on the mountain. They heard his voice out of the midst of the fire, and they were amazed that God speaks with human beings and that they remain alive.

Moses is speaking to the new generation, before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of what happened at Mount Sinai (Horeb). He quotes what the leaders and elders said to him after hearing the Ten Commandments. They felt great fear, and asked Moses to listen to God and then pass on his words to them.

For today: God speaks, and his Word deserves respect and attention. We can approach the Bible with humility and gratitude, remembering that listening to God is a privilege, and that he speaks to us to give us life, not to destroy us.
exp.4:25:
This verse is a question that expresses amazement and fear. "All flesh" means every human being, frail and mortal. The people are asking who could hear the voice of the living God, who spoke from the fire, and still remain alive. In other words, they feel small before the holiness of God.

Moses is reminding the people of what happened at Mount Horeb (Sinai). After hearing the Ten Commandments, the Israelites became afraid and asked that Moses speak with God on their behalf. God approved of that attitude of respect, as the following verses say.

For today: draw near to God with reverence and humility, without losing your confidence. Christians believe that through Jesus we can approach Him with confidence, but without forgetting that He is holy. Today, before you pray or read the Bible, acknowledge who God is and listen to Him with an attentive heart.
exp.4:30:
God tells Moses to stay here beside Him on the mountain. There He will give him all the commandments, statutes, and judgments (that is, the rules and fair decisions) so that Moses may teach them to the people. The purpose is that they carry them out, that is, that they do them, in the land that God gives them as an inheritance.

God speaks this after the people, frightened by the voice of fire at Sinai, asked that Moses listen on their behalf. God approved that request, and He wanted them to have a heart that respected and obeyed Him. Moses recalls this before preparing the people to enter Canaan.

For today: God does not only want us to hear His Word, but to live it. Choose a biblical command today and look for one concrete action to practice it this week.
exp.4:32:
This verse says that the people are to walk, that is, to live, following everything God commanded them. The promise is that in this way they will have life, things will go well for them, and they will live many years in the land they are about to receive. The verse's "walk" means to live, and a long life means a life that is lasting and secure.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, close to entering the promised land. He has just reminded them of the Ten Commandments and of how the people were afraid at the voice of God on the mountain. Now he asks them to obey without turning aside to the right or to the left. Their obedience would be a response to the God who had rescued them.

For today: God invites us to trust that his ways are good. Today you can choose one concrete step of obedience, such as forgiving, being honest, or setting aside time for his Word, and do it trusting that he cares for your life.
exp.5:2:
This verse says that Israel should listen carefully and also obey what God commands. If they do, it will go well with them and the people will increase, just as God promised. Practicing, or doing what one hears, is what the verse is calling for, and the image of a land flowing with milk and honey stands for a very fertile and abundant land. The "fathers" refers to the ancestors, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter the promised land. He repeats God's law to them so that they will teach it to their children and grandchildren. Right after this comes the well-known call, "Hear, O Israel," which urges loving God with one's whole being. Obedience springs from that love and from trust in God's promises.

For today: it is not enough to just listen to the Bible; decide today on one concrete action to put into practice what God has shown you, and do it with gratitude, not out of mere obligation.
exp.5:3:
Here the verse says that Israel must listen closely: the Lord, whom the people call "our God," is "one." The name of God is rendered in the traditional form. The phrase "the Lord is one" can be understood as meaning that the Lord is unique, or that only the Lord is our God. Scholars debate which nuance weighs more, and both fit with the rest of the Bible. "Hear" here means to listen and obey.

Moses speaks near the end of his life to a new generation ready to enter the promised land. He reminds them that God gave them his commandments so that they would respect him, so that things would go well for them, and so that they would pass them on to their children. This verse is the center of that message, and what follows is to love him with all one's being.

For today: before rushing off with your own concerns, take a few minutes to listen to God in his Word. Ask him to be first in your heart, without dividing your loyalty among many things.
exp.5:8:
He says God wanted his people to write his words on the doorposts of the house and on the gates, that is, on the frames of the doors and on the entrances of the city or the courtyard. In this way, every time someone went in or out, they would see God's commandments.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just reminded them to love God with all their heart and to teach his words to their children. Then he warns them that, when they receive houses and harvests they did not work for, they must not forget who gave them to them. Some Jews carry out this command literally with the mezuzah; others understand it as a way of living with God present.

For today: place in a visible spot in your home a verse that reminds you to trust God, and read it aloud with your family when you leave or come home.
exp.5:11:
This verse is a warning.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He tells them they will receive cities, houses, cisterns, vineyards, and olive groves that they did not work for. Moses fears that, once they are comfortable and satisfied, they will forget who gave them everything and turn to other gods, as the next verse says.

For today: when things are going well for you, it is not easy to remember God. You can pause each day, perhaps at mealtime, to thank him for something specific you received that you did not achieve on your own. Gratitude helps keep the heart close to God.
exp.5:14:
It says that the Lord, the jealous God, lives among his people. For that reason it warns that his anger should not be kindled against them, because he could destroy them from the earth. The phrase about the face of the earth refers to the surface of the earth. "Jealous" here means that God wants to be the only one his people love and worship, as in a covenant of faithfulness.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them not to follow the gods of the neighboring nations. Their closeness to God is a blessing, but also a serious responsibility, because God takes his covenant with them seriously.

For today: examine what things compete with God for first place in your heart, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Today, bring one of them before God in prayer and decide to give God his rightful place.
exp.5:16:
This verse calls the people to obey carefully everything God commanded. The words "keep" mean to carry out and to protect. The "commandments" are his orders, the "testimonies" are what God declared about himself and his covenant, and the "statutes" are his rules for daily life.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God is present among them and that they must not test him, as they did at Massah, when they doubted that he would take care of them. Obedience is presented as a response of trust in a faithful God.

For today: let us not treat the Word of God as optional. We can choose a specific teaching from the Bible and put it into practice this week, for example forgiving, telling the truth, or helping someone. Obeying is not a way to earn God's love, but a way of living that trusts in him.
exp.5:23:
He says that God commanded us to keep all his laws and to live them with respect and reverence toward him. Here "fear" does not mean being afraid, but honoring him and taking him seriously. "Statutes" are the rules God gave. The goal is twofold: that things go well for us always, and that he preserves our lives, as is already evident in the present.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He asks them to explain to their children why they obey: God rescued them from Egypt with great signs and promised them a land. Obedience springs from remembering what God has already done, not from mere obligation.

For today: before thinking about rules, remember how God has cared for you. From that gratitude, choose one concrete act of obedience today, and tell someone else why you are doing it.
exp.5:24:
It says we will be considered righteous when we carefully put into practice all of God's commandments, just as he gave them. Doing so means carrying them out faithfully. Here, being righteous means being in right standing with God and living in the way that pleases him.

Moses is speaking to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God brought them out of Egypt and gave them his laws so that they would live well and with reverence toward him. This obedience grew out of a relationship with the God who had already rescued them. Some understand righteousness here to mean living faithfully within the covenant.

Today we might ask ourselves: what do I know God is asking of me that I have not yet done? Choose one concrete thing this week and obey it with gratitude, not out of fear, but because God has already been faithful to you.
exp.6:2:
This verse says that the Israelites were not to marry their children into the families of the seven nations who lived in Canaan. It explains that to make marriages means to join families by marriage. Neither were the daughters of Israel to marry their sons, nor were their sons to take the daughters of those nations.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God would bring them in to possess it. The following verse gives the reason: such marriages could turn the hearts of their children toward other gods. The emphasis is spiritual, not a question of race.

For today: take care with your closest relationships, because they shape your faith. Before you commit to someone or to an important project, ask yourself whether it draws you closer to God or pulls you away. And seek wise counsel and prayer.
exp.6:7:
This verse says that God did not bring Israel out of Egypt because of the people's merit, but out of love and out of faithfulness to his promise. The oath was a solemn promise made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The mighty hand speaks of God's power. The house of bondmen was slavery, and to redeem means to set someone free by paying a price or by a powerful act.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God chose them, even though they were few and had nothing special about them. He wants them to avoid pride and to respond with gratitude and obedience, because God is faithful to his covenant.

For today: we do not need to earn God's love through our achievements. If you have received his help or his forgiveness, remember it with humility and gratitude, and let that motivate you to live faithfully and to treat others with the same grace you received.
exp.6:12:
God promises that he will love his people, bless them, and make them grow. That blessing would reach their children, their harvests, and their animals. The children are the fruit of the womb; the new juice of the grape is the wine; the young of your cattle are the calves. All of this would happen in the land that God promised with an oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God made a covenant with them and calls them to obey his commandments. The blessing is tied to that covenant relationship with God. It was given to Israel in their particular situation, so it should not be read as an automatic promise of wealth for everyone.

For today: God is faithful and generous, and every good thing we have comes from him. Today you can thank him for everyday things, such as your family, your food, and your work, and respond to him with trusting obedience.
exp.6:14:
This verse promises that God would take sickness away from his people. It also says that the terrible plagues of Egypt, which the Israelites knew well, would not fall on them. Those plagues would instead fall on those who hate them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the blessings of the covenant if they obey God and remain faithful to him, without following the gods of other peoples. This is a promise given to that nation in that covenant. Christians interpret it in different ways regarding how it applies today.

For today: we can trust that God cares for us and sustains us, even though he does not always keep us free from every illness. His faithfulness invites us to obey him with gratitude and to rest in his protection.
exp.6:22:
This verse says that God himself will hand over the enemy nations before Israel and throw them into great confusion and defeat, until they are overcome. The phrase about breaking them with great destruction means that God will defeat them completely, and the word about being destroyed speaks of the total collapse of their power.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He asks them not to be afraid, because God goes with them. This language of war belongs to that specific historical moment and to Israel's mission as a nation. Christians read it carefully and do not apply it to peoples of today.

Today we can take from this the confidence that God does not leave us alone before what seems impossible. When you face a big problem, such as a fear or a bad habit, remember that God works in his own time and often little by little. Ask him for help and keep going forward in faith.
exp.6:24:
This verse says that Israel was to burn the carved images of the gods of Canaan. They were not to desire the gold or silver that covered them, nor keep it for themselves. The reason is that they could be snared by it, because God regards such things as an abomination, something He utterly detests.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God Himself would defeat the nations who lived there. But he warns them that the danger was not only war, but that idolatry would draw them in and turn them away from God. For that reason they had to separate themselves completely from those objects.

Today we may not have wooden idols, but we do have things that can take the place of God, such as money, success, or certain habits. Ask God to show you what has hold of you, and stop keeping it just in case. Turning away from it is an act of love toward Him.
exp.6:25:
This verse commands that nothing abominable be brought into the house, meaning something God rejects, such as idols. If someone did so, they would become set apart for destruction, a thing devoted to be destroyed. For this reason the people were to utterly detest and reject such things.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just told them to burn the images of the gods of Canaan and not to keep their gold or silver. God wanted to protect his people from idolatry, which could trap them and turn them away from him.

For today: ask yourself what things you have let into your home or your life that compete with God or pull you away from him. It may be something you see, hear, or keep. Ask God for wisdom and, with humility, set aside whatever makes you stumble.
exp.7:0:
Moses tells the people that they must take care to obey all the commandments he gives them today. The reason is that in this way they will be able to live, grow in number, go into the land, and possess it. It is the land that God promised with an oath to their fathers, that is, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, just before they enter Canaan. He reminds them that obedience and God's promise go together. The verses that follow invite them to remember how God guided them, tested them, and sustained them with manna.

For today: God gives us his words so that we may live well, not to burden us. Today you can choose one specific command from the Bible that you already know and put it into practice this week, trusting that God is faithful to his promises.
exp.7:1:
God tells his people to remember the whole journey of forty years through the desert. There the Lord led them, humbled them (the word "humble" here means making them go through need and lowliness) and tested them, to show what was in their hearts: whether they would keep his commandments or not.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, just before they enter the promised land. He asks them to look back so they understand that the desert was not a meaningless punishment, but a time of teaching. God cared for them, but he also shaped them.

For today: think of a difficult season you have lived through. Ask yourself what it revealed about your heart and how God took care of you in that time. Remembering that can help you trust him more and obey him with humility.
exp.7:3:
What it says: Moses reminds the people that for forty years in the wilderness their clothing did not wear out until it was worn, and their feet did not swell from so much walking.

Context: Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He asks them to remember how God cared for them in their trials, with hunger and with manna. Some understand the clothing as a miraculous provision; others take it as a way of saying that God sustained them. The text does not explain how it happened.

For today: Before you worry about what lies ahead, make a list of the times God has sustained you. Remembering His care in the past helps you trust Him and obey Him with gratitude.
exp.7:4:
It says that Israel must acknowledge, that is, reflect on and accept in their hearts, that God corrects them the way a father corrects his son. The verse notes that the wording of the verse, in older language, carries the sense of correcting, disciplining and teaching, not of venting anger.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, just before they enter the promised land. He asks them to look back: the hunger, the manna and God's care all had a purpose. God was shaping them so that they would learn to depend on Him and to obey Him.

For today: when you go through a difficult season, do not immediately conclude that God has abandoned you. Ask Him sincerely what He wants to teach you, and trust that His correction comes from a Father's love. Seek His guidance in His Word.
exp.7:10:
It says we must be careful not to forget God, and that this forgetting shows up when we stop obeying what He commands.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He describes a land that is good and plentiful. But he warns them that when they have food, houses, livestock and riches, it will be easy to forget God and to believe they achieved everything on their own.

For today: when things are going well is when we most need to remember God. You can thank Him each day for what you have and ask yourself whether your comfort is pulling you away from Him or leading you to obey Him with greater gratitude.
exp.7:11:
This verse is part of a warning that begins in verse 11.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, after forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them that the abundance they will receive is a gift from God. His concern is that comfort will lead them to forget the one who gave it to them.

For today: when things are going well, it is easy to stop praying and giving thanks. A good habit is to thank God each day for what you have, food, shelter and work, and to remember that all of it comes from his generous hand.
exp.7:12:
This verse describes a time of prosperity: the herds grow, the silver and the gold increase, and everything the person has becomes more. The cattle and the sheep were the main form of wealth in that era. The word for "multiplied" simply means that they grow in number.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that abundance can bring a danger: thinking they are self-sufficient and forgetting God, who brought them out of Egypt and cared for them in the wilderness. The verses that follow make this clear.

For today: when things are going well, it is easy to stop praying and stop giving thanks. We can take a moment each week to thank God for what we have and ask him how to use it to help others.
exp.7:14:
This verse reminds us that God led Israel through a vast and terrifying desert, full of fiery serpents, whose bite was very painful, as if it burned, and scorpions. There was no water, but God brought water out of a rock so hard that it was like flint.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the Promised Land. He warns them that, when they have houses, livestock, and wealth, they must not become proud or forget God. He reminds them that it was He who cared for them when they had nothing.

For today: when things are going well for you, stop and remember the times God sustained you in hard seasons. Give Him thanks with humility, and do not think that you achieved everything by your own strength alone.
exp.7:19:
It says that if the people of Israel forget God, they will meet the same fate as the nations that God is going to destroy when they enter the land. The phrase about hearing and obeying the voice of God means having listened and obeyed. The word meaning "perish" means they will be destroyed or disappear as a people in that land.

Moses speaks to the Israelites at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, just before entering the promised land. He warns them that abundance can make them believe they achieved everything on their own. He reminds them that God is the one who gives the ability to prosper and that his covenant requires faithfulness. It is a serious warning, given with love, so that they do not repeat the mistakes of other peoples.

When things go well for us, it is easy to stop giving thanks and to stop listening to God. Today we can set aside a moment each day to thank him for what we have and to ask him how to obey him with it.
exp.8:1:
It says that Israel is going to face a people great and tall, descendants of the children of the Anakims, such as the Anakites. The Israelites had already heard of them and were repeating a saying: "Who can stand before the children of Anak?" The phrase about the children of Anak refers to people of great height and a reputation for strength.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they cross the Jordan, near the end of his life. He wants them to remember the fear they felt when the spies returned forty years ago. He reminds them that the victory will not depend on their strength, but on God, who will go before them.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, do not deny it, but do not let fear speak louder than God's promises. Do what is yours to do with confidence in Him, and if God gives you the victory, thank Him with humility instead of boasting.
exp.8:8:
Moses reminds the people that he went up Mount Sinai (Horeb) to receive the stone tablets, which represented God's covenant with Israel. There he stayed forty days and forty nights without eating or drinking. The name of God is LORD, and a covenant is a solemn commitment.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of their history so that they will not think they are righteous in themselves. While he was with God receiving the covenant, the people soon rebelled by making the golden calf. The text does not explain how he was able to sustain himself this way; it presents that time as the work of God.

Today we can remember that God is faithful even when we fail. Before judging others or boasting of our achievements, it is good to recognize with humility how much we need His grace and to return to Him sincerely.
exp.8:14:
Moses tells how he came down from Mount Sinai, which was burning with fire, carrying in his hands the two tables of the covenant, that is, the stones on which the Ten Commandments were written.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of their history so that they do not forget their failure. While he was receiving God's law, the people were already making a golden calf. That is why God calls them stiff-necked, that is, stubborn and rebellious.

For today: God gives us his word with great seriousness and love, and we fail with ease. Remembering our mistakes with humility leads us to ask for forgiveness and to obey again, trusting in God's mercy.
exp.8:15:
Moses says that he came down from the mountain and saw that the people had sinned. They had made a calf of cast metal, that is, a figure of a young bull made from melted metal. They turned aside quickly from the way that the Lord had commanded them.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, reminding them what happened at Sinai. He repeats this story before they enter the promised land, so that they do not think God gives them the land because they are good. Rather, they need to remember their need for God's grace and mercy.

Today we can learn that it is easy to turn aside quickly when we stop putting God at the center. It is wise to ask ourselves what things have taken his place in our hearts. And if we fail, we can return to him with humility, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.8:16:
Moses tells how he took the two tablets of the law, threw them down from his hands, and broke them before the eyes of the people. The verbs he uses mean that he threw them and that he broke them.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of their sin with the golden calf. When he came down from Mount Sinai he saw that the people had already broken their covenant with God. His action showed, with grief, that the agreement had been violated. Some also understand that it expressed his holy anger.

Today we can learn to take sin seriously, without excusing it or minimizing it. But, as Moses did afterward, we can also come to God with humility, ask him for forgiveness, and trust in his mercy.
exp.8:22:
God told Israel, from Kadesh-barnea, to go up and take the land he had already given them. But they rebelled against that command: they did not trust God, and they did not obey him.

Moses speaks to the people, now close to the promised land, years after those events. He reminds them that they do not deserve the land because they are good, but because of God's faithfulness. Kadesh-barnea was the place where, out of fear, they refused to enter (Numbers 13–14). Moses lists their failures to strip away any pride they might have.

Today we can ask ourselves: is there something God has clearly told us in his Word that we have not obeyed out of fear? We can confess it with humility and take a step of trust in him today.
exp.9:2:
Moses tells that he made an ark of shittim wood, which is acacia wood. He also hewed two tables of stone, like the first ones, and went up the mount having the two tables in his hand, just as God had asked him to do.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of his life, and he reminds them of their history. The first tables were broken when the people sinned with the golden calf. Even so, God gave a new opportunity and wrote his words again. Moses obeyed step by step.

God knows how to restore what was broken. If you have failed, do not stay in guilt: return to God, and obey what he shows you today, even if it is a small step. His mercy opens a new beginning.
exp.9:3:
This verse says that God wrote again on the new stone tablets the Ten Commandments, just as he had on the first ones. The Ten Commandments are also called the ten words. "The day of the assembly" refers to the day when the people were gathered at the foot of Mount Sinai. And at the end, Moses says that the Lord gave them to him.

Here Moses speaks, reminding the people of what happened after they sinned with the golden calf and he broke the first tablets. God, in his mercy, gave them a second chance and renewed his covenant. The tablets were kept in the ark.

For today: God knows how to forgive and to start over with us. If we have failed, we do not have to remain in guilt. We can come to him with humility, and he offers us again his guidance and his friendship.
exp.9:4:
Moses tells how he came down from Mount Sinai with the two new stone tablets and placed them in the chest he had made. The "tablets" were the two stones with the Ten Commandments. Moses adds that they are still there, just as the Lord commanded him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of his life and reminds them of their history. Earlier, the people had sinned with the golden calf, and Moses broke the first tablets. God, in his mercy, wrote new ones. Moses wants them to remember that grace and to be faithful.

God gives us his word to keep carefully and to obey. We can give it a central place in daily life: reading it, remembering it, and trusting it, grateful that God gives us new opportunities.
exp.9:5:
The verse tells how the Israelites set out from a place called Beeroth Bene-jaakan and arrived at Moserah. There Aaron, the first high priest, died and was buried. His son Eleazar took his place as priest.

The speaker is Moses, who reminds the people of their history before they enter the promised land. This verse seems to be a short note within the account of the tablets and the ark. It shows that, although leaders die, the service of God continues. Some scholars note that the order of the account differs from that in Numbers 33, and they explain this in several ways.

For today: God does not depend on a single person to carry forward his work. Value those who teach you and serve, but trust that God cares for his people from generation to generation. You too can prepare yourself to serve.
exp.9:8:
This verse says that the tribe of Levi did not receive a territory of its own like the other tribes of Israel. The word "inheritance" in the verse refers to the land or possession that is left to one's children. Instead of land, the Levites received God himself as their portion, just as he had promised them.

Moses speaks to the people and reviews their history after the sin of the golden calf. He explains that God set the Levites apart to care for the ark, to serve before him, and to bless in his name. Their lives would depend on serving God and not on owning fields. Some scholars see in this passage a brief note within the account of the journey.

For today: even though most of us are not priests, we can learn to find our main security in God and not only in money, a house, or a job. When material things are lacking or change, he remains our portion.
exp.9:9:
Moses recalls that he went up the mountain again, Sinai (also called Horeb), and stayed there forty days and forty nights, just as he had the first time. God listened to him once more and chose not to destroy the people.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel, who are now close to entering the promised land. He reminds them of what happened after the sin of the golden calf: he interceded for them, and God showed mercy. The verses that follow mention the Levites, and then God commands the people to move forward. The purpose is to show that God forgave them by grace, not because they earned it.
