For today: God listens to those who pray for others. Pray with confidence for someone who has failed, and remember that you too live by God's mercy, not by your own merits.
exp.9:11:
This verse sums up what God asks of his people: that they honor him with reverence (the sense of "fear" here), that they live according to his ways, that they love him, and that they serve him with their whole being. "Heart" and "soul" speak of the whole person: thoughts, desires, and will.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just reminded them that God forgave them, despite their sin with the golden calf, and that he continues to lead them. After so much mercy, Moses explains how they should respond: with a whole life of love and obedience.

For today: faith is not only keeping rules, but responding with warmth to a God who has already shown us his goodness. Today you can give God the first moment of your day, thank him for his mercy, and ask him to help you obey him with joy.
exp.9:13:
This verse says that everything belongs to God: the heaven, the heaven of heavens (a way of saying the highest and most distant heavens), the earth, and everything in it. Nothing is outside his ownership.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what God asks: reverence, love, obedience, and service with all their heart. Then he states that God owns everything, and yet he chose to love their ancestors and them. This shows that their being chosen was a gift, not something they earned.

For today: if everything is God's, then what we have is a loan that we should take care of. Today you can thank God for something specific you have and use it to help someone, with a humble and grateful heart.
exp.9:17:
This verse says that God defends those who have no one to defend them: the orphan and the widow. He also loves the foreigner, that is, the person who lives in a land that is not his own, and he gives him bread and clothing, which means what is basic for living. "He executes justice" means that he acts on their behalf.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He asks them for an obedient heart and reminds them that God does not show favoritism toward anyone and cannot be bought. Since God is like this, his people should imitate him, and the next verse reminds them that they too were foreigners in Egypt.

For today: notice someone vulnerable near you, such as an immigrant, a widow, or a child without support, and help them with something concrete: food, clothing, company, or your voice to defend them.
exp.9:18:
It says that the people must love the stranger, that is, the person who lives among them but comes from another land. The reason is that they themselves were strangers in Egypt.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just told them that God is just, defends the orphan and the widow, and loves the stranger by giving him food and clothing. If God cares in this way, his people should imitate him. Besides, they remembered what it was to live without a home of their own and without rights.

Today we can notice some immigrant, new neighbor, or person who feels out of place in our church or workplace. We can greet them, help them with something concrete, and treat them with respect, remembering how much God helped us.
exp.9:20:
He himself is the reason for his people's praise. He does not merely receive praise; he is the cause of it. The verse also states that he is "your God," the one who did things that were great and awe-inspiring, that is, astonishing, the kind that produce a reverent fear. Israel saw them with their own eyes, such as the departure from Egypt.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what God did so that they would remain faithful to him. Shortly before, he asked them to love the foreigner, because they had been foreigners in Egypt. Then he notes that seventy people went down to Egypt and are now countless like the stars.

For today: when it is hard to give thanks, make a list of concrete things God has done in your life. Remembering them will help you praise him with more sincerity and treat with kindness those who feel like strangers or alone.
exp.9:21:
This verse says that Israel's ancestors went down into Egypt as only seventy people. Now, by contrast, God has made them as numerous as the stars of the sky.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what God has done so that they will fear him, serve him, and remain close to him. The seventy refers to Jacob's family, according to Genesis 46. Moses uses this contrast to show God's faithfulness to his promise.

For today: when you feel small or think your beginnings were weak, remember that God can make grow what seems little. Make a list today of things God has done in your life, and thank him for them.
exp.10:1:
Moses tells the people to understand clearly what he is about to remind them of. He is not speaking to their children, who have not yet seen or experienced how God corrects and disciplines. The adults did live through it: God's greatness, his mighty hand, and his outstretched arm, which are expressions for his power to rescue and to act.

Moses speaks at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, shortly before Israel enters the promised land. He addresses the generation that left Egypt and saw the miracles with their own eyes. He asks them to love God and obey, relying on what they themselves witnessed.

For today: remember and tell what God has done in your life. Your experience with him can strengthen your obedience and help your children or younger people come to know him.
exp.10:2:
This verse continues a list of things Moses wants the people to remember. The "signs" are the miracles that showed God's power, and the "works" are the actions God performed. All of this happened in Egypt, before Pharaoh and all his land.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they themselves saw how God acted, not only their children who did not live through it. He calls them to love God and obey Him, using as the reason what He has already done for them. The plagues of Egypt are part of that memory.

For today: when you doubt or feel afraid, remember what God has already done in your life and in His Word. Recalling His faithfulness in the past strengthens trust and the desire to obey Him today.
exp.10:6:
This verse tells the people that they are not hearing about God's works secondhand, as old stories. Their own eyes saw the great works the LORD has done.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what God did in the wilderness, including when the earth opened and swallowed Dathan and Abiram because of their rebellion. That generation were direct witnesses, and Moses uses this to call them to obey God's commandments.

For today: remember what God has done in your life, whether as help, protection, or correction. Write it down if you can. Remembering his faithfulness in the past strengthens trust and encourages us to obey him today, even when the future seems uncertain.
exp.10:14:
God promises that if his people obey him, there will also be grass in the fields for the animals, and the people will have enough food.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the rain and the harvests depended on God, and that their well-being was tied to loving and serving him wholeheartedly. Then he warns them not to turn aside to other gods.

For today: we can see that everything we have, food, work, and health, comes from the hand of God. Today you can thank him before you eat and trust that he cares for you, remembering that God seeks our heart first, not just rewards.
exp.10:15:
Take heed to yourselves, so that your heart is not deceived. It means we must watch ourselves so that our heart is not led astray, not fooled, and not filled with pride and foolishness. When that happens, a person turns away from God, serves other gods, and bows down before them to worship them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. Just before this, he reminds them that God will give them rain and an abundant harvest. Then he warns them that if they worship other gods, the rain will stop. In that time, the harvest depended greatly on rain, and the neighboring peoples worshiped gods connected with it.

When everything is going well, it is easy to trust in what we receive and forget the One who gives it. Today we can guard our hearts by thanking God every day and asking ourselves what things are taking his place in our trust.
exp.10:19:
It says that Israel was to write God's words on the doorposts of their houses and on the gates, that is, on the entrances and the frames of the doors. The gates are the doors or entryways of the house and of the city. The idea is that, as they came and went, they would always see God's word.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He asks them to remember and obey the law, and to teach it to their children. Some understand this in a literal way, as many Jews do today with the mezuzah; others see it as a vivid way of saying that God should be present in everything.

Today we can put a verse where we can see it at home, at the entrance, or on our phone, and decide to read it together as a family. In this way the Word becomes part of daily life, not only of Sunday.
exp.10:22:
It says that God himself will drive out from before the people all those nations that lived in Canaan. Although those peoples were greater and stronger, Israel would take possession of their land. "Drive out" means to expel, and "possess" means that they will receive that land as an inheritance.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the promise depends on obeying God and loving him, as the verses before it say. He wants them to trust in God's help and not in their own strength. Scholars discuss how the conquest should be understood, but the text stresses that God is the one who acts.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, do not rely only on your own strength. Love God, obey him step by step, and trust that he sustains you.
exp.10:23:
It says God promises Israel all the territory that the soles of their feet tread on. The boundaries are the desert to the south, Lebanon to the north, the river Euphrates to the east, and the uttermost sea, which is the Mediterranean Sea, to the west.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The promise depends on obeying God and loving Him faithfully. It is not an automatic guarantee but an invitation to trust and walk with Him. Scholars debate how this extension of borders was fulfilled over the course of Israel's history.

For today: God often gives us what He promises step by step, as we walk with Him. If you feel faced with something great, take the next step in obedience and trust, without expecting to see it all at once.
exp.10:24:
No enemy will be able to stand against the people of Israel. God himself will put fear and dread of them over all the lands where they walk, just as he had promised.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan, near the end of his life. He reminds them that the victory would come from God, not from their own strength. But the next verse makes clear that the blessing depended on obeying his commands. The promise was tied to their faithfulness.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, do not rely only on your own strength. Seek God, obey him in what he has already shown you, and move forward with confidence, knowing that he goes before you.
exp.10:26:
This verse says that the blessing comes to the people if they listen to and obey the commands of God. The words quoted from the source are not in the verse you read, so I have left them out. In the Bible, the idea of listening includes paying attention and acting on what is heard, not just hearing it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He sets two paths before them: blessing or curse. He reminds them that God brought them out and cared for them, and he wants them to respond with trust and obedience. Afterward the ceremony on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal will take place.

Today we can remember that listening to God is more than knowing what the Bible says. It is deciding to put it into practice, even in small things. You might choose one clear command of God today and obey it with confidence in his goodness.
exp.10:27:
The passage says there will be a curse if the people do not listen to God's commandments and turn aside from the way Moses commands them. That turning aside consists of following other gods, that is, strange gods, which they had never known.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He sets before them two ways: to obey God and receive a blessing, or to abandon him and suffer the consequences. He reminds them of what God had already done for them, so that they will follow him with confidence.

For today: let us ask what things compete with God in our hearts. We can begin the day by listening to his Word and deciding to follow him, trusting that his way is the best.
exp.10:29:
This verse describes where Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal are located: on the other side of the Jordan, toward the west, in the land of the Canaanites who live on the open plain, near Gilgal and the plains of Moreh. The plain here means open, level ground. Some scholars debate whether this Gilgal is the same one mentioned later in Joshua, so it is not certain which place is meant.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that when they cross the Jordan, they are to proclaim the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal. He gives them a specific location so they will remember that this decision will be real, not just an idea.

For today: obeying God is not something abstract. Think of one particular place or moment this week where you can choose his way, and decide ahead of time what you will do.
exp.11:1:
It says that the people of Israel were to completely destroy all the places where the nations of Canaan worshiped their gods: on the high mountains, on the hills, and under every green tree.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter the promised land. He gives them the rules for living there. He wants them to worship only the LORD and not to mix in with the practices of the neighboring peoples. High places and leafy trees were common sites of pagan worship.

For today: this is not about destroying other people's things, but about examining our own hearts. We can ask ourselves what habits, influences, or "places" pull us away from God, and decide with courage to remove them from our lives so that we give Him first place.
exp.11:2:
It says that Israel was to tear down the altars of the peoples of Canaan, break their pillars or sacred images, and burn their wooden poles, which were posts or trees dedicated to the goddess Asherah. It also says they were to cut down the carved images of their gods and wipe out their names from that place.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them the laws for living there. He wants to protect them from idolatry, which could turn them away from God. The verses that follow say that they would worship God in a different way, in the place He chose.

For today: Jesus does not ask us to destroy other people's places of worship, but to guard our hearts. We can ask ourselves what thing has taken the place of God in our lives, such as money, fame, or pride. With God's help, we need to remove that place and put Him back first.
exp.11:5:
This verse lists what the people were to bring to the place of worship that God would choose: burnt offerings (offerings burned entirely), sacrifices, tithes (a tenth of what they earned), the heave offering (a portion presented to God), fulfilled vows, freewill offerings, and the firstborn males of their animals.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He tells them not to worship as the peoples of Canaan did, in any place they chose. God would choose one place for his name, and there they were to bring everything. This protected the purity of their worship and kept them united as a people.

For today: giving to God should be a deliberate and orderly act, not left to chance. We can ask ourselves whether we offer the best of our time, money, and affection with gratitude, or only what we have left over.
exp.11:9:
It says that the people of Israel would cross the Jordan River and live in the land that God was giving them as an inheritance. There God would give them rest from the enemies surrounding them, and they would live peacefully and in safety. Here, "inherit" means to receive as one's own property a gift that comes from God.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, shortly before he dies. He reminds them that they have not yet arrived at the promised land. For this reason he asks that, when they enter, they not each follow their own judgment, but worship God in the place he chooses, as the following text says.

For today: God promises rest, but he also asks for obedience. We can trust that he cares for our future and, in the meantime, live according to his Word and not according to what seems right to us at each moment.
exp.11:10:
He says that when Israel lives in the promised land, they must bring their offerings to one single place, the one God chooses so that his name dwells there. There they will bring the burnt offerings (offerings completely burned), the sacrifices, the tithes (the tenth part), the heave offerings (those lifted up before God) and the best of what they have promised in their vows.

Moses speaks to the people before they cross the Jordan. He explains how to worship God in the new land. The Canaanites worshiped wherever they wanted, but God wanted Israel to worship him with order, unity and obedience, according to his word and not according to their own ideas.

For today: God deserves the best of us, not what is left over. We can ask ourselves whether we seek him with sincerity and obedience, and whether we give him our time, affection and resources with joy and commitment.
exp.11:11:
This verse commands the whole people to rejoice before God at the place of worship. It includes the fathers, the sons, the male servants and the female servants. It also includes the Levite who lives within their gates. The word "gates" here refers to the towns and cities where they live, and an inheritance is a portion of land given as a family's share. The Levites received no land, so they depended on the generosity of the people.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that, once they settle there, they must bring their offerings to the place God chooses, and not to just any place. Worship was to be orderly, but it was also meant to be joyful and shared with everyone.

For today: when we worship or give thanks to God, we should not do it alone. Let us invite the family, the workers, and those who do not have much, so that they too may rejoice with us.
exp.11:13:
This verse says that God himself would choose a place, within one of the tribes of Israel, where the people were to offer their burnt offerings to him. A burnt offering was a sacrifice that was burned completely on the altar. There they were also to do all that God commanded them regarding their worship.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He warns them not to worship God in just any place, as the surrounding nations did with their false gods. God wanted an orderly and obedient worship, not one invented by each person. The text does not give the details of which place this would be here.

For today: worshiping God is not doing whatever seems right to us, but drawing near to him as he has made himself known. Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith rests on what God says or only on our own preferences.
exp.11:14:
This verse says that the Israelite could slaughter animals and eat meat in his own town, according to his desire and according to what God had given him. Both the person who was ritually unclean and the person who was clean could eat it, just as one eats the meat of the roe deer or the deer, animals that were hunted. The word "unclean" refers to ritual impurity, not to a moral failing.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He explains that sacrifices were to be offered only in the place God would choose, and here he makes clear that eating ordinary meat did not require going to that place. In this way the sacred is distinguished from the everyday.

For today: God allows us to enjoy everyday things, such as food, with gratitude, and to recognize them as his blessing. Before eating, we can give thanks from the heart, without turning it into an empty routine.
exp.11:18:
This verse says that the people of Israel were always to care for the Levites and not leave them without help as long as they lived in the land. To forsake someone means to leave them alone, without help or support. A Levite is a member of the tribe of Levi, set apart to serve in the worship of God.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The Levites did not receive a portion of land like the other tribes, so they depended on the tithes and offerings. That is why Moses reminds them to include the Levites in the feasts and meals before God, with joy and generosity.

Today we can think of those who devote themselves to serving in the church or teaching the Word. A practical way to do this is to support them with regular offerings, prayer, and encouragement, so that they lack nothing they need and can serve with joy.
exp.11:21:
It says that the meat of animals that Israel killed to eat at home could be eaten just like the meat of the roebuck and the hart, game animals that were not offered on the altar. The roebuck is a small kind of deer. The one who was ceremonially impure and the one who was not both could eat of that meat.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He explains that, when the place of worship is far away, they may eat meat in their towns and not only at the sanctuary. This was a practical allowance, on the condition that they not eat the blood.

For today: God cares for everyday life, such as food and the table. We can enjoy his gifts with gratitude and, at the same time, respect the limits he sets, without separating daily life from reverence toward him.
exp.11:28:
It says that when God has removed from the way the nations who live in the promised land, the people of Israel will take possession of it and live there. The verse of the word that meant ruined or laid waste is not needed here, since that word does not appear in the verse. For the idea of receiving the land as an inheritance, it means they would receive it as a gift and not by their own strength. Living there means dwelling in the land.

Moses is speaking near the end of his life. He is preparing Israel before they enter Canaan. He reminds them that God will act on their behalf, but that they must obey him. The verse is the opening of a warning: do not copy the religious practices of the peoples who will be displaced.

For today: when God gives us a new stage, such as a job, a home, or a community, it is easy to imitate the customs around us without thinking. Before adopting something, ask yourself whether it pleases God, and thank him for what you receive as his gift.
exp.11:30:
Deuteronomy 12:31 tells Israel that they must not worship the Lord by copying the practices of the peoples living in Canaan. Those nations practiced every kind of detestable thing that the Lord hates when they served their gods. They even burned their sons and daughters in the fire as sacrifices to their gods. God rejects such things, and He will not accept worship that imitates them.

Moses is speaking to the people before they enter the promised land. He warns them that once the Lord gives them that land, they must not be curious about how those nations worshiped or try to borrow their methods. The Lord wants to be worshiped in the way He Himself has directed, not according to human ideas or the religious fashions of other peoples.

For today, before adopting a spiritual practice, ask yourself whether it comes from God's Word or merely from a popular custom. A sincere heart also needs a faithful guide, and God gives us that guide in Scripture.
exp.12:1:
This verse speaks of a prophet or dreamer who announces a sign or wonder, and that sign really does come to pass. Yet he uses that fulfilled event to invite the people to follow other gods, meaning strange gods that Israel had not known, and to serve them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that a miracle is not enough to prove that someone speaks on God's behalf. According to the text, God allows that test to see whether they love him with all their heart and all their soul.

Today, let us not measure truth only by how impressive or successful someone appears. Let us compare every message with what God has already revealed in his Word, and let us remain faithful to Jehovah.
exp.12:3:
This verse brings together six actions of the faithful people: walking after the Lord, fearing him, keeping his commandments, obeying his voice, serving him, and cleaving to him, which means joining yourself to him and holding on to him with loyalty. "Fear" here speaks of deep respect and reverence, not of terror.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that a prophet with miraculous signs might invite them to follow other gods. Moses explains that God allows that test to show whether they love him with all their heart. The answer is not to be swayed by miracles, but to remain faithful to what God has already said.

Today, before following a teaching or a leader, let us compare what they say with the Word of God. A message is not true simply because it is impressive. Set aside time each day to listen to God in his Word and to obey him.
exp.12:6:
This verse continues a sentence that begins in the previous verse. It describes the gods that someone may try to persuade you to serve: the gods of the peoples who live near you or far from you, from one end of the earth to the other. The word "end" in that phrase is the one the verse itself uses, so the idea is that it does not matter where such false worship comes from, whether near or far; it is still a path that turns people away from God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that the temptation can come even from the people they love most, and that God, who rescued them from Egypt, deserves their complete loyalty. The severe penalty that follows reflects the law of Israel at that time, when the nation was a covenant with God.

For today: not everything that draws us away from God looks like a threat. It can come from people close to us or from popular ideas. Examine with humility which influences shape your faith, and stay firm in God with love and respect toward others.
exp.12:8:
It says that if someone tried to draw an Israelite away to worship other gods, that person should not be covered up or spared out of pity. The witness had to strike the first blow, and then the whole people would follow.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. God had rescued them from Egypt and made a covenant with them. At that time, idolatry was seen as treason against the King, and it could destroy the entire nation. This is a civil law for ancient Israel, not a command for the church today.

Today we do not use violence, but we can take seriously our loyalty to God. If anything or anyone pulls us away from Christ, we should not excuse it out of affection or comfort. With humility and love, let us put God first.
exp.13:3:
This verse opens the list of animals that the people of Israel were allowed to eat. It names three domestic animals that were common in their daily life: the ox (the bull or cattle), the sheep, and the goat. These were animals they raised in their fields and also offered in sacrifice.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God chose them as a holy people, set apart for him. For that reason, even what they ate was meant to show that they belonged to God. Scholars explain the reasons for these laws in various ways, and the Bible does not give all the details.

For today: God is interested in our whole life, even the everyday. We can ask ourselves whether our daily decisions, such as what we do and what we consume, reflect that we belong to him and give thanks to him.
exp.13:9:
Says that, among the water animals, the people could eat only those that had fins and scales, that is, common fish. Everything else, such as shellfish or eels, was to be avoided. "Unclean" means ceremonially impure, not fit for the people of God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them to live as a set-apart people. These food rules taught them to distinguish the clean from the unclean. Scholars explain the exact reasons in several ways: hygiene, symbolism, or setting themselves apart from other nations. The text emphasizes that they are God's holy people.

Today Christians do not follow these food rules, because Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). But we can learn to live with intention: asking whether our daily habits show that we belong to God.
exp.13:11:
It says that the people of Israel were not to eat certain birds of prey. Here the eagle, the ossifrage, and the ospray are named. The ossifrage is a bird of prey similar to a hawk, and the ospray is a small hawk. The exact Hebrew names are hard to identify, so some of these birds may vary from one translation to another.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them to live as a set-apart people. These rules about food distinguished them from other nations. Many think the birds listed were those that hunt or feed on dead flesh, although the Bible does not give a detailed reason here.

For today: Christians are not under these food rules (Mark 7:19; Acts 10), but we can learn to live with intention, letting God guide our daily decisions and set us apart by our love and obedience.
exp.13:15:
This verse is part of a list of birds that God declared unclean, meaning the Israelites were not to eat them. It mentions the little owl, the great owl, and the swan. Some of the ancient names are hard to identify: scholars are not sure which exact bird each one is, and translations vary.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them to live as a set-apart people, distinct from the neighboring nations. These food rules were part of that identity. The text does not explain the reason for each bird, so it is best not to invent reasons.

For today: although Christians are not under these food rules, the passage teaches us that God cares about every detail of daily life. We can ask ourselves whether what we eat, do, and say shows that we belong to Him.
exp.13:16:
This verse continues a list of birds that the Israelites were not to eat.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they are a holy people, set apart for God. These food laws helped them live differently from the neighboring nations and remember that they belonged to the Lord.

Christians are not under these food rules (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15). But we can still learn that God cares about our whole life, even the everyday things. Today you might ask yourself: what habit of my daily life can I offer to God to show that I belong to him?
exp.13:20:
It says that the Israelites were not to eat any animal that had died on its own. They could give it to the foreigner living in their towns, or sell it to a foreigner. The reason is that Israel was a holy people, set apart for God. Finally, it forbids boiling a young goat in its mother's milk.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land, reminding them how to live as God's people, even in what they ate. Scholars do not fully agree on why he forbids the young goat in its mother's milk; some think it relates to religious customs of other peoples, but this is not certain.

For today: our holiness shows in small, everyday things. Ask yourself which daily habit you can give to God, so that your way of living shows that you belong to him.
exp.13:25:
This verse says that the Israelite, on reaching the place of worship, could use the money from selling his tithe to buy whatever he wanted: cattle, sheep, wine, or strong drink (a fermented beverage, probably made from fruit). Then he would eat there, before God, and rejoice with his family.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. If the sanctuary was very far away, carrying the tithe in the form of produce was difficult, so they could sell it and carry money instead. The celebration was a feast of gratitude, and right after this the text reminds them to care for the Levite, who had no inheritance of his own.

For today: giving to God is not only an obligation; it can also include gratitude and celebration. Set aside time to thank God with your family, sharing a simple meal, and think of someone in need whom you could invite.
exp.14:1:
This verse explains how the year of release worked. A person who had lent money to a fellow Israelite was to let that debt go and not demand it back again. To release a debt means to cancel it or let it go. A loan is what was given, and a neighbor is the person living nearby or a fellow countryman. The word "proclaimed" in this context means announced publicly: it was God himself who declared that time of forgiveness.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. The law aimed to protect the poor and to keep anyone from being in debt forever. Scholars debate whether the debt was fully canceled or only its collection was suspended for that year, but the spirit of the law is compassion between brothers.

Today we can ask ourselves whether there is someone who owes us something, whether money or an offense, and whom God invites us to let go. Forgiving generously reflects how God treats us.
exp.14:2:
It says that a loan made to a foreigner could be collected, but the debt of a fellow Israelite was to be forgiven.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. Every seven years a release was given to debtors, to care for the poor and to keep anyone from being trapped in debt. Scholars discuss whether the debt was canceled completely or only suspended for that year. The foreigner, probably a passing merchant, was not under that same arrangement.

For today: if someone close to you owes you and cannot pay, ask God for a generous heart. Consider forgiving the debt or giving them more time, protecting their dignity and without humiliating them.
exp.14:4:
It says that the abundant blessing promised in the verses before depends on a condition: faithfully listening to the voice of God and putting all his commandments into practice.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains the law of the year of release, when debts between Israelite brothers were forgiven. The goal was that there would be no poor among them. This verse makes clear that the blessing and the mutual care go hand in hand with obedience to God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our obedience includes how we treat those who are in need. Listening to God is not only believing or feeling, but acting with generosity. This week, think of someone in need near you and help them in a concrete way.
exp.14:5:
He says that when God blesses Israel as he promised, they will have such abundance that they will be able to lend to many nations and will not need to borrow. The phrase about ruling over them means you will have dominance or influence over those nations, and the phrase about them not ruling over you means that no one will dominate you.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the blessing depends on faithfully obeying God. The passage speaks of the year of debt release and of caring for the poor, so that there would be no beggars among them.

For today: God's blessing is not only meant to be enjoyed, but also shared. We can live wisely in handling money, avoiding debts that enslave us, and be generous toward those who are in need. It is a promise given to Israel, so it should not be read as an automatic guarantee of wealth.
exp.14:6:
It says that when someone from your own people is in need within your city or your land, you must not harden your heart or close your hand. The word "poor" in the verse is the one that means needy, and "brother" refers to a fellow Israelite. Closing your hand means refusing to help.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains how to live there with justice. Just before this verse, he mentions the year of release, when debts were forgiven. God wants his people to care for the poor and not be selfish.

For today: when you meet someone in need, do not stop at good intentions alone. Ask God what you can give them, whether help, time, or money, and do it generously and without resentment.
exp.14:13:
This verse commands that when a Hebrew servant is set free, his master must not send him away empty-handed. The phrase "furnish him liberally" means giving to him generously, like someone filling a full supply. The "floor" is the place where grain was threshed, and the "winepress" is where grapes were trodden to make wine. In other words, the master was to give him from his flock, from his harvest of grain, and from his wine, according to what God had blessed him with.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In that time, a person could sell himself as a servant because of debt or poverty. After six years he was to go free. The law wanted him not to fall back into poverty, and it reminds Israel that they too had been servants in Egypt and that God redeemed them.

For today: if God has blessed us, we can give generously to someone who is coming out of a difficult situation, for example by helping someone who has lost a job or is starting over. Giving with gratitude reflects the kindness God showed us.
exp.14:14:
This verse asks the people of Israel to remember their past. They were servants, that is, slaves in Egypt, and God redeemed them, setting them free by paying the price of their liberty. That is why God gives them this command: to treat with kindness the one who leaves servitude.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He repeats the law about Hebrew servants, who were to be set free in the seventh year. When they sent them away, they were to give them generous provision. The reason for the command is memory: Israel knew from experience what it was to live without freedom and to receive the mercy of God.

For today: when you remember how much grace you have received from God, let that make you generous. Think of someone who needs help and share something concrete with them, expecting nothing in return.
exp.14:16:
It says that if a Hebrew servant had already completed six years and did not want to leave free because he loved his master and his household, the master was to take an awl (a pointed tool for piercing) and push it through his ear into the door. In this way he would remain a servant for life. The same applied to the female servant.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they were servants in Egypt and that God rescued them. For this reason the law commanded release in the seventh year and generous treatment of the servant. The act involving the ear was a public sign of a voluntary decision. Scholars do not fully agree on its exact meaning.

For today: remember how much you have received from God, and treat with generosity and respect those who depend on you, such as employees or family members. Let loyalty come from love, not from pressure.
exp.14:18:
It says that every firstborn male that is born from your cattle and your sheep belongs to God and must be set apart for Him. Therefore, that animal must not be used for work, nor may its wool be cut. "Set apart" means dedicating something to God, and cutting wool is shearing it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. Shortly before, he had commanded them to free their Hebrew servants and treat them generously. Now he reminds them that the firstborn of their herds also belongs to God. It then explains that they were to eat it before Him, in the place He would choose, together with their family, and that it had to be an animal without defect.

For today: we can give God the first and the best, not the leftovers. For example, setting apart with gratitude the first part of the day to pray, or a portion of our income to help others, recognizing that everything comes from Him.
exp.14:21:
This verse says that the firstborn animal that had some defect was not offered on the altar, but was eaten at home, within the towns of the people. Everyone could eat it, both the ceremonially unclean person and the clean one, just as one eats the meat of a roebuck or a hart, game animals that were not offered in sacrifice. The "gates" mentioned in the verse refer to the town gates, the places where the people lived and gathered within their settlements.

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that what is given to God must be the best, without defects. But the animal with a defect was not wasted: it served as food and was shared. Then follows the prohibition against eating blood.

For today: let us give God the best of our time, affection and resources, not the leftovers. And let us generously share what we have, without wasting or excluding anyone.
exp.15:1:
It says the people were to offer the Passover sacrifice to the Lord with animals from their flock, whether sheep or cattle. They were to do this only in the place God would choose, a place where God would be worshiped and remembered in a special way. The phrase about making his name dwell there means that place where God would be worshiped and remembered in a special way.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the Passover celebrates the night God brought them out of Egypt. By asking them to worship in one single place, he wanted the feast to be carried out with order and unity. Scholars often understand that this place was later Jerusalem, although it is not named here.

For today: let us not take for granted what God has done for us. We can set aside specific times to remember his deliverance and give him thanks, and to do it together with other believers, not only in private.
exp.15:2:
It says that during the Passover, the people were not to eat bread with yeast, that is, with fermented dough. For seven days they would eat bread without yeast, called "the bread of affliction," because they left Egypt in haste, that is, quickly. God wanted them to remember that day all their lives.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He repeats the Passover instructions so they will not forget how God freed them from slavery. The flat bread reminded them of the suffering and the speed of that departure.

For today: remember the times God has helped you and brought you out of trouble. You can write them down or tell them with your family. Remembering his faithfulness strengthens gratitude and trust when hard times come.
exp.15:4:
This verse says that the people of Israel could not sacrifice the Passover lamb in any of their towns, even though God himself was giving them those towns. The word "sacrifice" here means to offer and kill the animal for the feast. The sentence continues in the next verse: they were to do it only in the place that God would choose.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the departure from Egypt and teaches them to celebrate the Passover in an orderly way. By centering the feast in one place, the whole nation gathered to remember what God had done. Scholars agree that this place later became Jerusalem, although the text here does not name it.

For today: let us worship God as he asks, not only as is convenient for us. Setting a fixed place to remember his work, together with other believers, strengthens our faith.
exp.15:5:
It says that the Passover was no longer to be celebrated in any town, but in the place that God would choose for his name to dwell there. The sacrifice was made in the evening, at the going down of the sun, that is, at dusk, remembering the hour when Israel came out of Egypt. The phrase about the place God would choose is not explained further here.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He repeats the law to them and teaches them to worship God together, not each person in their own way. Over time, that place came to be associated with Jerusalem, although this verse does not name it.

For today: God invites us to remember his deliverance deliberately, not out of habit. We can set aside a fixed time, alone or with the church, to thank him for the salvation he gave us in Christ, and to do so with an attentive and obedient heart.
exp.15:6:
Moses says that the Passover lamb must be roasted and eaten in the place that God chooses, not in just any town. To "roast" is to cook over fire, and the phrase about returning to your home means going back to your house. Some understand that the "morning" is the one after the night of Passover, and others that it is at the end of the feast. The text does not fully make this clear.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the Passover celebrates the departure from Egypt. By asking for one single place to worship, he teaches them that the feast belongs to the whole people and that God is the one who sets how they are to draw near to Him.

For today: God calls us to gather to remember his work, but also to return home. May your time with him, alone and with other believers, renew you so that you live your routine with gratitude.
exp.15:7:
This verse commands eating unleavened bread for six days after the Passover. The seventh day would be a sacred gathering before the Lord, and no work was to be done on it. The term for unleavened bread refers to loaves made without yeast.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how to celebrate the feast that commemorated their departure from Egypt. The bread without yeast reminded them of that hurried departure, and the rest of the seventh day taught them to pause and honor God.

Today we too can set apart a regular time to rest from work and remember what God has done for us. A weekly pause, without rush or pending tasks, can help us give thanks, pray, and renew our trust that God sustains us.
exp.15:8:
It says the people were to count seven full weeks, beginning from the moment they first put the sickle to the ripe grain. The ripe fields ready for harvest are what the word refers to, and the sickle is the curved tool used for reaping. It was an orderly count between two harvests.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. After the Passover, which remembers the deliverance from Egypt, he explains the feast of Weeks, also called Pentecost in the New Testament. It was a festival of thanksgiving for the harvest, celebrated with joy, freewill offerings, and generosity toward the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow.

Today we can learn to count our blessings with intention. Before the season passes, take time to acknowledge what God has given you, and share something with someone in need, so that your gratitude becomes shared joy.
exp.15:10:
It says that at the Feast of Weeks the people were to rejoice before God, in the place where He would set His name. And not only the head of the household: also his sons, his servants, the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow. Here a "servant" means a worker of the house, and the Levite was a man from the tribe set apart for the service of worship, who had no land of his own.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This feast came after the wheat harvest, and each person gave a freewill offering according to what God had given him. The following verse reminds them that they were slaves in Egypt, so they were to treat those in need well.

For today: when God blesses you, do not celebrate alone. Invite to your table someone who is lonely or in need, and share generously.
exp.15:12:
This verse commands the people of Israel to celebrate the Feast of Booths for seven days. They were to do so after gathering in the grain from the threshing floor, the wheat and barley, and the wine and oil from the winepress, where the grapes were trodden.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the yearly feasts. This was a feast of thanksgiving for the harvest, and everyone was invited: family, servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans and widows. They were also to remember that they had once been slaves in Egypt. Other passages of the Bible say that living in booths reminded them of the journey through the desert.

For today: when God gives you something good, such as a job, a harvest or unexpected help, take some time to thank him. And share your joy with those who have less.
exp.15:13:
This verse commands rejoicing during the feasts, and that joy must include the whole household and the whole community. Holy festivals are the sacred feasts; the men and women who served in the house, whether as hired workers or as slaves, are included in the celebration; the towns or cities where people lived are the places where this community gathered. The Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow were people without land of their own or without anyone to support them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they were slaves in Egypt, and for that reason they must treat the most vulnerable with kindness. Here the text refers to the Feast of Tabernacles, which was celebrated after the harvest as thanksgiving to God for his blessing.

For today: when God blesses you, do not celebrate alone. Think of someone who is alone or in need, such as a neighbor, a migrant, or a widow, and invite them to your table. True gratitude becomes generosity.
exp.15:14:
This verse commands the people to hold a seven-day feast to God in the place he would choose. The reason given is that God blessed them in their harvests and in all the work of their hands, so they were to be very joyful.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains how to celebrate the feast of booths after the harvest. This joy was to include everyone: the family, the servants, the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. In this way no one was left out of the thankfulness.

For today: pause to thank God for what he has given you, and share that joy with someone who needs it. You can invite a person who is alone to a meal, or help someone with your time or your resources.
exp.15:21:
This verse forbids setting up a statue, that is, a pillar or sacred stone for worship. God says he hates this. The word "hates" means that he is deeply displeased by it. "LORD" is the name of the God of Israel.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for worshiping God in a pure way. The neighboring peoples used pillars and images in their worship, and God did not want Israel to mix its worship with those customs. Many scholars think this protected the people from idolatry, although some details of how those pillars were used are debated.

For today: examine whether anything holds in your heart the place that belongs to God. Worship him as he has revealed himself, with simplicity and truth, and not with things you invent or copy from others.
exp.16:1:
This verse begins a law about a serious case. It says that if, in any town that God gives to Israel, a man or a woman is found doing what is evil in the sight of God, breaking his covenant, action must be taken. The word "transgressing" means breaking faith or stepping over the line. A covenant is the solemn commitment between God and his people. The offense is made clear in the next verse: worshiping other gods.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that being God's people requires total faithfulness. Just before this, he spoke of offering God sacrifices without defect, and now he moves to something even more serious: loyalty of the heart.

For today: God cares about our loyalty more than about outward religious appearances. It is worth asking ourselves what things occupy God's place in our hearts, and returning to him with sincerity.
exp.16:3:
It says that if someone reports to the people a case of idolatry, action should not be taken right away. First one must listen carefully and inquire thoroughly, that is, investigate in depth. Only if it is confirmed that it is true and certain that this abomination (something God detests) was committed in Israel does one move to the next step.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the covenant with God demanded total loyalty, and that worshiping the sun, the moon, or the stars was breaking that covenant. Even so, he requires a fair investigation and, as the text goes on, more than one witness.

For today: before accusing someone or repeating a rumor, let us find out the facts carefully. Truth and justice matter just as much as faithfulness to God.
exp.16:7:
This verse says that when a case is too hard to settle in a city's courts, it must not be left without justice. It speaks of three kinds of cases: deaths, disputes between people, and wounds or assaults. The person was to go to the place that God would choose.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for living with justice. Earlier, he spoke of requiring enough witnesses, and afterward it says that the Levitical priests and the judge would give the final decision.

For today: when something is too complicated or unjust to resolve on your own, do not be carried along by pride or by haste. Seek wise and trustworthy counsel, and accept the guidance you are given.
exp.16:9:
It says that when a case is very hard to decide, the Israelite must go to the place the Lord chooses, listen to the decision given by the priests and the judge, and carefully carry it out. The decision or verdict is what the verse calls the sentence. The people who serve there as authority are the ones who inform the person. Carefully doing what is written means paying close attention to obeying everything that is told.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for living with order and justice. When local judges could not settle a complicated case, there was a higher court. In this way endless conflicts were avoided and justice was protected in the community.

For today: when you face a disagreement you cannot resolve, seek wise and trustworthy counsel, such as a pastor, a mentor, or a mediator. Then humble yourself to accept with respect what they advise, always comparing it with the Bible.
exp.16:15:
It says that the king of Israel was not to gather many horses for himself, nor send the people back to Egypt to get them. The Lord had already told them not to go back that way.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for the day they might ask for a king. In that time, horses were military strength, and Egypt was famous for them. Many understand that God wanted the king to trust in Him and not in his armed power. It also reminded them that Egypt had been the place of their slavery. The instructions that follow speak of not multiplying wives or riches.

For today: let us ask ourselves in what things we trust more than God, such as money, connections, or security. We may use them with gratitude, but without putting them in His place.
exp.16:17:
This verse says that when the king of Israel begins to rule, he must copy God's law by his own hand into a book. The copy was to be made from the original kept by the Levitical priests, who were in charge of guarding the law.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions in case they someday ask for a king. Earlier he had warned against accumulating horses, wives, and riches, things that could make a ruler proud or unfaithful. Copying the law was a way of reminding the king that he too was under God's authority.

For today: whoever has some authority, at home, at work, or in the church, needs to let God's Word correct him first. You could copy out one Bible passage by hand each week and meditate on it slowly.
exp.16:19:
This verse says that the king was to read God's law every day so that his heart would not be filled with pride over his fellow countrymen. It also says he was not to turn aside from the commandments, neither to the right hand nor to the left. If he obeyed, he and his children would reign for a long time in the midst of Israel.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions in case they someday ask for a king. That king would not be an absolute ruler, but someone under the authority of God's word, just like his brothers. Many scholars see here a check against the abuse of power.

For today: if you have any responsibility, whether in your home, your work, or your church, set aside a moment each day to read the Bible with humility. Ask God to remind you that you serve others and are not above them.
exp.17:0:
This verse says that the priests, the Levites, that is, the whole tribe of Levi, would not receive a territory of their own like the other tribes of Israel. Instead, they would live from what the people brought to God: the offerings made by fire, which were the offerings burned on the altar, and the Lord's inheritance, that is, the portion that belonged to Him.

Moses is speaking to the people before they enter the promised land. He explains how they are to care for the Levites, who served in worship and taught the law. Since they would have no land to farm, God himself would be their inheritance, and the people would support them.

For today: we can support with generosity and gratitude those who serve God and his people, and remember that having God is the most secure inheritance.
exp.17:1:
This verse says that the Levites would not receive their own piece of land among the other tribes of Israel. The word "inheritance" in the verse means the portion of land given to each family as its share. Instead of land, the Levites' inheritance was the Lord himself, just as he had promised them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the tribe of Levi was set apart for service in worship. Because of this, they would not have fields of their own, but would live from the offerings and firstfruits that the people brought to the Lord. In this way the people cared for those who served in the sanctuary.

For today: God wants to be our greatest wealth and security, more than money or possessions. We can also support, with generosity, those who serve in our church.
exp.17:2:
This verse says that when someone from the people offered an ox or a sheep, they were to give the priest three parts of the animal: the shoulder (the foreleg), the two cheeks (the jaws), and the maw (the animal's fourth stomach). That was the portion due to the priest by right.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The Levites would not receive land like the other tribes, so God sustained them through the offerings of the people. Their inheritance was to serve the LORD. Scholars explain the details of these parts in different ways, but the central idea is clear: a fair provision for those who served.

Today we can support with generosity and gratitude those who dedicate their lives to teaching and caring for others spiritually, and also remember that God himself is our greatest inheritance.
exp.17:6:
It says that a Levite who comes from another town to the place of worship may serve in the name of the Lord his God, just like his fellow Levites who are already there.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The Levites did not receive land of their own, so they lived scattered among the towns and depended on the offerings. Here, any Levite who sincerely wants to serve in the sanctuary is protected: he will have a place and a share just like the others.

For today: God values those who serve with a willing heart, no matter where they come from. In the church, let us welcome with joy anyone who desires to serve, and make room for them without comparing or excluding.
exp.17:9:
This verse forbids the people of Israel from practicing pagan customs. It speaks of making children pass through the fire, which probably refers to sacrificing them or offering them to false gods (some scholars debate whether it always meant death or sometimes a rite of dedication). It also forbids trying to learn the future, interpreting omens, casting lots for hidden purposes, and practicing sorcery.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He warns them not to imitate the practices of the nations living there, because those nations sought guidance and power apart from God. He wanted Israel to trust in Him alone.

Today we can ask ourselves where we look for security about the future. Instead of horoscopes, mediums, or other occult practices, we can pray, read the Bible, and seek wise counsel, trusting that God guides our steps.
exp.17:16:
Here Moses recalls that God answered him: "They have well spoken that which they have spoken." This refers to what the people asked for at Horeb (Mount Sinai): that they not hear the voice of God directly again, because the fire and the greatness of it filled them with fear. God approved that request and decided to speak to them through a prophet.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that God accepted their reverent fear and that he would send them prophets, from among their own brothers, to bring them his word. Many Christians see in this promise an announcement of Christ (as Acts 3:22 does), although it also applies to the prophets who would come afterward.

For today: God understands our fear and our need for him to speak to us with closeness. Listen to his Word with respect and seriousness, and remember that in Jesus God spoke to us clearly and accessibly.
exp.17:17:
God promises that he will raise up a prophet from among the people of Israel, one of their own brothers, like Moses. He will put God's words in his mouth, and that prophet will faithfully speak everything God commands him.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that at Horeb (Mount Sinai) they were afraid of God's voice and of the fire, and they asked for a mediator. God accepted their request. The verses that follow show that the true prophet was to be obeyed and the false prophet rejected. Many Christians also see here a sign pointing to Jesus, as the New Testament does in Acts 3:22; Jews have understood it in other ways.

For today: listen to God's Word with humility, and always compare it with the Bible before accepting what any voice says in God's name.
exp.18:1:
God commands Israel that, once they are living in the promised land, they are to set apart three cities within their territory. "Set apart" here simply means setting them aside on purpose, marking them out from the rest.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. These cities, called cities of refuge, were there so that someone who killed another person without meaning to could flee there and save his life. In this way, a relative moved by revenge could not kill him unjustly. The verses that follow explain that the road to the cities had to be kept clear and that the case in view is that of someone with no earlier hostility toward the person he killed.

For today: God cares about justice and also about mercy. We can imitate him by being people who are not carried away by anger, who can tell a mistake from an evil intention, and who offer a safe place and forgiveness to someone who got it wrong without meaning to.
exp.18:2:
It says that Israel was to prepare the roads well leading to the cities of refuge. It also was to divide its land into three regions, so that in each one there would be a city nearby. The phrase about preparing the way means that you shall prepare the way. A slayer is the one who caused a death, and fleeing means escape.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for when they are already living there. According to the verses that follow, these cities protected the one who killed without meaning to, so that an avenger would not kill him in the heat of anger. The law sought justice and mercy at the same time.

For today: God makes sure the way toward protection and forgiveness is clear. We can imitate him by removing obstacles so that others can find help, and by treating with compassion the one who made a mistake without bad intent.
exp.18:4:
This verse gives an example of accidental death. Two men go together into the forest to cut wood. One swings the axe, the head comes loose from the handle and kills his companion. The one who caused the death without meaning to may flee to one of the cities of refuge and save his life. Those cities are the ones God commanded to be set apart.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. God orders the creation of cities of refuge to distinguish between murder and accident. In this way, a relative moved by anger could not kill an innocent person, and justice was protected in the land.

For today: before judging someone, try to understand their intentions and the circumstances. God is concerned with the heart, not only with the result. This invites us to be fair, to show mercy, and not to act driven by anger.
exp.18:5:
This verse explains why God commanded that cities of refuge be set apart. If someone killed another person without meaning to, they could flee to one of them. This kept the victim's relative, burning with anger, from chasing the killer down and catching him if the road was long. Killing him would have been unjust, because there had been no hatred beforehand.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them this law to protect the innocent and to keep more unjust blood from being spilled. It distinguishes between an accident and a deliberate murder.

For today: when something angers us, it is wise to pause and look at the facts before reacting. Anger can blind us and lead us to do harm. Let us seek justice with calm, and care for the one who acted without evil intent.
exp.18:12:
It says that when someone deliberately kills another person and takes refuge in a city of refuge, the judges must not feel pity for him. The phrase about pity is explained as meaning that no compassion should be allowed to bend justice. In this way Israel is cleared of the guilt of blood that was shed unjustly, and things will go well for them.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The cities of refuge protected the one who killed by accident, but not the murderer who had planned the crime. God wanted to protect life and keep injustice from defiling the nation.

For today: compassion is good, but it must not be used to excuse wrongdoing. When you face a decision that affects others, seek to be just and honest, caring for the life and dignity of people, even when that costs you.
exp.18:13:
This verse forbids moving the boundary markers, that is, the stones or marks that separated one piece of land from another. Shifting a boundary stone to take a piece of someone else's land is what this law is about. The earlier generations who set those marks are the ones who placed them in the family's share, and that share of land is what each family received as an inheritance.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the land of Canaan. In that time land was the livelihood of each family and a gift from God. Changing a boundary was a quiet theft that harmed the most vulnerable. It appears among laws about justice, such as murder and witnesses, because God wants a people where no one is robbed.

For today: be honest in small things. Do not take advantage in measures, accounts, contracts or land, even when no one sees you. Respecting what belongs to another honors God.
exp.18:14:
This verse says that one person alone is not enough to accuse someone of a crime or a sin, whatever the offense may be. For a matter to be proven, the testimony of two or three witnesses was required. The phrase about the matter being settled means that the case was made firm. Where the verse speaks of the testimony, it refers to what a person states under oath.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them laws so that justice is even-handed and no one is condemned on the word of a single accuser, who could be mistaken or lying. What follows deals with the false witness.

For today: before believing or repeating an accusation against someone, do not rely on just one account. Ask, verify, and listen calmly. In this way you care for the truth and protect the good name of others.
exp.18:18:
The verse says that if a witness lied in order to harm his brother, the judges must do to him what he had planned to do to the other person. The false witness receives what he intended for his brother, and this removes the wickedness from the community.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law protected the innocent in legal cases. A false witness could destroy a life, so he had to face the consequence of his lie. The judges had to investigate carefully, and the punishment would also serve to make others afraid to lie.

For today: truth matters. A lie, a rumor, or a false accusation can deeply hurt another person. Let us try to speak honestly, not repeat what we have not checked, and defend the person who is unjustly accused.
exp.19:4:
Before a battle, this verse says, the officers would ask the people who had built a new house and had not yet dedicated it, meaning had not yet begun to live in it. That person was allowed to return home, because he might die in the war and another man would enjoy the house he had built.

This comes from Moses' instructions to Israel before they entered the promised land. First the priest encouraged the people to trust that God would go with them. Then the officers gave these exemptions. Many understand that they showed God's care for ordinary human life and that Israel did not depend only on the strength of its soldiers.

For today: God cares for our real needs and does not ask us to set aside what he himself has given us. We can serve him with courage, but also with wisdom, recognizing our limits and caring for our home and our family.
exp.19:5:
This verse says that a man who has planted a vineyard and has not yet eaten its fruit may go back to his house and not go to war. The reason is that if he died in battle, another man would enjoy what he had worked for.

The officers of the people speak to the Israelites before the battle, following the instructions that Moses gave them. First they are reminded that God fights for them. In the text, the vineyard is the second of several exceptions, together with the new house, the engagement to be married, and fear. Scholars explain the exact purpose in different ways, but a concern for people can be seen.

For today: God values our everyday life, our work, and our families. We can serve Him without neglecting what He has entrusted to us, and we should treat others with compassion.
exp.19:9:
When you approach a city to fight against it, you are to make an offer of peace. The wording here means drawing near to a city, and fighting against it means attacking it. Making an offer of peace means announcing it or formally putting it on the table. First, a way out without war was offered.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the land, giving rules for war. The verses that follow explain that if the city accepted, it came under tribute and service; if it did not, a siege followed. These instructions are for distant cities. For the nations of Canaan, the text gives stricter rules (vv. 15-18). Scholars debate how best to understand that difference.

For today: before entering a conflict, look first for dialogue and reconciliation. Offering peace first, with humility and clarity, can prevent wounds that later take a great deal of effort to heal.
exp.19:19:
It says that, if Israel besieged a city, they could cut down the trees that did not bear fruit for eating. With that wood they would build siege works against the enemy city, until they defeated it.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them rules for war. Shortly before, he had commanded them not to cut down fruit trees, because they were a source of food. Here he clarifies that they could use the other trees. The law sets limits even in war, and it cares for what serves to sustain life.

For today: even when we have to use resources or make difficult decisions, we can do so with care and without waste. Before destroying something, let us ask whether it can give life or food to others. God calls us to be responsible and just with what He has entrusted to us.
exp.20:1:
This verse says that if a man is found slain in the field and no one knows who struck him, the elders and judges of the people must go out to the place. There they shall measure the distance from the body to the cities around it. The verse of the verse's "measure" is that it means working out which city is nearest.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law was meant so that an unsolved death would not be ignored. Measuring the distance decided which city was responsible for carrying out the ritual that follows, to remove the guilt of blood from the land. The text does not say here why measuring was necessary, but the next passage makes it clear.

For today: God takes human life and justice seriously. We can take responsibility for what happens near us, by helping those who suffer and not looking away.
exp.20:2:
This verse says that when a dead body was found in the open country and no one knew who had killed the person, the leaders of the nearest city were to take a heifer, that is, a young cow. That heifer was not to have worked or pulled under the yoke, which is the wooden frame put on oxen for plowing. It was an animal that had never been put to use, set apart for this moment.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This ritual showed that innocent blood defiles the land and that the community is responsible for seeking justice, even when the guilty person is not known. The elders acted on behalf of everyone.

Today we can learn that injustice matters to all of us, even when we are not the direct guilty parties. We can ask God for wisdom to care for the vulnerable, speak the truth, and not look the other way.
exp.20:4:
This verse says that the priests, who were descendants of Levi, were to come forward at this time. God had chosen them to serve him and to bless in his name. In addition, whatever they decided would settle any dispute and any case of violence or injury.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He is explaining what to do when a dead body was found and it was not known who had killed the person. The priests were present as representatives of God, so that the process would be serious and fair, and the community would be cleared of guilt.

For today: God takes justice and human life seriously. We can learn not to ignore the injustices around us, to seek the truth with humility, and to ask for God's guidance when we face conflicts.
exp.20:7:
This verse is a prayer. It asks God to forgive Israel, the people He rescued. It also asks that God not hold against them the death of an innocent person. At the end, it promises that the guilt of that blood will be forgiven.

Moses is giving instructions for a special case: someone is found dead in the countryside and no one knows who killed him. The elders of the nearest town would carry out a ritual with a young cow and declare that they were innocent. Then they would pray in this way. This shows that God takes human life seriously, even when no guilty person is known.

For today: let us not be indifferent to injustice. Even if we have not done the harm, we can pray, seek the truth, and work to protect life. And we can rest in the fact that God forgives.
exp.20:9:
This verse begins a law about war. It says that when Israel goes out to fight against its enemies, and God gives them the victory, and they take prisoners, they must follow certain rules.

Moses speaks to the people in Deuteronomy, shortly before they enter the promised land. He reviews God's law for their life there. This verse opens a rule that protects a captive woman, since it limits what a soldier could do with her. It was a law given in an ancient and harsh world, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: even when we have power over others, God calls us to act with respect, limits, and justice, never with abuse.
exp.20:10:
This verse continues the previous sentence: when Israel wins a war and takes prisoners, and a man sees among them a beautiful woman, desires her, and wants to marry her. "Desire" here means wanting or being drawn to someone. The verse only describes the situation; what must be done comes afterward.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. This law regulates a situation of war in a very harsh ancient world. It sets limits: the woman must be brought into the home, have a month of mourning for her family, and only after that may she be married. Some readers see here a protection for her; others point out that even so it reflects a culture very different from our own.

For today: even when desire is strong, God calls us to restraint, to respect the dignity of the other person, and not to treat her as an object. Before acting, one must give time and think with justice and compassion.
exp.20:11:
