The verse says that the soldier was to bring the captive woman to his house, and that she would shave her head and trim her nails. The word "shave" here means to scrape off or shave the hair from the head. The Bible does not explain the meaning of these gestures: some see them as a sign of mourning, others as a rite of separation from her former life, and others as a way of leaving behind her status as a captive. There is no single certain interpretation.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law regulates a situation of war, which was common in that time, and sets limits to protect the woman: it gives her a month to mourn her family, forbids selling her, and protects her from abuse. It does not approve of war or violence, but rather restrains what would otherwise be cruel treatment.

Today we can learn that God cares about protecting the most vulnerable. If we have power over someone, we should use it with respect, patience, and compassion.
exp.20:12:
She was to take off the clothes she wore when she was captured, and live in the Israelite's house. There she would have one full month to mourn her father and mother. After that month, the man could marry her.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law regulated war in a very harsh world, where captive women were highly exposed to abuse. It required waiting, acknowledging her grief, and giving her a protected status. Interpreters debate how much this limited the customs of its time, but the text shows an intention to curb abuse.

For today: do not act on impulse toward someone who has less power than you. Give them time, respect, and space for their grief. God cares about the vulnerable, and we too should do the same.
exp.20:14:
This verse describes a specific case: a man has two wives, one he loves more and the other he holds in less favor, meaning he cares for her less or treats her with less affection. Both bear him children, and the firstborn son is the child of the wife he cares for less.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. The Bible does not approve of having several wives here; it simply regulates a situation that already existed and protects the most vulnerable. The law prevents a father's affection from taking away the firstborn son's rights of inheritance.

For today: justice must not depend on our likes and dislikes. In the family, at work, or in the church, God calls us to treat everyone fairly, even those we like less.
exp.20:17:
This verse describes a son who is "stubborn and rebellious": someone set against all authority, who resists being guided. It is not a passing mistake. His parents have already spoken to him and corrected him, and still he does not obey.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and explains how to live as a just community. This case comes after a law about inheritance, which protected the rights of the firstborn. The verses that follow show that parents did not decide alone: they brought the case before the elders. This limited the father's power. Scholars debate how this law was applied in practice.

For today: correction in the family requires patience, consistency, and also the support of a wise community. If you care for children or young people, seek help rather than acting in anger.
exp.20:18:
The verse says that the parents of the rebellious son were to bring him before the elders of the city. The elders were the leaders who judged cases. The gate of the city was the public place where legal matters were handled.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law was not about a mischievous child, but about a son who, even after being corrected, remained in total rebellion. The parents could not decide alone: the case was public and required a judgment. Scholars debate how many times it was actually applied in practice, and we do not know for certain.

For today: when a problem in the family overwhelms us, we do not carry it alone or hide it. Seeking the counsel of wise and mature leaders, with humility and patience, is always a good path.
exp.20:20:
The verse says that the men of the city would stone the rebellious son until he died. In this way the evil would be taken away from the midst of the community, that is, the wickedness would be removed from among the people. All Israel would hear of it and would fear, that is, have a serious respect for the law and for the authority of parents.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. This law refers to a stubborn son, meaning one who is obstinate and rebellious beyond remedy, who refuses all correction. It was not a matter of a mischievous child: the parents themselves brought him before the elders, and scholars debate how often it was applied. The Bible does not record a single case.

Today we do not apply this penalty, since Jesus calls us to grace and forgiveness. But the teaching remains: the family needs respect and loving correction, and we must take persistent rebellion seriously, seeking help and praying for restoration.
exp.21:0:
This verse says that if you see your brother's ox or sheep has gone astray, you must not pretend you didn't see it and simply walk away. The phrase about turning away from them means setting yourself apart from them, washing your hands of them. And the phrase about bringing them back means that without fail you must return them to him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and explains how to live as God's community. Animals were the livelihood of a family, so losing them was a serious blow. The law asks people to care for their neighbor's property, even if he lives far away or you don't know him.

For today: if you find something that isn't yours, such as a wallet, a phone, or money, make an effort to find its owner and return it. Loving your neighbor includes caring for what is his, even when no one sees you or requires it of you.
exp.21:2:
This verse says that the same rule given for the lost ox and sheep also applies to the donkey, to clothing, and to anything else that your brother loses and you find. The phrase about not being able to pull away means that you cannot pretend you did not see it or look the other way. You must help return it.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel, near the time they will enter the promised land, and explaining how to live as God's people. Here "brother" refers to a fellow Israelite. The law protects the property of one's neighbor and shapes a community where no one ignores another's need. The instructions that follow, about the fallen donkey, belong to the same line of thought.

For today: if you find something that is not yours, such as a wallet, a cell phone, or a set of keys, make a real effort to return it. Loving your neighbor includes caring for what belongs to them, even when no one is watching.
exp.21:3:
It says that if you see your brother's donkey or ox fallen down on the road, you must not pretend you did not see it or hide yourself from them. On the contrary, you must help him lift them up again. The word "donkey" here refers to the animal, and "brother" refers to another Israelite, your neighbor.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, explaining how to live as God's people. These animals were the livelihood of a family, so helping was a way of caring for their life. The previous verse asks you to return what has been lost; this one adds that it is not enough to avoid doing harm, you must also act. Some see here a principle that goes beyond animals.

Today, when you see someone in trouble, like a neighbor with a broken-down car or a coworker with too much work, do not look the other way. Offer your concrete help, even if it costs you time or effort.
exp.21:5:
If someone comes across a bird's nest along the way, in a tree or on the ground, with young birds or eggs and the mother sitting on them, they must not take the mother together with her young. According to the next verse, the person could let the mother go and take the young birds.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and explains how to live according to God's law. This rule appears among commands about helping one's neighbor and protecting life. It shows that God also cares for animals, and that what creation provides should be used without abuse. The text promises well-being and a long life to those who obey; some see in it a call to compassion and to thinking about the future.

For today: make use of what God gives you with respect and moderation, without abusing it or destroying its source. Take care of what sustains you, whether it is your work, nature, or your relationships.
exp.21:7:
This verse commands that when a new house is built, a low wall or railing (a parapet) be placed around the flat roof, the terrace of the house. The reason is to prevent someone from falling and dying, and so that the house does not carry guilt for a death that could have been prevented.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In those times houses usually had flat roofs, and people used them to rest, work, and gather. The laws near this one deal with caring for life and with order in everyday living. This law shows that God values life and expects responsibility.

For today: think of a risk you could prevent in your home, your work, or your church, such as a loose stair, damaged electrical wiring, or a place without protection for children. Fix it in time. Caring for the safety of others is also a way of loving your neighbor.
exp.21:8:
It says that an Israelite was not to sow other seeds in the middle of his vineyard. The source's quoted phrases are not to be carried over, so the verse of their meaning is rendered as: to be spoiled or set apart for another use, and the whole of what was sown together with the fruit of the vineyard.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and gives them laws to live as God's people. This command goes together with others about not mixing things, such as different kinds of animals or different kinds of cloth. Scholars do not fully agree on the reason: it may teach order, purity, and separation for God.

For today: seek not to divide your heart. Put God first, and take care that other priorities do not choke out the good that He wants to grow in you.
exp.21:10:
This verse forbids wearing a garment made from a mixture of wool and linen woven together.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, reminding them of God's laws. This command appears alongside others about not mixing seeds or different kinds of animals. Many believe it taught Israel to live separate and orderly as God's people. Others think it guarded against pagan customs. The Bible does not explain this clearly, so it cannot be stated with certainty.

For today: although Christians are not under this law about clothing, we can learn to ask ourselves whether in our lives we are mixing faith in God with things that weaken it, and to seek a whole heart, devoted to Him.
exp.21:11:
This verse says that the people of Israel were to put tassels or fringes on the four corners of the cloak they wrapped themselves in. "Corners" means the corners or edges, and fringes are hanging threads.

Moses speaks to God's people before they enter the promised land, giving them instructions for living as a set-apart people. The verse sits among laws about keeping different things separate and about everyday life. Numbers 15:37-41 explains the purpose: the tassels helped people remember the Lord's commandments. Other details about how they were used are interpreted in different ways.

For today: God is interested in the ordinary and wants us to remember him in simple things. We can choose a small habit, such as praying as we get dressed or reading a verse as we leave the house, that reminds us to obey him throughout the day.
exp.21:15:
Here the young woman's father speaks before the elders of the city. He says he gave his daughter to this man as his wife, and that now the man hates her, meaning he no longer wants her.

The setting is a public hearing at the city gate, where legal matters were settled. A husband had falsely accused his wife of not being a virgin in order to get rid of her. Her parents defend their daughter by presenting the evidence. The law protected the woman, who was vulnerable, and punished the man who slandered her. The details of the proof (the cloth) are understood in different ways among scholars.

For today: God takes truth and the good name of people seriously. Today we can guard our words, not make up accusations or damage anyone's reputation, and defend with courage someone who is treated unjustly.
exp.21:18:
It says that if a husband falsely accuses his wife of not having been a virgin and her parents prove the opposite, the man receives a punishment. He must pay one hundred pieces of silver (coins by weight) to her father. Next, he must keep her as his wife, and he may never divorce her.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law protected the woman and her family from false accusations that damaged her honor and her future. It obliged the husband to answer for his words. The text that follows deals with the opposite case, which is harsh, and it has been interpreted in several ways.

For today: our words can wound or protect others. Before accusing someone, let us seek the truth and take responsibility for what we say.
exp.21:19:
This verse continues a legal case. A husband accuses his newly married wife of not having been a virgin. The case is being discussed here: what would happen if the accusation were true and no proof of virginity were found.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, reminding them of the laws that would govern their lives in the promised land. This law was meant to restrain false accusations, since it punished the man who slandered without cause. It also reflected how seriously Israel regarded the marriage covenant and purity. The penalty was harsh, typical of that time and culture. Some scholars debate how it was applied and what kinds of evidence were accepted.

Today we learn that accusing someone requires truth and responsibility. Before speaking ill of another person, let us think about the harm our words can cause. Let us guard our words and always seek justice with mercy.
exp.21:21:
This verse says that if a man was found lying with a married woman, both the man and the woman were to die. The phrase about the wrongdoing being found out describes being caught in the act, and "lying with" means having sexual relations. The phrase about putting away evil from Israel speaks of cleansing the people from a serious wrong.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and he reminds them of the laws of their covenant with God. In that time marriage was a sacred covenant, and the whole community cared for its holiness. The law treats both the man and the woman equally, without favoring either one. Christians understand that Christ fulfilled the law and that today it is not applied in this way.

For today: this text reminds us that faithfulness in marriage is something very serious to God. Take care with your promises, avoid situations that tempt you, and if you have failed, seek God's forgiveness and reconciliation.
exp.22:3:
This verse gives the reason why the Ammonites and Moabites were not allowed to enter the congregation of the LORD. It says that they did not come out to meet Israel with bread and water when they came out of Egypt, and that Moab hired Balaam, the son of Beor, from Pethor in Mesopotamia, to curse the people. "Hired" means paid for, in exchange for payment.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, now close to the promised land, and reminds them of laws for living as God's people. The texts say that it was Moab who hired Balaam (Numbers 22). Scholars discuss how this restriction was applied, and later Ruth, a Moabite woman, was accepted and became an ancestor of David.

For today: hospitality matters to God, and hostility toward others has consequences. We can generously help someone who is on the way, without doing harm or taking advantage of anyone.
exp.22:5:
God tells Israel not to seek the peace or the prosperity of the Ammonites and the Moabites. The word "seek" here means to look out for, or to work toward. "Prosperity" is the word for good, which means their wellbeing and success. The point is not to make alliances with them or to help them grow strong, and this applies forever.

Moses is speaking to the people before they enter the promised land. He explains that these nations did not give them bread or water on the road, and that they hired Balaam to curse them. God turned that curse into a blessing. This is a rule for politics and for the nation, not a command of personal hatred. The verses that follow ask them not to despise the Edomite or the Egyptian.

For today: learn to be hospitable toward someone in need. And do not use this text to justify resentment; Jesus asks us to love our enemies and to pray for them.
exp.22:13:
This verse says that God walks in the middle of Israel's camp to protect them and to give them victory over their enemies. For this reason the camp had to be holy, meaning set apart and clean. That way God would not see anything unclean in them and would not turn away from them.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He is giving instructions for when they go out to war. The verse before this one commands them to dig a hole outside the camp to cover their waste. It was a rule of order and of respect for God's presence; it also clearly helped health, although the text emphasizes the spiritual reason.

For today: God wants to dwell in the middle of his people and in our daily life. Ask yourself what small or hidden mess you should clean up, such as a habit, an attitude or a debt, so that you can live with more reverence and closeness to God.
exp.22:15:
This verse says that a servant who runs away from his master and arrives among Israel may stay and live among them. He may choose the town and the place where he feels it is best for him.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them laws to live as a holy people, because God is present among them. Many understand this to refer to a slave who escapes from a foreign land, although the text gives no further details. Either way, it shows God's care for the vulnerable.

For today: let us be a safe refuge for anyone fleeing oppression or abuse. We can welcome, listen to, and help those who suffer, without taking advantage of their need.
exp.22:18:
It says that an Israelite was not to charge another Israelite any "interest" on what he lent. That is, no extra gain on the loan. This applied to money, food, or anything else that was commonly lent at a profit.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of God's laws. Loans in that time were usually meant to help a brother in need, not to make a business deal. That is why God asked for compassion and not for taking advantage of the poor. The next verse permits charging interest to a foreigner, and promises blessing to whoever obeys.

For today: when someone in your family, church, or close circle goes through a hard time, help them generously and without seeking to profit from it. Lend with their good in mind, not your own gain.
exp.22:19:
It says that a foreigner could be charged interest on a loan, but an Israelite brother could not. The reason given is that God would bless their work in the land they were about to possess.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He gives them laws for living as God's community. Lending to a poor brother was a way of helping him, not of profiting from his need. With the foreigner, who often borrowed or traded for business, the rule was different. Some understand this as a difference in economic situation, not in the worth of the people.

For today: when someone in your family or your church is in a difficult spot, help them with generosity and without taking advantage of their need.
exp.22:20:
If someone makes a solemn promise to God, they should not delay in keeping it. Fulfilling what was promised means carrying it out. God will require it, and to put it off or fail to keep it would be sin.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He repeats God's law for their life together in community. Vows were voluntary offerings or commitments made to God. No one was required to make them, but once spoken, they had to be kept seriously, as the following verses show.

For today: think before you promise something to God or to others. If you have already promised something, such as serving, helping, or giving, keep it without leaving it for later. And if you cannot keep it, pray and seek counsel with humility.
exp.23:0:
Here is what the verse says about Deuteronomy 24:1. It describes a man who takes a wife, and then she finds no favor in his eyes because he has found some uncleanness in her. In that case he is to write her a bill of divorcement, giving her a formal written document of divorce. He places it in her hand and sends her out of his house.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law does not command or approve divorce; it regulates it, to bring order and to protect the woman with a written document. What exactly the uncleanness was has been interpreted in various ways, and it is not known for certain. Jesus explained that Moses permitted this because of the hardness of the people's hearts (Matthew 19:8).

Today, this reminds us that marriage is serious, and that vulnerable people deserve respect and protection. Let us seek help, dialogue, and counsel before breaking a covenant.
exp.23:2:
This verse describes a second case within the same situation. The second husband comes to hate the woman, gives her a certificate of divorce, puts it into her hand, and sends her out of his house. Or else, that second husband dies. "Hate" here means to stop loving or to reject. The "certificate of divorce" is the document of divorce.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law does not command divorce; it regulates a practice that already existed, in order to set limits and give the woman legal protection. The verses that follow forbid the first husband to marry her again. Jesus later explained that God did not intend divorce from the beginning (Matthew 19:8).

For today: let us take marriage seriously and not lightly. Let us care for our spouse with respect, and if there are wounds or separations, let us seek the grace and wisdom of God.
exp.23:5:
This verse forbids a creditor from taking the lower or the upper millstone as a pledge from his debtor. The millstone was the stone used to grind grain into flour for bread. A pledge is an object left as security for a loan. And the millstone, whether the lower or the upper one, was essential, because without it the family could not prepare its food. That is why the verse says that taking it would be taking a man's life as a pledge.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel and passes on God's laws before they enter the promised land. The verses nearby aim to protect people: the wife, the newlywed, the brother who could be kidnapped. God wants a society where no one uses their advantage to harm another.

For today: if you lend money or collect a debt, do not demand what the other person needs to survive and work. Seek to be fair without taking away anyone's livelihood or dignity.
exp.23:9:
It says that if you lend something to another person, you may not enter their house to choose and take what they will give you as security.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of God's laws for living together in community. This rule protected the dignity and privacy of the person in financial trouble. The lender had to wait outside, and the debtor chose what to hand over.

For today: when someone owes you something or needs help, treat them with respect. Do not use your position to pressure them or to intrude on their privacy. Ask for what is fair, but always protect the dignity of the other person.
exp.24:3:
It says that when the ox is treading out the grain, that is, stepping on the grain to separate it from the straw, it must not be fitted with a muzzle. A muzzle is a piece placed over the animal's mouth so that it cannot eat. In this way, the ox could eat some of the grain while it worked.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in his final addresses before they enter the promised land. The laws nearby deal with justice and dignified treatment: even the person being punished was to have his dignity protected, and the widow was given protection. This rule shows that this compassion extended to animals as well. Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 9:9 and 1 Timothy 5:18 to teach that the one who works deserves to be supported.

Today we can pay those who work for us with justice and generosity, and support with gratitude those who serve us in teaching the Word. The one who works deserves to benefit from his labor.
exp.24:4:
This verse says that if two brothers live together (in the same land or family) and one dies without leaving a son, his widow must not marry someone from outside the family. His brother-in-law must marry her and fulfill toward her the duty of a close relative. This is called levirate marriage.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law protected the widow, who could be left without support, and cared for the name and inheritance of the family. The verses that follow explain that the first son would carry on the name of the dead man.

For today: God cares for those who are vulnerable. We can ask ourselves who near us needs help, such as a widow or a family in need, and help them with responsibility and respect.
exp.24:6:
This verse speaks of a man who refuses to marry his brother's widow. In that case, she was to go up to the city gate, where the elders gathered, and bring her complaint. Raising up a name for the dead brother meant giving continuity to his name through a son. The duty of family meant carrying out the obligation owed to a brother's household.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law, known as levirate marriage, protected childless widows and kept a family's inheritance and name from disappearing. The city gate was the place where legal matters were settled.

For today: God cares for the vulnerable, such as widows. We can fulfill our family responsibilities and generously help those who have been left alone or need support.
exp.24:8:
The text says that if a man refuses to marry his brother's widow, she will come before the elders of the town. She will take off his sandal from his foot, spit in his face, and declare that this is what is done to the man who will not build up his brother's house.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel and explains the law of levirate marriage. If a brother died without children, the other brother was to marry the widow so that the name and inheritance of the deceased would not be lost. If the brother-in-law refused, this public act shamed him and protected the widow. Scholars understand the gesture as a sign of giving up a family right or duty.

Today we do not practice this rite, but we learn that God cares for the vulnerable, such as widows. We can ask ourselves whom we should care for and not abandon: taking on our family and community obligations with responsibility and compassion.
exp.24:12:
It says we must not carry two different weights in our bag, one heavier and one lighter. In that time, merchants weighed metal or goods using stones as weights. The stone used to measure weight is what the verse calls a weight, so the word in the verse is the one to look at. Having two was a way of cheating: one for buying and another for selling.

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of God's laws for living in justice. The verse before this one deals with another matter, and scholars explain it in several ways. Here the subject changes to honesty in business. God promises blessing to those who act with justice.

Today we can apply this by being honest with money: charging what is fair, paying on time, and not deceiving in prices, accounts, or work, even when no one is watching.
exp.24:13:
This verse says that in your house you must not keep two different measures: one large and one small. The measure for grain and dry goods was a standard unit. Having two meant you could cheat: using the large one to buy and the small one to sell.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and he gives them laws for living justly. The verse before this one also forbids having false weights in your bag. Then it says that God regards fraud as detestable. Merchants of that time depended on weights and measures, and it was easy to take advantage of others.

For today: be honest in what you give and in what you charge. Whether in your work, your business, or your dealings, do not use two measures. Treat others as you would want to be treated.
exp.24:16:
It says that the people of Israel were to remember what Amalek did to them as they walked toward freedom, when they came out of Egypt. "Remember" is a command not to forget that injustice.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. Just before this, he speaks about using honest weights and measures. Then he recalls Amalek, who attacked from behind those who were weak and tired, without fearing God (Exodus 17). Some see a contrast: justice against the abuse of the strong over the weak.

For today: let us remember that God cares about the vulnerable. Let us be honest in our daily lives and take care of those who are tired and lagging behind us, rather than taking advantage of their weakness.
exp.24:17:
It says that Amalek came out to meet Israel on the way and attacked from behind the weakest, the stragglers at the back of the group, when the people were exhausted. The sentence about the rear guard being broken into means he destroyed or scattered those at the end of the line. Those who were weak or worn out are the ones meant. And the phrase about not fearing God means he showed no respect for God or for God's justice.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He asks them to remember this abuse, which happened after leaving Egypt (Exodus 17). He teaches them that God cares for the vulnerable and that cruelty against them is serious in God's sight.

Today we can care for those who are at the back: people who are tired, elderly, sick, or discouraged. One practical step is to call or visit someone this week who is going through a hard time, and never to take advantage of another person's weakness.
exp.25:10:
This verse says that the people were to rejoice in all the good things that God had given to them and to their household. It was not a solitary joy: the Levite and the foreigner who lived among them also took part. The phrase about God having given is rendered in plain modern English here, so the reader can follow the meaning directly from the verse as it stands.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains how to present the firstfruits, that is, the first part of the harvest, as an act of gratitude. The Levites had no land of their own, and foreigners were often vulnerable, so God includes them in the celebration.

For today: before enjoying your blessings, give thanks to God, and think about whom you can invite to share them. A meal, a helping hand, or time spent together can turn your gratitude into shared joy.
exp.25:12:
He says that the Israelite was to come before God and declare that he had already set apart from his house the holy portion of the tithe. He had given it to the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan and the widow, just as God had commanded.

It speaks of an Israelite who, in the third year, the year of the tithe, had shared his harvest with those in need. Before God he made a declaration of a clear conscience: he had obeyed and had not forgotten his commands. The Levites had no land of their own, and the other three groups were vulnerable.

For today: generosity is part of obedience to God, not an extra. We can ask ourselves honestly before Him whom I can help with what I have. And we can give with joy, without boasting, because everything comes from His hand.
exp.25:13:
This verse is part of a declaration that the Israelite made before God. He says that he did not misuse the sacred tithe: he did not eat from it while in mourning, he did not take any of it while unclean according to the law, and he did not spend any of it on offerings for the dead. He concludes that he obeyed God in everything God commanded.

The speaker is an Israelite who, every three years, gave the tithe to the Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows. Then he declared this before God. It was not boasting, but an honest account. Scholars explain the practices with the dead that are mentioned in various ways, but the general sense is that what was set apart for God was not to be mixed with what was unclean or with funeral rites.

For today: what we dedicate to God and to those in need deserves care and sincerity. We can ask ourselves whether we give with integrity, and obey with a grateful heart, not for appearance.
exp.25:14:
This verse is a prayer. The Israelite asks God to look down from his holy dwelling place, that is, from heaven, where He lives. He pleads that God would bless His people and the land He gave them, just as He promised them with an oath to their fathers. The phrase about the land flowing with milk and honey is a way of saying that the land was fertile and abundant.

A cruel-hearted person would not speak this way, but the speaker here is an Israelite who has brought the tithe of the third year before God. He has already declared that he gave it to the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow, and that he obeyed God's commands. Now, with a clear conscience, he asks for God's blessing. He does not demand a payment; he trusts in the promise God made.

For today: Obeying God and caring for those in need go hand in hand with praying with confidence. We can ask Him for His blessing, knowing that He keeps what He promises, and show our gratitude by sharing with those who have less.
exp.25:17:
This verse says that God chose Israel that day to be his special people, just as he had promised. That choosing had a purpose: that the people would obey all his commandments.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant: Israel declares that the Lord is their God, and God declares that Israel is his people. It is like a mutual commitment, and obedience was the response to his love and his care.

For today: God values us and calls us his own, and that gives us identity and security. We can respond with sincere obedience, not out of fear, but out of gratitude. Today you can choose one concrete action that honors God.
exp.26:0:
This verse says that Moses, together with the elders of Israel, gave a command to the people. He asked them to keep all the commandments that he was giving them that day. In this verse, "commanded" is the word for giving a firm order. It is interesting that here Moses does not speak alone, but is accompanied by the leaders of the people.

Moses is speaking almost at the end of his life, close to the entrance to the promised land. The people are preparing to cross the Jordan, and Moses reminds them that their life there must be guided by the law of God. The elders accompany him as witnesses and support, showing that this was a commitment of the whole community.

For today: obeying God is not only something personal; it is also strengthened in community. Seek out people of faith who encourage you to live out the Word with constancy, and encourage them too.
exp.26:5:
It says the altar for the Lord was to be made of whole stones, that is, complete, just as they were found, without being dressed or cut. On that altar the people would offer a burnt offering, that is, a sacrifice that was burned up entirely in honor of God. "The Lord" is the name of God, and "offer" means to present.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before his death. He tells them what they must do when they cross the Jordan and enter the promised land: build an altar on Mount Ebal and write the law. It was a way of renewing their commitment to God. Scholars explain in various ways why iron was not used; one common idea is that it emphasized that worship did not depend on human ingenuity.

For today: come near to God with sincerity and simplicity, without ornaments or pretense. He looks for a devoted heart, not a perfect image.
exp.26:6:
It says that, after offering the burnt offering, Israel was to present peace offerings, eat right there with their families, and rejoice before God. The peace offerings are sacrifices of fellowship or thanksgiving, of which the people could eat.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He tells them that, on crossing the Jordan, they are to build an altar on Mount Ebal, using uncut stones, and write down the law. That moment would be a renewal of the covenant: God was making them his people, and their response included dedication, gratitude, and celebration.

For today: life with God is not only duty, it is also joy. Make your gratitude something concrete: share a meal with your family or your church, thank God out loud for what he has done, and rejoice freely in his presence.
exp.26:11:
It says that, after crossing the Jordan, six tribes would stand on Mount Gerizim to pronounce a blessing over the people: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph (which includes Ephraim and Manasseh), and Benjamin.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before his death, when Israel is about to enter the promised land. He wants them, upon arriving, to renew their covenant with God in a public ceremony. The other six tribes would stand on Mount Ebal, facing them. Blessing and curse were meant to remind them that obeying or disobeying God brings real consequences.

For today: obedience to God is not a private matter, but something lived out and remembered in community. You could gather with other believers to read the Bible, encourage one another, and remember that God keeps his promises to those who trust in him.
exp.26:20:
This verse declares under a curse anyone who has sexual relations with an animal. The phrase that the old wording used for this act is not one your verse uses, so I will simply describe it. The people would answer together in agreement with the curse, meaning they affirmed it aloud and accepted it as true.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. A ceremony is commanded on Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, where the people would hear curses and accept them out loud. This sin also appears in other laws of Israel (Exodus 22:19; Leviticus 18:23). These are sins that often happened in secret, and God sees them.

For today: God calls us to live in purity even in what is hidden. We can ask him for help to guard what we look at, think, and do when no one sees us.
exp.27:0:
It says that if the people listen carefully to God's voice, not only hearing it but putting it into practice by obeying all his commandments, God will place them in a high position, that is, of honor and blessing, above the other nations.

Moses speaks to Israel on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God and presents the blessings that would come from obedience. Later in the chapter he also warns of the consequences of disobedience.

For today: listening to God is not only knowing what he says, but deciding to do it. Today you can choose one simple command from the Bible, such as forgiving or being honest, and put it into practice faithfully, trusting that God cares for those who obey him.
exp.27:1:
This verse promises that God's blessings will come upon his people and "overtake" them, as if they were chasing and catching up with them along the way. The condition is to listen closely to the voice of the Lord, which in biblical language means to listen and obey.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they obey him, they will live under his care. These blessings were given to Israel as a nation, within that specific covenant.

For today: God does not ask for obedience in order to control us, but to guide us toward a good life. Today you can choose one concrete action that God asks of you, such as forgiving or being honest, and do it with trust in his care, without using obedience as a formula to get things.
exp.27:2:
It says that God's blessing would reach all the people, both in the city and in the field. That is, in the work of trade and in the work of the land, in public life and in everyday life. "Blessed" means favored and cared for by God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they listened to his voice and obeyed, they would receive his favor. These blessings were tied to the life of Israel as a nation under that covenant, and so Christians read them carefully, without taking them as automatic promises.

Today we can learn that God wants to be Lord of every area of our lives. Ask yourself in which place, whether work, home, or school, you need to listen to him and obey him more.
exp.27:3:
This verse says that God would bless everything that gave life and provision to the people: their children (the fruit of the body), their beasts of burden and work (the animals used to carry loads and to plow), and their cows and sheep, that is, the livestock that gave them food, clothing and labor. The calves are the young ones born to the herd.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they listen to his voice and obey him, blessings would come upon their family, their work and their fields. It was a promise to Israel within that covenant, and not an automatic guarantee for every person today.

For today: recognize that family, work and provision are gifts from God. Thank him today for something concrete in your home or your work, and ask him to help you listen to him and live with gratitude.
exp.27:6:
It says that God will cause the enemies who attack Israel to be completely defeated. The phrase about the enemies being broken up is explained as meaning they will be beaten and thrown into disorder. They come against the people by one road, well organized, but they flee by seven, that is, in total confusion. "Seven" here expresses something complete.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings of the covenant if they obey God. This promise was given to Israel as a nation, within that covenant, and it is not an automatic guarantee of victory in every conflict.

Today we can learn that God cares for his people and that obedience is the way to live trusting in him. In the face of life's fears and opposition, we can pray, keep doing what is right, and rest in the knowledge that God is our refuge.
exp.27:8:
This verse says that God will establish Israel as his people set apart for himself, just as he promised with an oath. The verse's word "establish" means that he will make them firm and secure. "Holy" means set apart for God. This holds when the people keep his commandments and live according to his ways.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He presents the blessings of the covenant: if they obey, God will protect them, make them prosper, and the other nations will see that they belong to him. This promise rests on the oath God made to their fathers.

For today: obedience is not a burden but the path to living as God's people. Today you can choose one concrete step of obedience, such as forgiving, being honest, or setting aside time for prayer, trusting that God is faithful to his promises.
exp.27:11:
It says that God will open the heavens like a good and full storehouse, to send rain on the land of Israel at the right time, and to bless all the work of their hands. Because of this, they will have more than enough and will be able to lend to many nations without needing to borrow.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: the blessings come within a promise made to that nation, and they depend on obeying Him and not following other gods. For a people of farmers, rain was life.

For today: although this promise was given to Israel and does not guarantee wealth to every believer, it does teach us that everything we have comes from God. Work with effort, be thankful for what you receive, and live generously, trusting that God cares for you.
exp.27:13:
This verse calls for not turning aside from what God commanded, neither to the right hand nor to the left. The phrase about turning to the right or to the left means turning in any direction, and the other gods are the gods of other peoples. Serving them means worshiping them and obeying them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the blessings that would come if they kept the covenant with God. This verse closes that list of blessings, and right after it Moses warns of the consequences of disobedience. The central idea is exclusive faithfulness to God.

For today: ask yourself what things compete for first place in your heart, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Choose one concrete decision today in which you will put God first, and stay firm without turning aside.
exp.27:14:
This verse says that if the people do not listen to the voice of God, nor make an effort to keep all his commandments and laws, all the curses listed below will come upon them and overtake them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: obeying him would bring blessing, and turning away from him would bring painful consequences. He says this so that they will choose the right path with seriousness.

For today: obedience to God is not a burden, but a way of caring for our lives. Today, as Christians, we trust that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law (Galatians 3:13). Even so, we can ask ourselves: in what area do I need to listen to God more carefully and obey him with love?
exp.27:18:
It says the curse will reach the person in everything they do. The phrase "when you come in" and "when you go out" is an old way of speaking about all of daily life: coming and going, beginning and ending, working and resting. Nothing would be left outside. Being "cursed" means that God withdraws his blessing.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they obey, blessing will come; if they abandon it, serious consequences will follow. These words are a serious warning addressed to Israel, not a random threat.

For today: God cares for every part of our lives, not only the religious moments. We can ask ourselves whether we are including him in everyday things, such as work, home and decisions. Christians believe that Christ bore the curse for us (Galatians 3:13), so we can return to God with confidence.
exp.27:19:
This verse says that if the people abandon God, cursing, confusion, and failure will come upon them in everything they set out to do.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: obeying him would bring blessing, and turning away from him would bring serious consequences. These words are a solemn warning, given so that the people will choose the path of life.

Today we can remember that turning away from God is never a small matter. Instead of living in fear, we can honestly examine our hearts, return to him quickly when we go astray, and trust that his grace receives us when we repent.
exp.27:23:
What it says: Instead of rain, God would send dust and ash upon the land of Israel, like sandstorms falling from the sky. This would be a sign of total drought. The phrase "until you are destroyed" means until the people are wiped out or left in ruins.

Context: Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the covenant with God: blessings if they obey and curses if they abandon it. A heaven that is bronze and an earth that is iron describe a drought without hope. These were serious warnings, given so that the people would choose the good path.

For today: God speaks to us clearly because He wants us to live well. Today we can take His voice seriously, return to Him when we stray, and trust in His mercy, which in Christ is offered to all who repent.
exp.27:28:
In it, it says that, as punishment, the person will walk around groping at midday, just like a blind person in the dark. Nothing they set out to do will go well. They will live oppressed and stripped of their possessions every day, and no one will come to rescue them. "Grope" means to feel with the hands to find the way, and "prosper" means to go well for someone.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings for obeying God and the curses for abandoning his covenant. This verse is part of the consequences of disobedience. It was a warning so that the people would recognize how much they needed God.

For today: when we live without asking for God's guidance, we can feel lost even in the midst of what seems clear. Take a moment each day to pray and ask him for direction before you decide.
exp.27:29:
It says that, as a punishment, the person would make important plans and others would enjoy the result. They would become engaged to be married, but another man would take his wife. They would build a house, but would not live in it. They would plant a vineyard, but would not gather its grapes.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings for obeying God and the curses for breaking the covenant. This verse is part of the curses: it describes the loss and frustration that would come if the people turned away from God and fell under the oppression of their enemies.

For today: do not place all your security in your plans, your work, or your achievements, because they can be lost. Seek God first and live with integrity, trusting that he gives the true foundation for your life and your family.
exp.27:30:
It says that if the people turn away from God, they will lose what they have worked hardest for. Their ox will be slain before their eyes, and they will not even be able to eat it. Their donkey will be taken away by force, that is, seized from them, and it will never come back. Their sheep will pass into the hands of their enemies, and no one will rescue them. It is a picture of total helplessness: seeing the loss and being unable to do anything about it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In this chapter he presents blessings for obeying the covenant and curses for disobeying it. These words are a serious warning, given in the hope that the people will choose faithfulness to God.

For today: do not place your security in what you have, since everything can be lost. Put your trust in God, be thankful for what He gives you, and live in a way that honors Him in everyday life.
exp.27:33:
It says that the people, seeing with their own eyes the tragedies that will come upon them, will be so distressed that they will lose their reason.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In this chapter he sets out the blessings for obeying God and the curses for abandoning his covenant. This verse is part of a serious warning: disobedience brings painful consequences, such as invasion, oppression, and the loss of what is loved.

For today: when suffering overwhelms us, we should not carry it alone. We can bring our pain to God in prayer and seek the support of trusted brothers and sisters, and professional help too if needed. Moreover, this text invites us to take seriously the way of God, who seeks our good.
exp.27:34:
It says that God would strike the one who disobeyed him with a painful, malignant sore or ulcer in the knees and legs, one that could not be cured. It would spread from the sole of the foot up to the top of the head.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings for keeping the covenant and the consequences for rejecting it. These curses are serious warnings, growing harsher as they go, which culminate in oppression and exile among foreign nations. Some scholars think the illness is literal, and others think it describes total suffering.

For today: do not read this text to frighten yourself or to judge someone who is suffering, for illness is not always punishment. Rather, take it as an invitation to take God's voice seriously and to return to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.27:35:
It says that if the people are disobedient, God will allow them to be taken, along with their king, to a nation unknown to them and their ancestors. There they will have to serve false gods made of wood and stone, that is, idols.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings for keeping the covenant and curses for abandoning it. This warning describes the consequences of turning away from the living God. Many understand it to relate to the later exiles of Israel and Judah, though the text itself gives no dates.

For today: whatever we put in place of God, such as money, success, or approval, ends up enslaving us. Today you can ask yourself what holds first place in your heart, and return to trusting God with simplicity.
exp.27:36:
It says that the people of Israel, if they turn away from God, will become an object of horror, a case that others point to as a warning, and a subject of mockery or talk among all the nations where God takes them.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. After describing the blessings of obedience, he sets out the consequences of rejecting the covenant. This warning includes exile, and it was not an empty threat: it was meant to make Israel take its commitment to God seriously. Later texts of the Old Testament show that Israel did indeed live through something like this.

For today: our lives speak of what we believe. We can ask ourselves whether our decisions reflect faithfulness to God. When we go astray, He calls us to return with humility, and He always offers forgiveness to those who repent.
exp.27:39:
It says the people will have olive trees throughout all their land, but they will not be able to use the oil to anoint themselves, because the olives will fall before their time. "Territory" means land or region. "Anoint" means to rub oil on oneself, something common for caring for the body and for celebrating. Having the trees and not enjoying the fruit.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the Promised Land. He presents blessings if they obey God and curses if they turn away from him. This verse is among the consequences of disobedience: labor without fruit, as happens with the sowing and the vineyard that surround it.

Today it reminds us that having things does not guarantee enjoying them. We can examine whether we live thankful to God and in obedience to him, trusting that the true blessing comes from his hand, not only from our effort.
exp.27:41:
It says that the locust, that is, the insect that comes in swarms and devours everything, will consume all the trees of your orchard and the crops of your field. The trees in the orchard are the fruit trees, and the produce of your land are the crops. All the farmer's work would be destroyed.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In this chapter he presents blessings if they obey God and curses if they abandon him. This verse is part of the warnings: disobedience would bring losses, and the covenant with God was something very serious.

For today: our harvests, work and savings are not secure on their own. We can labor with diligence, but we must also trust in God, not in what we produce. Today, ask yourself: where am I placing my security?
exp.27:43:
The foreigner who lives among the people will have more money and power than they do. He will lend, and they will have to borrow. To be "head" means to be on top, with authority; to be the "tail" means to fall behind, to end up in a position of dependence instead.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings if they obey God and curses if they abandon him. This verse is a warning within the covenant: disobedience would bring loss, debt, and dependence on others.

For today: this text should not be read as a condemnation of the poor or those in debt, since poverty has many causes. It does invite us to live with wisdom and to trust God, taking care with our decisions about money and asking him for his guidance every day.
exp.27:46:
This verse says that the people did not serve God with joy or gladness of heart, even though they had all things in abundance. The complaint is not that they failed to serve at all, but that they served without a grateful heart.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience. Here he names the root of the problem: a heart that, in the middle of plenty, forgets to give thanks to God.

For today: even if you keep your religious duties, ask yourself whether you do them with gratitude. Before asking God for something, take a few minutes to thank him for what you already have. In this way your service to God comes from joy and not from habit.
exp.27:50:
It says that the foreign enemy will eat up the harvests and the livestock of the people until they are left ruined. The new juice of the grape and the young of the cattle are things the verse is listing among what would be taken from them. Everything that sustained the life of the people would be taken away from them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings if they obey God and serious warnings if they turn away from him. This warning describes a cruel invasion. Many believe it was fulfilled in the falls of Israel and Judah, although some also connect it to other moments in history.

Today we can remember that the goods of this life are not a secure foundation. Harvests, work and savings can disappear. It is good to thank God for what we have, to manage it with humility, and to place our trust in him, not in our fortifications.
exp.27:53:
It says that even the gentlest and most refined man, used to a comfortable life, will become hard toward his own brother, his wife, and the children who remain to him. The words used for him describe someone raised in great comfort. His eye will be evil means he will look at others with selfishness and refuse to share, even with those closest to him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings for obeying God and the curses for abandoning his covenant. This passage describes the horror of an enemy siege, with extreme hunger, as the consequence of turning away from God.

For today: scarcity and fear can harden even the kindest people. We can ask God to guard our hearts and practice generosity now, so that anxiety does not make us selfish toward our family.
exp.27:63:
It says that if the people of Israel turn away from God, He will allow them to be scattered among all the nations, from one end of the earth to the other. There, in exile, they would end up worshiping false gods that neither they nor their ancestors knew, that is, idols of wood and stone. Scatter means to disperse or spread apart. Strangers means foreigners or people from other nations.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the Promised Land. He sets before them the blessings for obedience and the consequences for disobedience, as part of the covenant with God. It is a serious warning, given so that they will choose faithfulness. Later, Israel's history shows periods of exile, and scholars discuss how these relate to this passage.

For today: when we move away from God, something else takes His place. Ask yourself which things, such as money or success, receive your trust, and return to God with sincerity, for He welcomes those who come back.
exp.27:65:
Your life will seem to hang by a thread before you, as if it could fall at any moment. You will be afraid day and night, and you will have no assurance that you will go on living.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains the blessings of obeying God and the consequences of turning away from him. This passage describes the wearing toll of living far from God, scattered among the nations, as a result of breaking the covenant.

For today: when fear and uncertainty take away your peace, do not carry them alone. Pray, rest in the faithfulness of God, and seek to live close to him, because in Christ there is a peace that the world cannot give.
exp.27:67:
It says that God would bring the people back to Egypt on ships, by a route they had been told they would never travel again. There they would try to sell themselves as male and female slaves to their enemies, but no one would buy them. The word "return" here means going back. It is an image of total humiliation: not even as slaves would they have any value.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This closes a long list of the blessings and curses of the covenant. It is the final warning about what would happen if they abandoned God: they would lose their freedom and return to the place of their former slavery. Some scholars see figurative language here, and others see a prediction of actual exiles.

For today: turning away from God leads us back into bondage that He has already rescued us from. Today you can guard your relationship with Him, thanking Him for his deliverance and obeying Him every day.
exp.28:1:
Moses gathers all the people of Israel and reminds them of what they saw with their own eyes: the works of the Lord in Egypt against Pharaoh, his servants (his officials and attendants), and all his land.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, on the plains of Moab, before Israel enters the promised land. He is renewing the covenant with a new generation, one that was young when they left Egypt. He reminds them of their history so that they will obey God faithfully. The next verse shows that seeing miracles was not enough: a heart that understands is needed.

For today: take time to remember the times God has helped you, and thank him. Remembering what he has done strengthens trust and helps us obey him, and we can ask him for an attentive heart to understand it.
exp.28:2:
This verse says that Israel saw with their own eyes the great trials, that is, the hardships and judgments with which God acted in Egypt. They also saw the signs and the great wonders, that is, the miracles. The word "trials" here refers to mighty acts that showed who God is.

Moses speaks to the people in Moab, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them what God did to Pharaoh in order to encourage them to renew their covenant with Him. But the next verse shows something sad: although they had seen everything, they still had not truly understood. Seeing is not the same as comprehending.

For today: it is not enough to remember what God has done in your life; ask Him to give you understanding and a grateful heart, so that what you have experienced leads you to obey Him and trust Him more.
exp.28:3:
This verse says that, although the people saw many miracles, God had not yet given them a heart that understood, eyes that truly saw, or ears that really listened.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel on the plains of Moab, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of what God did in Egypt and along the way, in order to call them to be faithful to the covenant. Interpreters explain this phrase in different ways: as a complaint about their hardness, or as a reminder that deep understanding is a gift from God.

For today: it is not enough to see good things from God; we need to ask him humbly to open our hearts so that we may understand and obey what he has already shown us.
exp.28:5:
For forty years in the desert the people had no bread, wine, or strong drink, as they would have had in a normal life with crops and vineyards. The "strong drink" was a strong fermented beverage, different from wine. God sustained them in another way, with manna and water, so that they would know that he is the Lord, their God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel on the plains of Moab, close to entering the promised land. He reminds them of what God did: he cared for them, gave them clothing that did not wear out, and victories over Sihon and Og. He wants them not to forget and to be faithful to the covenant.

For today: when you go through times of scarcity or change, do not look only at what is missing. Look at how God has sustained you until now. Write down three ways he has cared for you, and give him thanks; this strengthens your trust in him.
exp.28:6:
This verse recalls that, when the people reached the east side of the Jordan, they faced two kings: Sihon, king of Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan. Both came out to fight against Israel, and the Israelites defeated them.

Moses speaks almost at the end of his life to a new generation about to enter the promised land. He reviews what they have lived through in the wilderness so that they see God cared for them and gave them victories. He wants them to renew their covenant with Him and obey Him.

For today: when you face a difficulty, remember the times God sustained you before. That grateful memory strengthens trust and encourages you to obey Him, without assuming that the victory depended only on your own strength.
exp.28:9:
It says that the whole people of Israel were gathered that day before God. Moses names the leaders: the chiefs of the tribes, the elders (experienced men who guided the people), the officers (those in charge of carrying out the orders), and all the men. "Before the Lord" means in his presence, as one who gives an account.

Moses speaks near the end of his life, on the plains of Moab. A new generation is about to enter the promised land. He reminds them of what God has done and calls them to renew the covenant, that is, the commitment of faithfulness between God and his people. The verses that follow add the children, the women, and the foreigners.

For today: faith is not only for the leaders. Every person, whatever their place, stands before God and is called to obey him. Today you might ask yourself: what concrete step of obedience can I take?
exp.28:10:
This verse continues the list of those who were present before God: the little ones, the wives, and the foreigners who lived among the people. It even mentions those who did the simplest tasks, such as cutting firewood and carrying water. The phrase about those who lived within the camp means that they lived inside the encampment.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God. What matters is that no one is left out: everyone, from the leaders to the most humble, is invited to enter into God's promise.

For today: God does not show partiality in his calling. We can ask ourselves whether in our church or family there is someone we treat as if they mattered less. Today you can reach out to that person, include them, and let them know they are also welcome before God.
exp.28:17:
This verse is a warning. Moses says that there might be among the people a man, a woman, a family, or a tribe whose heart turns away today from the Lord our God, to go and serve the gods of other nations. He compares that sin to a root that produces poison and wormwood, a plant with a very bitter taste.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in Moab, when he renews the covenant with God before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the idols they saw in Egypt and along the way. He wants no one to believe that they can be unfaithful in secret and still remain at peace.

For today: a small turning away of the heart, if we let it grow, can make a whole community bitter. It is wise to examine honestly which things compete with God in our hearts and to ask him for help in time, before they take root.
exp.28:19:
It says that if someone hears the warnings of the covenant and still reassures himself, thinking "nothing will happen to me, I can follow my own desires," the Lord will not forgive him. The phrase about the anger smoking means that his wrath will burn against him. The phrase about blotting out his name means erasing it, making it disappear. The word for jealousy describes the love of God that will not tolerate rivals.

Moses speaks to the people in Moab, when he renews the covenant before they enter the promised land. He warns them against idolatry and against a heart that turns away in secret. The problem here is not a fall caused by weakness, but the stubborn attitude of someone who despises the warning and believes he is safe.

For today: do not use God's grace as an excuse to keep doing what you know is wrong. If you feel your heart growing cold, return to God with humility and do it in time.
exp.28:21:
This verse says that future generations, meaning the children of the Israelites and also foreigners who come from distant lands, will see the condition of the land and will ask what happened. The word "plagues" refers to blows or punishments, and "sicknesses" refers to the wounded and ruined land.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel as he renews the covenant with God before they enter the promised land. He warns them that abandoning God to serve other gods would bring serious consequences, and that this ruin would serve as a witness to other nations.

For today: our decisions affect those who come after us. It is worth guarding our faithfulness to God, because our lives can encourage or discourage our children and those who watch us.
exp.28:22:
It says the land would be like a burned-out desert: full of brimstone and salt, where nothing can be sown, nothing bears fruit, and not even a blade of grass grows. It would be like Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboim, cities that God overthrew, that is, utterly destroyed and tore down, in his anger.

Moses speaks almost at the end of his life, renewing the covenant with the people before they enter the promised land. He warns them what the land would look like if they abandoned God and worshiped idols. Those who came later, even foreigners, would ask what happened, and the answer would be: they forsook the covenant of the Lord.

For today: God is serious when he warns us, but he does so so that we will be faithful to him. Today you can examine whether anything is taking God's place in your heart, and return to him sincerely. His mercy is always near to whoever repents.
exp.28:23:
This verse shows a question that all the nations will ask when they see the land of Israel destroyed. They will wonder why the Lord did something so harsh, and what such a great anger means.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel just before they enter the promised land, while he renews the covenant with them. He warns them what the judgment would be like if they turned away from God. The answer comes in the following verses: the land would be left in that state because they abandoned the covenant and served other gods. In other words, the warning is meant to make them think about this before they reach that point.

For today: spiritual decisions leave marks that others can see. It is worth examining what we give first place to, and returning quickly to God with humility, because he is patient and seeks to restore us.
exp.28:24:
This verse is the answer to a question. The nations ask why God left the land of Israel as a desert of sulfur and salt. The answer is clear: the people abandoned the covenant, that is, the solemn promise the Lord made with their fathers when he brought them out of Egypt.

Moses speaks to the people on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He warns them what would happen if they left God. He wants them to understand that the punishment would not be random, but the consequence of abandoning the one who rescued them and gave them his promise.

For today: remember what God has done for you and do not let it be forgotten. Spend a few minutes this week thanking him for a specific help he gave you, and let that memory keep you faithful to him in your daily decisions.
exp.28:26:
This verse says that God became very angry with the land of Israel and brought upon it all the curses that were written in the book of the law.

Moses is speaking to the people before they enter the promised land. He describes what the nations would say when they saw a ruined land: that the people had abandoned the covenant with God and served other gods. It is a warning so that they would not repeat that mistake. The verses that follow speak of exile as the consequence.

For today: God takes our faithfulness to him seriously. Examine whether anything has taken God's place in your heart, such as money, success, or comfort, and return to him with sincerity. His warning aims to protect us, and his grace always invites us to return.
exp.29:0:
This verse begins a promise. Moses says that the people of Israel will experience the blessings and the curses that God has set before them. If they end up far from their land, scattered among other nations, they will take these things to heart, meaning they will reflect honestly and remember God.

Moses speaks to the people in his final addresses, before they enter the promised land. He had already warned them that obedience would bring blessing and disobedience would bring consequences. Here he shows them that, even after failure, there is hope of restoration, as the next verse continues.

For today: when you make a mistake or feel far from God, do not stay in guilt or distraction. Stop, reflect with honesty, and return to Him, because God still welcomes whoever comes back.
exp.29:2:
This verse promises that God will bring back his people who were held captive.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that if they turn away from God, consequences will follow, but that if they acknowledge their wrong and return to him with all their heart, God will restore them. His promise rests on his mercy, not only on what they deserve.

For today: if you feel far from God because of your mistakes, do not think there is no way back. Return to him sincerely, and trust that his mercy remains open to receive you.
exp.29:3:
It says that even if the people of Israel were scattered to the farthest place imaginable, to the edge of the heavens, the far end of the horizon, the limit of the known world, God himself will seek them out and bring them back. The verse's language of gathering and fetching shows God as one who will personally go to rescue them.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He warns them that disobedience would bring exile, but he promises that if they turn back to God wholeheartedly, he will have mercy on them and restore them. It is a promise conditioned on repentance and rooted in God's faithfulness.

For today: if you feel far from God because of your mistakes or because of your circumstances, there is no distance he cannot cross. Return to him sincerely, trusting that he will receive you with mercy.
exp.29:4:
It says that God will bring his people back to the land that their ancestors had received as an inheritance. There they will take possession of it, God will do them good, and he will make them grow in number more than their fathers.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that, if they turn away from God and suffer exile, they can still return to him. The promise shows that God's mercy is greater than the people's failure. Then the text adds that God will change their hearts so that they love him.

For today: if you feel that you have drifted away, or that your situation can no longer be repaired, remember that God knows how to restore. Come to him with sincerity, trusting in his mercy, and let him be the one who heals your heart.
exp.29:7:
This verse says that the people of Israel will return to God, listen to his voice, and obey all his commandments.

Moses is speaking to the people before they enter the promised land. He has warned them that disobedience would bring punishment and exile, but here he promises restoration. What stands out is that God himself circumcises their hearts (v. 6), that is, he transforms them so that they can love him. Obedience appears as the fruit of God's work in them.

For today: if you have drifted away from God, returning is possible. Ask him to change your heart, and take one concrete step of obedience today, trusting that he sustains you.
exp.29:11:
This verse says that God's command is not in heaven, meaning it is not out of anyone's reach. No one has to wonder who will go up to get it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that if they turn back to God with all their heart, they should not think that his law is too hard or far away. God has already given it to them in writing, and it is within reach.

The apostle Paul quotes this passage in Romans 10:6-8, applying it to faith in Christ.

Today, you do not need to wait for an extraordinary experience to know God's will. His Word is within your reach. Read a passage every day, and put into practice today one thing you clearly understand.
exp.29:17:
Here Moses says with great seriousness: "I warn you today that you will surely perish." To declare solemnly means to make a formal statement of warning, and the phrase about perishing means that they would be destroyed. If they turn away from God, they will not live long in the land they are about to receive after crossing the Jordan.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of his life, just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God and sets before them two paths: obey and receive blessing, or serve other gods and suffer the consequences. It is a call to decide.
