For today: God invites us to choose life by trusting in Him. Today you can make a concrete decision, such as praying before acting or giving up something that pulls you away from God, remembering that He Himself is your life.
exp.29:18:
Moses says that heaven and earth are called as witnesses that God has given the people two paths: life with blessing, or death with cursing. He asks them to choose life, so that they and their children may live.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, shortly before Israel crosses the Jordan and enters the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God. If they turn toward other gods, they will lose the land; if they love God and obey him, they will live there. The following text says that God himself is their life.

For today: choosing life is a daily decision, not only an idea. Today you can choose to listen to God, pray, and obey him in something concrete, knowing that your decisions also affect your family.
exp.29:19:
This verse sums up what God asks: to love the LORD, to listen to his voice, and to cleave to him, that is, to be joined to him and to stay close to him. The reason is that God himself is the life of his people and the one who gives them length of days. In this way they could live in the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of his life, before they enter Canaan. He has set before them two paths: life and blessing, or death and curse. He pleads with them to choose life, and here he explains that choosing life means loving and obeying God, who keeps his promises.

For today: a full life is not found in having more things, but in staying close to God. You can set aside a few minutes each day to read the Bible, listen to God in prayer, and obey what you understand, trusting that he is your life.
exp.30:0:
Deuteronomy 31:1 says that Moses went and spoke these words to all Israel. The verse notes that the wording used in this verse is an old form; today we would simply say the word as it appears in the verse. It is a simple sentence that opens Moses' final address, which continues in the verses that follow.

The speaker is Moses, the leader who brought Israel out of Egypt. He is at the end of his life, and the people are about to enter the promised land. He will not go in with them, so he says farewell and prepares everyone for the change, announcing that Joshua will lead them. Some scholars point out that the Hebrew text differs a little in this verse, but the general sense is clear: Moses is addressing the whole people.

For today: when a season of life changes, we can follow Moses' example. He spoke plainly, encouraged the people, and reminded them that God was going ahead of them. Our leaders change, but God remains faithful.
exp.30:2:
This verse says that God himself will go ahead of Israel. He will destroy the nations that live in the promised land, and the people will take possession of it as their inheritance. The word "possess" means that they will receive the land as a gift, not by their own strength. "Nations" refers to the peoples who live there. Joshua will also go before them, as the Lord had already said.

Moses is speaking, and he is one hundred and twenty years old. God has told him that he will not cross the Jordan. So he says goodbye to the people and assures them that they will not be left alone. God will continue to guide them, and Joshua will be the new leader who will bring them into the land.

For today: leaders and people change, but God remains. If you face a difficult change or a new season, remember that God goes ahead of you. Walk in obedience and trust, without depending only on your own strength.
exp.30:7:
This verse says that God himself goes before his people. He will be with Joshua, he will not fail him or leave him alone. That is why Joshua should not be afraid or feel weak.

Moses speaks in front of all Israel. He is old, he knows he will not cross the Jordan, and he is handing over leadership to Joshua. The people were about to enter the promised land and face strong enemies. Moses reminds them that the victory did not depend on them alone, but on God going with them, as he had promised their ancestors.

When you face a big change or a task that frightens you, remember that you are not alone. Pray, take the next step with humility, and trust that God goes before you. That does not remove the difficulties, but it gives you courage to keep going forward.
exp.30:9:
Moses gives the people a command: every seven years, in the year of release (the year when debts were forgiven), during the Feast of Booths (or Tabernacles, when they camped in shelters of branches to remember the wilderness), the law was to be read aloud.

Moses is about to die, and Joshua will take command. He has just handed the written law to the priests and the elders. Now he makes sure that Israel hears it regularly, so that the new generations, including children and foreigners, will know it and honor God.

For today: God wants his Word to be heard with constancy, not just once. We can set aside a fixed time each week to read the Bible as a family or with others, and so remember his promises and obey them.
exp.30:11:
Deuteronomy 31:12 says that Moses commands the whole people to be gathered together: men, women, children, and also the foreigners who lived within their towns. The purpose is that they hear the law and learn it, that they stand in awe of God and honor him, and that they make every effort to obey everything he has said. To carry out the law means to put it into practice.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, when Israel is about to cross the Jordan without him. He orders that every seven years, in the year when debts were released, and during the Feast of Booths, the law be read aloud. In this way the new generations, who had not lived through all that came before, would also come to know God.

Today, faith is learned in community and is not only for a few. We can set aside a regular time to read the Bible together as a family or in church, including the children and those who come from outside, and ask God for help to live out what we hear.
exp.30:13:
God tells Moses that the time of his death is drawing near. He instructs him to call Joshua, his successor, and to present themselves together at the tabernacle of the congregation, the tent where God met with his people. There God would give them their instructions. Moses and Joshua obey and wait together.

The Lord speaks to Moses near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. Israel is about to enter the promised land, and Moses will not go in with them. For this reason God prepares the transfer of leadership. Right away God appears in the cloud and tells Moses that the people, in time, will turn away from him. So Joshua receives his charge knowing the task will be hard.

For today: God makes sure his work continues when leaders change. If you serve in your church or family, prepare and encourage others, and wait on God before taking important steps.
exp.30:14:
This verse tells us that God made his presence known in the tabernacle, which was the tent where the people of Israel worshiped him. He did this through a pillar of cloud, which was a visible sign of his presence. The cloud stopped at the entrance of the tent.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Moses was already very old, and God had told him that his death was near. So Moses and Joshua went to the tabernacle, where God was going to entrust Joshua with the task of leading the people. Right away, God also warns Moses that the people would turn away from him.

For today: God continues to guide his people even when the leaders change. We can trust that he is present and seek his direction with humility and prayer.
exp.30:23:
Moses finished writing the words of this law in a book, down to the last line. That means he did not leave the teaching only to be repeated by word of mouth; he put the whole of it in writing.

Moses is about to die, and the people are going to enter the promised land with Joshua as their new leader. For that reason he leaves the law in writing, so that it may serve as a guide and as a witness. Scholars debate exactly how much "this law" covers: the whole book of Deuteronomy or only part of it. The text does not fully specify this.

God speaks and wants his word to be preserved. Today we can value the Bible we have and set aside a fixed time each day for it. Reading it faithfully helps us remember what God says when hard times come.
exp.30:27:
Moses asks for the elders of the tribes and the officers to be gathered together. He wants to speak some words to them so that they can hear them clearly. He also calls heaven and earth to witness against the people.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, shortly before Israel enters the promised land. He knows the people tend to rebel. That is why he has placed the law beside the ark and now asks for solemn witnesses. Afterward, he recites a song to them. Calling on heaven and earth was a firm way of putting a warning on record.

God speaks to us with clarity and with love, before we turn aside. We can take his Word seriously today, without waiting until we are in trouble. A good practice is to read the Bible every day and ask for help to obey it.
exp.31:0:
Moses calls on the heavens and the earth to listen to what he is about to say. "The words of my mouth" refers to the words he speaks. It is like opening a solemn speech, asking all of creation to pay attention.

This verse begins the Song of Moses, which he speaks at the end of his life, before Israel enters the promised land. Moses wants the people to remember God's faithfulness and not turn away from Him. Calling the heavens and the earth as witnesses was a way of giving weight to the message. The verses that follow compare his words to rain and dew that bring life.

For today: come to God's Word with attention and reverence, like someone receiving rain on dry ground. Before reading the Bible, pause and ask God for a heart willing to listen.
exp.31:3:
This verse says that God is the Rock: firm, secure, and unchanging. His work is perfect, that is, complete and without flaw. All his ways are judgment, that is, justice. He is a God in whom one can trust, and there is no wickedness in him; he is just and right.

Moses speaks, near the end of his life, in a song addressed to Israel. He has just invited the people to magnify God. The song then contrasts God's faithfulness with the people's corruption, since they turned away. The fault is not God's but theirs.

For today: when something in your life does not make sense or hurts, you do not have to accuse God of injustice. You can speak to him honestly and rest in the fact that his character is steady and good, even when you do not yet understand everything.
exp.31:12:
He says that God made his people ride on the high places of the earth, that is, on high and safe ground. There they ate what the fields produced. He also made them draw honey out of the rock and oil out of the hard stone. These are images of abundance that comes from places where no one would expect it. The verse of the word itself is left out here because it refers to a term that does not appear in the verse above.

Moses speaks near the end of his life, in the song he teaches to Israel. He recalls how God guided and cared for them, like an eagle with its young. He does this to show that when they later forgot God, their failure was ingratitude.

For today: God often gives good things even in difficult times. It is wise to thank him regularly, because the verse that follows shows that comfort can lead us to forget the Giver.
exp.31:15:
This verse says that the people of Israel provoked God to jealousy by worshiping foreign gods, that is, gods of other nations. The sentence about the word "provoked" can be rewritten: the verb here means they stirred God to anger. The "abominations" are practices that are detestable to God, above all idolatry and the things that went along with it.

Moses speaks in the song he leaves them at the end of his life, before Israel enters the promised land. He reminds them how God cared for them and made them prosper. But, once they felt satisfied, the people, here called by a poetic name for Israel, forgot God. God's jealousy is not a whim, but the pain of a faithful God when his people abandon him.

For today: when everything is going well for us, it is easy to put God in second place. Ask yourself which things occupy the place that belongs to Him alone, and thank Him today for what He has given you.
exp.31:16:
They sacrificed to demons, not to God, and the verse says Israel offered sacrifices to false spiritual powers rather than to God. The Hebrew word for these beings (shedim) appears only a few times and is usually understood as spirits or demons behind the idols. They were gods that had only recently arrived from neighboring peoples, gods that neither the people nor their ancestors had known or honored.

Moses speaks in his final song, shortly before he dies. He wants to warn the people that when they prosper and grow comfortable, they will forget God, their Rock and Creator, and will seek out other gods. God grieves and is angered by that unfaithfulness.

Today, when things are going well for us, it is easy to put our trust in new things: money, success, or passing trends. We can stop and ask ourselves: to what am I giving my time and my trust? Thanking God each day helps us remember who sustains us.
exp.31:24:
The verse says that judgment will come from every side: outside, the sword will bring death and destruction; inside, in the rooms of the houses, there will be terror. No one will be spared: not the young man, nor the young woman, nor the infant still nursing, nor the old man with gray hairs.

It is part of the Song of Moses, near the end of his life. God himself speaks and warns what would happen if Israel, after receiving so many blessings, turned away from him to follow other gods. These are harsh words, but they were meant to call the people to return and trust in God. Interpreters see here a serious warning, not any delight of God in suffering.

For today: do not take lightly the care of God. If you notice that you are drifting away from him, return soon, with humility and trust in his mercy.
exp.31:30:
Moses says that the gods of the neighboring nations cannot be compared with the God of Israel, whom he calls "our Rock," meaning a firm and secure refuge. He also says that the enemies themselves can judge and see this. Some understand that they themselves acknowledge it; the Hebrew text can be read in several ways.

Moses sings this poem to the people before he dies. He warns them that, if they turn away from God, they will suffer defeats. They would not lose because their enemies were stronger, but because God had given them over on account of their unfaithfulness.

Today, when something promises you security apart from God, such as money, success, or the approval of others, compare it with Him. Ask yourself what you can truly depend on when problems come, and return to God as your refuge.
exp.31:33:
God asks whether he has not stored up, as something sealed among his treasures, what is coming upon the wicked. "Sealed" means closed and secured, so that nothing is lost or changed. The idea is that judgment has not been forgotten; it is kept for its proper time.

These words are part of the Song of Moses, where God speaks about the rebellion of Israel and of hostile nations. The verses before describe their wickedness as bitter grapes and poison. Many understand that this refers to Israel's enemies, though some think it also reaches the unfaithful people. The verses that follow say that vengeance belongs to God.

For today: when you see injustice, do not grow bitter or take revenge on your own. Trust that God sees everything, keeps it in mind, and will act with justice in his time.
exp.31:34:
It says that only God has the right to punish wrongdoing and give what is justly owed. The word "vengeance" here means corrective justice, not resentment. The phrase about their foot sliding means that they will stumble and fall. The day of their calamity is near, and the punishment waiting for them is coming quickly.

It is part of the Song of Moses, which God gave to remind Israel of his faithfulness. It speaks of the enemy nations who oppress his people, whose wickedness is already stored up to be judged. The verses that follow show that God also judges his own people, but then has compassion on them. Some believe the passage also speaks of correction for Israel; the text allows for that reading.

When someone wrongs you, do not take payment into your own hands. Hand the hurt over to God, who is just, and ask for strength to forgive and to do good. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 12:19 for that same purpose.
exp.31:37:
God speaks with sorrowful mockery about false gods. These are the ones who received the fat from the animals offered and the wine poured out in the offerings. Now God asks: if they are so powerful, why do they not rise up to help and protect those who worshiped them?

God speaks within the song of Moses, near the end of his life. Israel had turned away from God to follow idols. God announces that when his people are left without strength, they will see that those gods cannot save. In this way he wants to bring them back to himself, the only God.

For today: think about what you give your time, your money, and your trust to. If something cannot sustain you in a crisis, it does not deserve first place. Turn your heart back to God, who does listen and does help.
exp.31:45:
Moses tells the Israelites to set their hearts, that is, all their attention and their will, on the words he is solemnly giving them today. Here "solemnly" carries the sense of declaring or warning with seriousness. They are to teach these words to their children and take care to put them into practice.

Moses has just recited the song of Deuteronomy 32 before the whole people, together with Joshua. He is about to die, and the Israelites are about to cross the Jordan into the promised land. He wants them not to forget God's law or set it aside once he is no longer with them.

For today: God invites us to take his Word seriously, not only to hear it. We can choose a passage of the Bible this week, think about it calmly, put it into practice in something specific, and share it with our children, family members, or younger friends.
exp.31:48:
God tells Moses to go up to Mount Nebo, in the Abarim range, in the land of Moab, facing the city of Jericho. From there he will be able to look out over the land of Canaan, which God gives to the people of Israel as an inheritance. An inheritance is something received as a gift, not earned by one's own merit.

The Lord speaks on the same day that Moses finished teaching his song to the people. After forty years in the wilderness, Israel is about to cross the Jordan. God allows Moses to see the land, but not to enter it, because at Kadesh he did not honor God before the people, as the following verses explain.

For today: God keeps his promises even when we do not see the full result. We can serve him faithfully, trust that his work continues, and learn to take seriously the call to honor him at all times.
exp.32:5:
He says that Reuben should live and not die, and that his men should not be few but should grow to a good number. The phrase about his men being numerous means that his people should be counted in great numbers and not be reduced. Some translators understand the verse to mean that his men should not be few, and the wording allows for both readings.

Moses speaks before he dies. He is blessing the tribes of Israel one by one. Reuben was the oldest son of Jacob, but he had lost his place of privilege because of a serious sin (Genesis 35:22; 49:4). This blessing seems to be a prayer for mercy, so that the tribe would not be wiped out.

For today: God knows how to give new chances to those who have failed. We can pray for people who carry mistakes from the past, asking that God sustain and restore them, and treat them with that same mercy.
exp.32:6:
Here Moses blesses the tribe of Judah shortly before he dies. He asks God to hear the voice of Judah and bring him back to his people, that is, to be with the other tribes. He also asks that his hands be sufficient for him, meaning that he would have strength to fight, and that God himself would be his help against his enemies.

Moses speaks to all Israel in his final words, blessing tribe by tribe. Some understand that Judah was separated or in danger, and so needed unity and protection. The text does not explain this with certainty. Later, from Judah would come King David.

For today: even when you do your part with your own strength, recognize that you need God and your community. Ask him for help in your struggles, and do not isolate yourself from your church or your family.
exp.32:9:
It says that the Levites would have two tasks: teaching and worship. They would teach Jacob's judgments (the decisions and commands of God) and the law to all the people. They would also offer the incense and the whole burnt offering (the offering burned completely) on God's altar.

Moses speaks just before he dies and blesses each tribe of Israel. Here he blesses Levi, the tribe set apart for service in the sanctuary. The verses before it recall their faithfulness to God in difficult moments. Some think it refers to the episode of the golden calf, although the text does not say so clearly.

For today: faith needs both the teaching of the Word and sincere worship. This week, set aside time to read the Bible and another time to pray and praise God, and share with someone what you have learned.
exp.32:20:
This verse says that the tribe of Gad chose for itself the first land conquered, east of the Jordan. There it was given a portion reserved by the lawgiver, that is, Moses. Even so, Gad did not settle back at ease: it marched at the head of the people to help conquer Canaan. In doing so it fulfilled the justice God required and what it had agreed with Israel.

Moses speaks before his death, blessing each tribe. Gad had asked to stay on the other side of the Jordan (Numbers 32), and Moses agreed on the condition that its warriors would fight alongside their brothers. Here he acknowledges that they kept that promise.

For today: Keeping what we promised, even after we have received our own share, honors God. We can ask ourselves whom we should help before we rest.
exp.32:21:
He says the tribe of Dan is like a lion's cub, young and strong, that leaps from Bashan. Bashan was a fertile region northeast of the Jordan, known for its mountains and forests. The word "leap" suggests a quick and brave movement.

Moses speaks just before he dies, blessing each tribe of Israel. Dan was a small tribe. Later, many of its people settled in the north, near Bashan, although it is not known for certain why Moses mentions that place. Some think the image refers to its impetus or its conquest of territory, but there are several interpretations.

For today: God can give strength and courage even to those who seem small or young. If you feel unable, remember that God equips you for what He asks of you. Trust in Him and take the first step with courage.
exp.32:23:
Moses says that Asher will be blessed with many children, that his brothers will look on him with favor, and that he will dip his foot in oil. The words "á" and "dijo" are from old spelling. Dipping one's foot in oil is a picture of great abundance, as if the oil were so plentiful that one could step in it.

Moses is blessing the tribes of Israel shortly before he dies. Asher would receive a territory in the northwest, and many understand that it was fertile land with olive groves. This is a common interpretation, though the text does not explain it in detail.

For today: God's blessing is not only for oneself. Asher would be loved because his abundance reached others. We can ask God that whatever he gives us, whether time, money or affection, may make us pleasant and generous toward the people around us.
exp.32:26:
This verse says that the eternal God, the one who has always existed, is a safe place where his people can hide and rest. Underneath you, there are strong arms that hold you up and never tire. God will also drive out the enemy, and the command to destroy them is understood as his order against those who opposed Israel in that conquest.

Moses speaks. He is close to death and blesses the tribes of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they will not advance alone: the same God who guided them through the wilderness will go with them and give them security.

For today: when you feel tired or threatened, do not depend only on your own strength. Stop for a moment, pray, and rest in God. He sustains you even when you feel you can no longer go on.
exp.33:3:
God tells Moses that this is the land he promised with an oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Moses sees it with his own eyes, but God makes clear to him that he will not enter it.

The Lord speaks, and Moses is on the mountain, looking out over the whole land: from Naphtali to Judah, the south, and the valley of Jericho. After leading the people for forty years, Moses cannot enter. Deuteronomy 32:51 connects this with his failure at Meribah, although the text here only stresses that the promise passes on to the next generation. Shortly afterward he dies.

God keeps his promises, even though we do not always see them fulfilled in our own time. You can serve faithfully and leave to others what you will not live to see. Trust that God finishes what he began, and accept with humility your part in his plan.
exp.33:8:
It says that Joshua, son of Nun, was full of the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him. For this reason the people of Israel obeyed him and did what God had commanded Moses.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who recounts what happened after Moses' death. Tradition attributes the book to Moses, but this ending is usually understood as added by another hand; scholars explain this in different ways. The people were in mourning and about to enter the promised land, so they needed a new leader. Laying on of hands was a gesture of blessing and of handing over authority (see Numbers 27:18-23).

Today we can learn that God takes care of his people through times of transition and change. If he calls you to serve, ask him for wisdom and do not rely only on your own strength. And if someone else receives a responsibility, support them with respect and prayer.
exp.33:9:
This verse says that, after Moses, there never arose in Israel another prophet like him. The Lord knew him face to face, that is, spoke with him in a very close and direct way. The word "prophet" refers to someone who speaks on behalf of God.

The narrator, who is not named in the text, closes the book of Deuteronomy and the whole Law of Moses. Israel has just mourned his death, and Joshua is now the new leader. The verse does not diminish Joshua's worth; it shows that Moses held a unique place because of his close dealings with God and the signs he performed in Egypt. Some scholars believe these lines were added later, but the text does not make this clear.

God desires a close relationship with us. We can speak to him with confidence in prayer and read his Word to know him better. We can also thank those who have guided us in the faith.
exp.33:10:
This verse continues the previous sentence: no other prophet arose like Moses, in the signs and wonders that God sent him to perform in Egypt. Those works were directed at Pharaoh, his servants (his officials and attendants), and all his land.

These words close the book of Deuteronomy. They were probably added after the death of Moses, and it is not known with certainty who wrote them. The text sums up the greatness of Moses, recalling the plagues and Israel's deliverance from Egypt, which showed the power of God.

Today we can remember that God is the one who acts and sustains his servants. Moses was great because God was with him. If God has given you a task, trust in his power more than in your own strength, and give him the glory.
exp.6:0:
He says that when God brings Israel into the promised land, he himself will drive out many nations from before them. Seven are named: the Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. They were larger and stronger than Israel. The phrase "to possess it" means to take the land as a possession.

Moses speaks to the people on the plains of Moab, just before they enter Canaan. He reminds them that the victory will come from God and not from their own strength. The verses that follow speak of destroying those peoples and avoiding alliances with them, since the danger was that Israel would turn away from God. Scholars debate how to understand that command of destruction, and it is best read in its particular historical context, not as a general command for today.

Today, when you face something that seems bigger than you, remember that God can work where your strength falls short. Trust in him, and keep faithfully doing what is your part.
exp.31:27:
This verse says that the people of Israel had made foolish and aimless decisions. The phrase "a nation devoid of counsel" means that their plans were of no use and led to failure. The phrase "with no understanding among them" means that they lacked the wisdom to see what was happening around them.

The one speaking is Moses, in the song he teaches the people shortly before his death. There he expresses how God feels: Israel had turned away from Him and therefore suffered defeats. Some scholars think this verse refers to Israel and others think it refers to the enemy nations; the following context favors Israel more.

For today: before deciding, ask God for wisdom and listen to His Word. Also pay attention to what is happening around you, because God often speaks to us through consequences, and learning to see them keeps us from following paths that lead nowhere.
exp.21:17:
It says that when a husband falsely accuses his wife of not having been a virgin, the leaders of the people, called the elders, must take him and punish him. The word "punish" here means that they would impose a penalty or correction on him. The verses that follow make clear that he would also have to pay a fine of one hundred pieces of silver.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law protected a young woman and her family from a false accusation that could ruin her name and her future. The parents would present the evidence before the elders, who acted as judges at the city gates.

For today: God takes seriously words that damage the reputation of others. Before accusing someone, or repeating a rumor, let us ask ourselves whether it is true and whether we are saying it out of a love for justice or out of resentment.
exp.18:3:
This verse explains who may flee to a city of refuge and save his life: the person who killed another person accidentally, without intending to harm him. The Hebrew idea of killing "unintentionally" is rendered in your Bible as "accidentally," and the phrase about having had no hatred or quarrel with the victim beforehand appears here as "without intending to harm him." The word "neighbor" refers to the other Israelite.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. God commands that three cities of refuge be set apart, with roads kept in good condition, so that an angry relative of the dead person would not kill, without justice, someone who was not guilty of murder. In this way life was protected, and a clear distinction was made between an accident and a crime.

For today: before judging someone, try to understand his intentions and the facts. God cares about justice and also about mercy, so we can avoid impulsive revenge and look for ways to protect the innocent.
exp.31:14:
This verse says that Israel, called here "Jeshurun" (an affectionate name meaning something like "the upright one"), grew fat and kicked like a bloated animal that has been overfed. The words "grew fat," "bloated," and "gorged" describe prosperity that had become excess. Then the people abandoned the God who made them and scorned the Rock of their salvation, the one who was their secure refuge.

Moses speaks in a song that teaches the people before he dies. He recalls how God cared for them abundantly in the promised land. He warns them that when everything is going well, they could forget God and turn to other gods, as the following verses show.

For today: when we are in times of comfort, it is easy to stop praying and stop depending on God. Let us pause to thank him for what we have and remember that everything comes from his hand.
exp.20:3:
The passage says that the elders of the city nearest to a body found lying in the field must bring a young cow to a valley with running water, where the ground has not been plowed or sown. There, by the stream, they are to break the animal's neck.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. If someone was found killed and no one knew who had done it, the land was burdened with guilt for the blood that had been shed. This ritual showed that the community took human life seriously and did not want to be indifferent. Scholars explain the unplowed valley and the running water in several ways, and the Bible does not detail it.

For today: let us not ignore injustice by saying "it's not my concern." We can pray, speak out, and help those who suffer near us.
exp.2:18:
This verse says that the wives, children, and livestock of the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh would remain in the cities Moses had already given them east of the Jordan. The word "only" marks the exception: the fighting men would cross over. "Your livestock" refers to the herds and flocks, and "I know that you have much livestock" shows that Moses was well aware of their situation.

Moses speaks to the people as he recalls what they have lived through in the wilderness. He reminds them of what he commanded these tribes: to help their brothers conquer the land on the other side of the Jordan before returning to their homes. Their families would be kept safe while they carried out that commitment.

For today: God blesses when a person cares for their own, but He also expects us to help others. Let us not rest thinking only of ourselves; let us look for ways to support those who are still fighting, without neglecting our family.
exp.23:17:
It says that the people must remember that they were once slaves in Egypt and that the LORD their God set them free from that place. For this reason God commands them to act with justice and compassion. Here "slaves" refers to people held in servitude, and the phrase "redeemed you" means that God brought them out of that slavery through his own action on their behalf.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He repeats God's law to them. Just before this, he asked them not to pervert justice for the stranger, the fatherless, or the widow, who were people without protection. Their own history of suffering was meant to make them sensitive toward the weak.

For today: when God has shown you mercy, use it as a reason to treat others well. Think of someone vulnerable near you, such as a migrant, an orphan, or a widow, and help them with something concrete this week.
exp.1:12:
He says that God, through Moses, commanded the people to arise and cross the Brook of Zered, and that they did so. A "brook" is a small stream of water, and here it marks a boundary on the road.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, and reminds them of their history. Crossing the Brook of Zered marked the end of thirty-eight years of waiting, counted from Kadesh-barnea, a time in which the generation that did not believe died out. The verses that follow explain this. The exact location of the brook is debated among scholars.

When God says "go forward," it is wise to obey without delay. Perhaps you have spent a long season of waiting or correction. God knows when it ends, and his call to move ahead comes at its appointed time. Respond in faith and take the step.
exp.11:16:
It says that the Israelite could not eat in his own town the things dedicated to God: the tithe of the grain, of the new wine and of the oil, the firstborn of his herds and flocks, any of the offerings he had vowed to give, and his freewill offerings and special gifts. A "town" here means the cities or villages where a person lived. "Firstborn" refers to the first young of the animals.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He teaches them that they could eat ordinary meat in any place, but what was set apart had to be brought to the place God would choose. There they would eat it as a family, with joy, together with the Levite. In this way, the worship and those who served in it were cared for.

For today: what we give to God is not a formality, but an act of gratitude. We can set aside the first of our resources and time for God, and share it joyfully, remembering also to support those who serve in the church.
exp.25:0:
This verse says that a time will come when the people of Israel enter the land that God gives them as an inheritance. There they will take possession of it and settle in it. An inheritance is something received as a gift, not earned by one's own merit. Taking possession means claiming the land as their own, and settling in it means making their home there.

Moses is speaking to the people near the end of his life, before they enter the land. This verse introduces a ceremony in which they bring the firstfruits, the first produce of the harvest, to God in gratitude. In this way they would acknowledge that the land was a gift from Him.

For today: before enjoying what you have, whether your work, your home, or your livelihood, pause to thank God. Give Him the first and the best, remembering that everything comes from His hand.
exp.24:5:
This verse says that the first son the widow bears will carry on the name of her dead husband's brother, so that his name will not be blotted out from Israel.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. This law of marriage to a brother-in-law protected a widow with no children, who was left very vulnerable, and it cared for the family's inheritance and memory. The verses that follow show that the brother-in-law could refuse, though that brought public shame. Scholars debate how it was applied in detail.

For today: God cares for those who are left alone and unprotected. We can ask ourselves who is near us, such as a widow, an orphan, or a relative in need, and help them with concrete commitment, not only with kind words.
exp.18:17:
The passage says that the judges must investigate the case thoroughly. If they find that the witness lied and falsely accused a fellow Israelite, that witness will be considered a false witness. "Investigate thoroughly" means they will ask questions and examine the matter with care. "Is proven to be a liar" describes how the truth becomes clear: the lie is exposed through careful examination.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He is explaining how justice was meant to work. An accused person could not be condemned on the strength of a single word, and the case was brought before God, the priests, and the judges. In this way the innocent were protected and the sin of lying was taken seriously.

For today: before repeating an accusation, ask questions, verify the facts, and do not let yourself be carried along by rumors. And if you are asked to give an opinion or testify about someone, say only what you truly know, because your words can either harm or protect another person.
exp.28:15:
Moses reminds the Israelites of something they lived through themselves: they lived in Egypt and then passed through the lands of other peoples on the way here. When he says "you yourselves know," he asks them to draw on their own memory. The word "nations" here refers to foreign peoples.

Moses speaks to the people on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He is renewing the covenant with God. He reminds them of what they have seen, because in the verses that follow he warns them about the idols of those peoples and the danger that someone might turn away from God.

For today: remembering what we have lived through and what God has done helps us stand firm. If we live alongside customs that draw us away from God, it is wise to examine our hearts honestly and remain faithful to him.
exp.6:9:
God does not leave those who hate him without a response. "He repays them to their face" means that he answers them directly and surely. "With destruction" speaks of a severe judgment. "He will not hesitate" means that he will not keep them waiting: God does not stay inactive, nor does he overlook persistent rejection of him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just reminded them that God is faithful and keeps his covenant with those who love him. This verse shows the other side: God is just. Interpreters debate the timing and the form of this repayment, but all agree that God takes wickedness and rebellion seriously.

For today: you can trust that God is faithful and also just. You do not have to take revenge on someone who has wronged you; hand that person over to God. And examine your heart so that you live close to him in love and obedience.
exp.16:13:
This verse speaks of a future time. When Israel has entered the land God is giving them, taken possession of it, and settled there, the people might say, "Let us set a king over us like all the nations around us." The words "when you enter" and "have taken possession" describe the moment the people are fully established in the land.

Moses speaks to the people before they cross the Jordan, repeating God's law. Just before this, he speaks of obeying priests and judges. Here God does not forbid having a king, but He sets out rules so that the king is someone chosen by Him, a brother among the people, and one who does not trust in human power. The phrase "like all the nations" shows the danger of copying others.

For today: before deciding something important, ask yourself whether you want it only because everyone else does. Seek God's guidance and do not imitate others without thinking.
exp.5:22:
This verse says that God brought his people out of Egypt with a purpose: to lead them into the land he had promised to their ancestors. The "fathers" in this verse refer to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He teaches them how to answer when their children ask about the meaning of the laws. They are to tell the story of their deliverance: God not only rescued them from slavery, he also fulfilled what he had promised. In this way, obedience grows out of gratitude and not merely out of duty.

For today: when I explain my faith to my children or to others, I can share how God has been faithful to me. Remembering his promises that have been kept strengthens trust and encourages us to obey him with joy.
exp.10:30:
This verse says that the people of Israel are about to cross the Jordan River to enter the land that God is giving them. It assures them that once they take possession of it, they will settle there. "Possess" means to take the land as one's own; "settle" means that they will make their home there.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, shortly before his death. He reminds them of God's promise and asks them that, upon entering, they proclaim the blessing and the curse on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal. Then he asks them to obey all of God's commandments.

For today: God keeps what he promises, but he invites us to respond with obedience. If you are facing a new step, trust in his faithfulness and walk day by day according to his Word.
exp.18:7:
It says that if the LORD your God enlarges your territory, just as he solemnly promised your ancestors, and gives you all the land he pledged to give them, then something more will happen (this is completed in the next verse). "Enlarges" means extends, and "territory" refers to the land and its borders. "Swore" indicates a solemn promise.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He had already commanded that three cities of refuge be set apart, where someone who killed another person without intending to could flee. Here he looks ahead: if the land grows, three more cities will be added, so that innocent blood is not shed. It is not certain when or how this was fulfilled in history, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: God cares for justice and mercy even when his people prosper. If we receive more blessings or responsibilities, we should also use them to protect and give opportunity to the vulnerable.
exp.17:8:
It says that when the people of Israel enter the land the LORD your God is giving them, they must not imitate the detestable ways of the nations living there. "Detestable ways" are customs that God rejects. "Imitate" means copying or adopting those customs.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter Canaan. He has just spoken about the Levites, who served God and lived from the offerings. Now he warns against magic, divination and contact with the dead, and reminds them that God himself would guide them, especially through his prophets.

Today we can ask ourselves where we look for direction and security. It is easy to copy the customs around us without thinking. This verse invites us to trust God, to seek his Word and to pray, instead of turning to horoscopes, spiritualists or superstitions.
exp.6:18:
This verse reminds the people of Israel what God had already done for them in Egypt. The "trials" are the plagues and hardships they saw with their own eyes. The "mighty hand and outstretched arm" points to God's power in rescuing them. And it says that God will do the same against any people they come to fear.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. They saw the nations of Canaan as more numerous and stronger. Moses encourages them to look back: if God defeated Pharaoh, he can also go with them now.

When you feel fear before a great problem, remember the times God sustained you. Write those moments down and go over them again. Recalling his past faithfulness strengthens confidence to face what lies ahead.
exp.16:6:
It says that when someone was condemned to death for idolatry, the witnesses who accused them had to throw the first stone, and then all the people. In this way Israel would purge the evil from the midst of the community. The phrase "purge the evil" in the verse above is the one this comment refers to, and it means to clear out or get rid of.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. This command deals with idolatry, which broke the covenant with God. Two or three witnesses were required, and they had to act first, so that no one would accuse lightly: whoever made a false accusation would bear the responsibility. Today many Christians understand this law as part of the old covenant with Israel, not as a current civil rule.

For today: before accusing someone, think about the weight of your words. Speak with truth, with evidence, and with humility, knowing that God asks for justice and care for your neighbor.
exp.6:1:
When the LORD your God hands those nations over to you and you defeat them, you must devote them to complete destruction. You were not to make any treaty with them or show them mercy.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter the promised land. He warns them that those nations were numerous and strong, and that the greater danger was not the war itself but the influence of their gods and customs. The verses that follow make this clear: they were not to intermarry with these peoples, so that they would not turn away from God. This command is difficult, and it has been interpreted in various ways; many see it as a unique charge given for that particular moment.

Today we are not commanded to fight anyone, but we are called to guard our faithfulness to God. We can examine which influences, habits, or relationships pull us away from Him, and be firm in turning away from them.
exp.21:25:
It says that nothing should be done to the young woman, because she has committed no sin worthy of death. The word "young woman" refers to a girl or woman who is promised in marriage. The text compares her case to a man who attacks his neighbor and takes his life: she is the victim, not the one at fault.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, and their laws distinguish two cases. If it happened inside the city, it was assumed she could have called for help, and the text takes this as a sign of consent. If it happened in the field, where no one would hear her, she is protected as a victim. Some scholars see here a protection of the woman; others point out that the law reflects the customs of its time.

Today we learn not to blame someone who suffers an assault. If someone trusts you with an account of abuse, listen to them with respect, believe them, stand up for them, and help them seek protection and justice. God takes the side of the one who has been hurt.
exp.9:12:
Moses tells the people to keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD, which he is giving them that day. Here "statutes" means rules or instructions, and the phrase "for your own good" means that it will go well with you. Obedience is not presented as a burden, but as a path to well-being.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God is not asking them for something impossible: he asks for reverence, love, and sincere service. He says this in the context of God's grace, who chose them even though the whole world belongs to him.

For today: remember that God's instructions come from his love and his desire to care for you. Choose one teaching from the Bible that you know you should practice today, and obey it with gratitude, not out of fear, trusting that God seeks your good.
exp.28:20:
This verse says that God will single that person out from all the tribes of Israel for disaster. All the curses of the covenant written in this Book of the Law will fall on them. The phrase "single him out" means that he will be picked out for judgment, and "for disaster" means that the outcome will be harmful to him.

Moses speaks to the people when he renews the covenant with God in Moab, before they enter the promised land. He warns anyone who hears the curses and thinks, "I will have peace, even if I do as I please." This is someone who despises the warning and follows his own heart, counting on a blessing he has never sought.

For today: do not take God's grace lightly or use his patience as an excuse to keep doing wrong. If you feel that God is speaking to you, respond with humility and repentance, not with a false sense of security. God welcomes those who return to him sincerely.
exp.1:13:
This verse says that the time from when Israel left Kadesh-barnea until they crossed the Brook of Zered was thirty-eight years. During that time, the entire generation of fighting men, meaning the adults fit for battle, died off in the camp. This happened just as the LORD had sworn it would. The words "until that entire generation... had perished" mean that the dying continued until none of that generation was left.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, and he reminds them of their history. At Kadesh, the earlier generation did not trust God and refused to enter the land (Numbers 14). Because of this, God swore that they would not see it. Moses tells them this so that the new generation will learn from it and obey.

For today: God's words are serious and faithful, both in his promises and in his warnings. Today you can trust him and obey him without delay, knowing that he does what he says.
exp.20:22:
It says that the body of a person condemned to death and hanged on a tree was not to be left there overnight. It had to be buried that same day. The phrase "anyone who is hung on a tree is under God's curse" means that someone hanged was left exposed as a sign of judgment. To "defile" means to make dirty or to profane, and the "inheritance" is the land the LORD gives to his people.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the land God has promised them. These laws aimed to take justice seriously, but also to respect human dignity, even that of a guilty person. Scholars explain in various ways how the condemned person was hanged, but the command to bury him promptly is clear.

For today: Paul quotes this text in Galatians 3:13 to explain that Christ bore our curse. Today you can give thanks for him and treat all people with respect and compassion, even those who have failed seriously.
exp.4:20:
It says we should not covet what belongs to another person: not his wife, not his house, not his field, not his servants, not his animals, nor anything else that belongs to him. The verse's own words "covet" and "desire" mean wanting something that belongs to someone else with a strong longing. The "manservant" and "maidservant" were the hired workers or servants of a household. "Neighbor" means the person who lives nearby, someone close to us.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel, reminding them of the Ten Commandments that God gave them on the mountain, before they entered the promised land. This commandment is different from the others, because it looks not only at what is done, but at what is in the heart, from which theft, lying and other wrongs come.

Today we can practice it with gratitude: when you feel envy for what someone else has, thank God for something specific he has already given you, and ask him for a contented heart.
exp.22:4:
God says he would not listen to Balaam, the man who was hired to curse Israel. Instead of letting that curse fall on the people, God turned it into a blessing. The reason the text gives is simple: God loves his people. The word "listen" here means "to pay attention to" or "to answer."

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that Moab and Ammon did not help them on the way, and that the king of Moab paid Balaam to curse them. Moses wants Israel to remember how God cared for them, even when they did not know what was being planned against them.

For today: when you feel that someone wishes you harm or that circumstances are against you, remember that God's love sustains you. Trust that he can work for good, and respond with gratitude rather than resentment.
exp.26:18:
It says that God pronounces a curse on the one who withholds justice from the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow. Withholding justice means denying people the fair treatment they are owed, whether by misusing the law or by failing to act when they need it. "Cursed" means that person falls under God's judgment. And all the people respond "Amen," that is, "so be it," accepting this warning.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. At Shechem, according to the passage, the people were to say these curses aloud as part of renewing their covenant with God. These three groups had no strong family or land to protect them, and God cares for them in a special way.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I treat fairly those who have less power than I do? It may be an immigrant, a child without support, or a widow. Standing up for them, rather than taking advantage of them, is obeying God.
exp.18:19:
When a false witness receives the punishment he deserves, the rest of the people will hear about it and be afraid. In this way they will never again do anything so evil among the people.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. God gives laws to protect the innocent in trials. If a witness lied to harm someone, he received the same penalty he had wished on his brother. The punishment aimed at justice and also at preventing wrongdoing. This is a law for the judges in Israel.

For today: our words carry weight. Telling the truth, especially when another person's good name is at stake, is a way of loving our neighbor. Before speaking about someone, ask yourself whether what you are saying is true and just.
exp.31:1:
Moses says that his teaching will fall gently, like the rain and dew that refresh a field. "Teaching" is what he is passing on, and "speech" is the words he speaks. "Tender plants" are young growing things, and "gentle rain" is a light, soft rain.

Moses speaks near the end of his life, in the song he gives to Israel before they enter the promised land. He calls the heavens and the earth as witnesses. He wants the people to remember who God is and not turn away from Him, since the song also warns about their future unfaithfulness.

For today: receive the Word of God like gentle rain, without hurry. Set aside a few quiet minutes to read a passage, and let it slowly nourish your heart and bear fruit over time.
exp.27:66:
It says the person will live with such distress that they will never be at rest. In the morning they will wish it were evening, and in the evening they will wish it were morning, longing to escape the dread. "If only it were evening" expresses a wish that the day were over. "Terrifying" describes sights that fill the heart with dread. The fear comes from the terrifying things they will see.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings of obeying God and the consequences of abandoning his covenant. This passage describes the last part of those warnings: exile, insecurity and slavery. It is a serious warning, not a hopeless threat, since other passages speak of restoration.

For today: when fear does not let you rest, do not keep it to yourself. Pray honestly, seek God, and also seek help from trusted people. His peace sustains the anxious heart.
exp.30:26:
Moses tells the people that he knows how rebellious and stubborn they are. He reminds them that they were already rebelling against the LORD while he was still alive and among them. So how much more would they rebel once he was gone?

Moses speaks at the end of his life, about to say farewell to Israel. He has just asked that the book of the law be kept beside the ark, as a witness. He knows the history of the people in the wilderness and speaks to them frankly, not out of contempt, but to warn them and to make them take the law seriously.

For today: it is not enough to depend on leaders or on good spiritual moments. Ask God for a humble heart willing to obey him, reading his Word honestly, even when no one is watching you.
exp.27:40:
It says that parents will have sons and daughters, but they will not remain theirs, because they will be taken away as prisoners to another land. "Captivity" means being carried off as a prisoner and living far from home.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In this chapter he sets out blessings if they obey God and curses if they turn away from him. This verse belongs to the curses: labors and joys that are lost. The nearby verses speak of vineyards, olive trees, and ruined harvests. Later, the history of Israel shows exiles, although how each passage relates to each event is understood in different ways.

For today: value your family as a gift from God, pray for them, and give them your time now. Put God first in your home, because what is dearest also needs his care.
exp.12:9:
It says that anyone who tries to lead God's people away from Him, even through deceit or signs, must be stoned to death. The reason is clear: that person tried to turn them away from the LORD, the God who brought them out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. To "try" means to attempt, and to "turn away" means to lead someone off course.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. Israel was a nation under a covenant with God, and idolatry was seen as treason against that covenant and as a danger to the whole community. This law was for that time and that structure of government; Christians do not apply it as a civil rule today.

For today: take faithfulness to God seriously, and guard your heart against voices that would pull you away from Him. Remember what God has done for you, and seek Christ with firmness, always responding in truth and love, never with violence.
exp.7:17:
This verse says that we should always remember the Lord, because it is God who gives us the power to gain wealth. He does this in order to confirm his covenant, that is, the solemn promise he made to Israel's ancestors, and that promise continues to stand even to this day.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how God cared for them in the desert with the manna. He worries that, once they prosper, they will think everything came from their own effort and forget God.

For today: when something goes well for you at work or in your finances, thank God and recognize that he gave you health, opportunities, and abilities. Also, use what you have with generosity and humility, without boasting.
exp.2:10:
This verse says that Og, king of Bashan, was the last of the giants known as the Rephaim. His bed was made of iron and measured nine cubits long and four cubits wide. A cubit is the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, about 45 centimeters, so the bed measured nearly four meters by almost two. The verse notes that this bed was still in Rabbah, the main city of the Ammonites. Some think "iron" could refer to basalt, a dark, hard stone, but this is not known for certain.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the victories God gave them over powerful kings. The bed served as a visible proof that Og had existed and had been defeated.

For today: when you face something that seems like a giant, remember that God has already overcome things far greater. Trust in Him and move forward in faith.
exp.8:28:
This verse says that the people of Israel belong to God. An "inheritance" means something very precious that a person owns and cares for, like something handed down to them. God brought them out of Egypt by his "great power" and his "outstretched arm," which are ways of speaking of his power to rescue.

The one speaking is Moses. He tells how he prayed to God after the people made the golden calf. Instead of defending the people on the basis of their merits, Moses appeals to God's character, to his promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to his reputation among the nations.

For today: when you fail, do not trust in your good behavior, but in the fact that God loves you and rescued you. That assurance is not an excuse to sin, but a reason to return to him with humility and to pray for others as well.
exp.31:20:
They have provoked My jealousy by worshiping what is not God, and they have enraged Me with their worthless idols. In return, God says He will make Israel jealous through those who are not a people, and He will make them angry through a nation without understanding.

God speaks within the Song of Moses, which warns Israel before it enters the promised land. God sees the unfaithfulness of His people and announces the consequences. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 10:19, and some connect it to the opening of the gospel to other nations, although it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: examine what things are taking the place of God in your heart, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Return to Him sincerely, for God desires to be loved with the whole heart.
exp.14:20:
It says that if the firstborn male of the cattle or the sheep had a defect, such as being lame or blind, or having any other serious flaw, it was not to be sacrificed to the LORD. The word "defect" in the verse means an imperfection or fault, so the verse covers any kind of serious flaw.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the firstborn belonged to God and that they were to bring them before Him each year. God asked for the best, not for what was left over. An animal with a defect could be eaten at home, but it was not offered on the altar.

For today: let us give God the first and best of our time, care, and resources, not just what we have left over. Giving with sincerity and effort shows that we truly value Him.
exp.11:4:
God himself would choose a place from among all the tribes of Israel to establish as a dwelling for his Name, and the people were to seek that place and go there. A "dwelling" is the place where God is present, and "his Name" speaks of his presence and authority.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He orders them to tear down the pagan altars of Canaan and tells them not to worship God the way those nations worshiped their gods. Worship was to be done as God directed, not as each person wished. The verse does not say here what that place would be.

For today: worshiping God is not a matter of following what seems best to us, but of drawing near to him as he has made himself known. We can ask ourselves whether our life of prayer and faith is guided by his Word and not only by customs or personal tastes.
exp.13:10:
This verse says that the people of Israel could eat any bird that was "clean," meaning the kind God allowed as food. The word "clean" does not refer to dirt, but to what was acceptable under the law. The text then lists the birds that could not be eaten, such as the eagle and the vulture.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them to live as a holy people. These rules about food set them apart from the neighboring nations. Scholars explain the exact reason for each rule in various ways, and the Bible does not always spell it out.

For today: God cares about every area of our lives, even the everyday, such as food. We can ask ourselves whether, in our daily decisions, we seek to please Him and to live with gratitude and self-control.
exp.13:4:
This verse continues a list of wild animals that the people of Israel were allowed to eat: the deer, the gazelle, the roe deer, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the mountain sheep. Some of these animals are hard to identify with certainty today, and scholars give different views on a few of the names. The word "ibex" refers to a wild goat of the mountains.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God called them to be a set-apart people, and so he gives them clear instructions about what they could eat. For them, even food was a way of obeying and remembering their identity.

For today: God is interested in the details of our everyday lives. We can ask ourselves whether what we do, eat, or decide each day reflects gratitude and obedience to God, not out of fear, but out of love.
exp.8:9:
This verse says that God gave Moses two tablets of stone. They were inscribed by the finger of God, a way of saying that the work came directly from Him. On them were written the exact words that the LORD had spoken to the people from the mountain, out of the fire, on the day of the assembly. The "day of the assembly" refers to the time when the people gathered before the mountain.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how they rebelled at Horeb, that is, Sinai. While he was receiving the law on the mountain, they were about to make a golden calf. Moses wants them to see that God was faithful, even though they failed.

God gave us His Word with clarity and care. Today we can read it not as a burden, but as a sign of His nearness, and respond with humble and grateful obedience.
exp.13:8:
This verse says that, of all the creatures that live in the water, you may eat anything with fins and scales. That means fish like the ones we commonly know. The word "may" shows permission, and "fins" are the parts a fish uses to swim.

Moses is speaking to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them so that they would live as a people set apart for Him. These rules about food were part of that covenant. The Bible does not explain every reason, and scholars offer different ideas: health, identity, or symbolism.

Today we are not under these dietary rules, since the New Testament teaches freedom in this matter. But we can still learn to ask ourselves whether our daily habits, even the simplest ones, show that we belong to God and obey Him with gratitude.
exp.28:27:
God uprooted his people from their land, the way a tree is pulled up by its roots. He did it in anger, in rage and great wrath, and sent them into another land. The words "where they are today" show that, for the one speaking, that situation is already visible.

Moses speaks to Israel in Moab, when he renews the covenant before they enter the promised land. He describes what future generations would say if the people turned away from God to serve other gods. It is a serious warning about the consequences of breaking the covenant, not a prediction that God would abandon them without any remedy.

Today we can take faithfulness to God seriously. Ask yourself what things occupy the place that only God deserves, and return to Him sincerely, trusting in His mercy.
exp.5:17:
This verse says that the people should do what is right and good in the sight of God. If they do so, it will go well with them, and they will be able to enter the good land and take it as their own, just as the LORD your God swore to give your fathers. The word "possess" means you will receive it as your own.

Moses speaks to Israel, about to enter Canaan, after forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them that obeying God is not a meaningless burden, but the way to live in the blessing he promised. He mentions earlier Massah, where they doubted God for lack of water.

For today: before deciding something, ask yourself not only "What is good for me?" but "What pleases God?" Obeying him in small things, with trust, teaches us to rest in his faithfulness, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that Moses was on the east side of the Jordan River, in the land of Moab, and that there he began to explain the law to Israel. The phrase "began to explain" means he set out to do it with determination. "To explain" here means to make the law clear, not merely to repeat it.

The narrator introduces the beginning of Moses' speeches. Forty years have passed since the exodus from Egypt, and the people are about to enter the promised land. Moses knows he will not cross over with them, so he uses this time to remind them of what God commanded them and of what they have lived through, so that the new generation may understand it.

For today: it is not enough to hear the Word of God; we should understand it and explain it patiently, especially to those who come after us.
exp.23:15:
This verse teaches that justice must be personal. Fathers are not to be put to death for their children's crimes, nor children for their fathers' crimes. Each person is to answer for his own wrongdoing. The phrase "to be put to death" here refers to the death penalty in Israel's courts.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the Promised Land, repeating God's law. This command stands among laws that protect the vulnerable: the poor day laborer, the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow. In this way, judges were not to punish innocent family members for another's guilt. Some scholars think it also corrects customs of other peoples of that time, but the text does not state this clearly.

For today: do not blame others for mistakes they did not commit. Do not use a family's past to judge a person. And when you are wrong, take responsibility with humility, trusting in God's mercy.
exp.3:46:
The verse says that the people of Israel took possession of the land of King Sihon and the land of Og, king of Bashan. These were the two Amorite kings who ruled across the Jordan River, to the east. The reference to the east is simply the direction of their land from the perspective of the Israelites.

Moses is speaking to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the victories God gave them after they left Egypt. With this he introduces the teaching of the law: God had already been faithful, so now they were to obey him.

For today: when you are unsure of what lies ahead, remember how God has helped you in the past. That grateful memory strengthens trust and encourages us to follow him in obedience.
exp.5:6:
This verse says that parents should teach their children the words of God, and do it consistently. It is not a one-day lesson: it speaks of talking about them at home, on the road, when lying down, and when getting up. The phrase "teach them diligently" means to teach with insistence, again and again.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that loving God with all the heart (verse 5) must pass from one generation to the next. These "words" are the commandments of God that Moses has given them.

For today: faith is best passed on in everyday life. Take simple moments, such as breakfast, a trip, or bedtime, to talk with your children about God, pray together, and tell them how God has helped you.
exp.25:4:
This verse says that the Israelite, when presenting the firstfruits of his harvest, was to remember his humble origins. The phrase "My father was a wandering Aramean" refers to Jacob, who is called an Aramean, from Aram, the region we now call Syria. The word translated "wandering" describes a person who moves from place to place without a settled home; it is also understood by some as a reference to someone who was near death. He went down to Egypt few in number, and there God made him a great nation, mighty and numerous.

Moses gives these instructions before the people enter the promised land. When they bring their basket of firstfruits to the priest, they are to speak this declaration before the LORD their God. It was not only an offering: it was telling the story of God's faithfulness, from a wandering family to a free people with their own land.

Before boasting of what you have, remember where God brought you from. Gratitude grows when you recognize that what you enjoy today was a gift, not merely the fruit of your own effort. Today, tell someone how God has sustained you.
exp.9:19:
It says that Israel must have a deep, reverent respect for God, obey and serve Him, and remain faithfully connected to Him ("hold fast" means staying close to Him with firm commitment), and use His name only to make true promises ("take your oaths in His name").

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the God who loves the fatherless, the widow, and the stranger is the same God who deserves their full loyalty. He also reminds them of their history: they were few in Egypt, and God made them a multitude.

For today: serve God faithfully in everyday life, and let your word be trustworthy. When you promise something, keep it, remembering that God cares for the most vulnerable and expects you to do the same.
exp.15:18:
It says that those who judge must not deny justice, nor show favoritism toward someone because of who they are, nor accept a bribe. "Showing partiality" means treating some people better than others because of their position or their friendship. A "bribe" is money or gifts given to sway a decision. The verse warns that a bribe blinds even the wise and twists the words of the righteous.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just commanded that judges and officials be appointed in every city. Because God is just, he wanted his people to reflect that character in their courts.

For today: be honest in your decisions, whether at work, in your family, or in your church. Do not let yourself be swayed by favors, sympathies, or self-interest. Before deciding something that affects others, ask yourself: "Am I being fair, or is something that benefits me influencing me?"
exp.16:14:
It says that, if Israel comes to want a king, God himself must be the one who chooses who it will be. That king had to be one of the Israelites, "one from among your brothers," and not a foreigner who is not one of your brothers.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He warns them ahead of time that one day they will want a king like the nations around them. He does not forbid it, but he sets limits: the king would not be the highest authority, but someone under God's direction and a part of the people. The verses that follow ask him for humility, without piling up horses, wives, or riches.

Today we can pray for those who govern us and remember that leadership is a service, not a privilege. Before choosing a leader, it is worth asking ourselves whether he or she is close to the people, has integrity, and respects God and the people.
exp.32:0:
This verse introduces the last words of Moses to Israel. It says that Moses, called "the man of God," pronounced a blessing on the Israelites shortly before his death. "Blessing" refers to words of favor and care from God. "Man of God" was a title for someone who spoke on behalf of the Lord. The phrase "before his death" shows that these are his final words.

Moses had led Israel out of Egypt and through the wilderness for forty years. Now the people were about to enter the promised land, and he would not go in with them. Like a father saying farewell, he blesses each tribe. This chapter resembles the blessing Jacob gave his sons in Genesis 49. Here the narrator introduces the speech, and then Moses begins to speak.

Even at the end of his life, Moses thought of the good of others. We can make the most of our opportunities to bless those we love: speaking words of encouragement to them, praying for them, and reminding them of God's faithfulness, without waiting until the last moment.
exp.7:2:
He humbled them, letting them go hungry in the desert, and then fed them with manna, a food neither they nor their ancestors had known. "Humbled" means brought low or put through hardship. The purpose was to teach them that a person does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of forty years in the desert, before they enter the promised land. He asks them to remember the path they have traveled. The hardships were not senseless punishment: God wanted to reveal what was in their hearts and whether they would truly obey him.

For today: even though we work and need material things, we also need to nourish the soul. We can set aside a moment each day to read the Bible and trust God, especially when we go through scarcity or uncertainty.
exp.27:62:
This verse says that just as it pleased the LORD to make you prosper and multiply, so it will also please Him to bring you to ruin and destroy you if you turn away from Him. Here "pleased" does not speak of cruelty; it means that God acts with complete resolve, whether to bless or to judge.
