Being "uprooted" means being pulled up from the roots, that is, driven out of the land you were about to possess.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings for obeying the covenant and the curses for disobeying it. His aim is that they take their commitment to God seriously. Some scholars see here very strong language meant to warn clearly; others see it as a foreshadowing of the later exile.

For today: God takes our relationship with Him seriously. Ask yourself in what area you need to obey Him again, and do it today, trusting in His mercy.
exp.13:17:
This verse continues a list of birds that the Israelites were not to eat. It names the stork, any kind of heron, the hoopoe, and the bat. The exact identities of several of the Hebrew birds are uncertain, and ancient and modern translations do not always agree. Today it is known that the bat is not a bird, but the Hebrew list groups together the animals that fly.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the dietary laws God gave them. These rules set them apart as a holy people, consecrated to God. The Bible does not explain the reason for each animal, so it is not appropriate to invent reasons.

For today: God wants his people to live with attention to him, even in everyday matters. We can ask ourselves which daily habits show that we belong to God, and offer them to him with gratitude and obedience.
exp.23:20:
It says that when the owner of the vineyard harvests the grapes, he must not go back over the vines to collect the clusters that were left behind. The verse itself explains what happens to those clusters: what remains is for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of God's laws. The three groups mentioned had no land and no family protection, so they depended on the generosity of others. The verse that follows asks them to remember that they themselves were slaves in Egypt.

For today: think about what you have in excess, whether time, food, or money, and share it with someone in need. For example, you can set aside part of your income to help a widow, a migrant, or a child without parents in your community.
exp.30:18:
God tells Moses and Joshua to write down a song and teach it to Israel, and to have the people recite it. The BSB's wording "write down for yourselves this song" is a plain way of saying the same thing. This song will serve as a witness from God against the people, that is, as a reminder of what He had already warned them about.

God speaks near the end of Moses' life. He knows that once the people enter the promised land and live in abundance, they will forget Him and follow other gods. The song (chapter 32) would stay in their memory and remind them that they had been warned in time.

For today: keep God's Word in your memory, perhaps through songs or verses you have learned. In times of comfort or of distress, those truths can bring you back to God.
exp.30:24:
This verse says that Moses gave this command to the Levites, who were responsible for carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD. It is an introductory statement: what Moses goes on to say comes in the next verse. The word "command" means an order, and the ark of the covenant was the sacred chest that reminded the people of God's agreement with his people.

Moses had already finished writing the law in a book and had encouraged Joshua, who would replace him. Now, before he dies, he speaks to the Levites so that they will keep that book beside the ark. There it would serve as a witness, because Moses knew that the people tended to rebel.

For today: God left us his Word to remind us of the way when we forget it. Set aside a fixed time each day to read the Bible, and let it speak to you, even when it corrects you.
exp.21:27:
It says that if a man encounters a young woman who is a virgin and not pledged in marriage, seizes her, lies with her, and they are discovered, what follows in verse 29 applies. The verse notes that the word for "young woman" means a young girl, and that the phrase "lies with her" means they had sexual relations. Another word here means a woman who is pledged to be married. The text on sexual violence is hard to read, and scholars debate how to understand each detail of this law.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land and repeats God's laws to them. In that society, a young woman who was dishonored in this way risked being left without support or a future. The law aimed to make the man answer for what he had done and to hold him responsible.

For today: God cares for those who have been hurt and expects justice. We can protect the vulnerable, listen to someone who has suffered abuse, and help them find support and justice.
exp.26:19:
The verse says that God pronounces a curse on the person who sleeps with his father's wife, because he has violated his father's marriage bed. The phrase "sleeps with" is a plain way of describing sexual relations. To violate a father's marriage bed means dishonoring him by taking for oneself what belongs to him within his marriage. All the people are then told to say "Amen," which means "so be it," accepting this warning as their own.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. Curses are pronounced in a ceremony where the people renew their covenant with God. This list deals with sins committed in secret, which the judges might not see. The verses nearby protect the weak and the purity of the family. Some think that "his father's wife" refers to a stepmother, not to one's own mother.

Today it reminds us to respect the boundaries of marriage and family. Even where no one sees us, we can take care of our relationships, honor our parents, and flee from what harms others.
exp.2:15:
This verse says that Moses gave the tribes of Reuben and Gad a territory east of the Jordan River. Their land ran from the Gilead region to the Arnon Valley, with the middle of the valley serving as the boundary. On the other side it reached to the Jabbok River, which was the border of the Ammonites.

Here Moses is speaking near the end of his life. He is reminding the people how the conquered land was divided before they entered Canaan. He reminds them that God kept his promise and that each tribe received a place with clear boundaries.

For today: God cares for us with order and generosity. We can learn to recognize what He has given us, live thankfully within our limits, and not envy what others have received.
exp.21:12:
This verse opens a law about a specific case: a man marries a woman, has relations with her, and afterward comes to hate her. The phrase about having relations is a plain way of referring to the intimate side of marriage. The verse does not finish the thought; the law continues in the verses that follow.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, explaining laws for living as God's people. This law seeks to protect the woman from a false accusation made by a husband who no longer wanted her. Her honor and her life depended greatly on her good name.

For today: let us guard the truth in our words about others, especially when there is anger or lack of love. We must never damage someone's reputation with lies.
exp.26:12:
This verse says that six tribes of Israel would stand on Mount Ebal to deliver the curse: Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali. Delivering the curse means declaring aloud the consequences of disobeying God. The other half of the tribes would stand on Mount Gerizim to bless.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He commands that, when they cross the Jordan, they hold a solemn ceremony between two mountains. The Levites would read out the curses, and all the people would respond with "Amen." In this way it was remembered that obedience brought blessing and disobedience brought consequences. It is not known with certainty why the tribes were divided in this way.

For today: it is not enough to hear the Word of God; we must respond to it. Saying "Amen" is a commitment. Today you can ask yourself in what area you need to obey God more sincerely, even in what no one sees.
exp.8:2:
This verse tells Israel to understand, as a settled fact, that the LORD their God is the one who goes across ahead of them. He is described as a consuming fire, a picture of his great power and of his holiness set against evil. "He will destroy them and subdue them before you" means that God himself will bring those nations down and leave them without the strength to resist. The promise is that God will win the battle, and that the people will take part by driving those nations out.

Moses is speaking just before the people cross the Jordan. They were afraid of walled cities and of people who were very tall and strong. Moses reminds them that the victory will not depend on their own strength, but on God. Right away he warns them not to think of themselves as better than others.

Today we may face problems that seem too big to handle. This verse invites us to trust that God goes ahead of us, to obey him and to act, and to give him the glory with humility.
exp.10:31:
The verse tells the people to be careful to follow all the statutes and ordinances that God is setting before them. The "statutes" are God's commands, and the "ordinances" are his rules for what is right and fair. "Follow" means putting into practice what one hears.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they cross the Jordan River to enter the promised land. He reminds them that God is giving them that land, and that living in it means obeying what God has taught them. Moses wants them not only to know the law, but to live it.

For today: it is not enough to hear or know the Bible. Choose one teaching you already know, such as forgiveness, honesty or helping someone, and practice it today with one concrete action.
exp.23:13:
It says we must not mistreat, deceive, or exploit a worker who is poor and needy and lives on his daily wage. A "wrong" means unfair treatment or harm. A day laborer is someone who works for pay each day, and a person in need is someone who lacks what is necessary. This applies equally to a fellow Israelite and to a foreigner who lives in one of the towns.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and he reminds them how to live justly. The verses before and after show God's care for the poor: returning the cloak by evening and paying the wage the same day. God hears the cry of the one who is treated unjustly.

For today: if you have someone who works for you, whether in your home or your business, pay them in full and on time, and treat them with respect.
exp.1:26:
It says that Israel wants to cross the land of King Sihon, but only along the main road. "We will stay on the main road" means they will not wander off it. "We will not turn to the right or to the left" means they will not go off the road to the right or the left, that is, they will not touch fields, houses or other property.

Moses is speaking, reminding the people what he asked of Sihon, king of Heshbon. He made the request with words of peace, before any fighting. He promised to buy food and water, and only asked for passage to the land God was giving them. The text shows that they first sought a peaceful agreement.

For today: when you face a conflict, try first to speak with respect and clarity. Say what you need, promise to act honestly and keep your word. Even if the other person does not accept, you will have acted with integrity and peace.
exp.27:25:
It says that if the people turn away from God, their dead bodies will be left lying out and become food for birds and wild animals. The phrase "your corpses" points to the same grim image, and the verse notes that there will be no one to scare the scavengers away or to give the dead a proper burial.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings for obeying the covenant and curses for breaking it. In the ancient world, being left without burial was a great dishonor. This image shows how serious it is to abandon God: defeat, shame, and abandonment.

For today: God speaks to us with seriousness because he loves us and wants us to live well. This week, prayerfully consider whether there is something you have been ignoring that God is asking of you, and take one concrete step of obedience, trusting in his mercy.
exp.27:51:
An enemy will surround all the cities of Israel with his army and keep them under siege. This will continue until the high, fortified walls in which the people trusted have fallen. The siege will reach every part of the land that the LORD their God had given them.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He is explaining the blessings of keeping the covenant and the serious consequences of abandoning it. This warning describes the horror of an invasion. Many see in it a foreshadowing of the later downfalls of Israel and Judah, though the text itself gives no dates.

It is easy to trust in our own high walls: money, work, health, or security. But none of these can take the place of God. Today we can ask ourselves what we rest our peace of mind on, and return with humility to trusting Him first.
exp.22:22:
This verse calls on us to follow through on the promises we make to God. The original word translated as "keep" means to carry out faithfully. The phrase "what comes from your lips" refers to the words you have spoken, and the reference to having "freely vowed" means you made the promise willingly, with no one forcing you.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and he repeats God's law to them. Vows were voluntary promises made to God, such as an offering or a commitment. No one was required to make them, but anyone who did make one was expected to keep it without delay, because God takes seriously the word that has been given.

For today: think carefully before you promise something to God or to others. If you have already made a promise, keep your word. And if you find you cannot keep it, it is better not to promise carelessly in the first place, but to speak with sincerity.
exp.26:7:
It says that, upon crossing the Jordan, the people were to write all the words of this law on these stones, and to do so distinctly, that is, in a way that is clear and easy to read. Earlier, verse 2 speaks of coating those stones with plaster.

Moses speaks, together with the elders of Israel, to a new generation that was about to enter the promised land. The stones would be a public reminder of the covenant with God, placed beside the altar where they would offer sacrifices and rejoice before Him. It is not known with precision how the text was carved or written, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: God wants His Word to be understood, not kept hidden. Make a habit of reading the Bible attentively and explaining it simply to your family, so that others can understand it too.
exp.10:20:
God wants the Israelites and their children to live many years in the land he promised to their ancestors. "Your days and those of your children may be multiplied" means that they would have long lives. "As long as the heavens are above the earth" is a way of saying "for a long time," for as long as the sky stays over the earth.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He asks them to teach God's commands to their children at all times: at home, on the road, when they lie down, and when they rise. The promise of a long life is tied to obeying and passing on their faith from one generation to the next.

For today: let us make faith a part of daily life. Let us speak about God naturally at home, at the table, or on the road, so that our children come to know him through our example and our words.
exp.22:0:
This verse says that a man whose genitals were crushed or severed could not enter the assembly of the LORD, that is, the official gathering of the people of Israel. The wording "crushed or severed genitals" refers to a man whose genitals were injured by a blow or a cut, or who was deliberately castrated.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, reviewing the laws of the covenant. Many believe this rule was meant to keep Israel separate from pagan practices, where mutilation was associated with the worship of gods. The text does not give all the reasons, so there are different interpretations.

For today: Isaiah 56:3-5 promises a place and a name in God's house to the eunuchs who remain faithful to him. In Christ, no one is left outside because of their body or their history; we can welcome everyone with kindness.
exp.16:18:
This verse says that the king of Israel was to keep his own copy of the law with him and read from it every day of his life. The purpose was that he would learn to fear the Lord, that is, to respect him and honor him with reverence, and that he would carefully observe all the words of this instruction and these statutes. The phrase "this instruction" refers to the law itself, and "carefully observing" means putting the commands into practice in daily life.

Moses is speaking to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions in case they ever asked for a king. That king was not to gather for himself many horses, many wives, or large amounts of silver and gold, but was to submit to the word of God, like any other Israelite. In this way he would not consider himself superior to his fellow Israelites.

For today: no one is so important or so mature that they can stop reading the Bible. Setting aside a moment each day to read it with humility helps us live out what we learn.
exp.8:25:
Moses recounts that he prayed to God and asked him not to destroy Israel. He calls them "your people" and "your inheritance," that is, the people God treasures above all else. To be "redeemed" means to be rescued through an act of deliverance that cost something. The "mighty hand" speaks of God's power in bringing them out of Egypt.

Moses speaks to the people, reminding them of their rebellion in the wilderness, especially when they made the golden calf. He tells how he interceded for them for forty days. He does not defend the people's sin; he appeals to what God had already done for them and to his promises.

For today: when you see wrongs in others, or in yourself, do not stop at reproach. Pray for them with humility and with confidence in God's mercy and promises, remembering that his work of rescue remains the foundation of our hope.
exp.15:20:
The verse says that the Israelite was not to set up any wooden Asherah pole beside the altar built for the Lord. The word "Asherah" refers to a wooden pole or tree-like object linked to the worship of a Canaanite goddess. Scholars debate its exact form.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He warns them not to mix the worship of the Lord with the religious practices of the neighboring peoples. That is why the next verse also forbids sacred stone pillars, which God detests.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are mixing our faith with customs or ideas that do not honor God. Worshiping him with simplicity and truth is better than decorating our faith with things foreign to his Word.
exp.31:35:
God says that he will vindicate his people, that is, he will judge them and also defend them. The phrase about God having compassion on his servants does not mean that God makes a mistake, but that he will change how he deals with them and will feel compassion. This happens when he sees that his people's strength is gone and that no one remains, slave or free, to help them.

God speaks within the song that Moses taught Israel before he died. God warns that the people will suffer because of their unfaithfulness, but he also promises that he will not abandon them forever. His compassion comes when Israel no longer has anything to trust in.

For today: when you feel without strength and without a way out, do not despair. Recognize your limits, return to God with humility, and trust that his compassion sustains you.
exp.23:8:
The verse says that the people must remember what the LORD their God did to Miriam, the sister of Moses, on the journey after they came out of Egypt. "The LORD" is the name of God, and "Miriam" is the same name that appears as "Mary" in some other English versions.

The text does not repeat the story here, but it refers back to Numbers 12, when Miriam spoke against Moses and was struck with leprosy for a time.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just given instructions about leprosy and about obeying the priests. This example shows that no one is above God's correction, not even a person very close to the leader. It is a warning to take sickness and obedience seriously.

For today: learn from the mistakes you already know. If God has corrected you, or you have seen how he corrects others, do not harden your heart. Guard your words, especially about those who lead you, and respond with humility.
exp.6:17:
He tells the people not to be afraid of the nations they are about to face. Instead of focusing on how strong those nations are, they should remember carefully what the LORD their God did to Pharaoh and to all of Egypt. The name "LORD" is the personal name of God, and "remember" here means to bring to mind deliberately and with care.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. They were thinking, "Those nations are greater in number than we are." Moses does not deny that they are many, but he reminds them of the plagues and of their deliverance from Egypt. If God overcame the mightiest power of that time, he could also carry out his promise against these peoples.

When a problem seems bigger than your own strength, do not start by staring only at the problem. Call to mind the times God helped you, sustained you, or brought you through. Remembering his faithfulness in the past strengthens your trust to face what lies ahead.
exp.11:24:
This verse repeats the prohibition against eating blood. "Do not eat it" refers to the blood of the animals. Moses adds a promise: if the people obey, it will go well with them and with their children, because they are doing what is right in the eyes of the LORD.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In that time, blood was connected with life, and that is why God asked for respect toward it. It was to be poured out on the ground, and the blood of the sacrifices was offered upon the altar. Some think that the aim was also to set Israel apart from the practices of other peoples, although the text mainly underlines the holiness of life.

Today we can learn that obedience to God affects not only us but also our family. Doing what is right, even in small things, leaves a good mark on those who come after us.
exp.0:17:
Moses reminds the people that, at that time, he gave them clear instructions about how they were to live and organize themselves. The phrase "all the things you were to do" means everything that was their responsibility to carry out. It is a summary of the commands he had already given them.

Moses is speaking to the new generation of Israel, close to entering the promised land. He reviews the history of the wilderness. Just before this verse he recalls that he appointed judges to decide cases fairly, without favoritism. Here he closes that topic: they were not left without guidance, but he explained to them how to act.

God gives us direction for living well, and that direction includes treating everyone with justice. Today we can apply this by listening to both sides before judging a conflict in the family, at work, or in the church, and not favoring anyone out of sympathy or position.
exp.12:15:
If a city in Israel turned away to worship other gods, all its plunder was to be gathered into the middle of the public square and burned along with the city, as a whole burnt offering to the LORD your God. "Plunder" means what is taken from a conquered city. The city was to remain a mound of ruins forever, never to be rebuilt.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He warns them against idolatry, which could corrupt the whole nation. The law requires careful investigation before any action is taken. Things set apart as "devoted" belonged to God and could not be used for personal gain. It is a hard text, tied to the unique situation of Israel as a nation under that covenant. Christians do not take it as a model for punishing others.

For today: God deserves total loyalty. Ask yourself what thing competes with God in your heart, and remove its place there with determination, not with violence toward anyone.
exp.11:7:
It says that when the people entered the promised land, they were no longer to worship God each one in their own way, as they had done in the wilderness. "Each one doing what seems right" reflects the phrase "everyone does what seems right in his own eyes." God was asking for order in worship.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they cross the Jordan. In the wilderness, life was temporary, without a land of their own. Once they settled, God would show them a chosen place to bring their offerings and to rejoice before Him. Some scholars also see here a warning against the practices of the neighboring peoples.

For today: it is not enough that something seems right to us when we worship God. We can ask what pleases Him according to His Word, and seek a sincere, orderly, and joyful worship, together with other believers.
exp.8:6:
This verse asks the people to remember and never forget something important: they angered God in the wilderness. From the day they left Egypt until they reached this place, they have been rebelling against Him. "Provoke to wrath" means to make someone angry, and that is how the verse describes what they did to God.

Moses speaks near the end of his life, before Israel enters the promised land. He has just told them that God is giving them that land not because they are good, but because of the wickedness of the nations living there and because of the promise made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Now he reminds them of their own record in order to strip away any pride.

For today: when God blesses us, remembering our failures keeps us humble. We can thank Him for His grace instead of thinking we deserve what we have.
exp.24:0:
This verse describes a legal situation: two people have a dispute and bring it before the judges. The judges must declare innocent the one who is in the right and guilty the one who acted wrongly. A "dispute" here means a disagreement or a legal case. Something "unjust" means unfair or wicked. To "acquit" means to declare someone free of blame.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for living with order and justice. This verse opens a law about punishments, which continues in the verses that follow: even the guilty person was to be treated with limits and with respect for their dignity.

For today: when there is a conflict, let us seek the truth honestly, without favoritism. And if someone turns out to be guilty, let us correct them without humiliating or exaggerating, remembering that they are still a person of value.
exp.7:6:
It says that God is leading his people into a good land, full of water: streams, springs, and fountains that flow through the valleys and the hills. Here the wording points to flowing water that comes up from the earth and moves across the land. Fertile lowlands are good ground for crops and pasture. For a people coming out of the desert, this image spoke of life and abundance.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the land, after forty years in the desert. He reminds them that God corrected them as a father corrects his child, and that the land is a gift from him. He asks them to obey and not to forget this when they have plenty.

For today: think about what God has given you and thank him in a concrete way. When things are going well, it is easy to forget; gratitude keeps us humble and attentive to him.
exp.27:48:
God says he will bring a nation from far away, from the ends of the earth, to swoop down on Israel like an eagle. Its language is one the people will not understand. The phrase "ends of the earth" means a distant place, far from home.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He lays out the blessings that come with obedience and the consequences that come with disobedience. This warning follows his concern that they would not serve God with joy, even though they would have everything they needed. Many see a foreshadowing of later invasions, such as those by Assyria or Babylon, though no single one can be pinpointed.

For today: let us not take God's blessings for granted. When life is going well, it is easy to forget him. Let us take a moment each day to thank him sincerely and to serve him with joy.
exp.19:3:
This verse says that God himself goes with his people into battle. He does not leave them alone: he will fight for them against their enemies and give them the victory.

The one who speaks is the priest, before Israel enters combat. Moses gives these instructions to the people who are preparing to enter the promised land. The priest reminds them that their confidence is not in the size of the army, but in the presence of God, who had already rescued them from Egypt. Afterward, the officers will give other instructions.

For today: when you face a situation that frightens you, do not face it alone. Before acting, pray and remember that God is with you. That does not remove your responsibility to do your part, but it allows you to do it with peace rather than panic.
exp.31:31:
They say that Israel's enemies have a vine that comes from Sodom and Gomorrah, cities famous for their wickedness. Their grapes are poisonous, that is, deadly, and their clusters are very bitter. It is an image: what those people produce with their lives looks like fruit, but it does harm.

The speaker is God, within the song that Moses taught Israel before he died. The verses before say that Israel would be defeated only if God allowed it. Interpreters debate whether "they" refers to the enemy nations or to Israel itself because of its unfaithfulness; the context favors the enemies. In either case, the message is that apart from God there is no good fruit.

For today: examine where what feeds you comes from, such as your habits, advice, and goals. If the root is far from God, the fruit will end up bitter. Seek to be rooted in Christ, who gives good fruit.
exp.3:20:
Moses says that the LORD was angry with him on account of the people. In the reader's wording, God swore that Moses would not cross the Jordan River or enter the good land that the LORD your God is giving the people as an inheritance, meaning as a possession received as a gift.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the land. He warns them against idolatry and reminds them that God brought them out of Egypt. His own prohibition from entering the land serves as a serious example. According to Numbers 20, Moses did not honor God as holy at Meribah. Here, however, he connects his own situation with the situation of the people.

For today: God is good, but he is also holy and serious. Obeying him matters, and his promises stand firm even when we face consequences. We can learn to take his word with respect and trust.
exp.27:31:
It says that the sons and daughters of the people will be given over to another nation. Their parents will watch it happen, and their eyes will grow weary from looking for them day after day. The phrase "with no power in your hand" means they will be unable to do anything to prevent it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He is explaining the blessings of obeying God and the curses of abandoning him. This verse is part of a warning: if they break the covenant, they will lose what they love most, even their family and their freedom.

For today: value your family and tend your relationship with God while you still have time. Invest in your children through prayer, presence, and a good example, and trust that God is merciful when a person returns to him.
exp.27:44:
All these curses will come upon the people of Israel. They will chase them and catch up with them until they are destroyed. The reason is plain: they did not obey the LORD their God or keep the commandments and statutes he gave them. "Destroyed" means they would be ruined. "Obey" means listening closely and doing what he says.

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He sets before them two paths: blessing if they obey, and curse if they turn away. These words are part of the covenant, a serious warning, given so that they would think carefully and choose obedience.

For today: God speaks to us frankly because he wants our good. We can ask ourselves which instruction of his Word we have been ignoring, and today take a concrete step to obey it, trusting in his mercy that goes with us.
exp.0:33:
God heard what the people of Israel had said, grew angry, and confirmed it with an oath, that is, a solemn promise. "Grew angry" means "became angered." "What you said" refers to the words the people spoke.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of what happened at Kadesh-barnea: after the report of the spies, the people doubted and complained, even though God had guided them with fire and cloud. Because of that lack of trust, that generation did not enter the promised land. Only Caleb, who followed God faithfully, would receive that promise.

God hears our words, including words of complaint and distrust. Today we can be careful about what we say in difficult times and, instead of grumbling, remember how God has guided us before and trust Him.
exp.22:11:
The passage says that within the camp of Israel's army there had to be a set-apart place outside the camp where people would go to relieve themselves. It was not done just anywhere, but in a designated spot.

Moses is speaking to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He gives them rules for when they go out to war. God was present in the middle of the camp, so it had to be kept clean and orderly. Besides, these rules helped protect everyone's health, although the text stresses above all holiness.

For today: God cares about the everyday, not only about what is "spiritual." We can honor him with order, cleanliness, and respect for others in the home, at work, and in church, remembering that he is close to us.
exp.26:8:
Moses and the Levitical priests speak to all the people. They ask them to be silent and listen carefully. They tell them that "this day" Israel has become the people of the LORD your God. The verse of "Be silent" is to stop and give careful attention, and the phrase "become the people" means that they are now confirmed as God's people.

Moses is taking leave and preparing the new generation to enter the promised land. Earlier, they had been commanded to write the law on stones and to celebrate with peace offerings. Here they pause to remind them who they are. The call to obey will come afterward. Some think that "this day" renews the covenant made at Sinai; the text does not explain this in more detail.

For today: before thinking about what God commands us, let us remember to whom we belong. Our obedience comes from a relationship with God, not from fear. Today you can stop, listen carefully to his Word, and respond with gratitude.
exp.27:54:
It says that during an enemy siege the hunger will be so terrible that a man will eat his own children, and he will refuse to share that flesh with anyone, because nothing else will be left to him.

The phrase "siege and distress" refers to the enemy surrounding the city and inflicting extreme anguish on the people inside its gates.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings for obeying God and curses for abandoning him. This scene is a very harsh warning about the consequences of rejecting their covenant. Later, the Bible records similar famines during sieges (2 Kings 6:28-29; Lamentations 4:10).

For today: let us take seriously our faithfulness to God, because turning away from Him brings deep harm. But let us also remember that He warns us out of love, and always invites us to return to Him.
exp.1:33:
Israel captured all of King Sihon's cities and destroyed the people of every one of them, including women and children, leaving no survivors. The word "devoted to destruction" describes setting something apart for God's judgment, and the "spoils" are the goods the people took after the victory.

Moses is speaking to the people, reminding them of what the LORD did when they entered the promised land. Sihon attacked Israel first, and the victory is presented as the work of the LORD.

This passage is hard, and interpreters understand it in different ways: as God's judgment on the peoples of that time, and always within a unique moment in Israel's history, not as a model for today.

Today we can learn to recognize that God is just and sovereign, and to trust that he judges with perfect justice. That frees us from taking revenge on our own and invites us to seek peace with humility.
exp.1:34:
The verse says that the Israelites, after defeating King Sihon, kept only the livestock and the plunder from the cities they had captured. "Livestock" means farm animals, and "plunder" refers to the valuables taken from the defeated. Everything else was destroyed.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, reminding the new generation how God gave them victory over Sihon, king of Heshbon. This account is harsh. Scholars understand it in several ways, and the text says that God himself handed over those lands and that he respected the boundaries he had set, such as those of Ammon.

Today we can learn that victories come from God, and that he also sets limits. Before we profit from an achievement, let us ask ourselves humbly: am I within what God permits me?
exp.27:12:
God says he will make his people the head and not the tail, meaning he will place them in a position of honor rather than humiliation. Being above and not beneath describes standing in a favored place. All of this depends on one condition: hearing and carefully following the LORD's commandments.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of their covenant with God: if they obey, blessings will come; if they turn away to serve other gods, curses will come. These promises were given to Israel as a nation under that covenant, not as an automatic guarantee of wealth for every believer.

Today we can learn that obeying God is the wise path, even though it does not always bring visible success. This week, choose a teaching of the Bible that you have neglected and put into practice one concrete step to fulfill it, trusting that God cares for you.
exp.17:11:
This verse says that God regards as detestable anyone who practices the things mentioned before: sacrificing children in the fire, divining, interpreting omens, casting lots, using charms, calling up spirits, or consulting the dead. "Detestable" means something God finds deeply offensive. The verse also says that the LORD your God is driving out the nations before you because of these detestable things.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them not to imitate the peoples they are about to replace. God wants a people who trust in him and not in hidden powers. The text says that these nations are being driven out in part because of these practices.

Today, when you are afraid or uncertain about the future, instead of looking for horoscopes or hidden spiritual advice, bring your worry to God in prayer and seek guidance in his Word and from wise people of faith.
exp.13:24:
If the road to the place of worship is too long to carry the tithe (grain, wine, oil, and animals), the Israelite may exchange it for money. The instruction "exchange it for money" means that the produce is turned into money. "Take the money in your hand" means you should keep it safe, perhaps in a pouch, and carry it with you to the place the LORD your God will choose.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions so that, when they live far from the place of worship, they can still honor God. The purpose was that they would learn to fear him and to celebrate with joy in his presence, together with their families and the Levites.

For today: God cares that we worship him with sincerity and joy, and he does not place impossible obstacles in the way. Think of a practical way to give or serve with joy, even when your circumstances are difficult, and do it with a grateful heart.
exp.19:2:
Before the battle, the priest speaks to the people and asks them for four things: that they not be fainthearted, that they not be afraid, that they not be alarmed, and that they not be terrified in the face of the enemy. The word translated here as "going into battle" means "gathering together to fight."

These words are part of the instructions Moses gives Israel before they enter the promised land. Before fighting, the priest would remind the people that God, who brought them out of Egypt, was going with them. The enemy might be more numerous and have horses and chariots, but Israel's confidence had to rest in God, not in their own strength.

For today: when you face a situation that frightens you, remember what God has already done for you and ask him to give you calm. You do not depend only on your own strength, and his presence helps you keep going with courage.
exp.16:2:
This verse describes the sin of an Israelite who turned away from the true God to go after other gods. He bowed down to them, whether to the sun, the moon, or any of the host of heaven, that is, the stars. The verse calls these "other gods" and adds that God had forbidden this kind of worship.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God had rescued them and made a covenant with them. Worshiping other gods was breaking that covenant, like a betrayal. That is why, in this law for Israel, the punishment was very severe and required a careful investigation before any action was taken.

Today we do not worship the stars, but we can give other things the place that belongs to God: money, fame, work, or pleasure. Ask yourself honestly what occupies your heart, and give God first place.
exp.0:23:
They say that the twelve chosen men set out, went up into the hill country, and came to the Valley of Eshcol. There they spied out the land. Here "spied out" means to explore and to observe carefully.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, and reminds them of what happened at Kadesh-barnea. It was the people who asked that scouts be sent, and Moses agreed. The twelve returned saying the land was good, but the people did not want to go up and rebelled against God.

For today: seeing the good that God has prepared is not enough; trust in Him and taking the step is needed. When God shows you an open door, ask Him for courage to obey instead of remaining paralyzed by fear.
exp.6:19:
It says that God himself will send hornets against the peoples of Canaan, until even the survivors who hide from you have perished. The word "perished" here is the one in the verse above, meaning that they die or are wiped out. Scholars are not sure whether the hornets are real insects or a picture of the terror and confusion that God would send upon them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. They feared nations that seemed larger and stronger. Moses reminds them how God delivered them from Egypt, so that they will trust that He will also fulfill His promise now.

For today: when you feel afraid in the face of a problem that seems enormous, remember the times God helped you in the past. That remembrance strengthens trust and encourages you to take the next step, knowing that God goes with you.
exp.6:4:
The verse says Israel was to tear down the places of worship of the nations of Canaan. The "altars" were where they offered sacrifices to their gods. The "sacred pillars" were stone pillars set up for worship. The "Asherah poles" were wooden poles dedicated to the goddess Asherah. The "idols" were carved images of their gods.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He warns them not to mix with those nations, because their worship could draw them away from God. Destroying these objects was a way of protecting their faithfulness, since God had chosen them as a holy people.

Today it is not about destroying other people's things, but about examining our own hearts. We can ask ourselves: what in my life is pulling me away from God? Firmly removing what competes with him, such as a habit, a relationship or a distraction, protects our faith.
exp.22:1:
Deuteronomy 23:2 says that no one of illegitimate birth may enter the assembly of the LORD, and neither may any of his descendants, even to the tenth generation. The Hebrew word here (mamzer) is unclear. Some believe it refers to a child born of a forbidden union, and others to someone of mixed origin or pagan worship. It is not known for certain.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. These rules, given to Israel under the covenant of the law, aimed to keep the people separate from the practices of the neighboring nations. The concern is participation in the assembly, not personal salvation.

Today, the New Testament shows that in Christ no one is left out because of their origin or their past (Galatians 3:26-28). We can welcome with compassion those who feel ashamed of their family history, reminding them that God calls them his children.
exp.4:24:
This verse says the people were afraid they would die. They had seen the mountain burning and heard the voice of God, and they thought that hearing it again would destroy them. "For this great fire will consume us, and we will die, if we hear the voice of the LORD our God any longer" means that if they heard God's voice any longer, the fire would consume them and they would die.

Moses is recalling what happened at Mount Sinai. The leaders of the tribes and the elders came to him, amazed that God had spoken to them and they were still alive. Even so, they felt that his presence was too overwhelming, and they asked Moses to speak with God on their behalf.

For today: God is holy and deserves reverence, but his nearness is not meant to frighten us without hope. Today we can draw near to Him with respect and confidence, listening to His word with a humble heart willing to obey.
exp.31:21:
For a fire has been kindled by God's anger, and it burns down to the depths of Sheol. The verse says it consumes the earth and its produce, and it scorches the foundations of the mountains. The fire is a picture of how serious God's judgment is.

God speaks in the Song of Moses, shortly before Moses died. God warns that Israel, after receiving so many blessings, would turn to idols. For that reason he announces harsh consequences, but the song also speaks of his compassion, for in the end he has pity on his people.

For today: let us not take faithfulness to God lightly. If anything takes the place that belongs only to him, it is wise to return to him soon, for he is just, but also merciful.
exp.2:14:
Deuteronomy 3:15 says: "To Machir I gave Gilead." The word "gave" here is the one the verse discusses, and it means "handed over" or "assigned."

Machir was a descendant of Manasseh, and Gilead was a region east of the Jordan River.

Here Moses speaks, reminding the people of Israel how the conquered lands were divided before they entered Canaan. God had given them victory over the kings of that area, and Moses assigned part of the territory to the half-tribe of Manasseh, in particular to the family of Machir. Some details of how that region was divided are explained more fully in other passages, such as Numbers 32.

For today: God takes care that each person and each family has a place and a responsibility. We can give thanks for what He has entrusted to us and manage it faithfully, without comparing ourselves to others.
exp.21:29:
This verse forbids a man from marrying his father's wife. The BSB words it as dishonoring his father's marriage bed, meaning the father's marriage and intimacy. Here the verse speaks of wronging the father by taking his wife. It is understood to refer to the stepmother, that is, the father's wife who is not the man's own mother.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of God's laws for their life in the family. This rule protected the honor of the household and prevented rivalries and abuses within the family. The same prohibition is repeated in Leviticus 18:8.

For today: let us care for respect within the family. God desires homes where there is trust and protection, not abuse or betrayal. We can ask ourselves whether our relationships honor those who live with us.
exp.5:13:
This verse commands the people of Israel not to follow other gods, meaning the gods of the nations around them. "Follow" here means to go behind someone, as a disciple does. The words "the gods of the peoples around you" refer to gods that belong to others, not to Israel. The phrase "around you" points to the nations living in the surrounding lands.

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the LORD brought them out of Egypt, out of slavery. He warns them that, by living among peoples with other religions, they could forget God. For this reason he asks them for complete faithfulness, and tells them that God is jealous, meaning that he desires a love with no rivals.

Today, idols can be money, success, or the opinions of others. Ask yourself what you follow more than God, and offer it to him in prayer.
exp.13:13:
This verse continues a list of birds that the Israelites were not to eat. Here the raven is named, and the words "any kind of raven" show that the prohibition covered every bird of that kind, not just one. The names of some birds on the list are hard to identify with certainty, but the raven is fairly clear.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them to live as a people set apart for Him. These rules about clean and unclean animals distinguished them from the neighboring nations. Many scholars also see in them reasons of health or symbolism, although the text emphasizes above all holiness.

For today: God cares for every area of our lives, even the everyday. We can ask ourselves what small habits, such as what we eat or do each day, show that we belong to Him and want to obey Him with gratitude.
exp.20:0:
This verse describes a specific case: someone is found dead, lying in a field in the land that the LORD was giving to Israel, and no one knows who killed him. "Found" means discovered, and "killed" means the person died by violence.

Moses is giving these laws to the people before they enter the land. God wanted the land not to be stained by a death that went unanswered. For this reason, the verses that follow ask the leaders to measure the distance to the nearby cities, and the nearest one takes on a public responsibility. In this way, no life was treated as something unimportant.

For today: human life matters to God, even when no one claims it. We can be people who care about justice, help those who suffer, and do not look the other way when someone is harmed.
exp.16:4:
If a person in Israel, man or woman, had worshiped other gods and the matter was clearly proven, the verse commands that they be brought out to the city gates (the entrance of the city, where judgment was given) and stoned to death. Stoning was the form of public execution used at that time.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. Israel lived in covenant with God, and idolatry was seen as a betrayal of that covenant, a serious unfaithfulness. Notice that the law required careful investigation and at least two witnesses, to prevent unjust condemnations. This law was for Israel as a nation under that ancient covenant.

For today: God deserves first place in our hearts. Today it is not about punishing anyone, but about examining what things occupy the place of God in our lives, and seeking the truth with justice before judging others.
exp.4:5:
This verse says that God presents himself by his name, the LORD, and reminds the people that he is the one who brought them out of Egypt. The phrase "out of the house of slavery" refers to a place of slavery, where the Israelites lived under forced labor. God begins the Ten Commandments by recalling what he has already done for them.

Here God speaks through Moses, who repeats the law to a new generation of Israelites before they enter the Promised Land. Moses reminds them that God spoke to them from the mountain, out of the fire, and that he himself served as the messenger. Before giving the commandments, God shows them who he is: their deliverer.

For today: before asking us for obedience, God reminds us of his love and his help. We can obey him with gratitude and not out of fear, remembering the times he has rescued and sustained us.
exp.5:0:
This verse introduces what follows in the book: the commandments, laws, and decisions that God instructed Moses to teach the people. The words "statutes" and "ordinances" refer to established rules and to fair decisions, and the purpose was that the people would follow them in the land they were about to enter and possess.

Moses is the one speaking. Israel is on the plains of Moab, about to cross the Jordan, after years in the wilderness. Moses reminds them of God's law so that a new generation would live by it in the promised land. This is the beginning of a major section of teaching in the book.

For today: God's word is not given to us only to know, but to live. Choose one biblical teaching you already know today and decide how you will put it into practice this week, at home or at work.
exp.30:21:
That very day Moses wrote down this song and taught it to the Israelites. The verse is plain: he wrote the song down and passed it on to the people. The song is the one found in Deuteronomy 32.

Moses speaks these words after God had told him that the people, once they were settled and well fed in the promised land, would turn away from Him and follow other gods. God wanted this song to serve as a witness, easy to remember, so that in times of distress the people would return to Him.

For today: what we sing and repeat stays in the heart. We can learn verses or hymns that remind us who God is, so that in difficult moments, or even in times of comfort, we do not forget Him.
exp.26:9:
This verse asks the people to truly listen to God and do what he commands. The word translated here as "obey" means to obey, not merely to hear with the ears. The phrase "follow His commandments and statutes" refers to the rules and regulations God gave to Israel. The words "today" stress that the decision is for that very moment.

Moses, together with the Levitical priests, speaks to all Israel. They are about to enter the promised land and have just heard that they are God's people. Before crossing the Jordan, they are reminded that being his people means living according to his law, written clearly on stones. Afterward will come a ceremony of blessings and curses.

For today: it is not enough to know the Bible or to agree with it. Choose one specific teaching you already know and decide to live it out this week, asking God for the strength to do so.
exp.22:10:
The verse says that when evening approaches, the man must wash with water, and when the sun sets he may return to the camp. "When evening approaches" means when the day is nearly over. "When the sun sets" is the time of sunset.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them rules for the military camp. God was present among them, so the camp had to be kept clean and orderly. The uncleanness in this law was ceremonial, not a sin. It was a way of teaching respect for the holiness of God.

For today: God cares about the details of our daily lives. We can care for our hearts and our habits, knowing that He is near, and return to Him with confidence whenever we need to be renewed.
exp.2:24:
Moses asks God to let him cross the Jordan River to see the good land on the other side. His request is humble and heartfelt, a plea from a man who has waited a very long time. The "pleasant hill country" probably refers to the mountainous region of that land, and "Lebanon" is the mountain area to the north, famous for its cedars.

Moses speaks after leading the people of Israel through the desert for many years. They had already defeated some kings, and he longed to enter the promised land. However, God told him he would not cross over, and allowed him only to look at it from Mount Pisgah. The text connects this with what had happened earlier between Moses and the people.

For today: we can bring our desires before God with sincerity, as Moses did. If the answer is no, let us trust that God remains good and wise, and give thanks for what he does allow us to see and live.
exp.14:11:
If a fellow Hebrew, a man or a woman, sold himself to another Israelite to serve him because he was in debt or in poverty, he was to serve only six years. In the seventh year, the master had to set him free. "Set him free" means "let him leave" or "send him away."

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and repeats God's law. Just before this, he asks for generosity toward the poor. This rule protected the most needy from endless servitude and reminded them that God had freed Israel from Egypt. Scholars discuss how it was applied in detail, but the intention of mercy is clear.

For today: if you have authority over someone, such as an employee, treat them with justice and dignity. Pay them well, do not take advantage of their need, and help them get ahead, remembering how much God has given you.
exp.28:25:
This verse describes what the people did: they went after the gods of other nations, served them, and bowed down before them. They were gods they had not known, and the LORD had never given them to the people. "Foreign" means strange, belonging to other peoples. "Bowed down" means they lowered themselves to the ground to worship them.

Moses speaks to Israel at the end of his life, when he renews the covenant with God before they enter the promised land. He warns them what would happen if they abandon it. The neighboring nations would see the land ruined and ask why. The answer would be this: they left the covenant with the God who brought them out of Egypt.

For today: ask yourself what things are taking the place of God in your heart, such as money, fame, or fear. None of them has given you what God has already given you. Give thanks to Him again and trust in Him.
exp.23:12:
If a poor man gives you his pledge (an item, usually his cloak or coat, that he leaves as security for a loan), you must return it to him by sunset. That way he can sleep in his own cloak and stay warm. He will bless you, and this will be credited to you as righteousness before the LORD your God. Here the phrase "be sure to return it" makes clear that this is not optional.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and explains how to live with justice. The law allowed lending, but it protected the poor so that their need would not be taken advantage of. The cloak was sometimes the only thing they had to cover themselves from the cold of the night.

Today, if you have power over someone because of a debt, a job, or a favor, do not take advantage of their need. Act with compassion and seek to treat them fairly and humanely, because God sees how we treat the weak.
exp.13:6:
It says that the Israelites were not to eat animals that chew the cud but do not have a completely divided hoof. As examples it mentions the camel, the rabbit, and the rock badger. It calls these animals "unclean," that is, forbidden as food under the law. Here, in plain terms, they are not to be eaten because of the law. Chewing the cud means that these animals bring up their food to chew it again. Some scholars are unsure which exact animal the rock badger is, since the original name may refer to another small animal that lives among the rocks.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them so that they would live as a people set apart, distinct from the neighboring nations. The text does not explain all the reasons for these rules, and scholars offer several explanations.

For today: God cares for every aspect of the life of his people, even everyday matters such as food. We can ask ourselves whether we are willing to obey him in small things too, showing that we belong to him.
exp.27:15:
This verse says that if the people disobey, the curse will reach them everywhere: "in the city" (where people live and trade) and "in the country" (where people work and farm). The word "cursed" here means being under painful consequences, without the blessing of God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they obey, blessing will come; if they abandon it to follow other gods, the consequences will come. This verse is the reverse of verse 3, where blessing is promised in the city and in the field.

For today: our obedience to God is not only for the temple or Sundays, but for all of life, at home, at work, and in the street. Let us ask him to guide every space of our day, trusting in his grace.
exp.9:7:
This verse says that God chose the tribe of Levi for three tasks: to carry the ark of the covenant, to stand before Him to serve Him, and to pronounce blessings in His name. "Set apart" means that He chose them and marked them out for a special purpose. "As they do to this day" means that this work was still going on when Moses was speaking.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and looks back over their history. The verses around it recall their journeys and the death of Aaron. It is then explained that the Levites did not receive a territory, because their inheritance was the LORD Himself. Many scholars see this passage as a reminder within Moses' account.

For today: God calls each person to serve Him with what they have. Ask Him how you can serve others this week, trusting that He is your greatest treasure.
exp.13:27:
This verse says that at the end of every three years, the Israelite was to set aside a tenth of all the produce from that year and store it in his own town. A tithe is the tenth part of the harvest or of earnings. Produce means the fruits of the land and of labor.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In the other years, the tithe was brought to the place of worship. But every third year it stayed at home to help the Levites, who had no land, and also foreigners, orphans, and widows.

For today: God joins worship with compassion. You might set aside in an orderly way a portion of your income to help someone in need near you, such as a widow, an immigrant, or a family in difficulty, and do so with joy.
exp.2:23:
Here Moses addresses God with respect and admiration. He tells him that he has already let his servant see the beginning of his greatness and his power. Then he asks who, in heaven or on earth, can perform works and mighty acts like God's.

Moses speaks near the end of his life, while Israel prepares to enter the promised land. He had just seen victories over the kings Sihon and Og. After praising God, he asks to enter that land, but God tells him no.

For today: before asking God for something, we can begin by remembering what he has already done. Sincere praise helps us to trust, even when his answer is not the one we expected.
exp.3:14:
It says that the people must be very careful about their inner life and their faithfulness to God. The reason is that when the Lord spoke to them from the fire on Mount Horeb, they heard his voice but saw no form of any kind. "Be careful" means to watch yourselves closely. "Form" means a visible shape or image.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant and the Ten Commandments. Since God showed no form, they must not make idols to represent him. It is a warning against idolatry, which comes up in the verses that follow.

Today we too can invent an idea of God that suits us. To take care of your soul, know God by what he has said in his Word, not by what you imagine or what is convenient for you. Read the Bible with humility and let it correct your ideas about him.
exp.30:25:
Moses commands the Levites to take this book of the law and place it beside the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God. There it must remain as a witness against the people. The words "Take" and "place it" carry the same sense as in the verse above, and "remain there as a witness" means that the book will stand as proof of what God said.

Moses speaks near the end of his life, just after finishing the writing of the law. He knows the people have been stubborn, and so he warns that they will rebel even more after he dies. The book was placed beside the ark, not inside it, and this placement points to a place of safekeeping and constant reminder.

God speaks to us clearly so that we cannot say we did not know. Today we can read his Word with humility, letting it correct us in time and guide us back to him.
exp.18:20:
The verse says that the judge must not feel pity or show favoritism when passing sentence. "You must show no pity" means "you shall not have compassion." The phrase "eye for eye" establishes that the punishment must match the harm caused, no more and no less.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. The passage deals with the false witness who accuses an innocent person. If the judges discovered this, the punishment was the one the accused would have suffered. It was a rule for the courts, not a license for personal revenge. Its purpose was to restrain evil and protect justice in the community.

Today we can learn that justice requires truth and honesty. Before speaking badly of someone, let us consider the harm that a false word can cause. Jesus, moreover, calls us not to take revenge and to respond with mercy in our personal relationships (Matthew 5:38-39).
exp.1:32:
It says that the LORD our God handed King Sihon over to Israel, and that the Israelites defeated him, along with his sons and his whole army. The phrase "delivered him over to us" means that God gave them the victory. The word "defeated" means that they overcame him in battle.

The one speaking is Moses, who is reminding the new generation of Israel, before they enter the promised land, of what happened when Sihon came out to fight against them at Jahaz. Moses wants them to remember that the victory came from God. These accounts of war are difficult, and they are read within the ancient history of Israel and its entry into Canaan.

For today: when you face something great, remember the times God has sustained you. Give thanks, trust in Him, and move forward with humility, without boasting in your own strength.
exp.3:7:
Moses asks what great nation has laws as righteous as the whole law he sets before them today. The word "statutes" refers to commands and rules, and "ordinances" refers to fair and right decisions. The question answers itself: no other nation had anything like it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of forty years in the wilderness, before they enter the promised land. He asks them to keep the law so that the other peoples will see their wisdom. Earlier he said that God is near to them whenever they call on him. Then he asks them not to forget what they experienced at Horeb and to teach it to their children.

For today: God's Word is a treasure, not a burden. We can read it with gratitude, put it into practice at home and at work, and share it with our children through our example and in simple words.
exp.17:4:
This verse says that the Lord your God himself chose the tribe of Levi, out of all the tribes of Israel, to serve him. "Minister" means to serve, and "in His name" means on behalf of God. That service would belong to the priests and also to their descendants, for all time.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He explains that the priests and Levites would not receive an inheritance of land like the other tribes, so the people were to support them with portions of the sacrifices and with the firstfruits, that is, the first of the harvest.

For today: God cares for those who dedicate their lives to serving him, and he invites us to be generous. We can gratefully support those who teach and serve in our church, giving joyfully from what God has given us.
exp.30:16:
God warns that if the people abandon him to follow other gods, his anger will burn against them. "I will hide my face from them" means he will withdraw his favor and protection. "They will be consumed" speaks of being overwhelmed by troubles. Then many disasters and afflictions will come upon them, and the people themselves will admit: "Have not these disasters come upon us because our God is no longer with us?"

The one speaking is God, addressing Moses in the tabernacle, shortly before Moses' death. God already knows that Israel, once in the promised land, will turn toward idolatry and break the covenant. For this reason he commands that a song be written to serve as a witness and reminder for the people.

For today: when hard times come, it is wise to examine with humility whether we have drifted away from God. And although the text is serious, it serves as a call to return to him, who always invites people to repentance.
exp.18:10:
If someone hates his neighbor, lies in wait for him, attacks him, kills him, and then flees to one of the cities of refuge, this case is different. "Hates" means despises and wishes harm; "lies in wait" means watching in secret in order to attack; "kills him" means striking him until he dies.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. The cities of refuge protected a person who killed without intending to. But here it is made clear that they did not protect a killer who acted out of hatred and planned the crime. In this way justice and innocent life were safeguarded.

For today: hatred kept in the heart can grow until it causes serious harm. Ask God to heal resentment before it becomes revenge, and seek reconciliation while you still can.
exp.18:6:
Moses reminds the people of a command from God: they were to set apart three cities within the land they would receive. Setting them apart means choosing them and dedicating them to a special purpose. These were cities of refuge, where a person who had killed someone without intending it could flee, such as a man whose axe head flies off the handle and strikes another person.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and repeats what God had commanded him. The purpose was to protect life in two ways: to prevent an innocent person from being killed out of revenge, and to keep innocent blood from defiling the land. God cares for justice and also for mercy.

For today: God calls us not to act in anger or revenge, but to make room for truth and compassion. We can be a place of refuge for others, listening before we judge and seeking justice with humility.
exp.8:21:
This verse names three places in the wilderness where the people of Israel provoked the Lord. Taberah, Massah and Kibroth-hattaavah are the names of those places. Taberah is related to a word meaning burning, and Massah is related to a word meaning testing. Kibroth-hattaavah is related to a word meaning graves of those who craved food. The phrase "You continued to provoke the LORD" means that the people kept making God angry.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they do not deserve the land because they are good, but that God gives it because of his faithfulness. In those places, according to the accounts in Exodus and Numbers, the people complained, put God to the test, and craved food. Moses lists these failures so that they will not feel proud.

For today: remembering our past mistakes helps us to be humble and thankful. Everything we have comes from the grace of God, not from our merits. When we complain, we can stop and give thanks.
exp.32:4:
This verse says that the LORD was king in Jeshurun, a poetic name for Israel that means something like "the upright one." The verse says he became king at a particular moment, when the leaders of the people gathered and the tribes of Israel came together. The text does not name who the king is in so many words, but most readers understand it to be the LORD. Some think it could refer to Moses.

Moses speaks just before he dies, blessing the tribes. Earlier he recalled how God gave the Law at Sinai. Here he shows that Israel, gathered under the Law, acknowledged God as its true ruler. Then he begins to bless each tribe, starting with Reuben and Judah.

For today: putting God as king over our life is not just an idea, it is a daily decision. We can gather with other believers and ask ourselves: in what area do I need to let God rule?
exp.6:15:
God commands Israel to destroy the peoples whom the LORD will hand over to them. "Destroy" here means to wipe out completely. The command not to look on them with pity means they must not hold back compassion. He also orders them not to worship the peoples' gods, because doing so would be a snare, a trap that would bring them down.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God fights for them, and the verse that follows tells them not to be afraid. His greatest concern is idolatry. Scholars debate how literal or total this command was, but the text stresses the danger of turning away from God.

Today this is not a call to violence. It invites us to be firm with whatever pulls us away from God, whether habits, ambitions, or influences, and to trust that he gives us strength.
exp.32:19:
Moses says, "Blessed is he who enlarges the domain of Gad." Gad is compared to a lion that lies down and then tears its prey apart. The phrase about tearing off an arm or a head means that Gad will overcome his enemies, striking at whatever he reaches.

Moses is blessing the tribes of Israel shortly before he dies. Gad received land east of the Jordan, and he agreed to cross over armed with the other tribes to help them conquer Canaan. The verses that follow remind us of this. Some understand the one who enlarges Gad as God himself, and that is the most common reading.

For today: God gives us room and strength, but not so that we can stay comfortable. We can use what God has given us to help others in their struggles, as Gad did with his brothers.
exp.14:22:
When someone eats the meat of an animal with a defect, one that is not fit to be offered on the altar, they must not eat its blood. They must pour it out on the ground, the way water is poured out. "But" here means "but with this condition." "You must pour it out" means "you must empty it out."

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that animals with defects were not offered to God, but they could be eaten at home. Even so, blood remained something special, because in the law it represented life and was connected with the sacrifices (Leviticus 17:11).

For today: although we no longer live under those rules, we can learn to respect what God calls valuable, such as life. We can give God our best and treat even everyday things with reverence.
exp.24:15:
This verse says that God detests whoever behaves dishonestly in these matters, which means whoever uses false weights and measures, and everyone who commits injustice or fraud. Whatever is called detestable is something God rejects strongly. Wrongdoing that harms another person is dishonesty toward them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that honesty in trade was part of living under the covenant with God. Then he mentions Amalek, who treated the weak without mercy; in this way dishonesty is set against the fear of God.

For today: be honest in your work and in your accounts. Do not cheat on prices, hours, change, or promises. Even if no one notices, God sees and values justice.
exp.17:19:
It says that a prophet who dares to speak a message in God's name that God has not commanded him to speak, or who speaks in the name of other gods, must be put to death. "But" simply introduces the contrast with the prophets God sends. "Dares" means he boldly goes ahead with arrogance. "Other gods" refers to gods that are not the true God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. God had promised to send them faithful prophets, so he warns firmly against false ones. At that time, speaking in God's name was something very serious, because the life and faithfulness of the people depended on it. This penalty corresponds to the law of Israel at that time.

Today it reminds us that speaking on behalf of God is a great responsibility. Before saying "God told me," it is good to check whether it agrees with the Bible. And when we listen to others, we can test what they teach with humility and with the Word.
exp.22:7:
The verse says that the third generation of children born to Edomites and Egyptians may enter the assembly of the LORD. Edom is the people descended from Esau, and the verse names them alongside the Egyptians. What that admission meant exactly, whether it concerned worship, legal rights, or full membership among God's people, is debated among scholars.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. Just before this, the law bars Ammonites and Moabites from the assembly. Here, by contrast, he asks for a more open attitude toward Edom, because Edom was related to Israel, and toward Egypt, where Israel had lived as a foreigner. The shared history is remembered.

For today: God invites us not to be carried away by old resentments. We can remember how we have been treated and offer others, even those who hurt us or are different from us, a patient and fair welcome.
exp.18:16:
Deuteronomy 19:17 says that when two people have a dispute, and one accuses the other before a witness who may be lying, both must stand in the presence of the LORD, before the priests and judges who are in office at that time. Both parties to the dispute must appear there, so the case is heard openly and in front of those responsible for judging it. The people in dispute are the ones who oppose each other in the case.
