Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the land. He gives them rules so that justice would be serious and fair. Requiring two or three witnesses protected the innocent, and bringing the case before the priests and judges reminded them that God sees everything.

For today: if you are in a conflict, do not speak on the basis of rumors or hasty accusations. Seek the truth, go to wise people, and speak as if the LORD were listening, because he is.
exp.12:10:
The passage says the punishment was to be public, so that all Israel would hear, be afraid, and never again do such a wicked thing among them. The phrase about a wicked thing refers to trying to lead others into worshiping false gods.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God brought them out of Egypt, and that their faithfulness to Him was the foundation of their life as a nation. This law deals with the extreme case of someone who drew others into idolatry. Many scholars see here a protection for the identity of the covenant people. We should read it in its historical context, not as a model for today.

Today we can take seriously whatever pulls us away from God, and lovingly care for those around us so that no one falls into what harms their faith. We can remember who has saved us and stand firm in Him.
exp.31:9:
This verse says that God found his people in a desert, a barren, dry and dangerous place. He did not leave them there: he surrounded them with his care, taught them and guarded them. "Barren" describes land that is bare and unable to support life, and "the apple of his eye" refers to the pupil, something very delicate that is protected with every ounce of strength.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in the song he leaves them before he dies. He reminds them that God chose them as his own and led them out of Egypt through the desert. Many understand the "desert" as that journey; others also see an image of Israel's fragile beginnings as a nation.

For today: when you find yourself in a desert, remember that God does not see you as a burden. He cares for you with tenderness, teaches you along the way and protects you. Respond with gratitude and trust.
exp.14:7:
This verse says that when a poor brother is in need, you should help him generously. "Open your hand to him" means giving gladly and without stinginess. "Freely loan him whatever he needs" means enough to meet what he truly needs. "Needy" means someone in want.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them laws to live as God's community. Shortly before this, he commanded that debts be forgiven every seventh year. Here he warns that no one should refuse to help on the grounds that the year of release is near and they would not get their money back.

For today: when you meet someone in difficulty, do not look for excuses not to help. Ask yourself what they truly need and give gladly what you can, whether money, food or time, trusting that God cares for you.
exp.9:0:
God tells Moses to chisel out two new stone tablets, like the originals, and to come up the mountain to Him. He also commands him to make an ark of wood. "Chisel out" means "cut" or "carve," and "come up to Me" means "come up to where I am."

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel, reminding them of what happened on Mount Sinai. The first tablets had been broken when the people made the golden calf. Even so, God decides to renew His covenant. The ark would serve to hold the new tablets. According to the next verse, the wood was acacia.

God knows how to give new opportunities. When we fail, He does not abandon us, but invites us to return to Him with humility. If today you feel you have ruined things, come to God with sincerity and let Him restore what was broken.
exp.6:3:
The passage warns that marrying people from those nations would put the faith of the Israelite children at risk. The one who "will turn your sons away" is the foreign spouse, who could lead your son away from following God. "Other gods" are the gods of other peoples. "Swiftly" means quickly, and "the anger of the LORD" refers to God's burning response to unfaithfulness.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the land of Canaan. He reminds them that God chose them as His own people, and he forbids alliances and marriages with the nations living there, because their idolatry could corrupt Israel's faith. Some scholars see the command to destroy them as a particular judgment of that time, and it is a topic that is interpreted in several ways.

Today we can guard the influences that most shape our heart and the heart of our family. Choose friendships, relationships, and habits that draw you closer to God, and not ones that little by little pull you away from Him.
exp.23:16:
This verse commands that justice not be denied to the most vulnerable. The "foreigner" is someone from outside the community who lives among the people, without family or land of his own. "Deny justice" means to treat someone unfairly in judgment or to take advantage of them. "Take as security" means to keep an item to guarantee a debt; here it is forbidden to do so with a widow's cloak, which was perhaps something she needed to cover herself.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and passes on God's laws to them. He reminds them that they were slaves in Egypt and that God rescued them. For this reason they must treat with compassion those who today have no one to defend them.

For today: if you have any power, whether as a leader, a neighbor, or a lender, use it with justice and tenderness. Think about who near you has the least voice, and make sure you treat them fairly, without taking advantage of their need.
exp.0:11:
Moses asks how he can carry by himself all the troubles that the people bring. The verse speaks of the trouble and weight of looking after so many people, the responsibilities that come with leading them, and the disputes and conflicts that arise between them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land, and he recalls what happened in the wilderness. God had multiplied them like the stars, just as he had promised their ancestors. But a people so large brought many conflicts. That is why Moses proposed choosing wise, understanding, and experienced men from each tribe to help him lead and judge.

No one was made to carry everything alone. If you feel exhausted by your responsibilities, ask for help and share the burden with trusted people. Doing so is not weakness; it is wisdom.
exp.5:1:
This verse says that God wants his people to fear him, meaning to respect him and hold him in reverence, and to keep all his statutes and commandments. This is meant to be passed down from generation to generation: you, your children, and your grandchildren. The word "statutes" refers to rules or laws, and the promise that your days may be prolonged means that God gives a long life to those who obey him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what God has commanded, so that they will keep it once they are there. Shortly after comes the well-known "Hear, O Israel: the Lord is one."

For today: if you are a parent or grandparent, do not keep your faith only for Sunday. Live it at home through your example, and talk about God naturally, so that the younger ones also learn to respect and love him.
exp.23:4:
He says a newly married man must not be sent to war or pressed into any duty. For one year he is free to stay at home and bring joy to the wife he has married. "Bring joy" here means giving her happiness, companionship, and security. The phrase about being pressed into duty means that no other task would be assigned to him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and repeats God's laws for life in community. This command protects the beginning of marriage. It belongs among laws that care for people, especially the most vulnerable, such as the wife and the poor. Some think it also aimed to keep a young woman from being left a widow without children, though the text does not say so.

For today: give your marriage real priority, especially at the beginning. Devote time, attention, and affection to your spouse, and do not let work take over everything.
exp.27:49:
It says the enemy people who would come would be cruel and harsh. "Ruthless" means showing no pity, with no softness in them. They would have no respect for the old, which was a very serious matter in that culture, and no pity for the young. In other words, they would show mercy to no one.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the Promised Land. He explains the blessings of obeying God and the consequences of abandoning him. This warning describes a foreign invasion as the result of breaking the covenant. Many relate it to later invasions, such as those of Assyria or Babylon, although the text gives no names.

For today: God speaks to us with clarity and with warnings because he loves us. It is worth listening in time, returning to him when we stray, and treating the elderly and children with respect and compassion, as that cruel people did not.
exp.14:3:
The verse says that among Israel there should be no needy person forced to beg. The reason given is that the LORD promised to bless His people in the land He was giving them to possess as an inheritance. The word "inheritance" refers to land passed down to a family as its property.

Moses is speaking to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He explains the year of release, when debts between fellow Israelites were canceled, so that no one would stay trapped in poverty. The verse ties God's promise to the people's obedience, as the verses that follow make clear. Later in the same chapter, the text admits that there would always be poor people, so the ideal depended on the people's faithfulness.

Today we can ask ourselves how we use what God has given us. One practical step is to help generously someone close to us who is in need, without belittling them and without expecting anything in return.
exp.4:4:
Moses says he stood between God and the people to pass on what God was saying. The people were afraid because of the fire on Mount Sinai and did not go up the mountain. Then Moses begins to repeat God's words.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what happened at Sinai, though they were children then or had not yet been born. He says the covenant is for them too. This seems to sit uneasily with the statement that God spoke to them face to face in the previous verse; many understand it as God's real nearness, with Moses as the mediator.

Today we can approach God with reverence, but without a fear that keeps us away. His Word calls us to hear it personally, not only through what others tell us.
exp.15:17:
This verse commands Israel to appoint judges and officials for their tribes in every town that the LORD their God was giving them. The "officials" mentioned here were overseers or assistants who helped carry out the judges' decisions. Their task was to judge the people with righteous judgment, that is, with uprightness and impartiality.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He has just spoken about the yearly feasts, when everyone presented themselves before God. Now he turns to daily life: worshiping God and practicing justice go together. The verses that follow call for not bending justice and not accepting bribes.

For today: if you have any responsibility over others, in your home, your work, or your church, make decisions with honesty. Do not favor anyone out of sympathy, self-interest, or pressure, and treat everyone with fairness.
exp.11:15:
It says that the people could eat meat in their own towns, but they were not to eat the blood of the animal. Instead, they had to pour it on the ground, like water. "But" marks a contrast with what came before, and "pour" means to let a liquid fall to the ground.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that the sacrifices were to be made in one place chosen by God, but that meat for everyday use could be eaten in any town. The blood was treated with respect because it represented life, and life belongs to God (Leviticus 17:11).

For today: We can learn to treat life as a gift from God, with gratitude and respect. Before eating, thanking God for food is a simple way to recognize that everything we have comes from Him.
exp.16:5:
This verse says that no one could be sentenced to death on the testimony of just one person. Two or three witnesses who agreed were required. The phrase "the testimony of two or three witnesses" in this verse refers to the statements of those witnesses, and the phrase "a man shall be put to death" refers to the person who deserved that penalty.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them laws to live justly. Before any serious punishment, such as in cases of idolatry, a thorough investigation was required. The witnesses were even expected to act first, which made them think very seriously about the truth of their words.

Today we can learn not to judge or repeat accusations based on a single rumor or a single version of events. Before forming an opinion about someone, let us look for facts, listen to more people, and be fair, remembering that the truth matters greatly to God.
exp.4:26:
Here the people ask Moses to go near to God, listen to all that He says, and then tell them everything God says to him. They promise: "we will listen and obey."

Moses is reminding the people of what happened at Mount Sinai (Horeb). The Israelites had heard God's voice from the middle of the fire and were very afraid. That is why they asked Moses to be their go-between. God approved what they said, though He wished that their hearts would truly be marked by reverence and constant obedience.

For today: promising to obey is easy; the hard part is keeping that promise every day. Before making a decision, you might read a passage of the Bible and ask God for a heart willing to put into practice what you are learning.
exp.27:64:
This verse says that among the nations where the people would be scattered, they would find no repose and no place of rest. "Not even a resting place for the sole of your foot" means they would have nowhere to settle. God would give them a trembling heart (filled with fear), failing eyes (tired eyes that grow dim from long waiting or weeping), and a despairing soul (a spirit weighed down with hopelessness).

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings if they obey and curses if they abandon the covenant with God. This passage describes the consequences of persistent disobedience: exile and anguish far from their land.

For today: a life far from God can fill us with restlessness, even when we have everything. We can return to Him with sincerity and rest in His forgiveness, for Jesus invites: "Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest."
exp.29:13:
This verse says that the word of God is not far away or hard to reach. It is very near you: in your mouth, because it is known and spoken, and in your heart, because it is kept within you. It also has a clear purpose: so that you may obey it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God's commands are neither a distant nor an impossible secret. God has already given them and explained them. For that reason they have no excuse for saying they cannot obey. Right after this, he sets life and death before them so that they may choose.

For today: do not wait until you feel ready or until you find something extraordinary to obey God. Choose a truth you already know from the Bible, repeat it aloud during the day, and look for one concrete action to live it out today.
exp.22:9:
If any man among you becomes unclean because of a nocturnal emission, he must leave the camp and stay outside. It describes something that happens to a man during the night, without his intent, while he is asleep, and the word unclean means he was ritually impure.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them rules for when they go out to war, and he places them alongside the command to keep themselves from "any wicked thing." God was present in the middle of the camp, so it had to be kept as a place set apart for Him. This impurity was ceremonial, not a sin.

For today: God cares about order and reverence, even in small things. We can ask ourselves which things, though not serious sins, we should set apart so that we can draw near to Him with a clean and attentive heart.
exp.3:39:
Moses asks the people to keep God's statutes and commandments. "Statutes" are the laws and rules that God sets down. If they obey, they will prosper, and so will their children after them, and they will live long in the land God is giving them. The words "for all time" most likely point to a lasting permanence, tied to faithfully following God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God brought them out of Egypt and will give them the land, and that the LORD alone is God. For this reason, obedience comes from recognizing Him and trusting in Him.

Today we can obey God not out of fear, but out of trust in his goodness. Choose a teaching from the Bible that you already know and put it into practice this week in your home. Your example also leaves a mark on your children and on those around you.
exp.14:15:
This verse speaks of a Hebrew servant who has finished his six years of service and could go free. But if he says, "I do not want to leave you," because he loves his master and his household, and things go well for him with them, he may choose to stay.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they were slaves in Egypt and that God rescued them. For that reason they must be generous to the servant who goes free. If he decides to stay out of love, he does so by his own choice, not out of obligation.

For today: treat with kindness and fairness those who work with you or depend on you. Let your treatment be so good that whoever is at your side feels valued, and not trapped.
exp.1:11:
The Horites lived in Seir before this time, but the descendants of Esau, also called the Edomites, drove them out. They destroyed the Horites and settled in their place. The word "drove them out" describes how these people took over the land and moved in where the Horites had been.

The one speaking is Moses, reminding the people of their journey through the desert before entering Canaan. This comment about Edom, Moab, and other peoples shows that God also guided the history of other nations. Some scholars think this explanatory note may have been added later, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: God cares for his people and also works in history in ways we do not always understand. We can trust that his promises are fulfilled in his time, even when the path is long.
exp.1:15:
This verse says that all the fighting men from that generation of Israel had now died. The wording "had died" shows that they passed away over time until none of them were left. This closes a long period of waiting in the wilderness.

Moses speaks to the new people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that their parents did not believe at Kadesh-barnea, and for that reason God declared that they would not enter. Thirty-eight years passed on the journey until that generation came to an end. Only after that did God give Moses a new direction to move forward.

For today: God keeps what He says, both His warnings and His promises. If you feel that you are in a time of waiting, trust that God is at work even there. Learn from the unbelief of the past, obey Him, and be ready to take the next step when He shows the way.
exp.12:2:
This verse says that if someone presents himself as a prophet or a dreamer, and even performs a sign that comes true, but invites people to follow other gods, they should not be listened to. The phrase about not listening is explained by its meaning: not listening to or obeying. Where the verse says that the LORD your God is testing His people, it means that God examines the heart of His people. "Other gods" are the gods of other peoples.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the Promised Land. He warns them that a miracle is not enough to prove that a message comes from God. What matters is whether that message agrees with what God had already said and whether it leads people to love Him alone.

Today we can measure any spiritual message, however impressive it may seem, by the Word of God. If something draws us away from Jesus and from the truth of the Scriptures, it is best not to follow it, even if it comes with signs or sounds very convincing.
exp.27:22:
The sky over your head would be like bronze, which does not let rain through, and the ground beneath you would be as hard as iron, which does not allow anything to grow.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they obey, there will be blessing; if they turn away from Him, consequences will come. This passage is part of the warnings, or curses, of the covenant. These were words for Israel within that specific agreement.

For today: we should not read every hardship as punishment from God, since the Bible does not teach that. But this text invites us to examine with humility whether we are listening to God, and to return to Him when we feel that the sky is shut.
exp.3:23:
He says that God is like a consuming fire, and that he is "jealous." "Consuming" means that he destroys whatever opposes him. "Jealous" does not speak of petty envy, but of an exclusive love: God does not share the loyalty of his people with idols.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He will not cross the Jordan, so he gives them a final warning: do not forget the covenant, and do not make images to worship them. He reminds them that God is holy and that his people, by being unfaithful, would face serious consequences.

For today: examine what things compete with God in your heart, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Take God seriously, but without servile fear, for his zeal springs from a love that wants what is best for you.
exp.27:5:
This verse says that God will bless his people in everything they do: "coming in" and "going out" refer to the comings and goings of each day, such as work, travel, and life at home. It is understood as a blessing that covers the whole of life.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they listen to his voice and obey, blessings will come. It is part of a list that includes fields, family, livestock, and harvests. Later he also warns of consequences if they turn away.

Today we can begin the day by entrusting to God our going out and our coming back with a simple prayer. It is not a guarantee that everything will be easy, but it is a reminder that his care accompanies us when we live trusting in him and seeking to obey him.
exp.8:0:
Moses tells the people that today they are about to cross the Jordan River to go in and take possession of the land. The nations living there were greater and stronger than Israel, with large cities fortified like strongholds. The phrase "fortified to the heavens" is an exaggeration meant to say that their walls seemed extremely tall.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, in his addresses before Israel enters Canaan. He reminds them of the reality without hiding the danger. The verses that follow explain that the victory will not depend on their own strength, but on God himself going ahead of them.

For today: there is no need to deny the size of our challenges. We can recognize them honestly and, at the same time, trust that God goes before us. His presence weighs more than our fears.
exp.22:23:
If someone walks through a neighbor's vineyard, the verse says they may eat grapes until they are full. But they must not put any grapes in their basket to take away.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law protected the poor and travelers, who could satisfy their hunger, and at the same time it looked after the owner, so that no one would take advantage of his generosity. It comes alongside commands about keeping promises and about honesty.

For today: we can be generous with those in need, and at the same time be honest people who do not take advantage of what others share. Receiving with gratitude, without exploiting others, is one way of loving our neighbor.
exp.1:21:
He says that God had already done something similar for the descendants of Esau, who lived in Seir. Before them, the Horites lived there, a people whom God drove out from before them. The descendants of Esau took their place and have lived in that land ever since, up to the time this was written. The phrase "to this day" means that they remained there until the present time, and the verse says "to this day," which conveys the same idea.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them that God had already given lands to other nations, such as Edom, Moab, and Ammon. In this way Israel understood that God rules over the nations and could also give them the promised land.

For today: if God cares for the nations and carries out his plans, he can also guide your life. Trust him when the way seems uncertain, and remember how he has helped you before.
exp.28:28:
The verse says that some things belong to the LORD our God alone and have not been made known to us. But the things He has revealed belong to us and to our children forever, so that we may follow every word of this law. The point is that we are to live by what God has made known. "Secret" refers to things that are kept hidden; "revealed" refers to what God has disclosed; "follow" means to obey.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in Moab, near the end of his life, as he renews the covenant before they enter the promised land. The verses just before this one speak of judgment on those who turn away from God. Perhaps questions remained about that punishment, and Moses reminds them that not everything is explained, but what is essential has already been given to them.

Today we can live in peace even when we do not understand everything God does. Instead of being troubled by what we do not know, let us put into practice what we do know of His Word, and teach it to our children.
exp.6:16:
It says that the people of Israel, looking at the nations of Canaan, might secretly think: "These nations are greater than we are; how can we drive them out?" The word "drive out" means to force people to leave a place completely. "Nations" here means peoples or nations.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter the promised land. He knows the fear they will feel before enemies who are stronger in number. So he names that fear honestly and immediately invites them to remember how God rescued them from Egypt with power.

Today, when a problem seems bigger than your strength, do not hide it in your heart. Bring it to God with sincerity and recall the times He helped you before. Remembering His past faithfulness strengthens confidence to face what lies ahead.
exp.1:3:
God tells Moses to give the people a warning: when they pass through the territory of their relatives, the descendants of Esau who live in Seir, those people will be afraid of them. Even so, the Israelites must be very careful not to stir up trouble with them.

Moses recalls how God spoke after many years of wandering in the wilderness. It was time to move forward toward the north. Edom, the land of Esau, belonged to the brother of Jacob, who is Israel, and God had given that land to Esau's descendants as their own. For that reason Israel was not to take it from them or fight with them.

For today: even when we have strength or advantage, God calls us to respect what he has given to others. We can act with humility, avoid unnecessary conflicts, and treat others justly, even those who fear us or think differently from us.
exp.10:3:
This verse recalls what God did to the Egyptian army: its soldiers, horses, and chariots. When they came pursuing Israel, God made the waters of the Red Sea engulf them, and he destroyed them completely. The words "even to this day" show that this display of God's power was still being remembered.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what they themselves saw, so that they will obey God with reverence and trust. Those events were a real proof of his faithfulness and his power.

For today: when you face a great fear or difficulty, remember the times God has cared for you and carried you through. Recalling his past faithfulness strengthens faith and encourages us to obey him today.
exp.27:59:
It says that if the people disobey, God will bring back upon them the same diseases they dreaded in Egypt. The words about them clinging to the people mean they will stay with them, like something that cannot easily be shaken off.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This chapter sets out blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience to the covenant. The plagues of Egypt fell on the Egyptians, and here God warns that if Israel turns against Him, they would lose that protection. The warning seeks to lead them to take their faithfulness seriously.

For today: God warns us out of love so that we do not turn away from Him. Today you can ask Him to help you obey Him from the heart, trusting that His way cares for your life.
exp.11:23:
This verse says that the people were not to eat the blood of the animals. When they killed an animal for food, they had to pour the blood out on the ground, like water. "Pour it on the ground" means to spill the liquid so that it falls to the earth. "You must not eat" means you must not consume it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that they could eat meat in their own towns, without bringing the animal to the sanctuary. But the blood remained special, because it represented life, and God had set it apart for sacrifice. For that reason, blood was not treated as ordinary food.

For today: life is a gift from God and deserves respect. We can practice this by caring for people and creation, and by thanking God for every food we receive.
exp.0:24:
This verse tells how the twelve men sent to explore the land took some of the fruit that grew there and carried it back to the people. Then the phrase "brought us word" means that they reported to them, and all of them said the same thing: the land that the LORD our God is giving us is good.

The one speaking is Moses, who reminds the people of Israel of what happened almost forty years earlier, near Kadesh-barnea. He reminds them that the spies confirmed the goodness of God's promise. However, the following context shows that, even with that good news, the people did not want to go up and did not trust God.

For today: sometimes God shows us clearly that his promises are good, and yet fear still holds us back. Let us remember what God has already done, and take the next step of obedience with confidence in his goodness.
exp.27:52:
This verse says that during a terrible siege, people would become so desperately hungry that they would eat their own children. The verse's phrase "the fruit of your womb" refers to the children. A siege is the enemy's blockade of a city, and the distress the verse describes is a very great anguish.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets out blessings if they obey God and curses if they abandon him. This is a very harsh warning about the consequences of breaking the covenant. The Bible records that something similar happened later, for example in Samaria (2 Kings 6:28-29) and in Jerusalem (Lamentations 4:10).

For today: let us take God's warnings seriously, not out of fear of punishment, but because he loves us and wants to care for us. Today we can examine our hearts, return to God with humility, and trust that Christ bore the curse for us (Galatians 3:13).
exp.32:10:
Moses asks God to bless the work of the tribe of Levi and to accept with favor what their hands do. He also asks that God crush their enemies, those who rise against them and those who hate them, so that they can never rise again. The phrase "smash the loins" is an old expression that means breaking the strength of the adversary, that is, taking away his power.

Moses is saying farewell to Israel and blesses each tribe. Here he speaks of Levi, the ones appointed to teach the law and offer the sacrifices. In the verse before, their faithfulness to God is praised, even above family ties. This prayer asks for protection for their service.

For today: pray for those who serve God in your church, such as pastors, teachers, and volunteers. Ask God to bless their labor and to sustain them against opposition. And offer your own work to the Lord, trusting that he receives it with favor.
exp.31:44:
This verse says that Moses finished reciting the whole song that God had given him, and that he did it in front of all the people of Israel. To "recite" means to say something out loud, either from memory or by reading it. "Finished" means that he had reached the end.

Moses is speaking near the end of his life, shortly before Israel enters the promised land. This song was a reminder of God's faithfulness and a warning against disobedience. Joshua was with him, since he would soon take his place as leader. Afterward, Moses asks the people to take these words seriously.

For today: hearing God's Word just once is not enough. Moses repeated it in full and asked that it be taught to the children. We can choose a fixed time each week to read the Bible as a family or with someone close to us, and talk about what we are learning.
exp.25:7:
He says that God brought Israel out of Egypt with a "mighty hand" and an "outstretched arm," that is, with visible power. The "great terror" refers to events that caused fear and amazement, such as the plagues. The "signs and wonders" were extraordinary acts that showed God was acting on behalf of his people.

Here the Israelite speaks as he comes to the sanctuary to present the firstfruits, the first produce of his harvest. Moses teaches him to recite the story of salvation: the oppression, the cry for help, and how God heard. In this way the offering is not merely a formality but a grateful response to what God has done.

For today: remember the times God helped you in difficult moments. Before asking for something new, thank him with concrete words and with a generous offering, acknowledging that what you have comes from his hand.
exp.17:20:
This verse raises an honest question people might ask themselves: "How can we recognize a message that the LORD has not spoken?" In other words, how can they tell a true prophet from a false one? The name "LORD" is God's name, and "speaking in his name" means claiming that a message comes from Him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just warned them against the fortune-telling practices of other nations, and he promises that God will raise up prophets to guide them. But he also knows there will be false voices, so God gives them a sign by which to test them (v. 22).

Today, not everything said to come from God really does. We can examine each message calmly, comparing it with what the Bible teaches, and without fear of whoever speaks with great confidence.
exp.28:16:
Moses reminds the Israelites of what they saw in Egypt and along the way. There they encountered abominations, things detestable to God, along with idols made of wood and stone, silver and gold. The phrase "among them" speaks of the peoples who kept those gods as their own.

Moses speaks to the people on the plains of Moab, when he renews the covenant with God, and he also includes future generations. He reminds them of what they saw in order to warn them: what is seen up close can attract. Right after this, he asks them to take care that no one turns away from God and becomes a bitter root that contaminates everyone.

Today's idols are not always statues; they can be money, success, or anything that takes the place of God. Ask yourself honestly which things attract you more than He does, and ask Him for help so that they do not take root in your heart.
exp.19:10:
It says that if a distant city accepted the offer of peace and opened its gates, all its people would become forced laborers, meaning they would work for Israel and serve it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. These rules refer to cities outside Canaan; for the cities of Canaan a different and harsher rule applied (vv. 16-18). First they were to offer peace, which limited violence. Today people debate how to understand these ancient laws of war, but it is clear that peace came first.

For today: when a conflict arises, before raising your voice or looking for a fight, offer a way toward peace. Speak first, listen, and work for reconciliation, as Romans 12:18 teaches.
exp.21:20:
If it was proven that a young bride had had relations before marriage and had hidden it, the men of her city would bring her out to the door of her father's house and stone her to death. She was charged with committing an outrage in Israel and with being promiscuous, meaning she had relations outside of marriage. The phrase "so you must purge the evil from among you" means removing from the community what was harming it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. These are civil laws for a nation under covenant with God, where faithfulness and purity in the family protected the community. The case assumes a judgment based on evidence, and the verse before it punishes a husband who made a false accusation. Christians often understand that these penalties belonged to Israel as a nation.

Today we can learn that God values truth, faithfulness, and justice. We should avoid false accusations and always seek the forgiveness and purity that Christ offers.
exp.22:2:
No Ammonite or Moabite, or any of their descendants, was allowed to join the assembly of the LORD, meaning the gathering of the people of Israel for worship and community life. The phrase "even to the tenth generation" points to a very long time. Some readers understand it as a way of saying the exclusion would last for a long, indefinite period rather than as an exact count of generations.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. The verses that follow give the reason: Ammon and Moab did not meet Israel with food and water, and Moab hired Balaam to curse them. Even so, God turned that curse into a blessing. Scholars debate whether this restriction applied to full participation in worship, in civic life, or both. Later, Ruth, a Moabite, was welcomed into Israel and became an ancestor of David.

Today we can remember that God sees how we treat his people. We can also trust that when someone tries to harm us, God is able to turn it into a blessing.
exp.7:9:
This verse says that the people will eat until they are satisfied, and that then they will give thanks to the Lord their God for the good land he has given them. The phrase "when you eat and are satisfied" means having enough to eat and no longer being hungry. Blessing the LORD here means giving thanks and praising God.

Moses speaks to Israel at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, just before they enter the promised land. He describes a land of plenty and teaches them to respond with gratitude. The verses that follow warn that abundance can lead them to forget God.

For today: before or after eating, pause and truly thank God. May comfort not lead you to forget that every good thing comes from him.
exp.21:1:
If you find a lost animal and its owner does not live near you, or you do not know who he is, do not leave it behind. You should take it home with you, care for it, and keep it until your brother comes looking for it. Then you give it back to him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how to live as God's people. Here, "brother" refers to a fellow Israelite and neighbor. The law shows that loving others is lived out in concrete actions, even when no one sees us or forces us to act.

For today: if you find something that is not yours, make a sincere effort to return it. Ask, let people know, or look for the owner. In this way you honor God with your honesty and your care for others.
exp.27:55:
This verse describes a woman who was so gentle and refined that she would not venture to set the sole of her foot on the ground. The phrase about her eye being evil refers to a begrudging and grudging attitude: she will resent sharing anything, whether with her husband, her son, or her daughter. The husband she embraces is the very one she would begrudge.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them of the consequences of abandoning the covenant with God. One of them would be a siege so terrible that hunger would lead to dreadful acts. It is a warning, not a promise of what God desires for them.

For today: disobedience to God and hardness of heart come at a very great cost. Today we can choose to trust God and care for those near us, sharing what we have instead of clinging to what is ours.
exp.7:15:
This verse says that God fed Israel with manna in the wilderness, a food that neither they nor their fathers had known. The phrase "to humble you and test you" means that God allowed hard moments in order to test and shape their character.

Moses speaks to the people near the entrance to the promised land. He reminds them of the forty years in the wilderness so that, when they live in abundance, they will not fill up with pride or forget God. The verses that follow warn against thinking that wealth comes only from their own effort.

For today: when you go through a difficult season, remember that God may be caring for you and shaping you at the same time. And when things are going well, pause to thank him, because everything good comes from his hand.
exp.10:11:
It says the promised land is a place that God himself cares for. "Cares for" means that he looks after it and attends to it. His eyes are always on that land, throughout the whole year, from beginning to end.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter Canaan. He explains that this land is different from Egypt, where they watered the crops through their own effort. The method described there likely refers to some manual system of irrigation, though its exact form is debated. In Canaan they would depend on the rain, that is, on God's provision. For that reason he asks them to obey him and to love him.

Today we can remember that we do not live alone or depend only on our own effort. God cares for us every day. We can work diligently and, at the same time, trust him and give thanks for every provision, because his eyes are on us.
exp.3:3:
This verse says that the Israelites who stayed loyal to God were still alive that day. The phrase "who held fast" means that they stayed close to Him and clung to Him, with loyalty and trust. The phrase contrasts with those who turned away from God and died.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what happened at Baal-peor, where many followed a false god and were destroyed (Numbers 25). He wants them to learn from that experience and to obey God's word without taking away from it or adding to it.

For today: faithfulness to God is not only a duty but a path of life. Today you can stay close to Him through simple decisions, such as praying each day, reading his word, and turning away from whatever pulls you away from Him.
exp.31:41:
God says, in very strong images, that his arrows will be drunk with blood and his sword will devour flesh. The arrows here are the arrows of war. The verse speaks of the blood of the slain and of captives, and it names the heads of the enemy leaders. The word "vengeance" here means just punishment.

God speaks within the Song of Moses, just before Israel entered the promised land. It is poetic language of war. It shows that God defends his people and that he does not leave evil without an answer.

For today: when someone hurts you, do not take payment into your own hands. Leave justice to God, as Romans 12:19 says, and ask him for strength to forgive, to do good, and to trust that he judges with perfect justice.
exp.29:8:
It says that if the people return to God, He will make them prosper in everything: in their work, their children, their animals, and their crops. "Abound" means to have more than enough, and "will again delight in your prosperity" means that God will take joy once more in blessing them, as He did with their ancestors. "For good" means that His purpose is good.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that, although they may fail and suffer the consequences, God will restore them if they repent and obey Him wholeheartedly. It is a promise given to Israel as a nation, within the covenant with God.

For today: God delights in blessing those who return to Him. If you have turned away, you can come back without fear, trusting in His goodness. His blessing is not always measured in money, but it is measured in His care and His presence.
exp.29:15:
This verse says that God, through Moses, commands his people to love him, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments, statutes, and ordinances. "Statutes" are his rules and "ordinances" are his decisions. If they do this, they will live and increase, and God will bless them in the land they are about to enter and possess.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before his death, when they are about to enter the land beyond the Jordan. He reminds them that God's word is not distant or out of reach: it is near them, in their mouths and in their hearts. He sets before them two ways, life and death, so that they may choose with understanding.

For today: love for God is lived out in daily decisions. Today you can choose one concrete action, such as praying before making a decision or being honest in a difficult situation, and do it out of love for God.
exp.24:11:
If a wife, wanting to defend her husband in a fight, grabs the other man in an improper way, by his private parts, her hand is to be cut off. The verse adds that the one judging must show her no pity. "Shame" refers to the private parts.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This is one of the civil laws that regulated community life. It protected dignity and the ability to have children, something very valued in that culture. It is one of the few biblical laws with this kind of corporal punishment, and scholars debate whether it was applied literally or whether it was replaced by a fine, as some later Jewish traditions did.

For today: even when we want to defend someone we love, we cannot do so by violating another person's dignity or body. A good end does not justify means that cause harm.
exp.31:5:
Moses asks the Israelites: "Is this how you repay the LORD, you foolish and senseless people?" He reminds them that God is their Father and Creator, the one who made them and established them as a nation. "Foolish and senseless" means without wisdom or understanding; "established" means set up firmly and made secure.

Moses is near the end of his life, and he teaches this song to Israel. Earlier he described God as a faithful and just Rock, and his people as crooked. Now he confronts them with sorrow: God cared for them, and they responded with ingratitude and disobedience.

For today: before we complain, let us remember what God has done for us. Today, thank God for one specific blessing, and respond with obedience in something you have neglected.
exp.4:27:
God heard what the people said to Moses and replied that all of it was good. "The LORD heard the words you spoke to me" means that God listened closely to them. "They have done well in all that they have spoken" means that what they said seemed right to him.

Moses reminds them of what happened at Horeb. After hearing God's voice from the fire, the people became afraid and asked Moses to stand between them and God. They promised to listen and obey. God approved their reverence, but in the next verse he expressed the wish that this fear would become a truly faithful heart.

God listens to us and values our respect for him. But what he desires most is that our promises be shown in steady obedience. Today you can tell him honestly in prayer what you want to do, and then take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.17:18:
This verse says that God will hold accountable anyone who does not listen to the words that the prophet speaks in his name. The phrase "hold accountable" means to call someone to answer for their response and to hold them responsible. In other words, God himself will deal with the one who refuses his message.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel, and he recalls what God told him at Horeb. The people had been afraid to hear God's voice directly, so God promised to raise up prophets who would speak for him. Christians often see here a reference to Jesus as well, although the text has first of all a meaning for the prophets of Israel.

For today: when we hear God's Word, we should not take it lightly. We can open the Bible with humility and ask ourselves what God is asking us to obey today.
exp.5:7:
God's words are meant to go with the people in everything they do. The phrase about tying them on your hands speaks of their actions, and the phrase about binding them on your foreheads speaks of what a person sees and thinks.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the command to love God with all their heart. Some Jews have taken this verse literally and use phylacteries, small boxes containing Bible passages. Others understand it as a figurative expression. Both readings exist.

Today we can let God's Word guide what we do and what we look at. For example, before starting the day, read a verse and ask God to direct your decisions, your work, and the way you treat others.
exp.2:25:
Here Moses tells how the LORD was angry with him "on account of you", that is, because of the people, and for that reason would not listen and did not allow him to enter the promised land. The words "That is enough" are God's way of closing the matter: he tells Moses not to keep pressing it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, near the Jordan, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them that he pleaded with God to be allowed to cross over. According to Numbers 20, Moses acted in disobedience at Meribah. Here he also connects this with the people. Even so, God lets him see the land from the top of Pisgah and charges him to encourage Joshua.

For today: sometimes God says "no" to a sincere request. We can pray with confidence, accept his answer with humility, and keep serving where he places us, preparing others for what is to come.
exp.15:0:
This verse tells the people of Israel to observe the month of Abib, meaning to keep it in mind and honor it. In that month they were to celebrate the Passover to the LORD their God. Abib means "ripening ears of grain," and it was the spring month when the barley ripens. Later it came to be called Nisan. The phrase "by night" points to the fact that God brought them out of Egypt in the depths of darkness.

Moses speaks to the people in Deuteronomy, shortly before they enter the promised land. He repeats the law so they will not forget what God has done. The Passover was a yearly celebration of remembrance and thankfulness for their rescue from slavery.

For today: make a habit of remembering how God has helped you. Once a month, write down something God has done for you and give him thanks. A grateful heart trusts God more easily.
exp.21:13:
This verse describes a man who, after marrying, stops loving his wife. He then accuses her of shameful conduct and begins speaking badly of her, saying that he married her and had relations with her but discovered she was not a virgin. Spreading a bad reputation means spreading claims that damage her good name. Having relations with her refers to sexual intimacy within the marriage.

Moses is giving laws to Israel before they enter the promised land. This law seeks to restrain false accusations and to protect the young woman. Parents could present evidence before the elders, at the city gate, where cases were judged. Some of that evidence has been understood in different ways.

For today: let us be careful with our words. Speaking badly of someone to justify ourselves or to harm them is unjust. Let us seek the truth and defend those who are accused without reason.
exp.23:14:
This verse says that a poor worker should be paid his wages each day, before sunset. A day's wage is the payment for one day of work, and the verse's word "wages" fits that meaning. "Depends on them" means that he relies on this money to feed himself and support his family. If he is not paid, he may cry out to God against his employer, and that would be sin for the one who kept back the payment.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of God's law. This command protects the poor day laborer, whether he is an Israelite or a foreigner. In that time many people lived from day to day and had no savings. God shows that he hears the cry of the weak.

For today: if you employ someone, whether in your business or in your home, pay them in full and on time. Do not use delays to gain an advantage. Paying justly is one way of honoring God.
exp.3:9:
This verse looks back to the day the people stood before the LORD your God at Horeb, another name for Mount Sinai. The LORD told Moses, "Gather the people before Me to hear My words." The purpose was twofold: that they would learn to fear God, meaning to respect and honor Him with reverence, all the days they live on the earth, and that they would teach those words to their children.

Moses is speaking to the new generation of Israel, before they enter the promised land. Many of them were children or had not yet been born when the people stood at Horeb. He reminds them of that encounter so that they do not forget what God said and what God did.

For today: faith is passed on from one generation to another. Set aside regular time, even if brief, to read the Bible with your children, nephews, nieces, or younger people, and tell them how God has worked in your life.
exp.25:11:
It says that when an Israelite had finished setting aside a tenth of all his produce in the third year, called "the year of the tithe," he was to give it to the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. To "tithe" means to set aside a tenth part. "Within your gates" refers to the towns or cities. They would eat there until they were full.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The Levites received no inheritance of land, and foreigners, orphans, and widows often lacked provision. This tithe every three years ensured their food. Then the Israelite declared before God that he had obeyed.

For today: God joins generosity with care for the vulnerable. We can set aside a fixed part of what we earn to help, with a name and a face, a person in need near us, and do it with gratitude, not out of obligation.
exp.32:22:
Moses says that Naphtali is abounding with favor, that is, rich in God's grace and goodwill. He is full of the blessing of the LORD and will take possession of the sea and the south. The words "the sea" can also be understood as "the lake," and it is not known with certainty which exact area they refer to.

Moses speaks shortly before he dies. He blesses each tribe of Israel before they enter the promised land. Naphtali was one of the tribes, and his blessing speaks of abundance and of an inheritance that comes from God.

For today: what we have comes from the goodness of God. Today you can give thanks for what he has given you and live content, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.3:38:
It says that today we should learn and take to heart one truth: the Lord is God, both in heaven above and on the earth below, and there is no other. "Know therefore this day and take to heart" means to bring this truth to mind and think it over until you take it very seriously. The name "the LORD" is the name of God.

Moses speaks near the end of his life, addressing the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how God brought them out of Egypt with great power, out of love for their ancestors. For this reason he calls them to acknowledge that only God deserves their loyalty, and then to obey him.

For today: when you feel fear or pressure, remember in prayer what God has done for you. Repeating that he rules over all helps you trust him and live in obedience, not just believe it in your mind.
exp.6:10:
This verse says that the people must take care to obey everything God asks of them. The word "keep" means to carry out with attention. "Commandments" are God's general orders, "statutes" are his fixed rules, and "ordinances" are his decisions about what is right. "Today" stresses that obedience is lived in the present.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God is faithful and that his covenant is real. That is why obedience is not a cold burden, but the response of a people who have already known God's faithfulness. Afterward, Moses speaks of blessings that accompany that path.

For today: do not wait until you feel ready to obey God. Choose one concrete step today, such as forgiving someone, being honest at work, or setting aside time for prayer. Do it trusting that God is faithful and good to you.
exp.8:3:
This verse tells Israel not to think, once the Lord their God has driven those nations out before them, "Because of my righteousness the Lord has brought me in to possess this land." The words "do not say in your heart" mean "do not think or tell yourself inwardly." "Wickedness" means evil and rebellion against God. According to the text, the Lord is driving out these nations because of their wickedness, not because of Israel's goodness.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. They will face strong enemies, and defeating them could fill them with pride. That is why Moses reminds them that the victory comes from the Lord, from his promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and not from their own merits. He even tells them they are a stubborn people.

For today: when you receive blessings or achievements, give thanks instead of boasting. Everything good comes from God's grace, not from our deserving it.
exp.24:7:
This verse describes what happens when a man refuses to marry his brother's widow. The elders of the city, who were the leaders and judges of the people, summon him and speak with him. If he persists and says, "I do not want to marry her," the matter moves to the next step.

Moses gives this instruction to the people of Israel. It was the practice known as levirate marriage: the brother was to give a son to the widow so that the name of the dead man would not disappear and the family would be cared for. Before any consequence is applied, the elders talk with him. In this way there is room for conversation and not a hasty decision.

For today: before judging someone for failing to keep a commitment, let us speak with him face to face and listen to his reasons. And when it falls to us to care for someone vulnerable, let us do so with responsibility.
exp.1:5:
Israel was to pay silver for the food and water it needed from the descendants of Esau. Food is the thing the verse speaks of here. They were not to take it by force or take advantage of them, but to pay for what they received.

Moses recalls what God commanded them while the people were traveling through the region of Seir, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. The Edomites were distant relatives, descendants of Esau, the brother of Jacob. God had given them that land, so Israel was not to take it from them or stir up conflict. Although the Edomites were afraid, Israel was to treat them with respect and honesty.

For today: We can trust that God takes care of us without having to take advantage of anyone. Deal honestly with those who have something you need, pay what is fair, and respect what belongs to others.
exp.2:2:
It says that the LORD our God handed Og, king of Bashan, and his whole army over to Israel. Israel struck them down until no survivor was left. The word "struck" means they attacked and defeated them in battle, and the phrase "into our hands" means that God gave them the victory.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them how God helped them before they entered the promised land. Og came out to fight against them, but God had already promised the victory, just as with King Sihon. This war is hard to read; the text presents it as a judgment and a unique action in Israel's history, not as a model for today.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, remember how God has helped you before. That remembrance strengthens confidence to keep going, without fear and with obedience.
exp.31:46:
It says that God's law is not an empty or worthless thing. It is the very life of the people. Obeying it would help them live many years in the land they were going to enter by crossing the Jordan. The word "idle" here means empty or of no importance, and the phrase "live long" means to live a long time.

Moses is speaking at the end of his last address to Israel. He is about to die and will not enter the promised land. He wants the people to take God's words seriously and to teach them to their children. Afterward, God tells him that he will go up Mount Nebo to see the land from a distance.

For today: let us not treat the Word of God as a decoration or a boring duty. Set aside a moment each day to read it, ask God to guide you, and look for one specific thing to put into practice. In this way it becomes a path of life, not just information.
exp.32:27:
The verse says that Israel, a descendant of Jacob, will live at rest and without fear, set apart from its enemies, in a land of grain and new wine. Dew will also drip from the heavens, which was an important source of moisture for the crops. "Dwells securely" means living safe, without depending on other peoples. "The fountain of Jacob" is understood as the offspring that springs from Jacob, though some interpret it in other ways.

Moses is speaking. He is blessing the tribes of Israel shortly before he dies. Just before this verse, he recalls that God is a refuge and that he drives out the enemy. For this reason, Israel's security does not come from its own strength, but from God's protection.

Today we can learn to rest in the fact that God cares for us. We can work hard, but without living ruled by fear, trusting that He is our refuge and provides what we need.
exp.31:25:
God says in the song of Moses that he had considered cutting Israel to pieces and erasing them from the earth. The phrase "I would have said that I would cut them to pieces" means that God had thought about destroying them completely. The words "blot out their memory from mankind" mean that people would not even remember that they had existed.

Here God speaks in the Song of Moses. Israel had been unfaithful, worshiping other gods, and for that reason God announces harsh punishments. But the next verse shows that God holds back: he does not want the enemies to boast that they won by their own strength and fail to acknowledge the LORD.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but his patience is greater than our failures. If you have drifted away from him, do not harden your heart; return with humility, trusting that his mercy is still open.
exp.2:0:
This verse says that the Israelites turned around and went up the road toward Bashan, a region north of the Jordan, and there Og, king of Bashan, attacked them. He came out with his whole army to meet them in battle near a city called Edrei.

Moses is speaking to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of what they have already lived through, before entering the promised land. He tells them this battle was not chance: God gave them the victory, as before with King Sihon. Moses wants them to remember and to trust God.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, remember how God has helped you before. That memory strengthens trust to keep moving forward.
exp.32:11:
He says that Benjamin, whom God calls "the beloved of the LORD," will rest secure in him. God shields Benjamin all day long, and Benjamin rests on his shoulders.

Moses speaks just before he dies, blessing each tribe of Israel. He blesses Benjamin with the image of a cared-for child. Some think the phrase about resting on God's shoulders points to Benjamin's land, where Jerusalem and the temple later stood, but this is not certain; others see it only as a picture of God's care.

For today: if you belong to God, you can rest in his care. When you feel fear or pressure today, pause for a moment and pray, remembering that God sustains and protects you.
exp.32:28:
Israel is called blessed, very richly blessed, because no other people is like them: the Lord saved them. God himself is their shield, the one who protects and helps them, and he is also the sword they boast in, the source of their strength and glory. Their enemies will cower before them, and Israel will trample the enemy's strongholds, the high and fortified places where they once felt safe.

Moses speaks just before he dies. He is blessing the tribes of Israel and closes with this song of praise. He wants the people to remember that their victory and their future depend on God, not on their own strength. Some scholars understand the trampling of high places as a military victory, and others as a picture of complete security.

For today: when you feel weak or threatened, remember that God cares for you and sustains you. Rest in his help, and give thanks for his salvation instead of trusting only in your own strength.
exp.33:1:
This verse continues the list of what God showed Moses from the mountain. It names the territory of Naphtali, the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, and all the land of Judah. The Western Sea, which is the Mediterranean, marks the western edge of the land. In this way, Moses sees the promised land from north to west.

The narrator tells of Moses' final moments. God himself shows him the land from Mount Nebo, before his death. Israel is about to enter Canaan, but Moses will not enter, as God had told him. The book is traditionally attributed to Moses, although this final chapter is told by another voice; scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: God keeps his promises, even though we do not always see them fulfilled in our lifetime. We can trust Him and work in faith, knowing that others will receive what God began with us.
exp.31:17:
This verse says that the people of Israel ignored God. It calls him "the Rock," an image of someone firm, secure, and faithful. It also says that God is the one who "brought them forth" and "gave them birth," meaning the one who gave them life and made them into a people. Here "gave them birth" means the one who brought them into being. To forget God is not only to fail to remember him, but to live as if he did not matter.

Moses is speaking. Before he dies, he teaches them a song to warn them. He reminds them that God cared for them, but they turned away after other gods. That is why, in the verses that follow, God grieves and becomes angry, and shows the consequences of their unfaithfulness.

For today: it is easy to forget God when everything is going well. You can set aside a few minutes each day to thank him for something specific he has given you, and so keep your heart steady in him.
exp.28:11:
This verse says that the whole people are gathered to enter into God's covenant. A covenant is a serious agreement between God and his people. The oath is the promise made with solemn commitment. God is making this covenant with them, and "today" stresses that it is a present and real moment.

Moses speaks to Israel on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He gathers everyone: leaders, men, children, women, and foreigners. His purpose is to renew the covenant with the new generation, so that they themselves choose to follow God and do not simply rely on the faith of their parents.

For today: faith is not passed down automatically; each person is invited to respond to God personally. You can pray a simple prayer today, renewing your commitment to trust Him and obey Him, regardless of your age or your story.
exp.5:10:
This verse describes what God would give Israel in the promised land: houses full of every good thing they did not fill, wells they did not dig, and vineyards and olive groves they did not plant. The phrase "when you eat and are satisfied" is explained by the verse itself, which describes the people eating and being satisfied. The sentence is left open and is completed in the next verse.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the land. He reminds them that everything they will receive will be a gift from God, not the fruit of their own effort. For that reason he warns them that, when they live in abundance, they must not forget the One who gave it to them.

For today: when you have food, shelter, work, or peace, pause to give thanks. Much of what we enjoy we receive from others and from God. A grateful heart helps us not to forget this in good times.
exp.21:28:
If a man takes a young virgin who is not engaged, lies with her, and they are discovered, he must pay her father fifty pieces of silver. She will also become his wife, and he may never divorce her for as long as he lives. "Lie with her" is a plain way of describing sexual relations. "He has violated her" means he wronged her and left her in a situation of shame and disadvantage.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, giving them laws for their life together as a community. In that society, a woman without a husband was very vulnerable. This law required the man to answer for what he had done, both financially and by taking on lifelong responsibility for her. Scholars debate whether the woman could refuse the marriage; the text does not make this clear.

For us today, the principle is that no one should use another person and then walk away. Every act has consequences, and we must honestly take responsibility for the harm we cause.
exp.13:23:
This verse deals with a practical problem. If the place God chose for worship was very far away, and the distance was too great for a person to carry the tithe (the tenth part of the harvest and of the animals), the person was not left without options. The phrase "carry that with which the LORD your God has blessed you" refers to carrying the tithe along that distance, as the verse itself says. The words "because the place where the LORD your God will choose to put His Name is too far away" show that the problem arises because God had given a good harvest.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for their life there. The tithe was to be eaten with joy before God, so that they would learn to revere and honor him. The law took into account the distance and the real difficulty people faced.

For today: God is concerned with our practical limitations, but he wants us to honor him with gratitude. When he blesses us, let us use what we have with joy, generosity, and thankfulness, without making excuses.
exp.25:6:
This verse says that the people of Israel called out to the LORD, the God of their ancestors, for help. The LORD heard their voice and saw their suffering. The word "affliction" means pain and distress; "toil" refers to the hard, exhausting work of slavery; "oppression" is the cruel treatment of someone who holds power over others.

Each Israelite speaks this when bringing the firstfruits of his harvest to God in the promised land. Moses teaches them to remember their history: they came from a wandering ancestor (many understand this to be Jacob) and were slaves in Egypt. In this way they acknowledged that the land was a gift from God, not their own achievement.

For today: when you are going through a difficult time, call out to God with confidence, because He sees and hears. And when He helps you, do not forget it; bring Him your gratitude and tell others what He has done for you.
exp.8:18:
Moses says he was afraid of the Lord's strong anger against the people, anger that was enough to destroy them because of their sin. But the Lord listened to him once more.

The words "anger" and "wrath" describe a very intense kind of displeasure, and "directed against" means the anger was aimed at them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, reminding them of what happened at Mount Sinai when they made the golden calf. He pleaded on their behalf during forty days of fasting. He tells them this so that they will not think they deserve the land because they are good, but so that they will recognize the Lord's mercy.

For today: praying for others, even for those who have failed us, is an act of love. God listens to those who come to Him with humility. We can ask for forgiveness and mercy for our family, our church, and our community, trusting that He hears.
exp.7:8:
This verse says that in the promised land the people will have food in plenty and will lack nothing. It describes a land rich in minerals: its rocks are iron, and from its hills copper can be mined. "Ready to be mined" means the metal is there to be taken out, and copper is the metal the verse names.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before they enter the land. He describes it to them with gratitude and hope. But he soon warns them not to forget God when they live in abundance.

For today: when you have what you need, do not take it as something you earned on your own. Make a habit of thanking God for your food, your work, and your home, and remember to obey him in the good times too, not only when you need help.
exp.11:19:
When the LORD expands your territory as He promised, and you crave meat and say, "I want to eat meat," you may eat it whenever you want. This verse says that once God enlarges Israel's land, as he promised, a person who desires meat may eat it freely, according to what their heart longs for. "Your" refers to each person, to one's own appetite and desire.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. Until then, animals for sacrifice were brought before God at one central place. Now, with a larger territory, many would live far from that place. That is why God permits eating meat at home, without it being an act of worship. Even so, the people are reminded to care for the Levites.

For today: God allows us to enjoy with gratitude what he gives, such as food. Let us enjoy without selfishness, remembering to share with those in need and to support those who serve.
exp.17:21:
It says that if someone speaks as a prophet in the name of the LORD, and the message does not come to pass or come true, then the LORD did not send that message. The prophet has spoken presumptuously, which means he spoke on his own authority while claiming to speak for God. For that reason the people were not to be afraid of him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He had promised them that God would raise up true prophets, and now he gives them a way to tell true prophets from false ones, since false ones could mislead them or lead them toward other gods. Some scholars point out that this verse is a test, and that it should be read together with the verse before it and with Deuteronomy 13, where it also matters that the message be faithful to God.

Today, let us not accept without examination everything someone says in the name of God. Let us compare their words with the Bible, observe their fruit, and not live in fear before voices that speak with great confidence.
exp.12:11:
This verse begins a new situation: God warns that Israel could hear a report about one of the cities He is giving them to live in.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. Shortly before, he dealt with the case of a person who led others to worship idols. Now he speaks of a similar problem, but one that affects an entire city. His purpose is to protect the people's faithfulness toward God, who brought them out of Egypt. Notice that he does not command action based on a simple report; he calls for careful investigation.

Today this teaches us not to believe or repeat everything we hear. Before judging, it is wise to investigate honestly and seek the truth, always taking care to remain faithful to God.
exp.28:0:
This verse introduces a new moment: God commands Moses to make a covenant with the Israelites in the land of Moab. This covenant is in addition to the one God had already made with them at Horeb, which is another name for Mount Sinai. The phrase "in addition to" in the verse means that this covenant comes alongside the earlier one, and the word "make" means that Moses was to set up or agree on this commitment with them.

Moses speaks at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. The generation that came out of Egypt was almost gone, and the Israelites were about to enter the promised land. That is why the covenant is renewed, so that the new generation would take it on as their own. Some understand this covenant as a renewal of the one at Horeb, and others as a complement to it; the Bible does not fully make this clear.

For today: it is not enough to inherit the faith of others. Each person can renew their commitment to God, remembering what He has done and deciding to follow Him sincerely.
exp.24:10:
It says that if two men are fighting and the wife of one comes to rescue her husband, but reaches out and grabs the other man's genitals, she would be committing a serious offense. The law that follows orders that her hand be cut off, without mercy.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, going over laws for their life together. The case protects the dignity of the body and the ability to have children, which was very valuable in that culture. The punishment is very harsh, and it is not clear how it was carried out; some scholars believe it was a symbolic or different kind of penalty, and this is debated.

For today: even with good intentions, such as defending someone we love, we cannot justify actions that harm or humiliate others. Let us look for ways to help that always respect the dignity of people.
exp.12:12:
