This passage describes a serious case: wicked men have arisen from among the people and led the inhabitants of their city astray, saying, "Let us go and serve other gods," gods the people had never known. To lead someone astray means to draw them away from what is right and pull them toward something wrong.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains how to act if someone leads them to abandon the God who rescued them. The command to investigate the facts carefully follows right away. The severity of the sentence reflects that Israel was a nation under covenant with God, and idolatry was treated as betrayal of that covenant.

For today: let us be careful about whose spiritual influence we accept. Let us test every teaching against the Bible and not follow anyone who would turn us away from Christ, even if they speak with conviction or are popular.
exp.23:21:
This verse reminds the people of Israel that they themselves were slaves in Egypt. That is why God commands them to leave some of the harvest for others. The word "slaves" here refers to people held in bondage. To "gather what is left behind" means going back over the field to pick up what remained, and to "harvest the grapes" means gathering the fruit of the vineyard.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land, and passes on what God orders. The laws in this passage protect the most vulnerable: the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow, who had no land and no one to support them. God appeals to Israel's memory: whoever was oppressed and rescued must treat the needy with kindness.

Today we can remember how much grace we have received and share from what we have. Perhaps by setting aside a part of our income or our time to help someone in need, without expecting anything in return.
exp.0:13:
This verse says that the people agreed with Moses' proposal. They answered, "What you propose to do is good." In other words, they judged that choosing leaders to help govern and settle the people's problems was a good plan.

Here Moses is speaking, reminding Israel of what happened years earlier, near Mount Sinai (Horeb). He felt weighed down by having to carry so many disputes and responsibilities alone. So he asked them to choose wise, understanding, and experienced men, and the people accepted. Afterward Moses appointed them as heads and judges.

For today: no one is made to carry everything alone. Asking for help and sharing responsibilities is not weakness but wisdom. And when someone gives us good advice, we can listen with humility and put it into practice, in the family, the church, or at work.
exp.32:16:
He says that Joseph is like a young bull, strong and full of majesty, like the firstborn bull of the herd. His horns are like those of a wild ox, and that animal was very powerful. With those horns he will gore the nations, pushing them out to the ends of the earth. Ephraim and Manasseh, the two sons of Joseph, are his myriads and his thousands, that is, great multitudes.

Moses speaks. Before he dies, he blesses each tribe of Israel. Here he blesses Joseph, represented by Ephraim and Manasseh, promising them strength and victory when they enter the promised land. It is poetic language, not a literal description.

For today: our strength does not come from ourselves, but from the grace of God, as the verse before it says. Trust that He gives you courage to face your challenges, and use it with humility.
exp.17:12:
It says that God's people must be "blameless" before Him. The Hebrew word behind this idea speaks of being whole, without duplicity, complete in loyalty. It does not mean having no faults, but belonging to God wholeheartedly, without mixing in other sources of guidance.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just warned them against sorcery, divination, and contact with the dead, practices of the peoples of Canaan. God promises them something better: a prophet who would speak to them on His behalf. Many Christians see in that promise an announcement of Jesus.

For today: when you seek direction, do not divide your loyalty between God and other voices such as horoscopes or superstitions. Pray, read the Bible, and seek counsel from mature believers. Trust God with a whole heart.
exp.30:12:
This verse says that the children of Israel, who did not yet know God's law, were to listen to it and learn to revere and honor the Lord. They were to do this for as long as they lived in the land they were crossing the Jordan to take. "Fear" here means holding the Lord in reverence and taking him seriously, not living in terror. The phrase "who do not know the law" identifies what the children lacked, and "as long as you live" points to the whole span of life in that land.

Moses is speaking to the people shortly before his death. He had already written the law and commanded that it be read aloud in public every seven years, at the Feast of Tabernacles. He wanted the new generation, which had not lived through everything in the wilderness, not to forget God in the new land.

For today: faith is not inherited on its own; it has to be taught. We can set aside regular time to read the Bible with our children or with younger people, and talk about it simply.
exp.30:29:
This verse says that Moses spoke to the whole assembly of Israel and recited the words of the song from beginning to end. The reader should know that the BSB says "recited aloud," which gives the sense that he said it so all could hear it. "Assembly" refers to the gathering of the people, and "song" is a chant or poem.

Moses is near the end of his life. God had told him that the people would turn away from Him after his death. For this reason, Moses gathered the elders and officers to leave them this song as a witness. His purpose was that, when troubles came, they would remember the warning and return to God. The song appears in chapter 32.

For today: we often forget easily what God has taught us. We can keep his word in our memory, perhaps through a verse or a song, so that it stays with us when we are weak or tempted to drift away.
exp.20:13:
If a man of Israel is no longer pleased with the captive woman he has taken as his wife, he must let her go wherever she wishes. He may not sell her for money or treat her as a slave. "Dishonored her" describes how he has wronged her by taking her as his wife in a way that leaves her without rights.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law addresses a situation of war in the ancient world and sets limits on what a man could do. The woman was not property. She had the right to mourn, and if she was rejected, the right to her freedom. Some see here a protection for her; others stress how harsh the context was.

For today: God cares for those who have less power. We should treat vulnerable people with dignity and never take advantage of them.
exp.19:0:
It says that when Israel goes out to fight against its enemies and sees horses, chariots, and an army larger than its own, they should not be afraid. The reason is that the LORD their God is with them, the same God who brought them out of Egypt.

Moses speaks to the people in his final speeches, shortly before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for war. Horses and chariots were the most feared military force of that time. Moses reminds them that their confidence is not in weapons, but in what God has already done in rescuing them from Egypt.

For today: when you face a problem that seems bigger than you are, remember how God has helped you before. Make a list of those occasions and use it to pray with confidence.
exp.13:7:
The verse says that pork could not be eaten by the people of Israel. The pig has a hoof that is split in two, but it does not chew the cud, which means it does not bring back up food it has already swallowed to chew again. Because of this, the pig is "unclean," meaning not fit for use by God's people. The verse also says that people must not eat its meat or touch its carcass.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them to live as a people set apart, holy to Him (Deuteronomy 14:2). Scholars explain the exact reason for these rules in different ways: some see a symbol of holiness, others reasons of health or of setting themselves apart from other nations. The Bible does not fully explain it.

For today: Christians are not under these dietary rules (Mark 7:19; Acts 10), but we can still ask ourselves how to live set apart for God in our everyday decisions.
exp.3:40:
Moses set aside three cities on the east side of the Jordan River, across the Jordan to the east. The word "set aside" in the verse means that he chose them and designated them for a special purpose. The verses that follow explain that they were cities of refuge.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. After asking them for obedience to God, he recalls this fact: a safe place had already been provided for the one who caused a death without intending to. In this way justice and mercy walked together. They were for cases of accidental death, not of planned wickedness.

For today: God cares for both justice and compassion. We can imitate him by being people who help others find protection and a new opportunity, without ignoring the truth or responsibility.
exp.27:56:
This verse describes something very painful. It speaks of a woman, once delicate and refined, who in the midst of famine will not share even with the child she has just given birth to, or with the children she bears. The newborn is the one that comes out from between her legs, and the phrase about eating them secretly describes doing so privately, because there is a lack of everything. The siege is the surrounding of the cities, when the enemy encircles them and cuts off supplies.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings for obeying God and, in very harsh words, the consequences of abandoning his covenant. It is a warning about the horror of war and hunger, not a command from God.

For today: obedience to God is the path of life. We can take his warnings seriously, seek his guidance every day, and remember that his correction aims to bring us back to him.
exp.28:4:
It says that during the forty years in the wilderness, the people's clothing and sandals did not wear out. The phrase "wear out" here means to become worn down or old through use. "Sandals" refers to footwear in general. God cared for them in a remarkable way.

Moses is speaking to the new generation of Israel, close to entering the promised land. He reminds them of what God did so that they might renew their covenant with Him. Here Moses says "I led you," speaking on God's behalf. Many of them were children or young people during those years, yet they had seen the signs and still found it hard to grasp their meaning.

For today: Remember how God has sustained you in difficult times, even if you did not notice it at the moment. Write down three specific ways God has cared for you in your life and give thanks for them, trusting that He will remain faithful in what lies ahead.
exp.1:29:
Here is what the verse says: Sihon, king of Heshbon, would not let the Israelites pass through his land. The verse says that the LORD your God had made his spirit stubborn and his heart obstinate. Stubborn means he would not change his mind, and obstinate means the same thing: he was set in his refusal. "As is the case this day" means the outcome is still visible now, as it was then.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, and he reminds them of what happened. Israel had asked for passage peacefully, offering to pay for food and water. Sihon rejected the offer and went out to fight. Scholars explain in several ways how God made his heart stubborn, but the text shows that Sihon made his own decision and that God was directing events toward his purpose.

For today: when someone shuts the door on your good intentions, do not become bitter. Do what is right with humility and trust that God governs history. And guard your own heart: do not harden it against the voice of God.
exp.3:37:
This verse says that God brought Israel out of Egypt to drive out before them nations greater and mightier than they were. Then he would bring them into the land of those nations and give it to them for an inheritance, that is, as a possession that is received as a gift and passed down to the children.

The phrase "as it is this day" means "as it is seen on this day," since the promise was already about to be fulfilled.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God spoke to them from the fire, loved their ancestors, and rescued them with great power. He wants them to respond with obedience and faithfulness.

For today: what we have is not due to our own strength, but to the grace of God. This invites us to live with gratitude and trust, and to obey him with humility, knowing that he cares for us.
exp.14:0:
Verse 1 says that at the end of every seven years the people of Israel had to cancel debts. The word "cancel" means ending what someone owes so they no longer have to repay it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land and repeats the law God had given them. This practice protected the poor so that a debt would not hold them down for life. It applied to fellow Israelites; a foreigner could be charged interest. Scholars debate whether the debt was canceled completely or whether only the collection of it was suspended during that year. The verse does not settle the question, but the law was given as a command that the people were bound to obey.

Today we can practice the same generosity: if someone in need cannot repay you, consider forgiving the debt or giving them more time, remembering that God has treated us with great mercy.
exp.20:15:
This verse says that when a father divided his inheritance among his sons, he could not name the son of the wife he loved most as the firstborn if the true firstborn was the son of the wife he loved less. The word "unloved" in the verse means less loved or less preferred. "Firstborn" refers to the eldest son and the rights that belong to him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law protected the weakest members of a family with several wives, something the Bible describes without presenting it as the ideal. The father's feelings were not to change what was just. The eldest son was owed a double portion.

For today: let us be fair even when our personal preferences lean us toward another side. In the family, at work, or in the church, let us give each person what is rightly theirs, without favoritism.
exp.3:31:
Moses invites the people to examine all of human history, from the day God created man on earth and from one end of the heavens to the other, to see whether anything as great as what Israel experienced has ever happened or been reported. The words "created," "one end of the heavens to the other," and "as great as this" are the ones the verse uses, so no further explanation of them is needed here.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God spoke to them from the fire on the mountain and brought them out of Egypt with great power. He wants their faith to rest on what God truly did, so that they will remain faithful to Him and not turn away after other gods.

For today: when you doubt or feel far from God, remember what He has done, both in the Bible and in your own life. Remembering His faithfulness strengthens trust and encourages us to obey Him with gratitude.
exp.0:22:
Moses says that the plan seemed good to him, so he selected twelve men from among the people, one from each tribe. "The plan" means the proposal the people had made. "Men" refers to adult males. Their job was to explore the promised land.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel almost forty years later, near the promised land, and he recalls what happened at Kadesh-barnea. God had already told them to go up and not be afraid, but the people asked to send spies ahead. Moses agreed to the plan. Later, most of the spies gave a report that caused fear. Here we see the beginning of that story.

For today: planning and seeking information is not wrong, but it should not replace trust in what God has already said. Before deciding, ask yourself whether you are looking for facts so you can obey better, or for excuses to doubt.
exp.27:37:
It says that you will sow much seed in the field but harvest little, because the locusts will consume it. The word "harvest" here means bringing in what has grown from the fields. The locust was a plague of insects that stripped the sown fields bare.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings if they obey God and curses if they turn away from Him. This verse is part of the warnings. His words remind them that life in the field depended entirely on God, and that turning away from Him would bring loss and sorrow.

Today we can remember that our effort, however great, does not guarantee everything by itself. Work with diligence, but trust in God and do not place your security in your own strength or your possessions. Give thanks for what you receive and seek to obey Him with humility.
exp.17:10:
This verse follows a list of forbidden practices. "Casts spells" refers to someone who uses charms or incantations. The person who "consults a medium or spiritist" seeks answers from a spirit, through a go-between who claims to speak for it. The one who "inquires of the dead" tries to speak with the dead to obtain answers.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them not to imitate the customs of the neighboring nations, who sought guidance from hidden sources. God wanted His people to trust Him and to listen to the prophets He would send, as the following verses show.

Today we can ask ourselves where we look for direction when we are afraid or doubtful. Instead of turning to horoscopes, fortune-tellers, or attempts to contact the dead, we can pray, read the Bible, and seek counsel from wise believers, trusting that God guides those who seek Him.
exp.26:10:
This verse is an introductory sentence. It says that Moses gave the people a command on that day. The word "commanded" means that he gave an instruction with authority. The colon at the end signals that what they were to do comes right after.

Moses speaks to Israel shortly before his death, when the people are about to cross the Jordan and enter the promised land. He had already reminded them to obey God. Now he gives them a specific instruction: a ceremony on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, where the tribes would speak blessings and curses. In this way the people would remember that their life in the land depended on their faithfulness to the covenant with God.

God speaks to us with clarity, and sometimes he asks for concrete actions, not just good intentions. Today you can choose one simple step of obedience, such as praying daily or forgiving someone, and put it into practice without waiting.
exp.3:12:
He tells us that God himself made his covenant known to them, that is, his solemn commitment to the people. He commanded them to follow it, and that covenant is summed up in the Ten Commandments. God wrote them on two tablets of stone. The word "declared" means that he made it plainly known, and "follow" means to live by it, not just to hear it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, now close to the promised land. He reminds them of the day when God spoke from the mountain amid fire and darkness. They heard his voice, but they saw no form at all. Moses stresses this so that they will obey God and not make images to worship.

For today: God spoke to us clearly, and his Word is not only to be admired, but to be lived. Today you can choose a teaching of the Bible that you already know and put it into practice in your home or at work.
exp.8:26:
Moses asks God to remember Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whom he calls "Your servants." He asks God to overlook the stubbornness of this people and the wickedness of their sin.

Moses speaks to the people and recalls how he interceded for them after they made the golden calf at Mount Sinai. He lay prostrate for forty days and forty nights. He does not defend the people by saying they deserve forgiveness; he appeals to the promises God made to the patriarchs and to God's own reputation among the nations.

For today: when you fail, do not trust in your own merits, but in the faithfulness and promises of God. And, like Moses, pray also for others who go wrong, asking for mercy for them instead of condemnation.
exp.10:28:
This verse says that when God brings Israel into the promised land, the people are to proclaim the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal. The word "brings" here means to lead someone into a place, and "proclaim" means to announce those words publicly so that everyone can hear them.

Moses speaks to the people before they cross the Jordan. He reminds them that obeying God brings blessing, and that turning away from Him to follow other gods brings a curse. These two mountains, facing each other, would serve as a sign to remind them of that choice. Later, in Joshua 8:30-35, the account tells us that this command was carried out.

For today: our daily decisions matter. Before we choose, we can ask ourselves, "Does this bring me closer to God or pull me away from Him?" Remembering His words regularly helps us walk faithfully.
exp.1:23:
God tells the people to get up, set out, and cross the Arnon Valley. He assures them that he has already delivered Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land into their hand. The phrase "engage him in battle" means to enter into combat with him, and "begin to take possession of it" means to start occupying that land.

Moses recalls what God commanded as the years in the wilderness were drawing to a close. Israel was near the promised land. It was an order for that specific moment in their history. According to the text that follows, Moses first sent messengers with words of peace to Sihon.

God often gives us promises, but he also asks us to take the step. Trusting him means moving forward in obedience and seeking peace first, without using this passage to justify violence today.
exp.31:49:
God tells Moses that he is going to die on the mountain he is about to climb, Mount Nebo. The phrase "be gathered to your people" is an old way of saying that he will die and join his ancestors. God reminds him how his brother Aaron died on Mount Hor and was gathered to his people. The word "unfaithful" in the older text means they failed in their duty, or were disloyal.

The Lord speaks on the same day that Moses finishes teaching the song to the people. Moses can see the promised land, but he will not enter it, because at Kadesh he did not honor God before Israel. Even so, God himself shows him how and where his journey will end, and does not leave him alone.

For today: our actions have consequences, and God is serious about obedience. But he is also faithful and close to us in our final days. We can live with humility, and trust that God cares for us until the last day.
exp.20:16:
This verse says that a father must recognize as firstborn the son who was born first, even when his mother is the wife he loves least. That son receives a double share, meaning twice the inheritance that the others receive. The phrase "his unloved wife" describes a wife the father cares for less, and it does not necessarily mean he hated her. The phrase "the firstfruits of his father's strength" refers to the fact that he was the father's first son.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and he passes on God's law to them. This rule protected the firstborn son from injustice or family favoritism, in a situation of polygamy, which the law regulates without approving it as an ideal.

For today: God calls us to treat everyone fairly, without letting our preferences or emotions decide what each person is due, especially within the family.
exp.21:22:
It says that if a young woman who is a virgin and already pledged to be married to a man is found in the city by another man, and he sleeps with her, the case that follows in the next verses applies. A "virgin" is a woman who has not had sexual relations, and "pledged in marriage" means formally engaged, something more serious than dating today.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and explains God's laws for their life as a nation. An engagement was taken as an almost marriage covenant. This case concerns what happens inside the city, where she could call for help; the case of the field is distinguished afterward. The details of how this law was applied are interpreted in various ways.

For today: God values faithfulness and protects commitments. Today we can keep our promises and always respect people, without taking advantage of anyone.
exp.30:8:
Moses wrote down "this law," meaning the instructions God had given Israel, and gave it to the priests, the sons of Levi, who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and to all the elders of Israel, the leaders of the people.

Moses is about to die, and Joshua will take command. Before he goes, Moses puts the law in writing and entrusts its care to both the spiritual and civil leaders. He then orders that it be read aloud every seven years, at the Feast of Tabernacles, so that all the people would hear it. Many scholars think "this law" refers to Deuteronomy or to a part of it, though not all agree.

For today: God's Word needs to be kept, read, and passed on. We can set aside a regular time to read the Bible as a family or in church, and not leave that to others on our behalf.
exp.6:6:
This verse says that God did not choose Israel because they were a great, strong, or numerous people. Instead, they were among the smallest. "Set his affection on you" means that God placed his love on them, and "choose you" means that he selected them for himself.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter the promised land. He has commanded them to tear down the altars of the idols, and he wants them not to become proud. He reminds them that their being chosen was not a reward for their merits. The following verse explains that it was because of God's love and his promise to their forefathers.

For today: God does not love us for what we accomplish, possess, or appear to be. If you feel small or inadequate, rest in the fact that his love does not depend on you. And if things are going well for you, live with humility and gratitude, not with pride.
exp.2:7:
This verse sums up the conquest of the lands east of the Jordan River. It says that Israel took the territory of the two Amorite kings, from the Arnon Valley in the south to Mount Hermon in the north. The phrase "across the Jordan" means the eastern side, where Moses was speaking.

Moses addresses the people near the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the recent victories over Sihon and Og, to strengthen their confidence that God keeps what he promises. Some readers feel uneasy about the violence in these accounts; the Bible presents them as part of a particular moment in Israel's history, not as a model for today.

For today: remember the times God has sustained you. Recalling his past faithfulness helps you face the challenges ahead with confidence.
exp.2:13:
This verse tells that Jair, a descendant of Manasseh, took control of the whole region of Argob, reaching as far as the border of the Geshurites and Maacathites. Afterward he renamed Bashan after himself, calling it Havvoth-jair, which means something like "the villages of Jair." The words "by which it is called to this day" mean that this name was still in use when Moses spoke.

Here Moses is speaking. He is recalling for the new generation, before they enter the promised land, how God gave them victories east of the Jordan and how that territory was divided among the tribes. Some scholars note that the phrase "to this day" may have been clarified later by an editor; there is no single agreement on that.

For today: God uses ordinary people to carry out his promises. Ask yourself what task, however small it may seem, God has placed in your hands, and do it with courage and faithfulness, trusting him with the outcome.
exp.33:0:
Moses goes up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, which faces Jericho. There the LORD shows him the whole land, from Gilead as far as Dan.

This is the beginning of the last chapter of Deuteronomy. Moses had already finished his speeches to the people. God had told him that he would see the land, but that he would not enter it. The text does not explain every detail here, but the scene marks the close of his life and of his leadership.

We can trust that God keeps his promises, even when we do not see them fulfilled in our own time. Moses served faithfully and accepted with humility what God decided. Today we can do the same: serve well, leave the future in God's hands, and rejoice in what others will enjoy after us.
exp.28:8:
Moses tells the Israelites to keep the words of the covenant closely, that is, the agreement God made with them, and to follow them. "Keep and follow" means to obey and to hold to what God has said, and to put it into practice. "Prosper" here means that things go well for them in life, in whatever they take on.

Moses speaks to the people on the plains of Moab, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them how God gave them victory over the kings Sihon and Og, and so calls them to renew their commitment to God before entering the promised land. The whole community was present, including children and foreigners.

For today: God's blessing is tied to a life of practical obedience. Today you can choose a teaching from the Bible that you already know and put it into practice this week, trusting that God cares for your path. This does not guarantee material success, but it does mean a life firmly rooted in Him.
exp.19:8:
This verse says that when the officers have finished addressing the army, they will appoint commanders to lead it. The phrase "have finished addressing" means the officers had completed their speech to the soldiers, and "appoint commanders to lead it" means that military leaders would be put in charge of the troops.

Moses is giving Israel instructions before they enter the promised land. The officers would first speak to the men and send home those who had unfinished business, such as a new house, a vineyard, or a promise of marriage, as well as those who were afraid. This looked after families and kept fear from spreading to the rest. After that, the commanders organized the army.

For today: before a difficult task, it is wise to stop and examine the heart and one's priorities. God cares about people, not only about results, and He invites us to move forward with order, honesty, and trust in Him.
exp.19:11:
If a city far away refuses the offer of peace and chooses to fight, Israel could surround it and lay siege to it. The verse says, "But if they refuse to make peace with you and wage war against you, lay siege to that city," so the instruction is clear: peace is offered first, and only when it is refused does the siege begin.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the land, giving them rules for war. The first step was always to offer peace. This passage refers to distant cities; for the peoples of Canaan, the same chapter gives other instructions, which are far more severe. These are difficult texts, and readers have understood them in different ways, but here it is clear that peace came first.

For today: when facing a conflict, look first for the path of peace. Offer dialogue, forgiveness, or an honest conversation before hardening your position or responding in anger.
exp.32:8:
This verse says that the Levites put loyalty to God above their family ties. The phrase "I do not consider them" does not mean they rejected their family, but that they did not let kinship bend their obedience. That is why they kept God's word and maintained his covenant. "Kept" means to carry out faithfully.

Moses is blessing the tribes of Israel before he dies. Here he speaks of Levi, the tribe of the priests. Many think it refers to the episode of the golden calf (Exodus 32:26-29), when the Levites sided with God, although the text does not name it and some interpret it more generally.

For today: loving our family is good, but when family pressure would draw us away from what God asks, we must choose to be faithful to Him, with respect and humility toward others.
exp.6:8:
This verse calls us to recognize and be certain that the LORD is the only true God, a faithful God. He keeps His covenant of loving devotion and shows His steadfast love to those who love Him and keep His commandments. The phrase "for a thousand generations" means for an extremely long time; many understand it as a way of saying that His faithfulness never runs out.

Moses is speaking to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God did not choose them because they were great, but out of love and because of the promise made to their ancestors. For this reason he calls them to trust in Him and to obey Him.

For today: when you feel small or insecure, remember that God does not love you for your achievements, but because of His faithfulness. Respond to that love with simple obedience each day, trusting that He keeps what He promises.
exp.26:17:
It says that God regards it as a very grave thing to deceive or lead a blind person astray so that they go wrong on the road. "Cursed" means that the one who does it falls under God's judgment. The people answer "Amen," which means: "So be it, we agree."

Moses speaks with the elders of Israel before they enter the promised land. He orders them to proclaim a series of curses from Mount Ebal, and the people accept them with their "Amen." Many of them deal with sins committed in secret, such as taking advantage of someone weak. This one protects the most vulnerable, just as those that speak of the orphan, the widow, and the foreigner do.

Today we can care for those who depend on our honesty: giving clear directions, reporting with truth, and not taking advantage of someone who knows less or cannot see the deception.
exp.3:10:
It says that the people of Israel came near and stood at the base of Mount Horeb, also called Sinai. The mountain was blazing with fire that reached up to the heavens, meaning it burned very high. It was wrapped in black clouds and deep darkness.

Moses speaks to the new generation, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the day God gave his law. He wants them not to forget what their parents lived through, so that they will fear God and teach it to their children.

For today: do not let your experiences with God grow cold. Write down what He has done in your life and tell it to your children, or to someone close to you, so that your faith and theirs stay strong.
exp.31:13:
This passage describes the abundance with which God fed his people: curds from the herd, milk from the flock, tender meat from lambs, rams from the region of Bashan (known for its good livestock), goats, and the choicest wheat. The phrase "with the choicest grains of wheat" is a way of saying the finest wheat. "The juice of the finest grapes" refers to the wine they drank.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, in a song addressed to Israel. He recalls how the LORD guided and sustained his people without the help of other gods. But the song also sets up a warning: the verses that follow say that, once they had grown fat, Israel forgot God.

For today: when God gives us blessings, it is easy to trust in them and not in him. Today you can thank him for something specific you have and ask him to keep you grateful and humble.
exp.2:5:
Moses reminds the people how Israel defeated the cities of King Og of Bashan. The phrase "devoted them to destruction" means they completely destroyed them, just as they had already done to Sihon, king of Heshbon. The text says this included the men, women, and children of every city.

Moses speaks at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before Israel enters the promised land. He reminds them of past victories so that they will trust God. This is a hard text. The Bible presents it as a judgment of God on the peoples of that time, and scholars debate how to understand the language of total destruction in these passages.

For today: when we remember how God helped us in the past, our confidence grows to face the challenges that lie ahead. And we should read these difficult texts with humility, never using them to justify violence today.
exp.11:0:
This verse opens a new section of laws. It says that what follows are "statutes and ordinances," that is, rules and decisions that the people were to follow carefully and put into practice. To be careful to follow means to carry them out faithfully. This was to be done in the land God was giving them, all the days they lived there.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, who are about to enter the land of Canaan after years in the wilderness. He reminds them that the land is a gift from the LORD, the God of their fathers. For this reason he asks them for faithfulness. What follows deals with removing the worship of other gods and worshiping the LORD as he directs.

For today: God's gifts are not meant for living by our own taste, but for obeying him with gratitude. Today you can choose one teaching from the Bible that you already know and put it into practice with steadiness, as a response of thanks for what God has given you.
exp.30:5:
Moses tells the people of Israel to be strong and courageous, and not to be afraid or terrified of their enemies, because the LORD their God is the one who goes with them. "Be strong and courageous" means to make yourselves strong and to take heart. "Never leave you nor forsake you" means God will not abandon them or desert them.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before he dies. They are about to enter the promised land, but he will not cross over with them. He reminds them how God helped them against the kings Sihon and Og, so that they can trust he will also help them in what is coming. Then he says the same thing to Joshua, the new leader.

For today: when you face something that frightens you, do not rely only on your own strength. Remember how God has helped you before, and take the next step with the certainty that you are not alone.
exp.5:20:
This verse says that when a son asks why God's laws exist, the father should answer by telling the story of deliverance. "Slaves" is the word for people held in servitude, and "a mighty hand" speaks of God's great power. "The LORD" is God's covenant name, the name he gave in his relationship with Israel. "You are to tell him" is a command: the parent must speak these words.

Moses speaks to the Israelite parents before they enter the promised land. He wants faith to be passed on from generation to generation. The answer does not begin with rules, but with what God did: he rescued them when they were slaves. Obedience grows out of that rescue.

For today: when your children or anyone else asks about your faith, do not begin with a list of rules. Simply tell how God has helped you and rescued you. Your personal testimony can open a heart.
exp.31:43:
This verse says that Moses went and recited the whole song to the people, and that Joshua, son of Nun, went with him. The phrase "in the hearing of the people" means that the people heard it directly. In this Bible, "Joshua" is the same leader who would later guide Israel.

The narrator of the book describes how Moses, near the end of his life, gives Israel a song that God had given him. This song recalls God's faithfulness and warns about the consequences of forgetting him. Joshua stands at his side because he would soon take up leadership. Afterward, Moses asks the people to keep these words and teach them to their children.

For today: God's truths are passed on when someone speaks them aloud and others listen carefully. Look for a moment this week to share with your family or friends a promise or teaching from the Bible that has strengthened you.
exp.31:23:
It says that God will send severe calamities on his people: hunger that wastes them away, a ravaging plague, bitter disaster, attacks from wild beasts, and deadly bites from vipers that slither in the dust. The phrase "wasted from hunger" means they will be worn down and destroyed little by little, and "ravaged by pestilence" means they will be consumed by disease.

It is part of the Song of Moses. God speaks through Moses and announces what would happen if Israel turned away from him to follow other gods. These are warnings about the consequences of breaking the covenant. The verses that follow show that God also limits the punishment and does not destroy them completely.

For today: God warns us out of love, because he does not want to see us suffer. Let us listen to his correction in time, return to him when we stray, and trust in his mercy, which always offers a way back.
exp.13:28:
The Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow who live within the gates of your towns may come, eat, and be satisfied. The Levite has no portion or inheritance among you, meaning no land passed down as a family share. The towns are the villages or cities where the people live. God promises to bless you in all the work of your hands when you care for them.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The Levites served in worship and did not receive land of their own, so they relied on the generosity of the people. Every third year, the tithe was stored in the towns to help them and the most vulnerable, who had no one else to support them.

For today: God cares for those in need, and our generosity is a way of obeying him. You could set aside a fixed part of your income to help a person or a work that serves the most vulnerable in your community.
exp.10:12:
This verse begins a conditional promise. God asks his people to obey carefully the commandments he gives them today, to love the LORD their God, and to serve him with all their heart and all their soul, that is, with the whole person, holding nothing back. The commandments are presented as things God is giving them now, as direction for daily life.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. That land depended on rain rather than on great rivers like Egypt's. Moses reminds them that God cares for that land, and that its blessing is tied to a life of faithfulness to him.

For today: God does not seek only the keeping of rules, but a love that is lived out in obedience. Today you can choose one concrete area of your life, such as your work or how you treat your family, and give it to God sincerely, trusting that he cares for you.
exp.22:16:
This verse forbids prostitution connected with religion in Israel. A shrine prostitute is a person who sells sex as part of religious worship. The verse applies to both women and men. Some scholars debate the details of this practice.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them laws to live as God's people, set apart from the Canaanite nations, whose worship sometimes included sexual acts. The surrounding context also shows a God who protects the vulnerable, such as the fugitive servant, and who desires pure worship.

Today we can learn that God cares for our dignity and that of others. Let us ask him for help to live with purity, not to use or exploit anyone, and to worship him with a whole heart.
exp.30:22:
God gives Joshua, son of Nun, a charge: "Be strong and courageous." He tells him that Joshua will bring the Israelites into the land that God swore to give them. And he adds: "I will be with you."

Moses is about to die, and Joshua will be the new leader. Before that, God warns that the people will turn away from Him, and for this reason Moses writes a song to serve as a witness. In the text, the one speaking here seems to be God himself, because he says "I swore" and "I will be with you." Some read these as the words of Moses, but the preceding context favors God.

When God gives you something difficult to do, your courage does not come from how strong you are, but from the fact that He goes with you. Take the next step by trusting in his promise.
exp.24:9:
This verse says that the man who refused to fulfill his duty to his widowed sister-in-law would receive a public nickname in Israel: "the house of the unsandaled." Being unsandaled meant that a man's sandal had been pulled off. It was a mark of shame, a reminder that he had refused to act on behalf of his brother's family.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, near the time they were to enter the promised land. This law of levirate marriage required that, if a man died without children, his brother should marry the widow so that the dead man's name would not be lost and she would be protected. If the brother refused, there was a public act before the elders. Scholars agree that the removed sandal pointed to giving up a right to an inheritance, although the details are interpreted in several ways.

Today we can learn that family responsibilities are not avoided in silence. God cares for the vulnerable, and he calls us not to abandon those who depend on us, but to serve them faithfully and honestly.
exp.29:9:
The passage says that the blessings God promises come when the people listen to him and obey what is written in his law. But it is not enough to keep rules alone: one must also turn back to God with all your heart and with all your soul, that is, with sincerity and wholeheartedly. The phrase "obey the LORD your God" means to listen to him and do what he asks, and "turn to Him" means to come back to him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He explains that, even if they fail and suffer the consequences, if they come back to God with sincerity, he will receive them again with compassion. The verse that follows makes clear that this command is neither impossible nor far away.

For today: if you have drifted away from God, you do not need a special feat to come back. Begin with a sincere prayer, and ask him for help to listen to him and obey him in one concrete thing this week.
exp.10:21:
This verse says that if you carefully obey all the commandments Moses gives you, doing them out of love for God, following his ways and holding fast to him, blessings will come. The phrase "hold fast" in this verse means to stay closely joined to God, to remain attached to him. "Keep" here means to obey. Love and obedience are joined together.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God freed them and asks them for faithfulness. After the verse, he promises that God will help them take possession of the land, even though the peoples living there were stronger than they were.

Today we can learn that obeying God is not only following rules, but a way of loving him and staying close to him. A practical idea: each morning, read a passage of the Bible and ask God for help to live it out that day.
exp.2:21:
There is no need to be afraid of the enemies, because the LORD your God himself is the one who fights for his people. The phrase "do not be afraid of them" means just what it says: do not live in fear of them.

The speaker is Moses, reminding the people of Israel what he had told Joshua. They had already seen how God defeated two kings east of the Jordan. Moses wanted Joshua to trust that God would do the same with the kingdoms they would face when Israel entered the promised land.

For today: when you face a problem that seems bigger than you, remember what God has already done in your life and in his Word. Do what is yours to do with responsibility, but rest in the fact that you are not alone. God is faithful and can work in the middle of what frightens you.
exp.1:16:
This verse is short: Moses tells that the LORD spoke to him, and what follows is what the LORD said to him. "Jehovah" is the name of God, and "the LORD said to me" introduces a command or instruction.

Moses is reminding the new generation of Israel of the years in the wilderness. The whole generation of fighting men who had rebelled had already died, just as God had said. Now, as that time of waiting comes to an end, God gives the first instruction: to pass through the region of Moab and not to trouble the Ammonites, descendants of Lot, because God had given them that land.

For today: God has his time and his tasks for each stage. After waiting, he speaks again and guides. We can learn to listen to his voice and to respect the limits he sets, without wanting to keep what does not belong to us.
exp.4:3:
It says that God spoke directly with the people of Israel on Mount Horeb, also called Sinai. "Face to face" is a way of saying it was a close and direct communication. The words "out of the fire on the mountain" show that God revealed himself with an overwhelming presence, surrounded by fire. "LORD" is the name of God.

Moses is speaking near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds the Israelites of God's covenant before they enter the promised land. He speaks to them as if they had all been there, because the covenant remains in force for every generation. The verses that follow clarify that Moses acted as a go-between because the people were afraid of the fire. Some understand "face to face" as an expression of closeness, not of seeing God's face.

God is not distant; he wants to have a relationship with you. Today you can speak to him in prayer and read his Word knowing that he listens. Do it with respect and confidence, and do not let your faith become merely an inherited custom.
exp.17:5:
If a Levite moves from any town where he lives in Israel and comes with all his heart to the place the LORD will choose, he may do so. "Moves from any town where he lives" means he is living as an outsider there, without land of his own. "With all his heart" means with sincere and deep longing.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The Levites did not receive territory, so they lived scattered among the tribes and depended on the offerings. Here, anyone who longs to serve God is protected: he must not be kept from doing so. The verses that follow say he would serve and receive a share equal to the other Levites.

For today: God values the sincere desire to serve him. If someone longs for that service, let us give them room and support, and if that longing is in you, do not put it out.
exp.22:14:
It says that if a slave runs away from his master and takes refuge with you, you must not send him back. "Return" means to give him back or hand him over to someone else. A "slave" is a person owned by another, and "master" is the owner. "Taken refuge" means he has fled to you for safety.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and passes on the laws of God. Many interpreters believe this refers to a slave who flees from a cruel master, perhaps from another nation. Others think the text is broader. The following verse lets him live among them freely, with no one oppressing him.

For today: God cares for those who flee oppression. We can be people who offer refuge, protection and fair treatment to those who suffer abuse, without taking advantage of their weakness.
exp.31:7:
God, the Most High, is the one who gave the nations their inheritance when the peoples were divided. To give each nation its inheritance means assigning each one its own land, and the boundaries are the borders that mark where each people lives. The verse says these borders were set "according to the number of the sons of God." Readers understand this phrase in different ways. Some take it to mean that God arranged the nations with his own purposes in view. Others see it as a reference to the heavenly beings who stand around God, and still others find here a link to the people of Israel.

Moses speaks in his final song, shortly before he dies. He wants the people to remember their history and not respond to God with ingratitude. He invites them to ask their fathers and elders what God has done.

For today: God governs history, even when the nations seem to be in confusion. You can rest in the knowledge that your life is not left to chance. Remember how God has cared for you, and give thanks.
exp.13:18:
It says that every flying insect was unclean for the Israelites and was not to be eaten. "Unclean" means it was not fit to eat under the law. Other passages allow certain locusts, so some believe this verse refers to flying insects in general.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the rules about food, together with the list of unclean birds. The text says that God had set them apart as a holy people, and these rules helped them live differently from the neighboring nations.

For today: although Christians are not under these food rules, we can learn to live set apart for God. Ask yourself what daily habit, large or small, you can give to Him to show that you belong to Him.
exp.24:18:
When the LORD your God gives you rest from all the enemies around you, in the land He is giving you to possess as an inheritance, you are to blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven. Do not forget!

This is a command about what the people must do once they are settled and secure in the land. Its focus is the removal of Amalek's memory, a people who attacked from behind the weak and weary when Israel came out of Egypt, showing no fear of God.

For today: do not repay evil with evil, but do not forget that God defends the weak. Care for those who are tired and lagging behind you, and trust that God will do justice in His own time.
exp.12:16:
It says that when an Israelite city was condemned for leading the people to worship other gods, no one was to keep anything from what was "devoted" to destruction, that is, what was set apart for destruction for God. If they obeyed, God would turn away from his fierce anger, would grant them mercy and compassion, and would multiply them, as he had sworn to their ancestors.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He is warning against idolatry, which put the covenant with God in danger. This command applied to one very specific legal case in ancient Israel; it is not a general instruction for today.

For today: God expects complete obedience, without holding on to "a little bit" of whatever pulls us away from him. We can ask ourselves what we are keeping that competes with our loyalty to God, and sincerely hand it over to him.
exp.19:12:
The verse says that when God gave a city into Israel's hands after a siege, the soldiers were to put to death every male in that city. "Put to the sword" means killed with the sword, leaving no survivors among the men. The phrase about God delivering the city into their hand means that God would grant them the victory.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land, giving rules of war. First, peace had to be offered; only if the city refused and fought was this applied. It refers to distant cities, not to the nations of Canaan, which had even harsher rules. It is a difficult text, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: this passage reminds us that God offers peace first. Before pursuing a dispute or conflict, seek reconciliation as the first option, as Jesus taught (Matthew 5:9).
exp.26:13:
This verse says that the Levites will proclaim in a loud voice to every Israelite. The Berean verse uses "every Israelite" rather than "all the men of Israel," so the verse speaks of every Israelite, and "loud voice" means that everyone could hear them clearly. It is the introduction to the solemn words that follow.

Moses gives these instructions to the people before they enter the promised land. When they cross the Jordan, the tribes will stand facing Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, some for blessing and others for cursing. The Levites will read the warnings aloud, and the people will respond with "Amen," that is, "so be it." It was a ceremony to renew the covenant with God.

For today: God's Word was given to be heard and answered. When you read it or hear it, do not stay silent inside: respond with a sincere "Amen," deciding to obey what God shows you.
exp.1:24:
This verse says that God, starting that very day, would begin to put dread and fear of Israel on the nations across the whole earth. They would hear reports of Israel, tremble, and be in anguish because of them. The phrase "the dread and fear of you" points to the terror that Israel's presence and reputation would stir in others. The words "This very day I will begin" show that this was a process only just starting.

The one speaking is God, addressing Israel through Moses. After nearly forty years in the wilderness, the people were about to enter the promised land. God encourages them to face Sihon, the Amorite king. It is notable that Moses, even so, first offers him words of peace (v. 26).

For today: when you face a great challenge, remember that God goes before you and prepares the way. Trust in Him, take your steps with courage, and seek peace before conflict.
exp.0:41:
God tells Moses to warn the people: do not go up to fight, because He is not with them. If they go anyway, they will be defeated by their enemies.

Moses is reminding the new generation of what happened in the desert. Because of their unbelief, the earlier generation had been condemned not to enter the land. Later they said, "We have sinned; now we will surely go up." But changing their minds was not the same as obeying. God had already told them not to go, and they went anyway. As the following text says, they lost the battle.

Today, obedience cannot be put off until it is convenient. Admitting a mistake in words is not enough if we keep acting on our own. Before we throw ourselves into a project, it is wise to pray, seek God's guidance in His Word, and ask ourselves: am I going with Him, or only with my own desires?
exp.29:12:
It says God's law is not on the other side of the sea, as if it were something far away and impossible to reach. No one needs to ask, "Who will cross the sea to get it for us and proclaim it, so that we may obey it?" Here "proclaim" means to announce or make known clearly, and "so that" means "in order that."

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of his life, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God has already given them his commandment and that they can understand it. He takes away the excuse that obeying is too hard or beyond their reach. Right after this, he calls them to choose between life and death.

Today we can stop making excuses like "I don't know enough" or "that is for more spiritual people." God has spoken clearly in his Word. You can start by reading one passage each day and putting into practice one simple thing you understand.
exp.5:15:
This verse says the people must not "test" God, that is, put him to the proof with distrust, demanding signs or doubting his care. "Massah" is the place where Israel did that. The word "test" here does not mean enticing someone toward evil, but trying God to see whether he is truly with them.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what happened at Massah (Exodus 17), when they were thirsty and asked whether God was among them or not. Moses wants them to learn from that mistake and remain faithful to him.

For today: trust God without demanding proof every time we go through a need. We can ask him sincerely, even with tears, but without threatening him or doubting his love. Remembering how he has cared for us before helps us wait with peace.
exp.0:14:
Moses reminds the people that he chose the leaders of each tribe, men who were wise and respected, and appointed them to lead the people. He organized them into groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. Those in charge of groups of ten led small units, and the officers were the ones who oversaw each tribe.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, in the wilderness, before Israel enters the promised land. He looks back over what they have been through. He could not carry all the people's problems by himself, and the people agreed to this plan. Afterward he commanded the judges to judge with justice, without favoring anyone. Scholars debate whether this arrangement was exactly the same as the one described in Exodus 18, but the account shows the same principle.

For today: no one should carry the whole burden alone. If you lead a family, church, or workplace, share responsibilities with wise and trustworthy people, and always seek to act with justice.
exp.31:6:
It says that the people should remember the past and think about what God has done across the generations. To do this, they should ask their father and their elders, who will tell them that story.

Moses speaks to Israel at the end of his life, in a song. Earlier he rebuked the people for their unfaithfulness and for forgetting that God is their Father, who made them and cared for them. Now he invites them to turn their attention to the history of God's faithfulness, which continues in the verses that follow.

For today: ask the older members of your family or your church how they saw God at work in their lives. Listening to them strengthens faith and helps us not to forget his faithfulness.
exp.21:24:
It says that if a man encounters a young woman who is engaged to be married in the open country, and he overpowers her and lies with her, only the man who did this must die. "Young woman" means a woman who is young, "engaged" means promised in marriage, and "overpowers" means seizing her against her will.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in his instructions before they enter the promised land. In the open country, far from other people, no one could come to help the young woman. For this reason the law presumes that she cried out and was a victim, and it declares her free of guilt. All the guilt falls on the attacker, and the text treats this crime as seriously as a killing.

For today: God takes the side of the person who has been attacked and does not blame her. We can imitate him by believing those who suffer abuse, caring for them carefully, and insisting that the one responsible answer for his actions.
exp.30:6:
Moses calls Joshua forward in front of all the people and tells him: "Be strong and courageous." He assures him that he will lead Israel into the land the LORD swore to their fathers to give them, and that he will give it to them as an inheritance.

Moses is 120 years old and will not enter the promised land. He is saying goodbye and hands the leadership to Joshua in public, so that the people will respect him and follow him. His encouragement does not rest on Joshua's abilities, but on God's promise, who goes with them.

When God gives you a task that feels too big for you, do not wait until you feel capable. Remember what He has promised, take the next step with courage, and encourage also those who are beside you.
exp.3:19:
God chose Israel and rescued them from Egypt, which the verse describes as a place of very harsh suffering and slavery, a kind of furnace. The word "yet" introduces the contrast with what the people were before. The phrase about being the people of God's inheritance means a people who belong to him in a special way, like a precious possession. The phrase "as you are today" points out that they were already like this at that very moment.

Moses speaks near the end of his life to the new generation of Israelites before they enter the promised land. He warns them not to make idols or to worship the sun, the moon, or the stars. He reminds them that, unlike the other nations, they were rescued and chosen by God.

For today: before we seek security or worth in created things, let us remember that God has rescued us and calls us his own. That grateful remembrance helps us to be faithful and not to depend on other things.
exp.27:47:
It says that if Israel turns away from God, they will have to serve enemies whom the LORD himself sends against them. They will live with famine, thirst, nakedness, and destitution. The "iron yoke" is an image of harsh oppression, like the heavy wooden frame that was placed on oxen, but here it would be made of iron. "Until He has destroyed you" shows that the harshness would reach very far.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He is renewing the covenant with God. Before this passage he listed blessings for obedience; here he warns about the consequences of rejecting God. The reason is clear: they did not serve him with joy when they had abundance. It is a warning to that people under that covenant.

When we have everything, it is easy to forget God. Today we can ask ourselves whether we give thanks to him and serve him with joy in abundance, not only when we need help.
exp.4:7:
This verse says that the people of Israel were not to make any carved figure or image of anything in heaven, on the earth, or in the waters, in order to worship it. An idol is an object made to stand in for God, and the verse's list of three places, above, below, and in the waters, covers all of creation.

Moses speaks to the people, recalling the law that God gave on Mount Sinai. God had just rescued them from Egypt, where they had seen many idols. The next verse makes clear that the problem was bowing down to those images and serving them, instead of the God who saved them.

Today we can ask what has taken God's place in our hearts: money, fame, work, or a person. Let us give God first place with gratitude, remembering all that he has done for us.
exp.8:23:
This verse says that the people of Israel have been rebelling against God the whole time Moses has known them. "Rebelling" refers to those who resist obeying. The phrase about rebelling against the LORD means "they have been rebelling against the LORD." The name LORD in the Old Testament is the name the text uses for God in that period.

Moses speaks near the end of his life, before the people enter the promised land. He reminds them of their failures: they complained in the wilderness and did not believe God at Kadesh-barnea. He does this so that they will not think they deserve the land for being good. Right after, he tells how he prayed for them, asking that God not destroy them, because they were his people.

For today: let us be humble and honest about our failures. Everything good we receive comes from God's grace, not from our merits. And like Moses, we can pray with love for those who have failed.
exp.3:11:
God spoke to the Israelites out of the fire on Mount Horeb, also called Sinai. They heard his voice and his words clearly, but they saw no form or shape at all. What they heard was the sound of the words, and nothing more was visible.

Moses speaks to the people almost forty years later, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of that day so that they will not forget what God said. Later he warns them not to make idols, because they never saw God in any form. What they received was his word, not an image.

For today: God makes himself known above all through his word. Instead of seeking spectacular experiences or images that picture God, we can set aside time to read the Bible and listen to him carefully, trusting what he has said.
exp.13:14:
It says that the people of Israel were not to eat certain birds: the ostrich, the screech owl, the gull, and any kind of hawk, along with all the birds like each of these. The exact names of these birds are hard to pin down. Scholars do not always agree on which animal each Hebrew word refers to, and that is why translations vary.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He repeats the laws that God gave them so they could live as his people. The list of clean and unclean animals set them apart from other nations. Many think these were birds of prey or birds that were active at night, but not everyone explains it the same way.

For today: God cares about the details of the daily life of his people. We can ask ourselves whether we also give him the ordinary things, such as what we eat, see, and do, so that we live in a way that shows we belong to him.
exp.0:7:
Here is what it says: God tells the people to see the land He has already placed before them, and to enter it and take possession of it. That land is the one He swore He would give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to their descendants after them. "Descendants" means their offspring. "Take possession" means to take hold of what has been given. "Swore" means that He made a solemn promise.

Context: Moses speaks to the people of Israel, near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of what God said at Horeb (Sinai), when He commanded them to leave that mountain and move forward. Moses wants the new generation to remember that the promise comes from God and that He is faithful.

For today: God keeps what He promises, but He often asks us to take steps of faith. Think of something God has shown you to do, and take one concrete step today, trusting His faithfulness more than your own strength.
exp.26:21:
It says God regards as cursed anyone who sleeps with his sister, whether she is the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother. The verse then calls on all the people to respond, "Amen," meaning "so be it," to show that they agree.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He orders a ceremony at Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, where the Levites would proclaim curses and the people would say "Amen." This list includes sexual sins and sins committed in secret, to protect the holiness of the family and so that the people would live in covenant with God.

Today it reminds us that God cares for the family and for healthy boundaries within it. We can ask him to help us live with purity, respect, and responsibility, even when no one sees us.
exp.3:16:
This verse is part of a list of things God forbids being made into an idol. Here it mentions the animals that walk on the earth and the birds that fly through the air. The word "likeness" means an image or representation. The phrase continues from the previous verse: do not make any image to worship it.

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that at Horeb they heard God's voice in the middle of the fire, but they did not see any form. Therefore they were not to invent a shape for God or worship creation.

For today: it is easy to turn good things in life, such as money, success, or fame, into "gods." Today we can ask ourselves what has taken God's place in our hearts, and return to worshiping only the one who created us.
exp.19:1:
This verse says that, just before the battle begins, the priest was to come forward and address the army. The phrase "come forward" is the key action here. It is not yet the message itself, but the indication of who would give it and when.

Moses is speaking to Israel before they enter the promised land. He has already told them not to be afraid, because God was with them, the same God who brought them out of Egypt. Now he explains that, on the battlefield, the priest would remind them of that truth. His task was to strengthen faith, not to direct military strategy.

For today: before facing a difficult moment, seek to hear the Word of God first. Pray, read the Bible, or ask someone of faith for encouragement. In this way your heart is steadied in God and not only in your own strength.
exp.11:12:
It says that the people of Israel had to be careful not to offer their burnt offerings, that is, offerings burned completely for God, in just any place they happened to see. The verse's wording is rendered here simply as "be careful."

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The peoples of Canaan worshiped their gods in any place, and God wanted Israel to worship him in the way he indicated, in the place he would choose. In this way the unity of the people and the purity of their worship were protected.

For today: worshiping God is not doing whatever seems best to us, but drawing near to him as he teaches us in his Word. Ask yourself whether your way of following him comes from what he says or only from your customs and preferences.
exp.21:14:
It says that when a husband accuses his wife of not having been a virgin, her parents must bring the proof to the city elders at the gate. The verse refers to her as a young woman, and the proof is described as the evidence of her virginity. The verse of what that proof was is left to the reader's own study of the surrounding verses.

Moses speaks to Israel, giving laws for life in community. The city gate was the place where legal cases were settled. This law protected the young woman and her family from a false accusation and from a damaged reputation invented by a husband who no longer wanted her.

For today: God cares about truth and about the honor of people. We should not spread accusations without proof or harm the reputation of others. Let us always seek justice and defend those who are slandered.
exp.27:10:
God will give His people abundance: children, livestock, and harvests. The phrase about having more than enough is rewritten here: it means to have more than enough. "The fruit of your womb" refers to children; the offspring of the livestock are the young animals; and the produce of the land is the harvest. All of this would happen in the land that God promised, with an oath, to your fathers.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the land. He presents the blessings of the covenant with God, which depended on obeying Him and walking in His ways. It was a promise to the nation of Israel within that covenant, not a guarantee for each individual person.

For today: God is a generous Father, and we can thank Him for what we have as a gift from Him. Moreover, obeying Him helps us live with trust and gratitude, without measuring blessing only by money.
exp.9:16:
This verse says that the LORD is the supreme God, above everything that people call god or lord. He is "the great, mighty, and awesome God," so majestic that he causes deep reverence. "Showing no partiality" means he plays no favorites, and "accepting no bribe" means he cannot be bought.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God chose them out of love, not because of merit, and he calls them to obey him wholeheartedly. Right away he shows what kind of God this is: he defends the orphan and the widow, and he loves the foreigner.

For today: if God shows no partiality and cannot be bought with anything, neither should we treat some people better than others because of their money or position. This week, make an effort to treat with respect and kindness someone who usually goes unnoticed.
exp.27:21:
The passage says that God would punish the people with serious diseases. The phrase "wasting disease" refers to an illness that slowly wears away the body, and the text also mentions fever, inflammation and scorching heat. It adds drought, which means long periods without rain. It names blight and mildew, which are harmful growths that ruin crops. All of this would pursue them until it brought them to ruin.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings if they obey and curses if they turn away from God. These words are part of the covenant with Israel, and they warn of the consequences of leaving Him. To see each suffering as a direct punishment in every concrete case would go beyond the text.

For today: do not use this passage to judge someone who is suffering. Use it as a call to take God seriously, to return to Him when you have drifted away, and to trust in His mercy, which reaches us in Christ.
exp.10:16:
It says that if the people turn away from God to serve other gods, the anger of the LORD will be kindled against them. He would shut the heavens so that there would be no rain, the land would not yield its produce, and they would soon perish from the good land that the LORD was giving them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the rain and the harvests depend on God, not on the gods of Canaan. The verse is a serious warning, part of the covenant: obeying brings blessing, and turning away brings consequences.

For today: let us not give anything the place of God, such as money, success, or comfort. Each day, thank God for what you receive and ask Him for a faithful heart that does not forget Him.
exp.21:9:
It says that the land should not be plowed by yoking together an ox and a donkey under the same yoke. "Together" means "at the same time," and "plow" means breaking up the ground to sow it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and gives them instructions for their daily life. It sits in the middle of laws about mixing: seeds, cloth. Some believe it teaches separation and order; others, that it protects the animals, since the ox is stronger than the donkey and the donkey would suffer. The text does not explain the reason, so we cannot be certain of it.

For today: although we do not plow with animals, we can learn to make sure no one carries a burden they cannot bear. Let us think about our work, our families, or our church, and share the tasks with fairness and compassion.
exp.25:2:
This verse says that the Israelite was to go to the priest who was serving at that time. There he would make a declaration. The phrase "I declare today to the LORD your God" means that he publicly states and admits that God has kept his promise. The word "swore" means that God made the promise with a solemn commitment. "Our fathers" refers to the ancestors, such as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the land. He explains how to offer the firstfruits, that is, the first fruits of the harvest, carried in a basket to the place that God would choose. By saying these words, each person remembered that the land was a gift from God and not merely the fruit of their own effort.

Today we can pause to acknowledge out loud what God has done for us. Before asking for more, give thanks in your own words for a promise he has already fulfilled in your life.
exp.24:1:
It says that if a guilty person deserves to be punished with lashes, the judge must order that he be laid down on the ground and flogged in his presence. The punishment must match the crime ("the number of lashes his crime warrants") and be counted out exactly. The guilty one is the "guilty man," "laid down" means stretched out on the ground, and "have him flogged" means the judge will have him beaten.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of laws for life in community.
