This rule limits the punishment: the judge watches to make sure it is fair, measured, and does not turn into revenge. The next verse sets a maximum of forty lashes, so that the person is not humiliated.

For today: when we have to correct someone, whether a child, a student, or an employee, let us do it with justice and with limits, without overdoing it or humiliating them. Correction seeks the good of the person; it is not meant to vent anger.
exp.20:8:
This verse says that the people of Israel would remove from among them the guilt of shedding innocent blood. They would do this by doing what is right in the eyes of the LORD. "The guilt of shedding innocent blood" refers to the responsibility for having killed someone who was not guilty. "What is right in the eyes of the LORD" means what God sees as just.

Moses speaks to the people in the book of Deuteronomy. Before this verse, a case is described in which a dead body is found and it is not known who the killer was. The elders of the nearest city would perform a ritual, declare their innocence, and ask God to forgive the whole people. In this way the land would not be stained by that injustice.

For today: God takes injustice seriously, even when we do not know the guilty person. We can do what is right by being honest, defending the vulnerable, and not looking the other way when others are harmed.
exp.30:15:
God tells Moses that he will soon die. "You will soon rest with your fathers" is a gentle way of speaking about death. He also warns that once the people enter the land they are about to receive, they will turn to the foreign gods of that land and give themselves to them, the way a person who is faithful to a spouse might betray that trust. In doing so they will forsake God and break the covenant he has made with them.

The Lord speaks in the tabernacle, where Moses and Joshua are waiting. Israel is about to enter the land, and God is preparing Joshua to lead them. God knows the hearts of the people and gives warning in advance. Afterward the consequences of that unfaithfulness are announced.

For today: let us not assume that we will remain faithful to God simply because life is comfortable. When everything goes well, it is easy to neglect prayer and the Word. Let us tend our relationship with God each day, so that other things do not take his place.
exp.19:13:
This verse says that in a war against a distant city that refused peace and attacked, the men would be killed, but the women, the children, the animals, and all the goods of the city would be taken as plunder for Israel. "Plunder" means the things taken from a defeated enemy. "Inheritance" is the land received as a possession.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. These rules of war belong to the old covenant with Israel, in a world where wars were brutal. Notice that peace was offered first, and that the nearby cities, within the promised land, were treated differently and more severely. Interpreters debate how to understand these commands, and it is honest to admit that they are difficult.

For today: Jesus calls us to seek peace and to love even our enemies. Before fighting or disputing, offer peace first, as this text shows it was to be done.
exp.30:17:
God says that when the people turn to other gods, he will hide his face from them. The phrase about the people's wrongdoing in the Berean Standard Bible is "because of all the evil they have done by turning to other gods," so the sense is that they have done these evil things by turning away to other gods.

God speaks with Moses shortly before Moses dies. He tells him that Israel, once settled in the promised land, will forget the covenant and worship idols. For this reason he commands Moses to write a song that will serve as a witness. God does not speak of punishment with pleasure; he warns honestly. Interpreters understand this hiding of the face as the consequences of turning away from him, not as a permanent abandonment.

For today: examine which things take God's place in your heart, such as money, success, or comfort. Return to him sincerely, for he always invites repentance.
exp.8:7:
At Horeb, which is another name for Sinai, the people of Israel angered God through their disobedience. The phrase "provoked the LORD" means they caused him to become angry, and the statement that he was "angry enough to destroy you" shows that their sin was so serious they deserved to be destroyed.

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He wants them not to think of themselves as better than other peoples. He reminds them that God gives them the land because of his goodness and his promise, not because they earned it. Next he recounts what happened at Horeb, when the people sinned while he was receiving the tablets of the law.

For today: when you receive blessings, do not think you deserve them because you are good. Remember your own failures and thank God for his patience and his mercy.
exp.29:10:
This verse says that what God commands is neither hidden nor out of reach. The word "intimate" (meaning to command or declare with authority) and the word "hidden" (meaning concealed or hard to understand) are both explained here. The phrase "not far off" means it is within the reach of the people.

Moses speaks to Israel at the end of his life, shortly before they enter the promised land. He has just spoken to them about returning to the Lord with their whole heart, with the promise that God would bless them again. Here he makes clear that obeying is not a task beyond their reach, because God has already given them his word in writing.

Today we can approach the Bible without thinking it is only for experts. Read one passage each day, ask God to help you understand it, and put into practice one simple step you see there.
exp.33:5:
God himself buried Moses in a valley in the land of Moab, facing Beth-peor. The verse says that to this day no one knows the location of his grave.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who closes the account of Moses. God had just shown Moses the promised land from the mountain, but did not allow him to enter it. Who wrote this ending is not known for certain; some think it was Joshua or someone else, and the Bible does not make it clear. It is also not known why God kept the grave hidden. Some believe it was to keep the people from turning it into an object of worship.

For today: God cares for his servants to the very end, and the glory belongs to him, not to people. We can serve faithfully without needing recognition, trusting that God takes care of us always.
exp.2:6:
It says that the people of Israel kept all the livestock and the plunder they took from the cities they had defeated. "Plunder" refers to the valuable things seized when winning a war.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life. He reminds them of the victories over Sihon and Og, kings east of the Jordan, before they enter the promised land. He presents those conquests as the work of God, and his purpose is to encourage them to trust Him. The text also mentions the total destruction of those cities, which is very harsh. Scholars interpret it in different ways, and it is best read within its specific historical moment.

For today: remember with gratitude how God has sustained you in the past. That strengthens your trust for the challenges ahead, and it helps you receive what you have as a gift, not as your own merit.
exp.31:11:
This verse says that the LORD alone was the one who guided his people, Israel. The phrase "led him" means that he guided him and took him along the way. The verse's line that no foreign god was with him means that no other god traveled with Israel or helped him. God had no partners in caring for his people.

Moses speaks in the song he left to Israel before he died. He recalls how God found them in the wilderness and cared for them the way an eagle watches over its young. He does this to show that Israel has no reason to go after other gods, because the LORD alone sustained them. The song also warns what would happen if they forgot him.

For today: remember the times God sustained you in difficult seasons. Thank him and trust in him, instead of looking for security in other things.
exp.0:34:
This verse says that none of the men of that evil generation will see the good land that God promised with an oath to Israel's ancestors. "Evil generation" refers to those who rebelled. The promise was made to the people's forefathers, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Moses speaks to the people as he recalls what happened near Kadesh-barnea. The Israelites were afraid, did not trust God, and grumbled, even though He had led them with fire and cloud. For this reason God swore that that generation would not enter the land. Only Caleb would be the exception, because he faithfully followed the Lord.

For today: unbelief has consequences, but faithfulness is also seen by God. When you are afraid, remember how He has guided you before and trust His promises, even when the path looks difficult.
exp.6:21:
God says he will drive the nations of Canaan out before you little by little, not all at once. The Berean Standard Bible words it this way: you will not be able to wipe them out completely in one go, or the wild animals would multiply around you. "Drive out" is the sense of the phrase, and "eliminate" means to remove them completely. The reason given is practical: if the land were suddenly emptied, wild animals would grow in number and become a danger to Israel.

Moses is speaking to the people just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the Lord will fight for them and urges them not to be afraid. The slow pace served a practical purpose, allowing Israel to care for the land and settle it step by step. Scholars understand in different ways how this came about, but the text stresses that God is the one who guides the pace.

For us today, this is a lesson in trusting God when things move slowly. If you do not see quick results, God may be caring for you and preparing you to hold on to what He is giving you.
exp.13:22:
You are to eat, in the presence of the LORD your God, a tenth of your grain, new wine, and oil, and the firstborn of your herds and flocks, at the place He will choose as a dwelling for His Name. The firstborn are the first young born to the animals; the herds are the larger livestock and the flocks the smaller. The purpose was so that you would learn to fear the LORD your God always, that is, to respect Him and live in reverence toward Him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they are a holy people, set apart for God. This tithe was brought to the place of worship and shared with joy, like a festival before the LORD.

For today: make your gratitude to God something concrete and constant. Giving generously, and gathering with others to celebrate His blessings, helps you remember that everything you have comes from Him.
exp.8:19:
This verse says that the Lord was angry enough with Aaron to want to destroy him, and that Moses also prayed for him at that time. Being angry enough to destroy someone means feeling a very strong anger, and destroying him means bringing his life to an end.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the sin of the golden calf, when Aaron took part in making the idol (Exodus 32). Moses wants them to remember that they were saved by God's mercy and not by their own merits. This verse shows that even the high priest needed forgiveness.

For today: praying for others, even for leaders who have failed, is an act of love. All of us need God's mercy, and we can ask for it for those around us too, without feeling superior.
exp.11:29:
Here is what it means: once Israel enters the land and God has destroyed the nations who lived there, the people must take care not to be trapped into copying them. "Be careful not to be ensnared by their ways" means being caught by adopting what they did. "Do not inquire about their gods" means: do not even be curious about how they worshiped, in order to imitate it.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land, in his farewell. He warns them that the danger would not only be war, but the temptation to mix their faith with the customs of the neighboring peoples. The verses that follow explain that those practices included terrible things, such as sacrificing children.

Today we too can fall into copying what most people do, even when it does not please God. Before following a trend or custom, ask yourself: "Does this honor God according to his Word?" Let that Word be your guide, not the crowd.
exp.22:8:
It says that when Israel's army was encamped against its enemies, the people had to keep themselves away from every wrong thing. The phrase "encamped against your enemies" describes the army stationed in a position of conflict, and "keep yourself" means take care of yourself and stay away from. The expression "every wrong thing" covers everything that was unclean or improper.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The verses that follow show that this "wrong thing" included ritual uncleanness in the camp, because God was present in the midst of his people. For Israel, war was not only a matter of strength, but also of living clean before God.

Today, when we face a difficult struggle, whether at work, in the family, or in health, we can ask ourselves which habits or attitudes we should leave behind. Taking care of our conduct and our heart helps us face problems with a clear conscience and trust in God.
exp.31:38:
God says: "Look carefully: I am He, and there is no God besides Me." He brings death and gives life, and he wounds and heals. No one can rescue anyone from his hand. The words "see" and "look" are the same command, and "deliver" means to rescue.

These words are part of the Song of Moses, near the end of his life. God himself speaks and rebukes Israel, who had turned away from him to follow idols. Earlier he mocks those false gods: where are they now to help? The passage shows that only the Lord has true power. Some understand that the wounding and the healing include God's discipline, which seeks to restore.

Today, when things do not turn out the way you hope, do not place your security in money, success, or people. Rest in God, who governs your life and sustains your future. Bring to him in prayer today whatever worries you.
exp.1:18:
This verse says that Israel was going to come near the land of the Ammonites, and that they must not provoke them or get into conflict with them. God gives the reason: he would not give the Israelites any of that land, because he had already given it to the descendants of Lot. The word "possession" in the verse above is the one used here; it means property that is received as an inheritance. "Get into conflict with them" means do not attack them or harass them.

Here Moses speaks, reminding the people of what the LORD told him during the journey through the desert, near the end of the forty years. The Ammonites were descendants of Lot, Abraham's nephew. God had given lands to other peoples, and Israel was to respect those boundaries while moving toward the promised land.

God rules over all nations and carries out his purposes with each of them. We do not need to fight over what God has already given to others, nor envy their blessings. We can live in peace, respect what belongs to others, and trust that God will care for what is ours.
exp.13:12:
This verse follows a list of birds that the people of Israel were not to eat. It names the red kite, the falcon, and any kind of kite, that is, these birds together with others of a similar kind. The exact identity of some of these birds is not known with certainty, but nearly all of them are birds of prey that feed on flesh.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they are a people set apart for God, and for that reason he gives them rules about what they could eat. The Bible does not explain every reason; some think it relates to holiness and obedience.

For today: God calls us to live differently, even in ordinary things. We can ask ourselves whether, in our daily decisions, such as what we look at, say, and do, we seek to please Him with an obedient and grateful heart.
exp.26:23:
God condemns the one who strikes another person in secret, that is, in hiding, where no one sees. The word "cursed" means under the judgment of God, cut off from his blessing. The word "neighbor" refers to any person nearby, such as a neighbor or a fellow countryman. The word "strikes" means to hit or attack, and under the law of Moses it can include an attack that ends in death. All the people answer "Amen," which means "so be it," accepting this warning.

Moses and the elders speak to Israel before they enter the promised land. The Levites would pronounce these curses, and the people accepted them as part of their covenant with God. Many of these sins were committed in secret, which is why the list stresses that God sees what human judges cannot see.

For today: take care how you treat others when no one is watching. God sees hidden harm, whether a blow, a slander, or a betrayal. Live with integrity in private too.
exp.17:7:
It says that a Levite who comes to serve at the sanctuary will receive a portion equal to that of the other Levites who are already there. The word "portion" refers to the share of food and provision that was due to them for their service. The phrase "even though he has received money from the sale of his father's estate" can be understood in two ways: either that he also received whatever he might have from his family or from selling his property, or that he received his share without anything being deducted because he had other income. Scholars do not fully agree.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The Levites had no territory of their own and lived from the offerings. Here the Levite who comes from another town is protected so that he is not treated as less.

For today: treat with equality and generosity those who serve in your church, regardless of where they come from or how long they have been there. Support with what you can those who dedicate themselves to the work of God.
exp.20:19:
This verse records what the parents were to say before the elders: that their son is "stubborn" (set in his ways, unwilling to yield) and "rebellious," that he does not obey them, and that he is a "glutton and a drunkard," meaning he gives himself over to excess without control.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law brought the case before the elders at the city gate, and it did not leave the parents to decide alone. It concerns persistent rebellion, even after being corrected. Scholars debate how often it was applied; later Jewish tradition set such strict conditions that it was almost never carried out.

For today: obedience and self-control matter. If you are a son or daughter, receive correction with humility. If you are a parent, correct with patience and love, seeking wise help when you need it.
exp.15:15:
This verse commands that all the men of Israel appear before the LORD their God three times a year, in the place He would choose. The feasts were the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Tabernacles. "Appear" means "present themselves," and "empty-handed" means arriving without bringing an offering.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that these feasts are for rejoicing and for giving thanks to God for His blessing. For this reason he includes servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows. The place of gathering would be one only, and the next verse says that each person would bring according to what God had given him.

For today: set aside regular times to meet with God and with His people, and come with gratitude. Give generously according to what you have received, and make sure that those in greatest need also have a place in the joy.
exp.2:27:
God tells Moses to commission Joshua, to encourage him, and to strengthen him. Joshua will be the one who crosses over ahead of the people, and the one who will enable them to inherit the land that Moses will only be able to see from a distance. The word "commission" here means to formally entrust him with the task, and "encourage" means to give him courage and confidence.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel, near the end of his life. He tells them that he asked God to let him enter the promised land, but God said no. Even so, God does not leave him with sadness without purpose: he gives him one last task, to prepare the one who will carry on leading the people.

For today: even though we may not achieve everything we hope for, we can keep serving. Encouraging and preparing others, in the family, the church, or the workplace, is a valuable way to take part in what God wants to do.
exp.14:17:
Do not regard it as a hardship to set your servant free. He has served you for six years, and that was worth twice the wages of a hired hand, that is, a worker who is paid by the day. The LORD your God promises to bless you in all you do when you let him go with generosity.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law protected those who fell into debt and sold themselves as servants: after six years they were to go free (vv. 12-17). Many understand the double value as a reference to the great worth of his labor, though some interpret it in other ways.

Today, when you have to release a debt, let an employee go, or be generous with someone, do it with gratitude and not with bitterness. God sees your generosity and cares for you.
exp.3:15:
This verse warns the people not to ruin themselves by making an idol in the form of any shape or figure, whether in the likeness of a man or of a woman. "That you do not act corruptly" means "so that you do not bring destruction upon yourselves." An "idol" is a carved or made object set up as a representation to be worshiped. A "likeness of a male" is the form of a man, and a "likeness of a female" is the form of a woman.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that when God spoke at Mount Horeb, they heard his voice from the midst of the fire, but they saw no form. For this reason they must not make an image to represent God.

Today we might ask whether we are reducing God to what is comfortable or familiar to us. A practical application is to know him through what he said about himself in the Bible, and not through our own ideas, customs, or mental images. In this way we worship him as he really is.
exp.26:24:
God condemns the person who accepts a bribe to kill someone who has done nothing wrong. "Cursed" means that person is under God's judgment and outside his blessing. The people then respond "Amen," which means "so be it," agreeing that this judgment is just.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He orders a ceremony between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, where the Levites read curses and the people respond. Many of these curses deal with sins committed in secret. In this way, the people commit themselves to obey God's law and to protect life and justice.

For today: do not use your influence, your money, or your silence to harm an innocent person. Defend the truth and reject every bribe or unjust deal, even when no one sees you.
exp.32:24:
This verse is part of the blessing on the tribe of Asher. "Bolts" refers to the bars of the gates, according to some translators, or to footwear; the word in the original is rare and is understood in several ways. "Iron and bronze" speak of firmness and protection. The second part promises that Asher's strength will match his days, meeting what he needs each day.

Moses speaks just before he dies. He blesses the twelve tribes of Israel, one by one. To Asher he speaks of abundance, with oil and good relations with his brothers. Then comes this promise of protection and strength. Afterward Moses reminds them that the true source of everything is God, who is a refuge and sustains with everlasting arms.

For today: God does not promise that there will be no hard days, but strength enough for each one. Today you can face your tasks and trials trusting that He sustains you, without being anxious about tomorrow.
exp.23:3:
A man who sent his wife away cannot take her back as his wife if she has since married another. "Defiled" means stained or made unclean. "Sent away" refers to a divorce. Scholars explain in several ways what exactly that stain consists of, and the text does not spell it out.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the land God promised them and reminds them of God's law. This rule was meant to restrain divorces made lightly and to keep a woman from being treated as an object that is discarded and reclaimed at will. Jesus later explained that Moses allowed divorce because of the hardness of the people's hearts.

Today we can take our commitments seriously and treat people with respect, never as things to be used and then thrown away. Before we promise something, let us think carefully about what we say.
exp.4:15:
It says that we should honor our father and our mother, as the LORD our God has commanded us. To honor means to give them respect and value, not merely to obey. The promise is that our days may be long and that it may go well with us in the land the LORD our God is giving us.

Moses speaks to Israel, about to enter the promised land, and reminds them of the Ten Commandments given at Mount Sinai. This is the first commandment about relationships between people, and it comes right after the command to keep the day of rest. The promise was addressed to the nation in its land, and it can be understood as an invitation to live in order and stability.

Today, honoring your parents can mean calling them, listening to them with patience, and caring for them as they grow old, even when you do not always agree with them.
exp.10:0:
Therefore you shall love the LORD your God and always keep His charge, His statutes, His ordinances, and His commandments. "Charge" is what God asks His people to guard; "statutes" are His set rules; "ordinances" are His just decisions; and "commandments" are His orders. "Always" means this is not something for a single moment, but for the whole of life.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they themselves saw the mighty works of God in Egypt. For this reason, their obedience should spring from what they have seen and from their relationship with God, not from rules alone.

For today: love for God is shown in daily obedience. Remember how God has cared for you, and choose today one concrete, small, and faithful action that pleases Him.
exp.19:17:
This verse gives the reason for the command just before it: Israel was to destroy the Canaanite cities completely so that those peoples would not teach them their detestable practices, meaning the religious customs that were abhorrent to God. The verse says the purpose is so that they cannot teach you to do all the detestable things they do for their gods, and so cause you to sin against the LORD your God. The danger was that Israel would copy the worship of those gods and in this way turn away from the LORD.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land, giving them instructions for war. This command refers only to those specific nations, and the text presents it as tied to their idolatry. It is a difficult passage, and scholars understand it in various ways. All agree that the emphasis is on protecting Israel's faithfulness to God.

Today we do not use violence, but we can take seriously the influences that pull us away from God. It is worth asking ourselves which things, friendships, or habits draw us into sin, and setting wise limits to protect our faith.
exp.3:45:
This verse tells where the people of Israel were when Moses explained the law to them. They were on the east side of the Jordan River, in a valley facing Beth-peor, in the land that once belonged to Sihon, king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon. Moses and the Israelites defeated him after they had come out of Egypt. The word "defeated" here means that they won the battle against him.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who presents the place where Moses spoke. Israel was about to enter the promised land. Moses was reminding them of the law and showing them how God had already given them victories along the way.

For today: when you doubt the future, remember how God has helped you in the past. That grateful memory can give you courage to obey Him and trust Him with what is ahead.
exp.27:61:
This verse says that the people of Israel, who had grown as numerous as the stars in the sky, would be reduced to very few in number. The reason is simple: they would not obey God. "Few in number" means small in count, and "obey the voice of the LORD your God" means listening to God and doing what he says.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He sets before them the blessings that come with obedience and the consequences of turning away from the covenant. This warning follows a long list of curses. It recalls the promise made to Abraham of many descendants, which here would be affected by disobedience.

For today: God gives us blessings and hopes that we will listen to him with a sincere heart. We can ask ourselves which area of our life needs more attention to his voice, and take one concrete step of obedience today, trusting in his goodness.
exp.31:2:
This verse says that Moses is going to proclaim the name of the Lord, that is, to speak about who God is and what he is like. Then it calls everyone to recognize and declare his greatness. Here "I will proclaim" means to announce openly. The phrase "Ascribe greatness" means: recognize and declare that God is great.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, near the entrance to the promised land. This song was given so that Israel would remember it. Before pointing out the people's failures, he begins by praising God. The verses that follow show him as a faithful and just Rock.

For today: before asking God for something or talking about your problems, begin by giving him thanks and remembering what he is like. This helps you see everything with more confidence and humility.
exp.15:11:
This verse says that the people of Israel had to remember that they were once slaves in Egypt. Because of that, they were to follow God's laws carefully. The word "slaves" here refers to people held in servitude, and "these statutes" are the commands and rules God gave them.

Moses is speaking to the people before they enter the promised land. He has just described the Feast of Weeks, a celebration in which everyone rejoiced together: family, servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows. Remembering their own time as slaves helped them treat with kindness those who were in need, because God had rescued them.

Today we can remember where God has brought us from and how much grace we have received. That grateful memory moves us to follow him and to be generous, including toward those who have less or who feel alone.
exp.25:16:
This verse says that the people of Israel declare today that the Lord is their God. The word "proclaimed" here means that they have openly affirmed him as God, giving him first place. With this declaration they commit themselves to walk in his ways, keep his statutes, commandments, and ordinances (that is, his laws), and listen to his voice. To listen to his voice here implies obeying, not merely hearing.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter the promised land. He explains a ceremony: when presenting the firstfruits, each Israelite would remember God's faithfulness and renew their commitment to him. It is a response of gratitude within the covenant. The following verse shows that God, in turn, acknowledges them as his people.

For today: we can renew our commitment to God with gratitude, not out of simple obligation. A practical step is to begin the day by thanking him for something specific and asking his help to obey him in one particular decision.
exp.3:33:
This verse asks whether any god has ever tried to take a nation out from the midst of another nation, as the LORD your God did for Israel in Egypt. The word "tried" points to a bold, deliberate act, and the verse lists the means by which God did it: trials, signs, wonders, war, a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and great terrors. Signs are actions that show his power; wonders are events that cause deep awe; the "strong hand and outstretched arm" speaks of God's power in action.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, now close to the promised land. He reminds them of what God alone did: he freed them from Egypt and spoke to them out of the fire. He wants them, with that memory, to recognize him as the only God and to obey him with gratitude.

For today: when you doubt or feel forgotten, remember what God has already done in your life and in his history with his people. Write down three things in which you have seen his help, and thank him for them.
exp.8:11:
God tells Moses to get up and go down from the mountain at once, because the people he brought out of Egypt have corrupted themselves. How quickly they have turned aside from the way God commanded them! They have made for themselves a molten image.

Here Moses is looking back on what happened at Mount Sinai. While he was receiving the tablets of the covenant for forty days, the impatient people made an idol for themselves. Moses reminds them of this to show that their entry into the promised land was not due to their own goodness, but to God's mercy.

For today: how easily we turn aside when we feel that God is slow. We can ask him to keep us faithful while we wait, and not to look for shortcuts or for things that take the place of his rightful place in our hearts.
exp.1:14:
It says that God himself acted against that generation of Israel until all the fighting men died in the wilderness. "The LORD's hand" is a way of speaking of his power in action. The phrase "to eliminate them from the camp" means to remove them from the people's camp, and "until they had all perished" means that not one of them was left.

Moses speaks, reminding the people of their history before they enter the promised land. That generation refused to trust God at Kadesh-barnea (Numbers 14), and God swore that they would not enter. They spent thirty-eight more years on the journey, until they crossed the brook Zered. Moses wants the new generation to learn from that.

For today: disobedience and unbelief have serious consequences, yet God is faithful to his word and carries on with his plan. Today we can ask ourselves in what area it is hard for us to trust God, and decide to obey him with humility and confidence, without putting it off.
exp.18:0:
When the LORD your God cuts off the nations whose land He is giving you, and you drive them out and settle in their cities and houses, they must do something. The phrase "cuts off" in the verse above means the same as "destroys," and "settle in" means receiving the land as your own. Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter Canaan, in his farewell in the book of Deuteronomy. This verse introduces a command: to set apart three cities of refuge, where a person who had killed someone without intent could flee. In this way the life of the innocent was protected and unjust revenge was prevented.

For today: when God gives us something good, such as a home, a job, or an opportunity, he also calls us to use it with justice and mercy. We can ask ourselves how we might help someone who needs protection or a second chance.
exp.7:16:
This verse warns against a dangerous thought: believing that you yourself, by your own strength and effort, have made yourself wealthy. The reader is warned about what goes on in the inner self, the private thought that may never be spoken aloud. The words "the power and strength of my hands" refer to one's own ability and labor.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God cared for them in the wilderness, providing water and bread from heaven. He warns that when they have houses, livestock, and abundance, they might forget the One who gave them everything and feel self-sufficient.

For today: working hard is good, but it is wise to pause and thank God for health, opportunities, and what we have. A simple practice is to pray giving thanks before each meal or when receiving a paycheck, and to share something with someone who is in need.
exp.33:2:
This verse continues the list of what God showed Moses from the mountain. Here the Negev is mentioned, the dry region to the south. Also named is the region from the Valley of Jericho, the fertile valley next to that city, called the City of Palms. The survey ends at Zoar, a place south of the Dead Sea whose exact location is not entirely certain.

The narrator of the book tells of Moses' final moments. God allows him to see from Nebo the whole promised land, although he will not be able to enter it. Who wrote this chapter is debated; many think another person added it after Moses' death.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even though we do not always see it fulfilled in our own lives. We can trust his promises and serve him faithfully, knowing that others will receive the fruit of what we sow.
exp.17:3:
It says the people were to give the priest the first and best of their harvests: the first of the grain, the new wine, the oil, and the first wool sheared from their flocks. The phrase "the first fruits" refers to the first produce of each season.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. The Levites would not receive a territory of their own, so God arranged for them to live from the people's gifts. It was a way of supporting those who served in worship, and also a reminder that everything they had came from God.

For today: before you spend or share what you have received, ask yourself how you can honor God first, with generosity toward your church and toward those who serve, trusting that he provides.
exp.16:12:
This verse says that when the punishment was carried out on someone who acted with arrogance against the decision of the priest or the judge, all the people would hear of it, would be filled with fear, and would no longer behave arrogantly. "Will hear" means they would find out about it; "be afraid" speaks of serious respect; "will no longer behave arrogantly" means they would stop acting with pride or rebelliousness.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions for resolving difficult cases at a central court. The sentence was severe because it dealt with deliberate rebellion, not a simple mistake. This was a time and a legal system particular to Israel.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we accept correction and authority with humility. When someone advises us with wisdom, it is good to listen before defending ourselves with pride.
exp.9:6:
This verse briefly recounts two stops of the people of Israel in the wilderness. They set out from Moserah toward Gudgodah, and from Gudgodah toward Jotbathah, which the Bible describes as "a land with streams of water", that is, a place with streams of water. "Traveled" means that they set out on their way. It is not known with certainty where these places are today.

Moses speaks to the people and reminds them of their history. He reviews the journey they have made, the death of Aaron and the service of the Levites, so that they can see how God guided and sustained them. This verse sits within a parenthesis in his account.

For today: in the midst of long and weary roads, God also prepares places of rest and provision. You can remember with gratitude those "streams" He has given you and trust that He will guide you through the next stage.
exp.8:10:
At the end of the forty days and forty nights that Moses spent on the mountain, the LORD gave him the two stone tablets. They are called "the tablets of the covenant" because they held the terms of the agreement between God and his people.

Here Moses speaks, near the end of his life, recalling the people's history. He tells them this so that they will not think they are righteous on their own. While God was giving him the law, the people had already turned away from Him by making a calf idol.

For today: God speaks to us with clarity and invites us into a relationship of faithfulness. We can set aside time to listen to His Word calmly, and remember that His grace sustains us when we fail.
exp.14:8:
Be careful not to let a wicked thought take root in your heart. Someone might think: "The seventh year, the year of release, is near," so it's better not to lend anything. Looking at the needy with a begrudging eye means regarding them with selfishness or resentment. The poor brother is a person in need. If he cries out to the LORD against you, your refusal will be counted as sin.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the land God promised them. He explains the law of the year of release, when debts were to be cancelled. God wanted to prevent anyone from using that law as a reason not to help.

Today, we can examine our motives when we give or help. If someone is in need, let us not look for excuses to refuse. Let us ask God for a generous heart and help in practical ways, according to what we are able to do.
exp.4:21:
This verse says that God spoke the Ten Commandments to the whole gathering of the people from the mountain, out of the fire, the cloud and the deep darkness, with a loud voice. "He added nothing more" means that God did not add other words at that time. Then he wrote those words on two tablets of stone and gave them to Moses. "Assembly" refers to the gathering of the people, and "deep darkness" describes the thick cloud that surrounded the mountain.

The one speaking is Moses. He is reminding the new generation of Israel, before they enter the promised land, what happened at the mountain. He wants them to remember that the law was not a human idea, but the direct word of God, given with solemnity and in writing.

For today: God wanted his word to be clear and firm. We can take the Bible seriously and with reverence, setting aside a fixed time each day to read it and ask ourselves: "What is God asking of me today?"
exp.8:5:
He says that God does not give Israel the promised land because they have earned it. Here "righteousness" means being good or upright before God. "Stiff-necked people" means stubborn and foolish, unwilling to be corrected, like an animal that will not bend its neck to take the yoke.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He warns them not to become proud when the LORD drives out the nations who live there. God gives them the land because he keeps the promise he made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and because of the wickedness of those nations. Then Moses reminds them of their rebellions in the wilderness.

For today: everything good we receive from God is a gift, not a reward. When things go well for us, let us give thanks with humility instead of boasting.
exp.32:2:
Deuteronomy 33:3 says that God loves his people, and that all his holy ones are in his hand. Those holy ones sit down at his feet, the way a student sits to listen to a teacher, and each one receives his words.

The verse speaks of the people God loves and the holy ones who belong to him, and it pictures them settling in at his feet to be taught. Some readers take "the people" to mean the tribes of Israel, while others understand it more broadly, as the nations.

Here Moses speaks at the end of his life, blessing the tribes of Israel. He has just recalled how God revealed himself at Sinai and gave his law. This verse shows God's care for his people, who receive his word.

For today: God holds us in his hand, and our natural response is to come close to him and listen. We can set aside a moment each day to read his Word carefully and seek to obey it, trusting that his love cares for us.
exp.3:47:
This verse marks the boundaries of the land that Israel conquered east of the Jordan. It ran from Aroer, on the rim of the Arnon Valley (to the south), as far as Mount Siyon, which is another name for Mount Hermon (to the north). This is not the Siyon of Jerusalem.

The one speaking is Moses. He is on the plains of Moab, about to die, and he reminds the people how God gave them victory over the kings Sihon and Og. He gives them the exact boundaries so that they will remember that this land was a real gift, not a legend.

Today, remembering in detail what God has done for you strengthens your trust. Write down a few specific times when he helped you, and use them to thank him and to face what lies ahead with faith.
exp.27:27:
This verse says that the LORD would afflict the people with "madness," meaning a loss of sound judgment; with "blindness," which can be physical blindness or a lack of clarity in seeing the way ahead; and with "confusion of mind," a phrase that speaks of a mind thrown into disorder and a heart paralyzed by fear.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings if they keep the covenant and curses if they abandon it. These words are a serious warning, not a desire for punishment, so that Israel will faithfully choose God.

For today: turning away from God brings confusion and inner fear. We can seek his guidance every day, ask him for wisdom and peace, and trust that Christ offers us forgiveness and a renewed heart.
exp.26:22:
Whoever sleeps with his mother-in-law falls under a curse. "Sleeps with" is a plain way of describing sexual relations. The people answer "Amen," which means "so be it," and by saying it they agree that this conduct is serious before God.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives instructions for a ceremony on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, where curses would be spoken and the people would respond with "Amen." These are warnings about sins, many of them committed in secret, and about protecting the family. This list of forbidden relationships appears alongside other similar laws, such as those in Leviticus 18 and 20.

Today, this verse invites us to care for holiness in the family. We can set clear boundaries, flee from temptation, and respect our relatives, so that our home is a safe and trustworthy place.
exp.11:8:
This verse says that the people of Israel had not yet entered the land God promised them, which here is called the "resting place" and the "inheritance." An inheritance is property that is given as a gift and passed down to the children. The phrase "not yet" means that the arrival was still ahead of them.

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they cross the Jordan, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He explains how they must worship God once they live in the land. In the wilderness each person did what seemed right to them, but there they would have a place of worship that God would choose. Moses reminds them that the best was still to come.

For today: sometimes we live in a season of waiting, not yet seeing what God has promised. While you are on the way, do not simply do whatever seems right to you. Follow God with order and gratitude, trusting that he keeps what he promises.
exp.25:1:
Once the people were living in the promised land, they were to set apart the firstfruits, meaning the first part of each harvest. They would put it in a basket and take it to the place God chose as a dwelling for his Name, the place of worship where he would be honored.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter Canaan. He teaches them how to thank God when they receive the land he promised to their ancestors. The firstfruits were a way of acknowledging that the harvest was a gift from God, not only the result of their own effort.

For today: before you spend or share what you receive, set something aside for God first, with gratitude. It can be money, time, or service. This helps you remember that everything you have comes from his hand.
exp.8:27:
Moses asks God not to destroy Israel, so that the nations watching will not think badly of Him. They could say that the LORD was not able to bring His people into the land He had promised them, or that He hated them and so brought them out to kill them in the wilderness.

Moses speaks to the people and reminds them of his prayer after the sin of the golden calf. He had pleaded for them on the mountain. He does not defend Israel's behavior, which was stubborn and rebellious, but appeals to God's reputation, to His promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and to His work of rescue.

For today: when we pray for others, or for ourselves, we can rely not on our own merits but on the character and promises of God. And let us remember that the way we live as believers speaks of God to those who observe us.
exp.32:14:
It says that the land of Joseph will also be blessed with the best of the ancient mountains and the bounty of the everlasting hills. The best and bounty of the ancient mountains and everlasting hills are the good and valuable gifts God gives. The mountains and hills are called ancient and everlasting because they have existed for a very long time, and that conveys the idea of a firm and lasting blessing.

Moses speaks just before he dies. He blesses each tribe of Israel, and here he addresses Joseph, that is, the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh. He promises them a fertile land, with water, fruit and good pasture. Some think the images of the mountains refer to the abundance of the land they would receive.

For today: learn to see the good things in your life, such as provision, nature and family, as gifts from God. Give thanks for them and share them generously.
exp.4:13:
It says that the seventh day is a day of rest dedicated to the Lord your God. No one was to do any work: not the head of the household, nor his sons or daughters, nor his male or female servants, nor his oxen or donkeys or other livestock, nor the foreigner living within the town gates. The reason given is that the servants may rest just as you do.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and repeats the commandments to them. Here the rest is not only for the head of the household, but for everyone. Afterward he reminds them that Israel was a slave in Egypt and that God set them free.

For today: set aside a regular time to rest and give thanks to God. And notice those who depend on you or work with you, so that you also give them space for rest and fair treatment.
exp.30:10:
This verse commands that when all Israel comes before the Lord their God at the place he will choose, this law be read aloud so that everyone can hear it. The word "comes" describes people gathering or arriving, and "before the LORD your God" means coming together to worship him. The phrase "in the hearing of all Israel" means they were to hear it directly.

Moses speaks shortly before he dies. He has already written the law and handed it to the priests and the elders. He orders that every seven years, during the Feast of Tabernacles, it be read before the whole people: men, women, children, and foreigners. He wanted the people not to forget the covenant when they entered the promised land, and for the new generations to also learn to fear God.

For today: God's Word is not only for specialists. Find a regular time to read and listen to it, at church or at home with family, and include the children so that they also come to know it.
exp.8:12:
This verse says that God spoke to Moses and told him that he had seen his people, Israel, and that they were stiff-necked. The neck is the back of the head or the throat area. An animal with a stiff neck will not let its owner guide it. It is a way of saying that the people were stubborn and rebellious.

Here Moses speaks, reminding the people of what happened at Mount Sinai. While he was receiving the tablets of the covenant, Israel made a cast calf. God tells Moses what he sees and says that the people had turned aside very quickly from the way he had commanded them.

For today: stubbornness closes our ears to God. We can ask him for a heart willing to listen and to correct itself. When someone corrects us with love, it is better to bow the head than to stiffen the neck.
exp.28:14:
God's covenant, this explanation says, is not only for those who were present that day but also for those who were not there. The word "but" here carries the sense of "rather": the covenant includes everyone. The phrase "those who are not here today" is understood as referring to Israel's future generations, although some also see a reference to those who were unable to attend.

Moses speaks to the people in Moab, at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He is renewing the covenant with God before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that this promise goes back to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and that it must be passed from generation to generation.

For today: faith is not inherited automatically, but it can be shared. Think of someone in your family, a son, a nephew, or a young friend, and this week tell them how God has been faithful to you.
exp.0:3:
This verse says that Moses spoke to the people after God had given them victory over two powerful kings: Sihon, king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan, who lived at Edrei. The word "defeated" means that the kings were beaten in battle.

Moses speaks at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. Israel is east of the Jordan, about to enter the promised land. Before he says goodbye, he reminds them of what God did, so that they will trust Him and obey His law with a new generation.

For today: remembering the past victories God has given us strengthens faith in the face of the challenges ahead. We can write down the times God helped us and read them again when we feel afraid or doubtful about the future.
exp.6:20:
This verse says that the people of Israel should not lose heart or give up before their enemies. The reason is that God himself is present among them. The word "terrified" in the verse refers to being overcome by fear, which the verse describes as losing strength or courage out of fear. "Awesome" does not mean evil, but that God inspires respect and wonder because of his power.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how God brought them out of Egypt with signs and wonders. If God did that once, he can do it again against the nations that now frighten them. The hornets can be understood literally or as a picture of God's judgment; scholars interpret this in different ways.

When you face something that frightens you, remember what God has already done in your life. His presence with you is greater than your fear. You can pray calmly and take the next step trusting in him.
exp.28:7:
This verse says that Israel took the land of the kings Sihon and Og, who had come out to fight against them, and gave it as an inheritance to three groups: the tribe of Reuben, the tribe of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. The wording "gave it as an inheritance" means the land was handed over to them as their own. An inheritance is a portion of land received as a possession.

Moses is speaking, near the end of his life. He is reminding the people of what God did for them in the wilderness and in the recent victories. He recalls this so that they will renew their covenant with God on the plains of Moab, before entering the promised land. Those victories and that inheritance were evidence of God's faithfulness.

For today: remembering what God has already done in our lives strengthens trust and obedience. Recalling his past help helps us follow him with gratitude today.
exp.31:32:
Deuteronomy 32:33 says that the "wine" of God's enemies, meaning what they produce and what fills them, is like the venom of serpents. The verse calls these creatures serpents and describes the poison as the deadly poison of cobras. The picture is of something that looks appealing but kills.

This is part of the Song of Moses, which Moses teaches to Israel before he dies. God himself, through Moses, warns that nations without God, and also a people who turn away from him, bear bitter and destructive fruit. Interpreters debate whether "they" refers only to hostile nations or also to an unfaithful Israel. The context that follows speaks of God's justice and judgment.

Today we can ask what "wine" we are drinking: ideas, habits, or pleasures that seem good but harm the soul. It is wise to examine the fruit and return to the Rock, who is God.
exp.27:24:
It says that if the people turn away from God, he will allow their enemies to defeat them. They would march out to fight against their enemies in one direction, but they would flee from them in seven directions. "You will be an object of horror to all the kingdoms of the earth" means they would be looked at with shock and disgust by the nations around them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings for obeying the covenant and curses for disobeying it. This verse is part of the warnings, and it aims to make Israel take its commitment to God seriously.

For today: obedience to God is not a burden but a path of protection. When you notice that you are drifting away from him, do not harden your heart; return soon, confess, and ask for his help. God is patient and seeks to restore.
exp.5:19:
This verse looks ahead to a future moment: when a son asks his father what the decrees, statutes, and ordinances the LORD our God has commanded them mean. The "decrees" are the reminders of what God has said and done, the "statutes" are his instructions, and the "ordinances" are his just decisions. "In the future" simply means the time to come.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He asks them to obey God and also to teach their children. After the verse, the answer they are to give does not begin with rules but with the story: God brought them out of slavery in Egypt.

For today: if your children or people close to you ask why you follow God, do not answer only with rules. Tell them simply what God has done for you, and let your testimony explain your obedience.
exp.32:15:
Moses asks that the land of Joseph be blessed with its choice gifts and everything within it, and that the favor of God, the one who dwelt in the burning bush, rest upon Joseph. The image of the blessing resting on his head and crowning his brow pictures honor placed on Joseph. The phrase "the prince of his brothers" points to a man set apart from his brothers and raised above them. The thought is of Joseph, sold by his brothers and later honored.

Moses speaks shortly before he dies. He is blessing the tribes of Israel, one by one. Here he blesses Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph. He mentions the bush because it was there that God called him and promised to be with his people (Exodus 3).

For today: even if you have been rejected or left alone, God does not forget you. His grace can cover you and give you a place. Trust that the God who drew near to Moses is also near to you.
exp.6:11:
If the people listen to God's laws and carefully follow them, this verse says, God will keep his covenant with them and the loving devotion he promised to their ancestors. "Ordinances" means God's rules or decrees. "Keep them carefully" means they follow them faithfully and sincerely. "Swore" means God made the promise with a solemn commitment.

Moses speaks to Israel, who are about to enter the promised land. He reminds them that God is faithful and calls them to respond with obedience. After this verse, Moses describes the blessings that will come. It is a covenant: God has already chosen them out of love, and now he invites them to live according to that relationship.

For today: God is faithful to his promises, and our obedience is a response of trust, not a way of buying his love. Today you can choose one concrete step of obedience to what you already know God asks of you.
exp.0:8:
Here Moses reminds the people of what he told them at Mount Horeb: "I cannot carry the burden for you alone." He means that he by himself could not carry the responsibility of guiding, caring for, and settling the problems of a nation so large. The phrase "I said to you" is simply the plain sense of the speech, and "carry the burden" means bear the weight of leading and looking after you.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, before Israel enters the promised land. He goes over the history of the journey. Just before this, God had commanded them to advance and take possession of the land. And just after, Moses gives thanks that God had multiplied them like the stars of heaven, as he had promised Abraham. The burden was great precisely because God had kept his promise.

For today: recognize that we do not have to carry everything alone. Asking for help, sharing responsibilities, and working as a team is not weakness, but wisdom.
exp.16:11:
This verse says that whoever acts presumptuously, refusing to listen to the priest who serves the LORD your God or to the judge, must be put to death. The phrase "acts presumptuously" describes someone who behaves with arrogance and deliberate defiance. "Purge the evil from Israel" means that this wickedness had to be removed from the people so that it would not spread.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. In difficult cases they were to go to the place God would choose and accept the decision of the priest and the judge. The penalty was severe because Israel was a nation under its covenant with God, and open defiance of that justice threatened the unity of the people. This law was meant for that time and that nation.

Today we can learn to live with humility: to listen to wise counsel, to respect fair authorities, and not to harden our hearts when someone corrects us.
exp.15:16:
Every person was to bring their offering according to what God had given them. Not everyone gave the same amount; each one gave in proportion to what they had received. The phrase "as he is able" means what a person could give, and "blessing" refers to what God had given them, such as the harvest and their work.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains the three festivals of the year: the feast of unleavened bread, the feast of weeks, and the feast of booths. These were times of joy and thankfulness. For that reason, no one was to appear before God empty-handed, but with a grateful offering.

For today: give with gratitude and in keeping with what God has given you, without comparing yourself to others. What matters is not the amount, but a joyful heart that recognizes that everything comes from God.
exp.0:18:
It says that the people left Horeb, which is Mount Sinai, and went through the vast and terrifying wilderness, the one they themselves had seen. They set out toward the hill country of the Amorites, just as the LORD their God had commanded, and they reached Kadesh-barnea, a place on the border of the promised land. "Terrifying" here means that the wilderness caused fear and awe.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of their history so that they will obey God. After speaking about the judges, he goes over the journey. Kadesh-barnea was the point where God invited them to enter the land.

For today: God guides us even along difficult paths, and remembering how He sustained us before strengthens our trust for the next step. If today you are going through a "wilderness," obey what God shows you, one step at a time, remembering that He has already brought you this far.
exp.33:11:
This verse closes the book of Deuteronomy and the story of Moses. It says that no prophet arose in Israel like Moses, one who performed all the mighty acts of power and awesome deeds he did before the eyes of the whole nation. The verse looks back on his ministry and sums up what made him unique.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book, not Moses, since the account already describes his death. Tradition attributes it to Joshua or another later writer, though this is not known for certain. The purpose is to sum up who Moses was: a unique servant, whom God dealt with face to face, and through whom He delivered Israel with the signs in Egypt and in the wilderness.

For today: God does great works, but He does them through people who obey Him. Moses is remembered for his power, but that power came from God. We can serve with humility, trusting that God works through us and giving Him the glory.
exp.23:6:
It says that if someone kidnaps a fellow Israelite and treats him as a slave or sells him, that kidnapper must die. "Kidnapping" means that the thief seized and carried off a human being. "Treating him as a slave" means that he used the person as property to be traded. And "purging the evil from among you" means that the people were to remove that wickedness from their community.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and he repeats God's laws to them. The commands nearby protect the most vulnerable: the newly married wife and the poor man who gives something necessary for living as a pledge. Here the freedom of people is protected, since they are worth too much to be treated as things.

For today: God values the freedom and dignity of every person. We can reject every form of exploitation or human trafficking, and support those who help the victims.
exp.17:13:
These nations that Israel was going to displace in the promised land listened to conjurers and diviners, people who claimed to foretell the future and who practiced magic. But God did not permit Israel to do the same. The phrase "as for you" marks that Israel's situation was different.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He has just forbidden practices such as divination and consulting the dead, and he explains that these customs were part of why God judged those nations. Instead, God promised to send a prophet to guide his people with his word.

For today: when you feel anxiety about the future, avoid seeking answers in horoscopes or occult practices. Turn to God in prayer and to his Word, where he makes himself known and guides with confidence.
exp.27:17:
It says that if the people turn away from God, the blessings they would otherwise receive would become a curse. It speaks of their children ("the fruit of your womb"), their harvests ("the produce of your land"), and their animals: the calves of their herds and the lambs of their flocks. In other words, family, food and work would be placed under misfortune.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: obeying him would bring blessing (Deuteronomy 28:1-14), and disobeying him would bring serious consequences. It is a warning meant to help them choose the path of faithfulness.

For today: do not see what you have, whether family, work or possessions, as secure in itself. Everything comes from God. Each day, put him first with gratitude and obedience, and trust him more than your achievements. Christians believe that Christ bore that curse for us (Galatians 3:13).
exp.16:10:
When a case was too difficult to decide, the Israelite was to accept the ruling given by the Levitical priests and the judge. The instruction not to turn aside "to the right or to the left" means not to depart from the decision they declare; that is, not to go against what they pronounce. A "verdict" is the final decision of the case.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. In the verses just before this one, he explains what to do with disputes that the local judges could not settle. They were to go to the place that God would choose, where there was a central court, so that there would be order and justice throughout the nation.

For today: we can learn to respect authorities and wise counselors, without stubbornness or pride. When someone with wisdom and grounded in the Word of God corrects us, it is worth listening with humility.
exp.26:2:
This verse says that, after crossing the Jordan and entering the promised land, the people were to write all the words of this law on the stones. The phrase about plastering the stones with plaster, meaning covering them with a white coat, is not in this verse, so it is left out. The description of the land as flowing with milk and honey is also not in this verse's wording, but the phrase "a land flowing with milk and honey" is, and it describes a good and abundant land. The LORD is the name of God.

Moses, together with the elders of Israel, speaks to a people about to enter the land. He already knows he will not cross with them. He wants Israel to remember that the land is a gift from God and that living in it means obeying his word. Scholars debate exactly how the law was written on the stones, and the text does not make this clear.

For today: before beginning a new stage, put God's Word in a visible place. You could note a verse in your home or in your planner, so that it guides your decisions.
exp.9:14:
It says that God set his love on the ancestors of Israel, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and loved them. Afterward he chose their descendants, the people listening to Moses, above all the other peoples. "Descendants" here means the offspring who come after, and the phrase "set his affection on them" means that he placed his love upon them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God owns the heavens and the earth, so his choosing of them was not because of anything they had earned, but out of love. For that reason he asks them to obey with a willing heart, not a hard one.

For today: if God has reached you with his love, it was not because you deserved it. Let that gratitude lead you to obey him with sincerity and humility, not out of mere obligation or pride.
exp.27:4:
This verse says that God will bless what the people use to store and prepare their daily food. The basket in which the fruits of the harvest were carried is what it refers to. The word translated as "kneading bowl" is an old one, and some understand it as a trough, the container in which bread was mixed. So the verse speaks of never lacking food.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that if they listen to and obey God, their daily life, in the field and in the home, will be under divine care. This is part of a covenant, and not a general promise for everyone in every age.

For today: we can thank God for our daily bread and trust that He cares for everyday life. We can also live generously, sharing what we have with those who are in need.
exp.16:8:
This verse says that when a case was too hard to settle, the person was to go to the Levitical priests and to the judge who was presiding at that time. There he was to inquire of them, and they would give him the verdict in the case.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions so that there will be justice in the cities. When the local judges could not decide, there was a central place, the one God would choose, where the difficult cases were resolved on the basis of God's law.

For today: you do not have to settle the complicated matters alone. When you are unsure between what is right and what is wrong, seek wise, humble counsel grounded in God's Word, and then be willing to obey what you learn.
exp.31:40:
God says that when he sharpens his flashing sword and his hand grasps it in judgment, he will take vengeance on his adversaries and repay those who hate him. The phrasing about grasping judgment follows the verse's own words, "My hand grasps it in judgment," and the vengeance and repayment are described using the verse's wording, "take vengeance" and "repay."

It is part of the Song of Moses. God speaks to the people of Israel, who often abandoned him for other gods. He reminds them that he alone is God, that he gives life and takes life, and that in the end he will defend his people and bring justice against evil and oppression.

For today: we do not have to take revenge on our own. We can hand over to God our wounds and injustices, trust that he is just, and ask him for strength to forgive and to do good, as the New Testament teaches in Romans 12:19-21.
exp.1:19:
This verse says that the land of the Ammonites was also regarded as a land of the Rephaim, a people who lived there long ago. The Ammonites called these people "Zamzummites." The reader's wording here is "regarded as," so the verse points to how people viewed the land at that time. The Hebrew name Rephaim is not fully understood, so it is not known for certain what these people were like.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them that God commanded them not to trouble the Ammonites, because that land had been given to the descendants of Lot. This detail shows that God had already assigned other lands before, even when it meant removing powerful peoples.

For today: God governs history and keeps His promises in His time. We do not need to take what He has already given to others, nor envy it. We can trust what He has promised us and respect the limits He sets.
exp.25:8:
This verse says that God brought his people into the promised land and gave it to them. The verse here points to the words "brought" and "gave," which are the verse's wording in the Berean Standard Bible: "He brought us" and "gave us." The phrase about the land is a way of saying it was a fertile land, good for living and with plenty of food. In this verse's wording, that is the phrase "a land flowing with milk and honey."

The speaker is an Israelite who arrives at the sanctuary with the firstfruits, that is, the first products of his harvest. He was to recite this short confession of faith before the priest. By remembering the oppression in Egypt, the people's cry, and God's deliverance, he acknowledged that the harvest was a gift and not merely the fruit of his own effort.

For today: before thinking about what we lack, we can stop to remember how God has helped us in the past. Giving thanks sincerely, and sharing some of what we have, helps us live with a grateful and generous heart.
exp.31:28:
This expresses a sad wish: if only the people were wise and would understand what is happening to them. Their fate is where their path leads and how it will finish.

This verse is part of the song that Moses taught Israel before they entered the promised land. God speaks through Moses. Many understand that it refers to Israel, which turned away from God and did not see that its defeats came from its unfaithfulness. Some apply it to the enemy nations, but the following verse supports the first reading more strongly.

Today we can take time to think about where our decisions are leading us. Ask God for wisdom to see the end of the road before you travel it, and return to Him with humility when you notice that you are straying.
exp.26:15:
It says that God takes very seriously anyone who dishonors their father or mother. To "dishonor" someone here means treating them as if they were worth little: mocking them, ignoring them, or being disrespectful toward them. "Cursed" means that the person falls under God's judgment and outside his blessing. And the people respond with "Amen," which means "so be it": they acknowledge that this warning is just.

Moses gave these instructions before Israel entered the promised land. The Levites would read aloud a series of curses, and all the people would respond. It was a public way of renewing the covenant with God. Here sins are mentioned that are sometimes committed in secret, such as hidden idolatry, along with wrongs within the home.

For today: honor your parents with respectful words, with your time, and with concrete help. If they are elderly, call them, visit them, and listen to them with patience, even when things are not easy.
exp.0:19:
Moses reminds the people that they had already reached the hill country of the Amorites, a region that the LORD our God was giving to them. The Amorites were one of the peoples living in Canaan. The verse names God as "the LORD our God," and the phrase "is giving us" shows that the land was a gift from Him.

Moses speaks at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, just before Israel enters the promised land. He goes over their history to remind them how, at Kadesh Barnea, they came close to receiving the promise but doubted and sent spies instead of trusting.

Today we can learn that God often brings us to the doorway of what He promises. When He gives us a clear direction, it is wise to obey with confidence, rather than letting fear make us hesitate.
exp.11:3:
The verse says that the people of Israel were not to worship the LORD in the way the neighboring nations worshiped their gods. The words "You shall not worship the LORD your God in this way" point back to what comes before: altars on high places, green trees, images, and sacred groves.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He orders them to destroy the places of pagan worship, and then tells them to worship God in the place He would choose. He wanted to protect them from mixing true faith with false practices. Scholars debate how this was applied over time, but the central idea is clear.

For today: God deserves to be worshiped as He asks, not as it seems right to us or as fashion dictates. Let us examine whether anything in our faith has been mixed with customs that do not honor God, and return to His Word.
exp.25:3:
This verse describes what the priest did when the Israelite arrived with his first fruits. The priest would take the basket from the person's hands and place it in front of God's altar. What the people brought passed from their hands to the place where God was worshiped.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He explains how to give thanks to God once they are living there and eating from their harvests. The first fruits were the first things the land produced. Giving them was a way of acknowledging that the land and the harvest came from God, not only from one's own effort.

For today: before you spend what you receive, whether money, time, or talents, give God the first of it with gratitude. Do it as an act of recognition and not out of obligation, remembering that everything good comes from Him.
exp.29:5:
It says that the LORD your God himself will circumcise your heart and the hearts of your descendants. To circumcise the heart means to remove the hardness that keeps a person from loving God. The words "so that" point to the result: loving God with all your heart and all your soul, and living.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, near the entrance to the promised land. Earlier he had said that, if they turned away and later returned to God, he would gather them from among the nations.
