Here he promises something deeper: that God himself would change their inner life. Many Christians see in this a foretaste of the new covenant, although there is debate about how it is fulfilled.

Today you can ask God each day to soften your heart. The love of God does not arise from your effort alone; he gives it and makes it grow. Pray simply: "Lord, give me a heart that loves you."
exp.1:10:
This verse says that the Emites, the ancient inhabitants of the land of Moab, were regarded as Rephaim, just like the Anakites. The word "regarded" in the verse means "considered" or "thought of as." The Moabites called them Emites, a name that some understand to mean "dreadful" or "frightening," although the exact meaning is uncertain.

Moses reminds the people what God told him as they were on their way to Canaan. God forbade them to fight against Moab, because He had given that land to the descendants of Lot. This aside explains that God had already made room for Moab, even though a great and strong people had once lived there.

For today: God cares for other peoples and has a plan for each one. If He can bring down giants to make room for those He has chosen, we can trust that He also guides our path, without envying what He gives to others.
exp.21:16:
Here a trial at the city gate is described. The husband accuses his wife of shameful conduct, claiming she was not a virgin when they married. The girl's father responds by presenting the proof of her virginity, which was a sheet or cloth, and they spread it out before the city elders. To bring false charges against someone means to accuse or discredit them. A young woman is a girl. But means "but."

Moses gives this law to the people of Israel. Its purpose was to protect the woman from a false accusation and to punish the husband who slandered her. The elders judged at the city gate. Scholars do not fully agree on exactly what the cloth proved, but the central point is clear: the accusation had to be proven, and the one who slandered her paid the penalty.

For today: do not repeat or believe serious accusations without evidence. If someone is slandered, defend them with truth and justice. God cares for the honor of people.
exp.0:44:
This verse says that the people came back after their defeat and wept before God, but God did not listen to them or pay attention to what they said. "You returned" means they came back to the camp. "He would not listen to your voice" means he did not respond to their plea.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, who are now close to the promised land, and reminds them of what happened forty years earlier. God had told them not to go up to fight, but they, in pride, disobeyed and were defeated by the Amorites. Afterward they wept, but without any real change of heart. Moses speaks to them so they will not repeat that mistake.

For today: weeping or regret does not replace obedience. When we fail, God looks for a humble heart that listens and corrects itself in time, not just tears after the consequences. Today you can ask yourself in what area you need to obey God without waiting to regret it afterward.
exp.22:21:
No one is required to make vows to God. If you decide not to make a promise, you do not commit sin. "If you refrain from making a vow" means "if you choose not to do it," and "vow" refers to making a solemn promise to God.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the law about vows: they were voluntary, but once made, they had to be carried out promptly. God takes seriously the words spoken in his presence. That is why this verse gives freedom: not making a vow is no fault, but making a vow and not keeping it is.

Today we can think before we say "I promise you" or "I promise God." It is better to speak little and follow through than to promise much out of emotion and fail afterward. Be sincere and careful with your word.
exp.16:16:
What it says: God sets limits on the future king of Israel. He must not take many wives for himself, because that could lead his heart astray from God. Nor should he accumulate large amounts of silver and gold. "Go astray" means to wander off the right path. "Large amounts" means gathering wealth in great quantity.

Context: Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land, reminding them of God's instructions for a future king. Together with the prohibition against multiplying horses, these rules keep the king from trusting in power, pleasure, or wealth. He is then commanded to copy the law and read it every day. Many see here a foreshadowing of the failings of King Solomon, though the text itself only gives the warning.

For today: When you have power, money, or influence, set simple limits for yourself and read God's Word faithfully. In this way your heart will remain loyal and will not depend on what you accumulate.
exp.23:18:
If, while harvesting your field, you forget a sheaf (a bundle of stalks tied together), you must not go back to get it. It is to be left for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. The verse promises that the LORD your God will bless you in all the work of your hands.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they were foreigners and slaves in Egypt and that God rescued them. For that reason they must care for those who had no land and no protection. The verses that follow apply the same principle to the olive trees and the vineyard.

For today: practice generosity without making it burdensome. You can deliberately set aside a part of your income, your time, or your food to help someone in need, without seeking recognition. Remember that everything you have comes from the grace of God.
exp.27:7:
It says that God will decree a blessing on your barns, the places where grain and provisions were kept, and on everything you put your hand to, that is, your work. It also promises that the LORD your God will bless you in the land he is giving you.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they obey him, they will live under his care. This promise was addressed to Israel as a nation and, according to the context, is tied to keeping God's commandments.

For today: we can work with confidence, remembering that everything we have comes from God. That confidence is shown in being honest, thankful, and generous. The Bible does not promise that everything will be easy, but it does invite us to place our work in God's hands.
exp.1:2:
God tells Moses that the people have already been going around this hill country long enough, meaning the hill country of Seir. He tells them to turn and head north.

Moses is reminding the new generation of Israel about their journey through the desert, after years of wandering that followed the unbelief of the earlier generation. God speaks and marks the end of that stage. Right away he tells them how to pass through the land of Edom, the descendants of Esau, without fighting them, because God had given that land to them as an inheritance.

For today: sometimes we go around in circles for years in the same situation, without moving forward. Ask God for clarity, and when He shows you that the time has come, be bold enough to obey and take the next step.
exp.2:12:
Moses says that he gave to the half-tribe of Manasseh the rest of Gilead and all of Bashan, which had been the kingdom of King Og. He also mentions the region of Argob, within Bashan. The BSB notes that this whole territory used to be called the land of the Rephaim, a people of great stature who had lived there.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of the forty years in the desert. He reminds them how God gave them victory over Og and Sihon, and how the lands east of the Jordan were divided among Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. He wants them to remember God's faithfulness before they enter Canaan.

For today: God keeps what He promises, even when the obstacles seem enormous. Remembering how He helped us in the past strengthens our confidence to face the giants of today, such as fear or debt, and encourages us to give thanks.
exp.20:6:
The verse says that the elders of the city will declare aloud: "Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it." The word "declare" here means to state solemnly, not to complain. They speak of their innocence in an unsolved murder case.

Moses gives this instruction to the people before they enter the promised land. If someone was found dead in the field and it was not known who had killed him, the nearest city carried out a ceremony with a heifer and the priests who were present. Washing their hands showed that they were not guilty, and they asked God not to hold that blood against his people. Every human life mattered greatly to God.

For today: let us take seriously the injustice around us. Even if we are not directly guilty, we can pray, speak, and help so that truth and justice are cared for.
exp.26:16:
Deuteronomy 27:17 speaks of the one who moves his neighbor's boundary stone, that is, who shifts the stones or markers that set the boundary of a field in order to take a piece of his neighbor's land. The words "Cursed is he" mean that such a person stands under God's disapproval and judgment. And all the people answer "Amen," which means "so be it," agreeing that this is just.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. Each family had received its inheritance, and the boundary stones protected that gift from God. This list of curses names sins that could be committed in secret, and so the people publicly commit themselves to reject them.

Today we can be honest in small matters: not taking advantage of someone's oversight, not altering measures, papers, or agreements to gain what is not ours. God sees what is hidden and cares for our neighbor.
exp.32:13:
Here Moses continues blessing the tribe of Joseph. He asks that its land receive the best of the sun and the seasons: a bountiful harvest from the sun and the abundant yield that each season brings. The idea is of rich, valuable produce, the very best that the land can give.

Moses speaks shortly before he dies. He is taking leave of Israel with blessings for each tribe. For Joseph he wishes a fertile land, and all of it is understood as a gift from God, not as the result of one's own merit.

For today: learn to see everyday things, such as food, the weather, and the work that bears fruit, as gifts from God. Give thanks before you eat, and share generously what you have received.
exp.33:7:
It says that the Israelites grieved for Moses on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan, for thirty days. The word for "grieved" describes deep sorrow, and the phrase "time of weeping and mourning" refers to the period of grief. When those thirty days ended, the time of sorrow was considered complete.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who tells of the end of Moses' life. Moses had led the people for forty years in the wilderness. Now Israel is about to enter the promised land, and the account shows that they first paused to honor their leader. Then Joshua takes command, as the following verses say.

For today: grief is healthy and needs time. God does not ask us to hide our pain, but to live through it with honesty and hope. Then, like Israel, we can move forward with confidence that God is still guiding us.
exp.0:38:
The verse says that the little ones the people had said would become captives, along with the children who did not yet know good from evil, would be the ones who entered the land. God would give it to them, and they would possess it. The phrase "little ones" refers to young children, and the people had feared that these children would become captives in war.

Moses speaks to the people in the wilderness, near the end of his life, and recalls what happened at Kadesh-barnea. The adults did not trust God and were afraid to enter the land, so that generation did not go in. Even so, God kept his promise through the next generation. Moses also mentions that he himself would not enter.

For today: God can carry out his plans even when we fail. When fear or doubt holds us back, we can return to trusting him, knowing that he cares even for those we worry about most, such as our children.
exp.27:26:
God would afflict Israel with diseases like the "boils of Egypt," sicknesses like those the Egyptians suffered. Tumors are painful swellings, and the scab is a skin infection. Being unable to be cured means there would be no human remedy.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He sets out blessings for keeping the covenant and curses for abandoning it. These warnings were meant to lead them to take their faithfulness to God seriously.

For today: we should not see every illness as punishment, since the Bible does not teach that. But we can take God's voice seriously, live with humility, and turn to Him when we feel there is no way out.
exp.11:26:
This verse tells the Israelite to bring his burnt offerings, the whole offering burned up for God, with both the meat and the blood, to the altar of the LORD his God. For his other sacrifices, the blood was to be poured out beside the altar, but he could eat the meat himself.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them instructions so that worship would be orderly and obedient, in the place that God would choose. Shortly before, eating blood is forbidden, and they are promised that things will go well for them if they do what is right before the LORD.

For today: God cares about how we approach him, not only about what we do. We can ask ourselves whether we worship him with obedience and reverence, and not out of habit. Christians see in Christ the complete sacrifice, and we respond with gratitude and a life given over to him.
exp.27:58:
It says that if the people disobey, God will bring extraordinary disasters on them and on their descendants. "Disasters" are blows or calamities; "descendants" means their children and later generations; "lasting" means they cannot be easily removed; and "severe and lasting plagues" and "terrible and chronic sicknesses" describe serious, prolonged afflictions.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: obeying it would bring blessing, and rejecting it would bring painful consequences. It is a serious warning, given so that the people would take God and his law seriously. Some understand these words as directed mainly to Israel under that covenant.

For today: God calls us to take his voice seriously, not out of empty fear, but because our decisions affect others, especially our family. Today you can choose one concrete act of obedience and do it with confidence in his grace.
exp.30:1:
Moses tells the Israelites that he is now one hundred and twenty years old and that he is no longer able to come and go as he once did, meaning he no longer has the strength to lead the people as before. He also reminds them that the LORD has told him, "You shall not cross the Jordan."

Moses speaks at the end of his life, on the plains of Moab, just before Israel enters the promised land. He encourages them by reminding them that God himself will go before them and that Joshua will be the new leader. Some think that being unable to come and go refers to his age; others, to his limit as a leader. The text joins both ideas.

For today: all of us reach stages in which we must let go of responsibilities. We can do so with peace, preparing others and trusting that God continues to guide his work, even when we are no longer at the front.
exp.1:7:
Israel went on its way without fighting the descendants of Esau, whom the passage calls "our brothers." They passed the Arabah road that comes up from Elath and Ezion-geber, places near the Red Sea. Then they turned away and traveled along the road of the Wilderness of Moab. "We passed by" means "we went past without stopping or attacking."

Moses speaks, reminding the people, almost at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. God had commanded them to respect the land of Edom, because it was the inheritance of the descendants of Esau, relatives of Israel. Moses reminds them that God took care of them and that nothing was lacking to them.

For today: God asks us to respect the boundaries and dignity of others, even when we have the strength to impose ourselves. We can trust that he provides, and so live without envy, without quarrels, and with honest dealing toward others.
exp.24:14:
This verse commands the use of accurate and honest weights and measures when buying and selling. "Accurate" and "honest" mean true to the standard and free of deceit. The ephah was a measure for dry goods, such as barley or flour. God promises that whoever lives with this honesty will live long in the land He gives.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter Canaan. He reminds them of laws for living justly in community. The verses before this one forbid having double weights, one for buying and another for selling, which harmed the poor above all. The verses that follow say that God detests fraud.

For today: be honest with your money and your work. Charge what is fair, pay what you owe, keep what you promise, and do not take advantage of someone who trusts you. Integrity in small things honors God and builds trust around you.
exp.10:18:
This verse commands parents to teach God's words to their children, speaking about them at all times: at home, along the road, when lying down and when getting up. The pairing of these moments covers the whole of daily life, from morning to night, indoors and out. It describes a constant and natural kind of teaching, not just a special class.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that obeying God brings blessing and that forgetting him brings serious consequences. For this reason he asks them to keep his words in their hearts and pass them on to the next generation.

For today: make faith part of daily life. You can pray with your children in the morning, talk about a verse at mealtime, or speak about God while driving or walking together, letting the conversation flow simply.
exp.7:18:
If you ever forget the LORD your God and go after other gods to worship and bow down to them, God warns you with complete seriousness that you will perish. The words "I testify against you today" mean that Moses is solemnly declaring this warning, the way a witness would speak under oath. To bow down and worship means to bend low in devotion. "Other gods" refers to the gods of other peoples.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He has just told them that there they will have abundance, and he warns them of the danger of thinking that their wealth is only the fruit of their own effort. He reminds them that God is the one who gives the strength to prosper. Forgetting him would lead to idolatry and to the same consequences suffered by the peoples of Canaan.

For today: when things are going well, it is easy to trust only in yourself. Set aside a moment each day to thank God for what you have, and put God first before money, work, or success.
exp.27:38:
The verse says that the people would plant vineyards and care for them, but they would not drink the wine or gather the grapes, because worms would destroy the fruit. "Cultivate" means to tend and work the ground. "Gather" means to pick the harvest.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He sets out blessings if they obey God and curses if they turn away from him. This verse is part of a warning: disobedience would bring loss, frustration, and finally exile. What they worked so hard for would not bear fruit.

For today: God invites us to trust him and not only in our own effort. We can work with diligence, but we should also ask ourselves whether we are placing our lives in his hands. His guidance gives meaning and fruit to what we do.
exp.28:13:
God is not making this covenant and this oath only with the people standing there that day. "Covenant" means an agreement, and "oath" is a solemn promise. Moses makes clear that the commitment to God reaches beyond those who were listening at that moment.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel on the plains of Moab, at the end of forty years in the wilderness, before they enter the promised land. He is renewing the covenant with a new generation. The next verse says it also includes those who are "not here with us today," which many understand as the children and future generations.

Our decisions of faith can affect others. If you follow God, your example, your prayers, and your teaching can leave a mark on your family and on those who come after you. Live today with them in mind.
exp.30:20:
God says that when many troubles and afflictions come upon the people for turning away from Him, the song that Moses will teach them will speak against them as a witness. That song will not be forgotten, because their descendants will keep repeating it.

Here the word "inclination" means what is in their mind and heart, the direction their desires and choices tend to go. God already knows them, even before they enter the land He swore to give them.

God speaks with Moses shortly before Moses dies. God knows that Israel, while living in abundance, could forget Him and follow other gods. For this reason He commands that a song easy to remember be put in writing, so that it would serve as a warning and also as a call to return.

For today: let us not wait for troubles to remember God. Let us learn His Word or a faithful song by heart, so that in good days it guards our heart and in difficult days it guides us back to Him.
exp.0:28:
Moses reminds the people of what he told them as they were about to enter the promised land. He told them not to be terrified or afraid of the inhabitants of Canaan. "Terrified" describes a sudden, overwhelming fear, and "afraid" repeats the same idea: not letting fear take control.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, and he reviews their history. Forty years earlier, at Kadesh-barnea, the Israelites heard that the peoples were great and strong, and they grumbled against God in their tents. Moses reminded them that God was going before them and had already cared for them before.

When fear makes us doubt God, it helps to remember how he has helped us before. Looking back with gratitude gives us strength to take the next step with confidence, instead of complaining or freezing up.
exp.22:12:
This verse says that every soldier was to carry a digging tool along with his weapons. When he went out to relieve himself outside the camp, he was to dig a hole and then cover his waste. The waste is what gets buried, and the hole is dug with the tool he carried.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. These instructions were for when the army camped in time of war. The reason the text gives is that God walks in the midst of the camp, so the place had to be kept clean and respectful. In addition, this practice helped protect the health of the group, although the text emphasizes the spiritual reason.

For today: God is concerned with everyday life, even with the small and unpleasant things. We can honor him by caring for the order and cleanliness of our home, our work, and our church, and by faithfully doing what no one sees.
exp.4:9:
God shows loyal, faithful love to a thousand generations of those who love him and keep his commandments. Here "loving devotion" means steady, faithful love that keeps its promises. A "thousand generations" is a way of saying a very long span of time, reaching far into the future. Some read the phrase as a literal count of generations, and others take it as a vivid way of describing a very large, lasting blessing.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel, who are about to enter the promised land. He is repeating the Ten Commandments to them. Just before this, God speaks of his strong opposition to idolatry and of the consequences that follow from sin. This verse sets up a contrast: God's faithful love lasts far longer and reaches much farther than his judgment.

For today: loving God and obeying him is not a cold burden. It is a response to someone who loved us first. Today you can choose one concrete act of obedience, and trust that God is faithful and kind.
exp.30:3:
This verse says that the LORD will do to the peoples of Canaan what He did to Sihon and Og, the kings of the Amorites. He has already destroyed these kings, along with their land, and He will do the same to the nations Israel is about to face, giving the land to His people.

Moses is speaking. He is 120 years old and already knows that he will not cross the Jordan. He says farewell to the people and reminds them that God will go before them, and that Joshua will be the new leader. Moses points to a recent victory, one they saw with their own eyes, to strengthen their trust before they enter the promised land.

For today: when you face something that frightens you, remember how God has helped you before. What you have lived through with Him yesterday can give you courage to trust Him tomorrow.
exp.3:4:
Moses reminds the Israelites that he taught them the statutes and ordinances just as the LORD his God commanded him. The "statutes and ordinances" are the rules and the decrees that God gave to his people. The goal stated in the verse is that the people follow them in the land they are about to enter.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the land, and he will not go in with them. He has just reminded them of the punishment for following Baal-peor and of the life of those who stayed faithful to God. He warns them that obedience is not optional: it is what will set them apart before the other nations.

For today: faith does not stop at knowing what God says, but lives it out where we are. Choose one teaching from the Bible that you already know and practice it this week in your home, your work, or your community.
exp.29:1:
It says that, after having turned away from God, the people return to Him and obey Him again. "Return" means to come back, to change direction toward God. "Obey His voice" means to listen to what He commands and do it. This is to be done together with the children, and "with all your heart and all your soul," that is, with sincerity and complete devotion, not just on the outside.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has set before them the blessing and the curse of the covenant. He warns them that they could be scattered because of their disobedience, but he gives them hope: if they return to God, He will restore them, as the following verses say.

For today: if you feel that you have drifted away from God, you can always come back. A perfect life is not required, but a sincere heart is. Start today with an honest prayer and one concrete step of obedience, and invite your family to walk with you.
exp.11:31:
This verse says that the people must take great care to do everything God commands. They must not add their own rules or practices to his commands, and they must not leave out parts that they find unappealing. "See that you do" means the same as "take care to do"; adding means putting something extra in, and subtracting means taking something out.

Moses is speaking to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He has just warned them not to copy the way the peoples of the land worshiped their gods, since those practices included things God hates, such as burning their children. God wants to be worshiped as he himself has directed, not as people happen to think of.

For today: when you read the Bible, try to receive it as it is, without bending it to your tastes or to the culture of the moment. Ask yourself honestly: "Am I adding something God did not ask for, or ignoring something he did say?" Then ask God for help to obey him with humility.
exp.28:18:
This verse speaks of someone who hears the words of this oath and takes them lightly. He invokes a blessing on himself in his heart, reassuring himself and saying, "I will have peace, even though I walk in the stubbornness of my own heart." The verse then warns that this will bring disaster on the watered land as well as the dry. The image of the watered and the dry points to the whole land being harmed, not just the one who makes the promise.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in Moab, when they renew the covenant before entering the promised land. He warns them against idolatry and against a heart that turns away in secret, like a root that sends up poison and bitterness, a bitter plant.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are deceiving ourselves with thoughts like "God will understand, it's no big deal." A false peace does not heal. Let us rather listen to God with humility and return to Him in time.
exp.8:17:
Moses tells how he fell down before the LORD, as he had done the first time, for forty days and forty nights. He did not eat or drink during that time. Falling down here means bowing low to the ground in humble prayer. He did this because of the sin of the people, who did what was evil in the LORD's sight and provoked Him to anger.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the episode of the golden calf, so that they will not think they deserve the land for being good. What he recounts here is that he interceded for them when they deserved punishment.

Today we can imitate Moses by praying for others, even for those who have failed. Instead of only criticizing the mistakes of family, friends, or our community, we can ask God for mercy for them and for ourselves.
exp.11:6:
This verse says that the people would eat in the place God chose, in his presence, and would rejoice together with their families over all they did with their labor. "There, in the presence of the LORD your God, you and your households shall eat and rejoice" describes a shared meal and celebration before God. "All you do" means what they produced through their effort. The blessing came from God.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that they must worship God in one chosen place, not wherever each person wanted, as they had done in the wilderness. There they would bring their offerings and celebrate with joy, like a thankful family feast.

For today: before you worry about what is still missing, pause with your family to thank God for what you have. A shared meal with gratitude can be a simple and joyful act of worship.
exp.31:8:
This verse says that the people of Israel are the portion that belongs to the LORD. The word "portion" means what falls to God as his own. Here the BSB's "allotted inheritance" takes the place of the older "lot," and it names the same idea: Jacob is the share God has set apart for himself as his own possession.

Moses speaks in a song meant to teach the people before his death. He wants them to remember how God cared for them from the beginning, so that they would not turn away from him. The verses that follow show that care: God found them in the wilderness and guarded them as the apple of his eye.

For today: if God considers us his own, our worth does not depend on what we accomplish. When you feel alone or unimportant, remember that God cares for you with love and sustains you as the eagle carries its young.
exp.12:5:
This verse speaks of someone very close to you, such as your very own brother, your son or daughter, the wife you embrace, or your closest friend. It describes a person who secretly urges you to worship other gods. To entice someone means to coax or push them toward doing something.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He had already warned them about false prophets, and now he shows that the temptation can also come from the people they love most. God wanted to protect the people He had rescued from Egypt.

For today: do not underestimate an influence that pulls you away from God just because it comes from someone you love. Love that person, but stay firm in your faith, and seek God in prayer and in His Word.
exp.6:13:
It says that God would bless Israel more than all the other peoples. No man or woman among them would be barren, that is, unable to have children. The same would hold for their livestock, which would reproduce well. The word "livestock" refers to domestic animals.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God will bless them if they obey him and keep his covenant. This promise was given to a specific nation, under the covenant of Moses. For that reason it is not a guarantee that every believer will have children or prosperity.

For today: learn to see life and what you have as a gift from God, and respond with obedience and gratitude. If you are going through a painful situation, such as not being able to have children, remember that God loves you and is with you just the same.
exp.2:22:
This verse says that Moses began to pray to God at that moment. The verse for "I pleaded with the LORD" is simply that Moses pleaded with the Lord. It is only the introduction to a prayer that continues in the verses that follow.

The speaker is Moses, as he reviews the history of Israel before the people, now close to the promised land. He had just encouraged Joshua not to be afraid, because God fights for his people. Then Moses asks God to let him cross the Jordan and see the good land. Later God answers him that he will not cross over (Deuteronomy 3:26-27). The reason is explained in other passages of the book.

For today: when you have a deep desire, bring it to God with sincerity and humility. And if the answer is not the one you hoped for, keep trusting that he is good and faithful.
exp.9:10:
Then the LORD said to me, "Get up. Go on ahead of the people, so that they can enter and take possession of the land I promised on oath to give their fathers." In plain terms, God told Moses to get up and lead the people forward, so that Israel would enter the land and make it their own. "Go on ahead of the people" means to walk at the front. "Promised on oath" means God bound himself by a solemn pledge. "Their fathers" refers to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the ancestors of Israel.

Moses speaks to the people and reminds them of what happened after the sin of the golden calf. He interceded on the mountain, and God did not destroy them. Now God renews the command to move forward. This shows his mercy and his faithfulness to the promise. Moses will soon explain what God expects of them: to fear him, love him, and obey him.

For today: when God gives us a new opportunity after we have failed, let us not stay trapped in guilt. Let us respond with gratitude, trust, and obedience, and take the next step he shows us.
exp.22:6:
This verse says that Israel was not to despise the Edomites, because they were their relatives, descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob. Nor was Israel to despise the Egyptians, because Israel had lived as a foreigner in their land. This verse says that "to despise" means to look down on someone with disgust, rejection, or contempt.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land, giving them rules for living as God's people. Just before this, Ammonites and Moabites are mentioned, who were barred from entering the assembly. Here a different treatment is shown for Edom and Egypt, appealing to kinship and to memory. The Egyptians had oppressed Israel, but they had also taken them in during times of famine. Interpreters explain this in several ways.

For today: even when someone has hurt us, remembering our own history of need helps us treat others with respect and humanity.
exp.1:30:
God told Moses that he had already begun to hand Sihon, king of the Amorites, and his land over to Israel. Now it was their turn to act: to begin to conquer and possess that land. The wording "begin to conquer and possess" comes straight from the verse above, so the focus falls on the people taking the first step.

Moses is speaking to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of what happened before they entered the promised land. Sihon refused to let them pass, and the text says that the Lord hardened his spirit. This has been understood in several ways, but here God is shown at work within that king's decisions.

For today: God sometimes has already begun to act, but he waits for us to take the first step of faith. Trust his promise and act in obedience, without simply waiting around.
exp.32:17:
Moses blesses two tribes of Israel. To Zebulun he says to rejoice "in your journeys", that is, when he travels out to his labors. To Issachar he says to rejoice "in your tents", that is, in his life at home. The two tribes are mentioned together, as sisters.

Moses speaks shortly before his death, and blesses each tribe. Some understand that Zebulun went out to trade or to sail, and that Issachar stayed in the field and the home. The text does not explain this, so that is an interpretation. What we do see is that God gives different tasks to each tribe.

For today: God calls us in different ways, and all of them have value. You can rejoice in your work outside the home as well as in your life at home, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.0:26:
This verse says that the people of Israel complained quietly, inside their tents. "Grumbled" means to protest in private, without facing the matter openly. They said that the LORD hated them and had brought them out of Egypt to hand them over to the Amorites, a people who lived in Canaan, so that they would be annihilated.

Moses is speaking about forty years later, reminding the new generation of what happened at Kadesh-barnea. The spies had brought back good news about the land, but the people became afraid and did not want to go in. Moses shows them that their problem was not only fear of their enemies, but that they doubted the LORD's love.

For today: when we are afraid, we should not draw conclusions about God from our fear. Instead, let us remember what He has already done for us, and bring our doubts to Him in prayer, not in hidden complaints.
exp.31:36:
God asks, with irony, where the false gods are that his people turned to for safety. He describes them as "the rock in which they took refuge," that is, the place where they sought shelter and protection. To take refuge in something means to rely on it, to put yourself under its safety.

This is part of the Song of Moses, where God himself speaks. Israel had turned away from him to follow idols, and now it faces the consequences. God lets the people see that those gods cannot save anyone in the time of distress. But the passage also shows that God will have compassion on his servants when he sees their helplessness. Some see here a mockery by God, and others a painful call to return.

For today: ask yourself what you rely on when a crisis comes, such as money, work, or the approval of others. Place your confidence in God, for he alone is a firm rock.
exp.12:7:
If someone close to you secretly invites you to worship other gods, you must not yield to them or listen to them. Show them no pity, and do not spare them or shield them. The word "yield" here means to give in to their pressure.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. God had made a covenant with them, and loyalty to Him was the foundation of the nation. This law, part of the framework of ancient Israel, treats idolatry as serious betrayal, even among family members. The verses that follow mention a death penalty, which belonged to that society and that covenant.

For today: do not place any bond, not even the dearest one, above your faithfulness to God. When someone invites you to turn away from Him, be firm and kind, without giving in or keeping your faith silent out of pressure or affection.
exp.10:4:
This verse recalls what God did for his people during the years in the wilderness, from the time they left Egypt until the moment they reached the plains of Moab. The phrase "until you reached this place" marks the point where that journey ended. God cared for them, corrected them, and sustained them along that whole journey.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, just before they enter the promised land. They had seen the works of God with their own eyes, and Moses brings those works back to memory to encourage them to love the LORD and obey him. Remembering his faithfulness would give them firmness for what was coming.

For today: think about how God has sustained you in your own wildernesses. Write down three moments when he helped you and give him thanks. Remembering his faithfulness strengthens confidence for what lies ahead.
exp.9:15:
This verse says that the people must remove whatever blocks their heart, just as the flesh was cut away in circumcision. The skin cut away in circumcision is the image here, and it stands for inner hardness. The phrase "stiffen your necks no more" describes being stubborn and refusing to obey. God asks for an open and teachable heart.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God, the Lord of the whole universe, chose them out of love and not because of merit. Furthermore, God is just, does not accept bribes, and cares for the orphan, the widow, and the foreigner. For this reason he asks them for an obedience that springs from the heart and not only from an outward sign.

Today we can ask ourselves in what area we have become stubborn before God. With humility, let us ask him to soften that point, and let us obey with love, especially by treating well those who need it most.
exp.6:23:
It says that God would give the Israelites victory over the kings of the nations of Canaan. "He will hand their kings over to you" means that God would give them the triumph. "Wipe out their names" means that their memory and their power would disappear. "No one will be able to stand against you" promises that no enemy would stop them while God was at work.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that the victory would come from God, not from their own strength. This is the language of conquest typical of that moment and of that covenant with Israel. Moreover, the following verse shows the central concern: that the people not fall into the idolatry of those nations.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, trust that God sustains you, but obey Him faithfully. His help is not an excuse for complacency, but a reason to remove from our lives whatever draws us away from Him.
exp.7:13:
When you have plenty of food, good houses, and a lot of money, there is a danger: that your heart will become proud and you will forget God. He is the one who brought Israel out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. Here the word "lest" introduces a warning: be careful that this does not happen.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the hard years in the wilderness, when God cared for them with water and manna. He fears that, once they prosper, they will think they achieved everything on their own.

For today: when things are going well for you, take a moment to thank God. Think of one specific blessing you have and give thanks for it in prayer, remembering that everything good comes from Him.
exp.18:15:
If a false witness testifies against someone, accusing him of a crime, the law of God takes that seriously. The verse opens a teaching about what to do when someone stands up to bring a false charge against another person. The word "crime" here refers to a serious wrongdoing, such as breaking what God has commanded. The verse does not finish the thought; the answer comes in the verses that follow.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just explained that one witness alone is not enough to condemn someone. Now he teaches how to protect the innocent from false accusations, bringing the case before the priests and judges, before the LORD.

For today: before repeating an accusation against someone, make sure it is true. If you are not sure, it is better to stay silent, because a lie told against another person can do them great harm.
exp.3:22:
It says the people must be very careful not to forget the covenant God made with them. "Be careful" is the main instruction here. An idol is an image made of material, shaped or carved to look like something, and God forbids them to make one to worship, in the form of anything at all. So he forbids them to make idols in the form of anything he has prohibited.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He himself will not cross the Jordan, so he warns them with urgency. He wants them, once he is no longer with them, to remember what God commanded them. He is also speaking with their children and grandchildren in mind.

For today: we can ask ourselves what things have taken the place of God in our hearts. To avoid forgetting him, it helps to read his Word every day and to remember with gratitude what he has done for us.
exp.32:25:
This verse says that no god compares to the God of Israel. "Jeshurun" is a poetic name for Israel, which probably means "the upright one" or "the beloved." The image of God who "rides the heavens" pictures him moving across the sky and the clouds, showing his power and majesty, and doing so to help his people.

Moses is speaking. He is about to die and, before Israel enters the promised land, he blesses each tribe. With verse 26 he finishes the blessings tribe by tribe and begins a song of praise to God. He reminds them that their strength and their victory do not come from themselves but from God, who protects them and will give them rest in the land.

When you feel small before a problem, remember that God is above all things and comes to your aid. You can pray with confidence, saying to him: "Lord, you are greater than this."
exp.4:19:
This commandment says that we must not lie about another person, especially in order to harm them. To "bear false witness" means to declare something that is not true, as a lying witness would do. Your neighbor is anyone close to us, the person who lives beside us.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, who are about to enter the promised land. He reminds them of the Ten Commandments that God gave at Mount Horeb (Sinai). This new generation needed to hear the law again in order to live in justice and trust with one another. In legal cases, a lie could ruin the life of an innocent person.

For today: before repeating a rumor or posting something about someone, ask yourself whether it is true and whether you would say it to their face. Caring for the truth protects the good name of others.
exp.11:25:
This verse says that the gifts a person had set apart for God, and the promises he had made, were not to be left at home or taken to just any place. They had to be taken and brought to the place God would choose. The word meaning "but" is not part of the verse, so it is not explained here. Instead, the verse uses "you are to take" to introduce the point. "Set apart" means dedicated to God, and "vows" are promises made to Him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that once they settled there, worship was to take place in the place God designated, and not in just any place. Earlier, the text speaks of not eating the blood, because the life was in it. All of this aimed at order, reverence, and obedience.

For today: if you have promised something to God, such as serving, giving, or changing a habit, do not put it off for later. Keep what you have promised sincerely and in an orderly way, with a grateful heart.
exp.27:57:
If you are not careful to keep all the words of this law written in this book, the verse begins a sentence that continues in the verses that follow. "If you are not careful to observe" means "if you do not make the effort to keep" the whole written law. It also calls for fearing the name of God, that is, respecting it with deep reverence. The phrase "this glorious and awesome name—the LORD your God" speaks of a majestic God worthy of awe.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. After the blessings for obedience, he warns them of the consequences of abandoning the covenant. The images before this are very harsh, and they show how serious it would be to turn away from God.

For today: obedience to God grows out of a heart that respects and loves him. We can ask ourselves which teaching of the Bible we have stopped practicing, and ask God for help to take one concrete step of obedience today.
exp.3:36:
It says that God loved Israel's ancestors, that is, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Because of that love he chose their descendants and brought them out of Egypt by his presence and great power. The phrase "by his presence" means that God himself brought them out, being with them.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what God did so that they will not forget who their God is. Their deliverance was not because of their own merit, but because of God's love and his faithfulness to his promises.

For today: when you doubt your worth, remember that God loved you first. Your life does not rest on your achievements, but on his faithful love. Respond with gratitude and obedience, trusting that he keeps what he promises.
exp.1:9:
This verse is an explanatory note placed in parentheses. It says that before the Moabites lived in that land, the Emites lived there. They were a great people, numerous and tall, as tall as the Anakites. The name "Emites" probably means "the terrible ones" or "the ones who cause dread," though its exact meaning is not entirely certain.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel and recalls their journey through the wilderness. God had commanded them not to fight against Moab, because He had given that land to the descendants of Lot. Moses adds this detail to show that God had already done the same with other peoples, removing some and giving the land to others according to His plan.

For today: God governs history, even when something seems huge or intimidating. We can trust that He carries out His plans and respect what He has given to others, without envy or violence.
exp.21:26:
It says the man who attacked a young woman betrothed to be married in the field is the only guilty party. "Betrothed woman" refers to a young woman who is already engaged to be married. "Cried out" means she shouted for help. "There was no one to save her" means nobody was near enough to defend her. Since no one could come to her aid, the law considers her innocent.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, explaining laws for living justly. This law distinguishes between what happened in the town, where she could cry out and be heard, and what happened in the field, where she could not. In this way the victim is protected and only the attacker is condemned. Scholars point out that the text does not leave her under suspicion, since it declares her without fault.

For today: when someone suffers abuse, we must not blame them or doubt their pain. We can listen to them, believe them, defend them, and seek fair help for them.
exp.5:12:
This verse says the people must have the LORD as their only God: they are to revere him, serve him only, and, when they take an oath, take it in his name. The word "fear" means a deep respect, not a dread that drives people away. "Serve him only" means living for him in obedience and giving him alone the devotion that belongs to God. "Take your oaths in his name" means making a promise before him, in truth, and not before other gods.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that when they have houses, vineyards, and plenty of food that they did not work for, they must not forget the one who brought them out of Egypt. Comfort can make people forget God and turn to other gods.

For today: when things are going well, pause and thank God for what you have. Let your well-being not draw you away from him, and let your words and promises be honest, as one who knows they stand before him.
exp.1:0:
Then the people of Israel turned back and set out for the desert, heading toward the Red Sea, just as the LORD had instructed Moses. For many days they wandered around the mountain of Seir.

The one speaking is Moses, near the end of the people's time in the wilderness. He reminds them of their history before entering the promised land. He speaks of the years after the people refused to trust God at Kadesh-barnea. The following verse shows that the detour lasted until God pointed them in another direction.

For today: sometimes we go around in circles for a long time in the same place, without moving forward. It is good to stop, to listen to God, and to be ready to change direction when He shows us the way.
exp.23:11:
If the person who borrowed is poor and has left a pledge as security, you must not keep that item overnight. A "pledge" is something a person hands over as assurance that they will repay their debt. The phrase "you must not go to sleep with the security in your possession" means not spending the night with it in your possession, since the following verse makes clear that it was the cloak the poor man used to keep warm.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and repeats God's laws to them. This rule protected the most vulnerable. Lending was permitted, but one could not take advantage of another's need or force your way into the debtor's house.

Today we can learn to help without taking advantage. If we lend something or demand payment, we should take care that the person does not lose what is basic to living with dignity. God calls for mercy and justice in how we treat those who have less.
exp.3:1:
This verse says that the people must not add anything to what God commands, nor take anything away from it. The purpose is that they can obey God's commandments just as he gave them, without changing them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that obeying God will give them life and allow them to possess the land. Next he recalls what happened at Baal-peor, where those who followed other gods died, while those who stayed faithful to God remained alive.

For today: we can read the Bible with humility, without twisting it to say what suits us or ignoring what makes us uncomfortable. Before deciding what to think, ask yourself: "What does God's Word actually say?" And then ask him for help to obey it.
exp.31:47:
This verse says that the LORD spoke to Moses on that same day, right after Moses finished teaching the people. The words "the LORD said" mean that God himself gave him a message. "On that same day" points to the day when Moses sang and repeated the law to Israel.

The speaker here is the narrator, who presents God's words to Moses. Moses had just urged the people to keep the law as their life. Now God tells him that he must go up to Mount Nebo, look out over the promised land, and die there. So his long task as leader comes to an end, though he will not enter Canaan.

For today: God keeps speaking to his people through his Word, and sometimes he reminds us that our time of serving has an end. We can live each day faithfully, teaching the truth to others and trusting that God cares for what comes next.
exp.23:1:
This verse says that once a woman has left her husband's house with a certificate of divorce, she is free to go and become another man's wife. The phrase "after leaving his house" means she has already been sent away, and the wording shows that she had permission to remarry.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel and gives a rule about divorce. He does not say that God approved of divorce as an ideal; the law regulated a practice that already existed. Its effect was to protect the woman, since the certificate proved she was free and could rebuild her life. Jesus commented on this passage in Matthew 19:8, explaining that Moses permitted it because of the hardness of the people's hearts.

Today it reminds us that God cares for the vulnerable when relationships break down. We can treat those who have gone through a separation with respect and justice, without judging them or leaving them without support.
exp.0:31:
This verse says that, although the people had seen so many signs of God's care, they still did not trust Him. In this passage, trusting God means more than accepting that He exists: it means relying on Him and obeying Him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of what happened at Kadesh-barnea, when they were afraid to enter the promised land. Moses shows them that God had carried them as a father carries his son, and yet they did not trust Him. That is why God was angry.

For today: when you are afraid, remember how God has cared for you before. Write down those moments and use them to trust Him today, even when the road looks hard.
exp.8:13:
In this verse God says to Moses, "Leave Me alone," that is, "do not stop Me." He says that He intends to destroy the people and blot out their name from under heaven, meaning from the earth, so that no one will remember them. Then He promises to make Moses into a nation greater and mightier than they are.

Moses is telling the people what happened at Mount Sinai. While he was receiving the tablets of the law, the people made a golden calf. God calls them a stiff-necked people, stubborn and unyielding. Moses recalls this so that the people will not think they are good on their own account. Some see in God's words, "Leave Me alone," an opening for Moses to plead on the people's behalf, and that is what he did.

For today: when you see the wrong of others, pray for them before you condemn them. And remember that God treats us with mercy, not according to what we deserve.
exp.31:39:
Here God speaks as if he were making a solemn oath. In ancient times, lifting the hand toward heaven was a way of swearing. "I lift up My hand" means that God commits himself with complete seriousness. And he declares, "As surely as I live forever," that is, that he is eternal and that his word cannot fail.

The one speaking is God, in the Song of Moses, near the end of Moses' life. God reminds Israel that its idols could not help them. Only the Lord has power over life and death, and he promises to act with justice against his enemies.

For today: when everything around you changes or falls apart, rest in the fact that God is eternal and faithful. You can trust him more than anything that passes away, because his word remains.
exp.25:9:
This verse says that the Israelite brings the firstfruits to God, meaning the first portion of his harvest, and acknowledges that the Lord gave him the land. The verse's words "behold, I have brought" present the offering as something done right now, and the instruction to place the basket before the LORD your God and bow down before Him points to an act of worship and humility. Here the text moves from the prayer to the command to leave the offering and worship.

Moses is speaking, instructing the people before they enter the promised land. He teaches them a prayer to say when they offer the firstfruits. Before this verse, the person recalls the deliverance from Egypt. In this way the offering is not a mere formality, but gratitude for what God has done. Afterward comes the shared joy with the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.

Today we can give God the first and not what is left over, remembering that everything comes from Him. Giving with gratitude also moves us to share with those in need.
exp.7:7:
This verse describes the good land that God was going to give Israel. It names the main products of that land: wheat, barley, vines (grapes), fig trees (figs), pomegranates (pomegranate fruit), olive trees (olives), and honey. The word "and" in the list is simply the ordinary connector between items, and the olives are the olive trees themselves. Many believe the "honey" could be bee honey or a sweet syrup made from dates or grapes; the text does not make this clear.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, just before they enter Canaan. He reminds them that this abundance comes from God and that they must obey him. Later he warns them not to forget God when they are satisfied.

For today: look at what you have on your table as a gift from God, not only as the fruit of your own effort. Before you eat, give thanks from the heart, and let that gratitude lead you to obey him and to share with others.
exp.26:25:
It says that whoever does not put the words of this law into practice falls under a curse. The phrase "put into practice" means to act on the law in daily life, not merely to know it; the word "cursed" means that such a person falls under God's disapproval and its consequences. All the people respond "Amen," which means "so be it," accepting the commitment.

Moses speaks to Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He orders a ceremony in which the Levites proclaim twelve curses, and the people respond to each one. This is the last and sums up all of them: it is not enough to know the law, it must be obeyed. Paul quotes this verse in Galatians 3:10 to show that no one keeps the law perfectly, and that is why we need Christ.

For today: do not be content with just listening to the Bible; choose one teaching and put it into practice this week. And when you fail, remember that Christ bore that curse for us.
exp.30:4:
God himself will hand the nations of Canaan over to Israel. After that, the people were to act toward them exactly as God had already commanded. "Will deliver them over" means he will put them under their control. "Exactly as" means in full agreement with what he had told them. The victory comes from God, but the people must obey his instructions.

Moses speaks here as an old man, shortly before his death. He knows he will not cross the Jordan, so he encourages the people and Joshua, his successor. He reminds them of what God did to Sihon and Og so that they will trust that he will keep his promise. The orders about Canaan were tied to that specific time and place in Israel's history.

For today: when you face a great challenge, trust that God goes before you, but do not stand still. Do your part in obedience, following what he has already shown you in his Word.
exp.31:22:
God says he will bring disasters upon his people. "Heap" means to gather or pile up, and "arrows" are the weapons God says he will spend against them. The arrows stand for the punishments God will send, one after another, until his supply is used up, as the next verse describes with famine, plague, and war.

This is part of the Song of Moses, where God speaks. Israel had abandoned him for idols, which were not God, and God answers with grief and judgment. The context shows this is not a whim of anger but the consequence of breaking the covenant. Scholars understand the language of arrows and fire as poetic images of judgment.

Today we can take seriously that turning away from God to trust in empty things, such as money, success, or image, brings painful consequences. But the song does not end in judgment; further on it speaks of compassion. Examine where you have placed your trust, and return to God with humility.
exp.19:15:
Here the word "however" links this verse to what comes before it. The word "inheritance" describes land given to Israel as something they would possess. Moses commands that in the cities of the nations that the LORD was giving to Israel, nothing that breathes was to be left alive.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. The text gives the reason: to keep Israel from learning the detestable practices of those nations and sinning against the LORD. It is a very harsh command, tied to that moment and to those nations. Scholars understand it in different ways: as divine judgment, or as the exaggerated war language of that time, since those nations remained in the land afterward. It is a difficult passage, and we should not soften it.

Today it does not justify any violence. Jesus teaches us to love our enemies. It does invite us to be serious about whatever pulls us away from God, and to cut firmly from influences that harm our faith.
exp.1:31:
This verse tells how King Sihon came out with his whole army to meet Israel and fight at a place called Jahaz. The phrase "came out against us" means that he came out to oppose us. It was not a meeting of peace but a battle.

The one speaking is Moses, who reminds the new generation of Israel of their history before entering the promised land. Israel had asked for peaceful passage, but Sihon refused. The text says that God hardened his spirit, and this has been understood in several ways: as a judgment on a king already opposed to God, or as the biblical way of saying that God governs even human decisions. The verses that follow include a total destruction, something difficult that we must read with humility.

For today: Moses recalled what had been experienced in order to strengthen trust in God. Remembering how God has helped you before can give you courage to face the challenges of today.
exp.3:5:
It says that Israel must keep God's laws, not just hear them. "Observe" means to obey them carefully, and "do" means to put them into practice. Doing this would show their wisdom and understanding before the other peoples, who, on hearing those laws, would say that Israel is a wise and great nation.

Moses speaks near the end of his life. He is on the plains of Moab and addresses the new generation of Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God gave them his commands and that obeying them would set them apart among the nations. The verses that follow show that what makes them great is having God near and having just laws.

For today: wisdom lies not only in knowing what God says, but in living it. Choose today a biblical teaching you already know, such as forgiving or being honest, and practice it in a concrete way. Your way of living can speak well of God.
exp.13:0:
You are sons of the LORD your God, so the command is that you must not cut yourselves or shave your foreheads on behalf of the dead. Because you belong to him, you are not to mark your bodies in grief as the surrounding nations did.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they belong to God and must live differently from those around them. Many neighboring peoples had mourning rites that involved cutting the flesh, and some scholars connect these practices to pagan religious customs, though the exact details are not fully known. The next verse gives the reason: they are a holy people, chosen by God.

For today: we can truly grieve those we lose, since mourning is a natural part of being human. But we do it as children of God, with hope, without despairing or harming ourselves, trusting that our Father cares for us.
exp.33:6:
Moses was one hundred and twenty years old when he died, yet his eyes were not weak, and his vitality had not diminished. Despite his age, he could still see well and kept his strength. The words "his eyes were not weak" mean that he did not lose his sight, and "vitality" means his strength and energy. This suggests that his death did not come from weakness or from extreme old age.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who closes the account of Moses. Tradition holds that Moses wrote most of the first five books of the Bible, but this ending was probably added by someone else, and there is no certainty about who that was. The text emphasizes that Moses died "according to the word of the Lord," and that Joshua then took over the leadership of Israel.

God can sustain a person until the end of their service. Today we can serve God wholeheartedly at every stage of life, without thinking that age takes away our worth. We can also trust that God cares for us and for those who will come after us.
exp.25:5:
This verse tells that the Egyptians mistreated the people of Israel. "Mistreated" and "afflicted" speak of abuse and suffering. "Putting us to hard labor" means they were forced into heavy work, like that of a slave.

The one speaking is the Israelite who brings the first part of his harvest to the sanctuary. The priest receives the basket, and the person recites this brief history of the people. Moses gives these instructions before they enter the promised land. Remembering the past pain, and also how God rescued them, gave meaning to their offering of gratitude.

For today: when you thank God, remember also the difficult times from which He sustained or delivered you. Seeing your whole story, with its struggles and its help, makes your gratitude more honest and more deep.
exp.0:16:
Israel's judges were required to judge with complete impartiality. "Show no partiality" means not favoring someone because of their importance, their wealth, or their position. Both the small and the great were to be heard alike. The judges were not to be intimidated by anyone, because judgment belongs to God, meaning the one who judges stands in God's place. If a case was too difficult for them, they were to bring it to Moses so that he could hear it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how, in the wilderness, he appointed wise leaders and judges to help him govern. He gave these instructions so that justice would be fair for everyone, including the foreigner.

For today: when you have to decide or give your opinion about someone, whether at work, in the family, or in the church, try to hear everyone with the same respect. Do not let yourself be swayed by pressure or by likes and dislikes, and ask for help when the matter is beyond you.
exp.14:9:
It says we should give generously to the needy, without hesitation and without resentment. "Give generously" means give freely and with an open hand. A stingy or resentful heart is one that gives reluctantly, grudgingly, looking for a way out. God promises to bless the one who gives with a good attitude, in all their work and in everything they set their hand to, which means in all they undertake and put effort into.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. Near the seventh year, debts were forgiven, and someone might refuse to lend so as not to lose his money. Moses forbids this and reminds them that God sees the heart of the one who gives.

For today: when you help someone, do it willingly, without complaints or calculations. Before giving, check your attitude and ask God for a generous and joyful heart. God not only looks at the help, he also looks at how we give it.
exp.4:10:
It says we should not use God's name in an empty, false, or disrespectful way. "Taking in vain" can include swearing falsely, using his name carelessly, or calling on him to deceive. "Will not leave anyone unpunished" means that God will not overlook this offense.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, who are about to enter the promised land. He repeats to them the Ten Commandments, given earlier on Mount Sinai. This is the third commandment. The name of the Lord represents who God is, and for that reason it should be treated with reverence and truthfulness.

For today: take care with your words about God. Avoid saying "I swear to God" over small things, or using his name in jokes or in anger. Also strive to make your life consistent with what you say you believe, so that his name is honored.
exp.15:9:
This verse commands that the Feast of Weeks be celebrated for the Lord. A "solemnity" is a sacred feast. The phrase "a freewill offering that you give" means an offering given willingly, in proportion to what each person has received. The measure is how much the Lord has blessed you.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the yearly feasts, which were counted from the start of the harvest. This feast came seven weeks later, and it is the one later known as Pentecost. It was a time of thanksgiving for the harvest, which everyone was invited to share, including the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow.

For today: give with generosity and joy, not out of obligation, remembering that what you have comes from God. And think about who near you needs you to share.
exp.27:20:
This verse says that if the people turn away from God, a deadly sickness will come upon them and cling to them, meaning it will reach them and will not let them go. "Plague" refers to death in large numbers, like an epidemic. "Exterminate" here means to bring them to an end, until they are removed from the land they were about to take possession of.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of their covenant with God: obedience would bring blessing, and abandoning him would bring serious consequences. These warnings show how seriously God took the faithfulness of his people.

For today: let us not take God's blessings for granted. We can humbly examine whether anything is pulling us away from him, and return to him promptly, trusting in his forgiveness and his mercy.
exp.1:17:
God tells Moses that the people of Israel are going to cross the border of Moab today, at the city of Ar. The source's comment about the word "boundary" and the old spelling of "to" does not apply to this reader's verse, so it is left out.

Moses is reminding the people of their journey through the desert. About thirty-eight years have passed, and the fighting men of that generation, who did not trust God, have already died. Now a new generation is moving toward the promised land. God shows them the way to go, and in the verses that follow, he asks them to respect Moab and Ammon, since God had given those lands to the descendants of Lot.

For today: God guides step by step and also sets limits. We can trust his direction and learn to respect what does not belong to us, without envy or abuse.
exp.31:19:
He says that God, grieved by his people's abandonment, decides to pull back his visible care from them: "I will hide my face from them." He wants to see what their end will be, meaning how things will finally turn out for them. He calls them "a perverse generation," twisted and rebellious people, "children of unfaithfulness," who are not loyal and cannot be relied on.

God himself speaks here, within the Song of Moses. Moses teaches it to Israel before he dies, so that they will remember what happens when they turn away from God, the Rock who formed them, and go after idols. God does not act on a whim; he responds to repeated betrayal.

For today: let us not take God's presence for granted. If we notice that we have grown cold, let us return to him soon and sincerely. The Bible also shows that God welcomes whoever repents and comes back.
exp.20:5:
It says that the leaders of the town nearest to where a murdered man was found had to wash their hands by a stream over a young cow whose neck had been broken. A "heifer" is a young cow, and the verse describes the animal's neck being broken as part of the ritual.

Moses gives this law to Israel before they enter the promised land. When a dead body was found and the person responsible was not known, the community had to acknowledge that the blood that had been shed had weight before God. Washing the hands was a public act: they declared that they were not guilty and asked God to forgive his people.

For today: God takes injustice seriously, even when no one has resolved it. We can be sensitive to the pain of others, ask for justice, and live with honesty, without washing our hands when we are able to help.
exp.5:21:
This verse says that the LORD inflicted great and devastating signs and wonders on Egypt, and that the people saw them with their own eyes. These wonders fell on Pharaoh and all his household and his people. The word "devastating" here means damaging or painful, because they were hard blows against Egypt. The "signs" are events that show the power of God.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He teaches them how to explain to their children why they obey the law of God. The answer is to tell the story: they were slaves, and God rescued them.

For today: when you teach the faith to your children, or to others, do not limit yourself to giving rules. Tell also what God has done in your life and in his people. Obedience is better born from grateful remembrance.
exp.10:17:
The verse says that the people should keep God's words in the deepest part of themselves, in their hearts and minds. They should also keep them constantly in view: tied as reminders on the hands and bound on the forehead. The forehead is the place where the eyes look and the mind takes in what it sees, so the picture is of God's Word shaping what we do and what we see.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just warned them not to turn after other gods. He wants them to remember the LORD and his command. Later, some Jews took these words literally and wore small boxes containing scripture passages. Others understand them as a figure of speech. Both readings exist.

Today we can choose one verse each week, memorize it, and go over it on the way to work or before going to sleep. In this way the Word guides our daily decisions and actions.
exp.24:2:
If a court sentenced someone to be beaten, the punishment had a limit: no more than forty lashes. The verse notes that the verse means the judge would have the guilty person struck. The phrase about the person being degraded in your sight means being humiliated and shamed. The reason is that the guilty person was still "your brother," that is, a member of the people.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. In this part of the law he explains how the judges were to act. The punishment was to fit the offense and be carried out in an orderly way, before the judge. Even a person who did wrong kept his dignity. Some think that later thirty-nine strokes were used so as not to go over the limit, but that is a later tradition.

For today: even when we must correct or set limits, let us do it without humiliating or exaggerating. Every person still has value before God.
exp.0:9:
Moses tells the people that God has greatly increased their numbers. Today they are so many that they are as numerous as the stars in the sky. "Has multiplied you" means that God made them grow in number.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God fulfilled what he promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob about a large number of descendants. Moses explains that governing a people so large was too heavy a burden for him alone, and for that reason leaders were later appointed to help him.

For today: when you look at what God has done in your life, take a moment to thank him for his promises fulfilled. And if responsibility feels heavy to you, do not carry it alone; ask for help and share it with others.
exp.1:1:
