This verse says that God spoke to Moses. The name "LORD" is the name of God used here. It is a short phrase that serves as a bridge: the people had been going around in circles, and now God is going to give them new direction.

Moses is speaking to Israel and recalling their history. They had circled the mountain of Seir for many days without making much progress. Then God steps in and tells them that it is enough and that they should turn toward the north. The verses that follow show that God guides them with care, even in how they treat their neighbors.

For today: sometimes we go around in a situation without moving forward. Stop to pray and listen to God through his Word. He can show you when it is time to change course.
exp.5:18:
It says that if the people obey God, He himself will drive out all their enemies from before them. The phrase "driving out" means pushing back or removing. And "as the LORD has said" reminds us that this is a promise God had already made before.

Moses speaks to the Israelites before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that obeying the commandments is tied to possessing that land. Notice that the victory is presented as the work of God, not only of the people's own strength. The conquest of Canaan is a subject that many scholars debate, and it is best read within its historical context and the whole biblical account.

For today: when we face struggles, we can trust that God keeps what He says, and respond with simple, daily obedience, without relying only on our own strength.
exp.31:51:
God tells Moses that he will be able to see the promised land from a distance, but he will not enter it. "You shall see from a distance the land" means that Moses will look out over it, though he will never set foot there. The land is the one God is giving to the Israelites.

God speaks on Moses' last day, shortly before his death on Mount Nebo. The previous verse gives the reason: at Kadesh, by the waters of Meribah, Moses and Aaron did not honor God as holy before the people. Scholars understand in different ways exactly what the failing was, but the text calls it a lack of trust and of honoring God.

For today: God is merciful, but actions have consequences, even for his most faithful servants. We can humbly accept what God permits, and trust that his plan continues, even when we do not live to see everything fulfilled.
exp.31:42:
It says the nations should rejoice along with God's people. The word "rejoice" here invites celebration. God will avenge the blood of his children, that is, he will not leave unanswered the wrongs done to those who were mistreated. The phrases "He will take vengeance on His adversaries" and "repay those who hate Him" mean that God will bring justice against his enemies. The phrase "He will cleanse His land and His people" means that he will purify and restore the land and the people.

This is the end of the Song of Moses. Moses recites it before Israel shortly before he dies, to remind them that God is faithful, that they tend to turn away from him, and that even so God will do justice and show mercy. The verse also calls on the heavens and God's angels to rejoice and worship him, and scholars read this opening line in several ways.

For today: when you are treated unjustly, do not carry the burden of revenge. Leave the matter in God's hands, for he judges with perfect justice, and ask him to help you forgive and to do good.
exp.8:20:
Moses describes how he took the golden calf, which he calls "that sinful thing," and destroyed it completely. He burned it in the fire, crushed it and ground it to powder as fine as dust, and cast that dust into the stream that came down from the mountain.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of their rebellion at Sinai, when they made the calf while he was on the mountain (Exodus 32). He wants them to understand that they do not deserve the land because they are good, but because of God's mercy. Destroying the idol showed that it had no power.

For today: it is not enough to regret what draws us away from God; we must remove it at its root. Ask God to show you what has taken his place in your heart, and with his help, rid yourself of it, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.2:1:
God spoke to Moses when Og, king of Bashan, came out to fight against Israel. God told him not to be afraid, because he had already handed the king, his people, and his land over to Moses. He said that Moses would do to Og what had been done to Sihon, the king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon. The phrase "delivered him into your hand" means that God had already given Israel the victory.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of his life, in the book of Deuteronomy. He reviews what they experienced in the wilderness so that they will trust God before entering the promised land. By recalling the victory over Sihon, he encourages Israel to believe that God will remain faithful. This story also shows how God acted during that time and place with his people.

For today: when you face a great fear, remember how God has helped you before. That memory strengthens your confidence to take the next step.
exp.4:31:
So be careful to do exactly what the LORD your God has commanded you. Do not turn aside to the right or to the left. "Be careful" means pay attention, and "not turning to the right or to the left" means staying on the path and not wandering off it, like someone walking down a road and not stepping off into the ditch.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, now close to the promised land. He reminds them of what happened at Mount Sinai, when the people were afraid of God's voice and asked that Moses hear it for them. Now Moses asks them to obey what God said, so that things will go well for them in the land they are about to receive.

For today: obeying God is a steady path, not an impulse of one day. You can choose one clear teaching from the Bible and put it into practice this week, even if it is difficult or unpopular, trusting that God cares for those who follow him.
exp.2:28:
This verse says that the people of Israel stayed in the valley opposite Beth-peor. The word it quotes, "stayed," simply means they remained or stopped in that place, so this is a plain note of location that marks where they were when the events before it took place.

Moses is speaking to the people near the end of his life, recalling what happened on the journey. Just before this verse he tells how God did not allow him to cross the Jordan, though he did let him see the promised land from Pisgah and charged him to encourage Joshua. Beth-peor appears later in the book as the place where Moses gives his teaching to the people. We do not know exactly where it was, but it lay in the region east of the Jordan.

For today: God also watches over times of waiting and transition. Even when we cannot see the end of the road, we can encourage and support those who come after us, trusting that God continues his work.
exp.19:7:
The officers would speak to the people again before the battle. They would ask whether anyone was afraid or fainthearted. That person could go home. The reason was to keep his fear from spreading to the men beside him. "Afraid" describes someone who feels fear, and "fainthearted" describes someone whose courage is weak or easily broken, the kind of person who could lose heart and discourage others.

Moses is giving Israel instructions about war. The officers, who were responsible for passing orders on to the people, would speak before the commanders took charge. Earlier, they had already allowed anyone with unfinished business to return home. Here the unity of the army is being protected. Some think the teaching also was that victory depended on God, not on the number of soldiers.

For today: be honest about your fears and ask God for help. Also watch your words, so that instead of spreading discouragement, you encourage those who stand beside you.
exp.12:17:
This verse finishes a condition: God will show mercy and bless Israel when the people obey him, keep all the commandments he is giving them, and do what is right in his eyes.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the Promised Land. The chapter deals with an Israelite city that had turned to idolatry, and the order to destroy it was very severe. Moses ends by reminding them that what matters most is complete obedience to God, not isolated acts. It is a hard passage, and Christians read it carefully, within the particular history of Israel.

For today: obedience to God is not lived halfway or only when it is convenient. We can ask ourselves with humility: "Is there any area of my life where I am not doing what is right before God?" And we can ask him for help to change.
exp.31:50:
God tells Moses why he will not enter the Promised Land. In the Berean Standard Bible, God says that both Moses and Aaron broke faith with him at the waters of Meribah-kadesh, in the Wilderness of Zin, by failing to treat him as holy in front of the Israelites. God says that Moses and Aaron did not honor him as holy before the people, at the waters of Meribah, at Kadesh, in the wilderness of Zin.

God speaks shortly before Moses' death. He commands Moses to climb Mount Nebo to see the promised land. The episode is recorded in Numbers 20, when the people complained for lack of water and Moses struck the rock instead of speaking to it, as he had been instructed. Interpreters point to different details of his failure, such as anger, disobedience, or taking credit for the miracle.

For today: those who serve God are responsible for honoring him through their attitude and obedience, even under pressure. God forgives, but some consequences remain. With humility, let us ask him for help to reflect his character.
exp.25:15:
The LORD your God commands you today to follow these statutes and ordinances, that is, his laws and rules for living. "Following" them means carrying them out in your daily life, not just knowing them. And you are asked to do this "with all your heart and with all your soul," that is, with sincerity and total devotion.

Here Moses speaks to the people of Israel, close to entering the promised land. He has just explained the ceremony of the first fruits and the tithe, where the Israelite declared that he had obeyed. Now he closes that section with a call to obey sincerely. What follows shows that this is a covenant relationship: God and his people belong to each other.

For today: choose a teaching from the Bible that you already know and practice it this week with sincerity, not just to fulfill an obligation, but out of love for God.
exp.11:20:
This verse says that if the place God chooses for worship is very far away, the Israelite may kill animals from his herd and flock in his own town and eat them there, whenever he wants. "Within your gates" means inside your city or village. "Whenever you want" describes the freedom to eat as much as you desire.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. Until now they were to bring their offerings and sacrifices to the place God chose. Moses makes clear that eating meat at home, in everyday life, was permitted and was not a sacrifice. God did not want to make daily life impossible because of distance. But he still required that they respect the blood.

For today: we can receive our daily food with gratitude as a gift from God, without unnecessary guilt. At the same time, we can eat with thankfulness and moderation, remembering that everything comes from his hand.
exp.16:0:
It says that Israel was not to offer to God an ox or a sheep that had a defect or serious flaw, such as a deformity or an illness. The words "defect" and "serious flaw" in the verse refer to physical problems with the animal. "Detestable" means something that God firmly rejects.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land, reminding them of God's law. The verse sits in the middle of instructions on how to live faithfully within the covenant. Right after this, he speaks about idolatry, so offering what is defective seems to show a divided or half-hearted heart toward God. Scholars connect it with that idea, although the text does not fully explain it.

For today: let us give God our best and not what we have left over. It can be our time, our money, or our attention, offered with sincerity and gratitude.
exp.4:28:
God expresses a deep longing: "If only they had such a heart" means "I wish it were so." He desires that the people have a heart that holds him in reverent awe ("fear") and that they keep all his commandments always. God wants things to go well for them and for their children forever.

Moses recalls what happened at Mount Sinai (Horeb). The people were afraid to hear God's voice directly and asked that Moses speak for them, promising to obey. God says that what they said was good, but he makes clear that what matters is not only the words, but a heart that truly follows him.

Obeying God is not just keeping rules on the outside. God looks at our heart, and his desire is our good and the good of our family. Today you can pray, "Lord, give me a heart that honors you," and take one concrete step of obedience at home this week.
exp.13:1:
This verse says that Israel is a people set apart for God, that is, dedicated to him. God himself chose them to be his prized possession, special and unique among all the peoples on the face of the earth.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. Shortly before, he forbade them the mourning customs of other peoples, such as cutting the skin or shaving the forehead for a dead person. Their identity as God's people was to be seen in the way they lived and the way they grieved. Afterward come the laws about food.

For today: if you belong to God, your worth does not depend on what people think of you. Ask him to help you live with hope, even in pain, showing that you are his child.
exp.15:3:
The passage says that during the seven days of the Passover feast no leaven was to be found in all of Israel's land. It also says that none of the meat sacrificed in the evening of the first day was to remain until morning.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how they left Egypt in haste, and that is why they ate bread without leaven, called "bread of affliction." These rules helped Israel not to forget what God did in freeing them. Some see in leaven an image of sin, but in this passage the main thing is memory and obedience.

For today: take a moment to remember with gratitude how God has helped you, and obey Him without putting off until tomorrow what He asks of you today.
exp.31:4:
Moses says that God has no part in the people's corruption. The fault is theirs: they have acted corruptly toward him, and the blemish on them is no longer that of his children. He calls them "a perverse and crooked generation," that is, people who turned away from the straight path. This verse can be read in more than one way, but the central idea is clear: the blame is not God's.

Moses sings this song shortly before he dies. He has just presented God as the perfect and righteous Rock. Now he contrasts him with Israel, which responded with unfaithfulness. He wants the people to remember who formed them and how he cared for them.

For today: when we fail, let us not blame God or our circumstances. Let us acknowledge our error with humility and return to the One who is faithful and upright.
exp.10:13:
It says that God himself will provide rain for the land of Israel in its proper season. The autumn rains softened the ground for sowing, and the spring rains helped the harvest ripen. In this way there would be grain (wheat and barley), new wine, and oil (from olives).

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God cares for that land throughout the year. The promise depends on obeying him and loving him with all your heart. In contrast with Egypt, where they watered the land by their own effort, here they would depend on the rain that God provides.

For today: you can work hard and at the same time recognize that everything you have comes from the hand of God. Before planning your day, give thanks for what you have already received and trust that he cares for you, while you obey him with love.
exp.26:3:
It says that, after crossing the Jordan River, the people were to set up large stones on Mount Ebal and coat them with plaster. Plaster is a mixture spread in a layer over a surface.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before his death, when they are about to enter the promised land. He orders them to write God's law on those stones, as a visible reminder of their covenant. We do not know for certain whether the words were written on the plaster or in some other way; scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: God wants his Word to be in plain sight and not forgotten. You can choose a verse and place it where you will see it every day, and let it guide your decisions as you begin a new stage of your life.
exp.30:19:
God says he will bring Israel into the land he promised to their ancestors, a land that flows with milk and honey, meaning very fertile and rich. There the people will eat their fill and prosper. But God warns that then they will turn to other gods, worship them, reject him, and break his covenant.

God speaks to Moses shortly before Moses' death. God knows that the people, once they are comfortable, will tend to forget him. For this reason he commands that a song be written, which the Israelites will learn and which will serve as a witness when troubles come. It is not a wish of God's, but an honest warning.

For today: prosperity can also be a test. When everything is going well, it is easy to stop praying and trusting God. Thank him today for what you have and look for a simple habit to remind you of it each day.
exp.21:6:
This verse says that the mother bird must be let go, and only the young may be taken. "Let go" means to set her free, and the phrase "so that it may be well with you" means that God promises blessing to the one who obeys. The verse's wording about "prolonging your days" speaks of a long life.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of God's laws. This rule appears among other instructions about daily life, such as putting a railing on the roof to protect others. Together, they show care for life and respect for what God has created. Some think it also protected future provision, since the mother could keep laying eggs.

For today: practice compassion and restraint. When you use something God has created, do not take everything you can, but leave room for life to continue.
exp.13:26:
This verse says that the Israelite must not neglect or leave without help the Levite who lives in his town. "Neglect" means to fail to look after someone who depends on you. The reason is that the Levite has no portion or inheritance of land among the people, as the other tribes did, so he has no means of his own to support himself.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He teaches them to bring their tithe to the place of worship and to celebrate with joy before God. In the middle of that feast, he reminds them of the Levites, who served God and depended on the people's generosity. Then he also mentions the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow.

For today: when you enjoy what God has given you, think about who needs support, such as a pastor, a missionary, or a neighbor in need, and share generously.
exp.12:13:
It says that if someone hears a rumor that people in a town are being led to worship other gods, they should not act on impulse. They must "inquire, investigate, and interrogate thoroughly," that is, look into the matter carefully and ask many questions. Only if it is established with certainty that this abomination has been committed among them is it something God detests.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. At that time God was their King, and idolatry amounted to betrayal of the covenant. The verses that follow give a very severe punishment, which is understood within that particular covenant with Israel. But this verse first asks that the facts be looked into with justice.

For today: before accusing someone or repeating a rumor, especially in matters of faith or about people, investigate patiently and seek the truth.
exp.21:23:
This verse speaks of a young woman who was promised in marriage and who has relations with another man inside the city. Both would be brought out to the gate of the city, where judgment was given, and stoned. "Cried out" means that she did not call for help by shouting. "Violated" means that he dishonored and wronged her. The law assumes that, in the city, she would have cried out if she were being forced.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. These civil laws protected marriage and the community. A promised woman was already considered committed as a wife. The verses that follow protect the young woman attacked in the field, where no one could hear her.

Today we do not apply those civil penalties. But we do learn to respect commitments, to care for purity, and to defend those who suffer abuse. Jesus also showed mercy toward sinners without making light of sin.
exp.4:6:
This is the first commandment. "Other gods" means foreign gods, different from the true God. "Before me" can mean "in my presence" or "above me." Either way, God asks to be the only one we worship and serve.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel, who are about to enter the promised land. He reminds them of what God said at Mount Sinai. Before giving the command, God presents himself as the one who freed them from slavery in Egypt. His demand rests on what he has already done for them and on the relationship he has made with them.

Today we can ask ourselves what holds first place in our hearts: money, success, a person, or our comfort. This week, put God first with a daily moment of prayer, and bring him your decisions and worries.
exp.19:18:
It says that if Israel surrounds an enemy city and attacks it for an extended time, they must not destroy its trees by putting an axe to them. The phrase "lay siege" means surrounding a city in order to capture it. The verse speaks of the city's trees, and the command is not to cut them down. The reason given is that the people can eat their fruit. The text then asks whether the trees of the field are human that they should be besieged, which makes the point that trees are not enemies to be fought.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He gives them rules for war. This law limits destruction and protects the food they will need later. Some understand that it also cares for the land, but the text mainly stresses the usefulness of the fruit.

For today: even in the middle of a conflict, do not destroy what you or others will need later. When you argue or are upset, take care of the good things God has given you, such as relationships, work and creation.
exp.21:4:
It says that a woman must not wear men's clothing, and a man must not wear women's clothing. "Detestable" means something God strongly rejects. The Hebrew word translated as "clothing" can also include weapons or tools.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and gives them instructions for living as God's people. Neighboring texts speak of caring for what belongs to others and of respecting life. The exact reason is not known with certainty; some think it was meant to avoid pagan religious practices, others to protect order and identity within society.

For today: fashions change according to culture, so rather than focusing only on clothing, we can ask ourselves whether we live with honesty and respect for how God created us, without disguising who we are or mocking others.
exp.4:0:
Moses gathers all the people of Israel and asks them to listen closely. He is about to repeat God's laws and commands to them. "Statutes and ordinances" are the commands and rules that God gave. "Observe them carefully" means actually doing them, not just hearing them. The call is to learn them and then carry them out.

Moses speaks at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, before Israel enters the promised land. Many of the listeners had been young or children when God spoke at Horeb (Mount Sinai). That is why Moses reminds them of the law and shows them that the covenant is theirs too, today.

For today: it is not enough to hear God's Word in church or read it at home. We can choose one teaching from the Bible this week, review it, and ask God for help to live it out in one concrete action.
exp.4:11:
God commands that the Sabbath day be set apart as a special day. The word for "observe" means to look after it and take it seriously. Keeping it holy means treating it as something separated and dedicated to God, different from the other days. The verse then adds "as the LORD your God has commanded you," meaning this had already been taught to them before.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He repeats the Ten Commandments to them. This commandment included sons, servants, animals, and foreigners, so that all could rest. In this version of Deuteronomy, moreover, the rest is linked to the remembrance that God freed them from slavery.

Today we can set apart a weekly time to rest, pray, and be with God and family, without living as slaves to work. We can also look after the rest of those who work alongside us.
exp.19:16:
The passage says that Israel was to completely destroy six peoples who lived in the promised land: the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. "Devote them to complete destruction" means destroying them entirely, with nothing held back. It is a command that, according to the text, the LORD your God had already given.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, instructing the new generation before they enter Canaan. The command is limited to those peoples, and the text gives the reason: so that they would not teach Israel their idolatrous practices. It is a very difficult passage, and scholars interpret it in different ways, for example as divine judgment or as the typical language of warfare of the time.

For today: God takes very seriously everything that draws us away from him. We can ask ourselves what influences today pull us toward sin, and turn away from them with determination, without harming anyone.
exp.13:5:
This verse gives a general rule: Israel could eat any animal that had a split hoof divided in two and that also chewed the cud, that is, that brings back up and chews again the food it has already swallowed. The animals in the list before this verse meet that rule.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them so that they would live as a people set apart for Him. The verses that follow give examples of animals that were considered unclean. Scholars explain the purpose of these rules in several ways: identity, obedience, or symbolism of purity. The Bible does not give all the reasons.

For today: although Christians are not under these dietary rules, we can learn to obey God in everyday life, even in small things, remembering that our whole life belongs to Him.
exp.32:1:
God revealed himself to his people like a light that rises with the dawn. First he "came" from Sinai, then he dawned upon them from Seir and shone forth from Mount Paran, places near the desert where Israel traveled. To "shine forth" means to give light, and to "dawn" means to appear like morning light coming over the land. The "holy ones" here are often understood as angels or heavenly beings who accompany him. "With flaming fire at His right hand" pictures the fire of Sinai beside him.

Moses is speaking shortly before he dies. He is blessing the tribes of Israel and begins by recalling how God made himself known to them and gave them his law. Some scholars debate exactly how to understand the phrase "myriads of holy ones" and the flaming fire, but the general sense is the greatness of God in giving his law.

Today we can remember that God's Word is not simply advice, but a gift that comes from a holy and near God. Before asking him for something, you can begin by reading his Word with respect and gratitude.
exp.12:14:
It says that if a city in Israel was proven guilty of collective idolatry, its people had to be put to the sword and the city devoted to destruction, including all its people and livestock. "Surely" means there was to be no exception and no pardon. "Put to the sword" means executed with the sword.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. Israel was a nation bound to God by a covenant, and idolatry was seen as a betrayal of that covenant. Before any action was taken, the matter had to be carefully investigated and confirmed to be true. This is an ancient law for that nation, and Christians do not apply it as a rule for today.

For today: this passage shows how seriously God takes exclusive faithfulness to Him. Today the response is not violence, but examining our hearts and removing from them whatever takes the place of God, always seeking the truth before we judge.
exp.31:29:
This verse asks how one enemy could chase down a thousand Israelites, or two enemies could put ten thousand to flight. The answer is that their Rock, meaning God, had handed them over and given them up to the enemy. The phrase "given them up" describes being left in the hands of the enemy. The word "end" refers to what awaits them afterward.

Moses speaks in his song near the end of his life, before Israel enters the promised land. He warns that if they turn away from God and follow their own foolishness, their defeats will not be bad luck but the consequence of having lost his protection. Some think that "their Rock" here refers to the God of Israel, and the contrast with "their rock" in verse 31 speaks of the gods of the nations.

For today: when you face failures or struggles, examine your heart with humility and ask whether you have turned away from God. He corrects those he loves, and he is always ready to restore whoever returns to him.
exp.33:4:
This verse says that Moses, whom the Bible calls the servant of the LORD, died in the land of Moab. The phrase "as the LORD had said" means that everything happened in line with what God had declared, as He had said it would. Some readers also understand the moment as one that God Himself guided.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, not Moses. God had just shown him the promised land from the mountain, but told him he would not enter it. This verse closes the life of a man who led Israel for forty years in the desert.

For today: our life has an end, and perhaps we will not see fulfilled everything we long for. Even so, being faithful to God until the last day is worth more than any achievement. We can trust that He fulfills His plan.
exp.3:44:
This verse gives a summary of what Moses is about to teach. It names three kinds of instruction: the "testimonies" (what God has spoken as a sign of his covenant), the "statutes" (the lasting ordinances), and the "ordinances" (the fair decisions for living together in community). The word "proclaimed" means he made them known, he made them clear. This happened after the people had come out of Egypt.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He has just named the cities of refuge, and now he introduces the law that follows. He reminds them that this teaching is not new: it comes from God and from the journey they have already made since Egypt.

For today: God does not guide us blindly; he speaks to us clearly. We can read his Word not as a burden, but as a guide that helps us live with wisdom, justice, and gratitude for what he has already done.
exp.8:4:
This verse says that Israel does not enter the promised land because they are good or have pure hearts. God drives out the peoples who lived there because of their wickedness, and also to keep the promise he made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The phrase "drive out" means to force out.

Moses speaks to the people shortly before they enter Canaan. He wants to keep them from becoming proud when they have victories. Right away he reminds them of their stubbornness and their rebellions in the wilderness. The land is a gift, not a reward. Some scholars note that the judgment on those peoples is also a warning for Israel.

Today we can remember that everything good we receive comes from God's grace and faithfulness, not from our merits. That leads us to gratitude and humility, and to treating others without feeling superior.
exp.3:29:
This verse says that when the people are in distress and all these things have happened to them, they will still have a way back: they can return to the Lord their God and listen to his voice. The phrase "in distress" describes a time of hardship, and "in later days" points to a future time when all of this takes place. The sentence is left open and is completed in the next verse.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that if they turn away from God and worship idols, consequences and exile will follow. But he also gives them hope: God is merciful and does not forget his covenant with them.

For today: if you are going through a difficult time, or if you have drifted away from God, do not think it is too late. Return to him sincerely, pray, and listen to his word. He welcomes whoever comes back wholeheartedly.
exp.3:0:
Moses asks the people of Israel to listen closely to the laws and commands he is teaching them. The words "statutes and ordinances" refer to the fair rules and decisions that God gave. Here, "follow" means to carry them out and put them into practice. The purpose is that they obey, live, enter the land, and take possession of it.

Moses speaks at the end of the forty years in the wilderness. A new generation is about to enter the land, and he reminds them that life there will depend on following God's word. Shortly after, he mentions what happened at Baal-peor, as a warning of what happens when people turn away from Him.

For today: hearing God's Word is not enough; it must be practiced. You might choose a Bible teaching you already know and decide this week how to live it out in one concrete step, such as forgiving, being honest, or helping someone.
exp.32:12:
He says that Moses asks God to bless the land of Joseph, that is, the territory of his descendants. He speaks of the "precious dew from heaven above," that is, the good things that come from above, such as the rain and the dew. He also mentions "the deep waters that lie beneath," which refers to the underground waters that rise from the earth and make it fertile.

Moses is near the end of his life and blesses the tribes of Israel before they enter the promised land. Here he addresses Joseph, represented by Ephraim and Manasseh. His blessing shows that the fertility of the land depends on God. Some scholars see in these words an echo of the blessing Jacob gave to Joseph in Genesis 49.

Today we can remember that everything that sustains our life, such as food, water, and weather, is a gift from God. Before you worry about what is missing, give thanks today for a simple provision you already have.
exp.32:18:
They will call the peoples to a mountain, and there they will offer sacrifices of righteousness, meaning offerings made in uprightness. For this reason, Zebulun and Issachar will feast on the wealth of the sea and the hidden treasures of the sand along the shore. The words "they will feast on" mean that they will be nourished by, or will benefit from, that abundance.

Moses speaks before he dies and blesses each tribe. Here he addresses Zebulun and Issachar, who lived near the coast and along trade routes. It is not known for certain which mountain is meant; some think of Mount Tabor or of a place of worship. Others see an image of nations drawn toward the God of Israel.

For today: material blessing is not an end in itself. We can recognize what we have as a gift from God and respond with honesty, generosity, and an upright life.
exp.0:45:
This verse says that the people of Israel stayed in Kadesh for a long time. The phrase "for this reason" points back to what had just happened, and the wording "a very long time" makes clear how long the stay was. No one knows exactly how many years it was.

Moses speaks to the new generation before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what happened when they did not trust God at Kadesh, tried to conquer on their own, and were defeated. After they wept, God did not change the situation, and they had to remain there for a long time.

Today we learn that disobeying God can bring consequences that last. But we can also listen to his voice in time and obey him with humility, instead of grieving when it is already too late.
exp.3:35:
This verse says that God let his people hear his voice from heaven, with a purpose: to discipline them and teach them. He also showed them his great fire on the earth, and they heard his words coming out of the fire. The phrase "let you hear" means that God himself spoke so that they heard him.

Moses speaks to Israel, toward the end of their time in the wilderness, before entering the promised land. He reminds them of what happened at Mount Horeb (Sinai), when God gave the commandments. Moses wants them not to forget that the LORD is the only God and that he spoke to them clearly and really.

For today: God continues to speak to teach us and guide us, today above all through his Word. We can read it with respect and attention, without taking it for granted, and put it into practice, because God speaks to us so that we may know him and live according to his will.
exp.5:9:
This verse says that God is going to bring his people into the land he promised, under oath, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. There they will find great and splendid cities that they did not build. The phrase "brought in" means taken inside, and "swore" means that God bound himself solemnly to his promise.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter Canaan. He has just taught them to love God with their whole heart and to teach his words to their children. Now he warns them that they will receive blessings they did not earn with their own effort, and that this gift can lead them to forget God.

For today: when you have plenty, remember that much of what you have is a gift. Today, thank God for something you received without having earned it, and think about how you can share it.
exp.18:9:
This verse says that the cities of refuge exist so that innocent blood is not shed in the land that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance. "Inheritance" means property received as a family gift. The phrase "so that you will not be guilty of bloodshed" means that if an innocent person was killed by mistake or injustice, the guilt would fall on the people.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. God commands them to set apart cities where a person who killed without intent could flee, so that he would not be put to death in revenge without a trial. But the following text makes clear that a murderer acting out of hatred would not be protected there.

For today: value life and justice. Avoid judging or taking revenge in haste, seek the truth before acting, and protect the person who could be treated unjustly.
exp.27:9:
This verse says that all the nations of the earth will notice that the people of Israel belong to God. The phrase "you are called by the name of the LORD" means that God acknowledges them as his own, like someone who puts his family name on his household. "They will stand in awe of you" here speaks of respect and admiration, not of terror.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains the blessings that would come if they obeyed God and walked in his ways. That visible blessing would serve as a testimony before the other peoples. The verse is tied to that condition of obedience.

For today: those of us who follow Christ bear his name, and people are watching us. Today you can live with honesty, kindness and faithfulness at your work and at home, so that others see that God is at work in your life, without showing off or seeking applause.
exp.11:27:
It says that God wants his people to be careful to obey everything he commands. The reason is so that things may always go well for them and for their children after them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just given them instructions about worshiping God in the place he chooses, with offerings and sacrifices. He reminds them that obedience is not a meaningless burden but a path of blessing for them and for the generations that follow. Then he warns them against imitating the pagan nations.

Today we can ask ourselves not only what seems good to us, but what is good and right in the eyes of the Lord. Obeying him in our everyday lives also leaves a good mark on our children and on those who come after us.
exp.26:14:
It says that whoever makes an idol, whether carved from wood or stone or cast from molten metal, and sets it up in secret, falls under a curse. God calls it an "abomination," something He utterly rejects. A carved idol is an image cut from wood or stone, a molten image is one made of poured metal, and a craftsman is a skilled worker. At the end, all the people say "Amen," which means "so be it" or "we agree."

Moses gives these instructions before the people enter the promised land. The Levites would proclaim twelve curses before the gathered tribes between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim. This one concerns secret idolatry: even though no one saw it, God did. The people were renewing their covenant with Him.

Today we can ask ourselves what hidden things in our hearts occupy the place that belongs to God. Let us bring them into the light and surrender them to Him.
exp.29:6:
It says that when God restores his people, the curses that had fallen on Israel because of their disobedience will turn against the enemies who persecuted them. The word "hate" in the verse refers to those who hate. The phrase "in this context" means "command."

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that if they turn back to God after failing, God will gather them, give them a heart willing to love him, and restore them. Some understand this verse as God's justice toward those who oppressed them; others see it as part of the promise of national restoration.

For today: we can trust that God sees injustice and that justice belongs to him. So instead of taking revenge, we hand our pain over to God and return to him with a sincere heart.
exp.13:19:
It says that the people of Israel could eat any bird that God had declared "clean." This is the conclusion of a list of forbidden birds that appears just before it. "Clean" here does not refer to hygiene, but to what God allowed as food for his people.

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, about to enter the promised land. He reminds them of the laws God gave them. The rules about food set them apart from other peoples, since the text says: "for you are a holy people to the LORD your God." Scholars explain the reason for each forbidden animal in several ways, and not everything is clear.

For today: God calls us to live differently, and that begins in everyday life. Ask yourself in which daily decisions you can show that you belong to God, with gratitude and not with fear.
exp.26:1:
And on the day you cross the Jordan into the land the LORD your God is giving you, the Israelites were to set up large stones and coat them with plaster. Plaster is a layer spread over a surface to cover it. Crossing the Jordan means going over the river. The plaster made a smooth, pale surface that was good for writing on.

Moses speaks, together with the elders of Israel, shortly before he dies. The people were about to enter Canaan, and Moses wanted them always to have the words of God's law in view. The verses that follow say that on those stones they would write the law, and that they would set them up on Mount Ebal. Scholars do not fully agree on how the writing was done, but the purpose is clear.

For today: God wants his Word to be clearly visible in our lives. We can choose a verse and put it where we see it every day, as a sign that we want to obey him.
exp.14:19:
It says that the firstborn male of the cattle and of the sheep, already set apart for God, was to be eaten each year before the Lord. You and your household ate it together, in the place the Lord would choose to worship him.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them how to live grateful to God. Just before, he speaks of freeing servants generously, and here he commands them to give God the first and to celebrate it together as a community. Many understand that it was a feast of thankfulness, not only a duty.

For today: set aside time to thank God as a family or with your church. You can share a meal, remember God's blessings from the year, and give him the first and the best, not what is left over.
exp.3:42:
This verse names the three cities that Moses set apart east of the Jordan. Bezer was in the wilderness, on the plateau belonging to the Reubenites. Ramoth, in Gilead, belonged to the Gadites. Golan, in Bashan, belonged to the Manassites. These were cities of refuge. "Unintentionally" means without meaning to, by accident.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of God's law. These cities protected anyone who caused a death without intent, so that an angry avenger would not kill them and justice could be carried out calmly. In this way both life and justice were cared for.

For today: God cares about justice and also about mercy. We can imitate him by not judging in haste, by listening before we condemn, and by offering a safe place to someone who has made a mistake and needs help to get back on their feet.
exp.10:5:
It says that God also acted against Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab, of the tribe of Reuben. The earth opened its mouth and swallowed them, along with their households, their tents, and every living thing that belonged to them, all in the sight of all the Israelites.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of what they themselves saw: the rescue at the sea and the judgment on the rebels. This event is told in Numbers 16, when Dathan and Abiram rose up against the leadership that God had put in place. Moses wants that memory to lead them to obey.

For today: remembering what God has done helps us take it seriously and walk in humility. When I feel pride or the urge to rebel, I can stop, ask forgiveness, and trust again in his guidance.
exp.22:24:
It says that if you walk through another person's field of grain, you may pick the heads of grain with your hand and eat them. But you must not put a sickle to your neighbor's grain, the curved tool used for cutting it. The phrase "grain" here refers to the ripe crop still standing in the field, and "neighbor" means the person who lives next to you.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. This law protected poor and hungry travelers, who could satisfy their hunger. It also protected the owner, because no one could carry off the harvest. Jesus mentions this practice in Matthew 12:1, when his disciples pick heads of grain on the Sabbath.

Today we can learn to combine generosity with respect. Helping someone in need is good, but without taking advantage of what belongs to others. We can be generous with what we have, and grateful and honest with what others share with us.
exp.31:18:
Deuteronomy 32:19 says that the Lord saw what his people had done, and he rejected them. Here "rejected" means that he turned away from them in deep displeasure, because his own sons and daughters had provoked him to anger.

Moses is speaking in the Song of Deuteronomy 32, shortly before his death. He reminds the Israelites how God cared for them, and how they forgot him and went after other gods. God's anger here is a response to betrayal, like that of a father hurt by children who turn away from him.

For today: God is not indifferent to our rejection, because he loves us as a Father. Today we can ask ourselves what things we have put in his place, and return to him with gratitude, remembering all that he has given us.
exp.13:21:
This verse tells Israel to set aside a tenth of all the produce brought forth each year from their fields. "Be sure to" means it was not optional but something they had to do without exception. A tithe is a tenth, or ten percent. The reference to seed points to the grain that was sown, and the produce is what the fields yield at harvest.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they are a holy people to God. According to the verses that follow, this tithe was eaten before God in the place he would choose, so that they would learn to revere him and to depend on him each day.

For today: before you spend what you receive, recognize that everything comes from God. Set aside a portion first for him and for helping others. Do it with gratitude, not out of obligation, and in this way you will learn to trust his provision.
exp.0:25:
This verse says that the people of Israel did not want to enter the land that God had promised them. The word "unwilling" in the verse above means they were not ready or did not want to go. The phrase "you rebelled against the command of the LORD your God" means that they opposed the word or command of God. It was not a lack of information, but a decision not to obey.

Moses speaks to the people near the end of the forty years in the wilderness. He reminds them of what happened at Kadesh-barnea. The spies had seen that the land was good, but fear grew when they heard about large peoples and walled cities. Instead of trusting God, they grumbled and doubted his love.

For today: we often know that God calls us to something good, but fear holds us back. Before deciding, let us remember what God has already done for us and trust his word, even when the path seems difficult.
exp.18:11:
It says that if someone deliberately kills another person out of hatred and flees to a city of refuge, he will not go free from guilt. The leaders of his hometown, called "elders," will send for him, bring him back, and hand him over to the "avenger of blood," the family member responsible for seeking justice for that blood. So the guilty person will pay with his life. The phrase "hand him over" is simply the verse's own wording, meaning the elders will hand him over.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. The cities of refuge protected someone who killed without meaning to, but they were not to shelter a murderer. The purpose was to protect the land from the guilt of innocent blood.

For today: God takes human life and justice seriously. We can seek forgiveness sincerely, but we must not hide the wrong we do, and we should defend the innocent.
exp.27:42:
It says that the foreigner who lives among the people will keep rising higher and higher in power and wealth, while the Israelites will keep sinking lower and lower. It is a picture of reversal: the outsiders on top, the insiders below. "Higher and higher" and "lower and lower" show a steady, growing change.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In Deuteronomy 28 he sets out blessings for obeying God and curses for disobeying him. This verse is part of the warnings: if the people abandon the covenant, they will lose their stability and their place. These words were addressed to Israel under that particular covenant.

Today we can learn that ignoring God's voice leaves us without the foundation that holds our lives up. A practical application: before making important decisions, set aside time for the Bible and prayer, and ask yourself whether you are listening to God or only to your own desires.
exp.3:18:
Moses warns that when you look up at the sky and see the sun, the moon, and the stars, all the host of heaven, you must not be enticed to bow down and worship them. The key points in the verse are the warning against looking up and being drawn in, and the danger of bowing down to what the heavens hold. The final phrase, about what the LORD your God has apportioned to all the nations under heaven, can be understood in several ways: that God gave those heavenly bodies to all the nations to give them light, or that God allowed other nations to look upon them with reverence. Scholars do not fully agree.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that at Sinai they saw no form of God, so they must not make images or worship creation. He wants them to remain faithful to the God who brought them out of Egypt.

Today we can admire the beauty of creation without making it the most important thing. Give thanks to God for what you see, and worship only the Creator.
exp.23:7:
In cases of infectious skin diseases, the people had to be very careful and follow closely everything the Levitical priests instructed them to do, because God had already commanded it.

Moses is speaking to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of laws for living as a just and protected community. The priests served as guides in these cases, and the following verse mentions Miriam, who was affected by this disease. The word translated here as "infectious skin diseases" may have included several conditions, not only the one we call leprosy today.

For today: when we receive wise warning about our health or our lives, it is good to listen with humility and act in time, without thinking we know better.
exp.4:29:
God tells Moses to go and say to the people: "Return to your tents." "Tents" are the tents where families lived in the desert. The verb "return" is an order to go back to their homes.

God is speaking to Moses. The people had just heard his voice at Mount Sinai, and, frightened, they asked Moses to be the one to listen to God and then tell them what he said. God approved that request, but he wanted their hearts to always respect and obey him. While the people returned to their tents, Moses stayed with God to receive the commandments.

For today: Listening to God does not stay in one exciting moment; it is lived out in the routine of the home. After reading the Bible or praying, ask yourself: "What concrete change will I make today at home or at work?"
exp.30:28:
Moses says that he knows that, after he dies, the people will become utterly corrupt and turn away from the path God commanded them. The phrase "utterly corrupt" means that they will become morally perverted. "In the days to come" means future times, not necessarily the end of the world. "The work of your hands" refers to their actions, and probably also to the idols they would make.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, alongside Israel, before they enter the promised land. That is why he gathers the elders and officers, and calls heaven and earth as witnesses. Then he teaches them a song so that they will remember this warning. He does not speak with contempt, but with sorrow and honesty.

For today: it is not enough to rely on good leaders or an inherited faith. It is wise to cultivate our own relationship with God, to read his Word faithfully, and to surround ourselves with people who help us stay firm.
exp.7:5:
This verse calls the people to obey God's commandments, to walk in his ways, and to fear him. Where the verse says "keep," it means to follow through and take care of what God has commanded. The phrase about walking in his ways means living each day as God teaches. The idea of fearing him speaks of deep respect and awe toward God, not of a fear that pushes him away.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God cared for them, corrected them as a father corrects his child, and sustained them. For this reason he encourages them to respond with obedience and respect.

Today we can remember how God has cared for us and corrected us in the past. That memory helps us obey him in the small matters of each day, with gratitude and not out of mere obligation. You might choose one decision for today and ask yourself how it would please God.
exp.0:27:
This verse says that the people of Israel lost their courage before the promised land. "Our brothers have made our hearts melt" means that their report drained away the people's courage. The spies reported that the people were larger and taller, that the cities were large with walls reaching up to the heavens (this is an exaggeration meant to say the cities were very high), and that they saw the descendants of the Anakim there.

Moses speaks at the end of the wilderness journey and recalls what the people said forty years earlier. The Israelites rebelled, complained, and even doubted God's love. Moses reminds them that God had already fought for them in Egypt, and that they should trust him.

Today, when a problem seems enormous, let us not allow fear and the comments of others to take away our faith. Let us remember how God has helped us before, and ask him for courage to take the next step.
exp.5:5:
These words I am commanding you today are to be upon your hearts. In biblical language, the heart is the center of a person: their thoughts, their will, and their affections. It is not only a matter of knowing the words, but of carrying them inside, very close, and letting them guide one's life.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just reminded them that God is one and that they must love him with all their being. Now he shows them how that love is lived out: by keeping his word in the innermost place, and then teaching it to their children.

For today: choose a verse this week, read it each morning, and repeat it through the day. In this way, little by little, that word stops being only on the page and begins to shape your way of thinking and acting.
exp.27:45:
This verse says that the curses described earlier will be upon Israel as a sign and a wonder, that is, something that draws attention and serves as a warning to everyone. The phrase "your descendants" means the effect would reach their children and grandchildren as well, upon them forever, that is, for a long time.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: if they obey, there will be blessing; if they turn away from Him, there will be serious consequences. What is especially emphasized is the lack of gratitude and joy in serving Him, even while having abundance.

For today: let us not take God's blessings for granted. We can begin the day by thanking Him sincerely and obeying Him with joy, not out of obligation, knowing that our decisions also affect our family.
exp.3:27:
It says that if the people turn away from God, they will end up serving false gods, made by human hands, of wood and of stone. These are idols that cannot see, cannot hear, cannot eat, and cannot smell; in other words, they have no life and no power. The phrase "you will serve" points to the lands where they will be scattered.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that if they fall into idolatry, God will allow them to be scattered among the nations. But the verse that follows shows hope: from there they can seek the Lord with all their heart, and they will find him.

Today we may not carve idols of wood, but we can place our trust in things that cannot save us, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Ask yourself what has taken the place of God in your heart, and return to seeking him; he remains willing to hear you.
exp.1:8:
God tells Moses not to harass the Moabites or start a war with them, because he will not give the Israelites any of their land. That land, called Ar, had already been given to the descendants of Lot. "Harass" here means to provoke or bother them, and "provoke them to war" means not to start a conflict with them. Land given to a family as its own is what the verse means by a possession.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel almost at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, and he reminds them of what God commanded him. Israel was passing near Moab, a people related to them through Lot, Abraham's nephew. God had already assigned lands to other peoples, and Israel was to respect those boundaries while they moved toward their own promise.

For today: God also cares for those who are not part of our own group. We do not have to take from others what God has given them. We can wait peacefully for what He has promised us, without envy or unnecessary quarrels.
exp.5:4:
It says God deserves complete love. The command to love is an order, but it grows out of a relationship. "Heart" was the center of thoughts and decisions; "soul" is life itself, the whole person; "strength" means all that you have and are able to give. Your verse uses "strength," so the verse of "might" is replaced with that wording.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God is one and calls them to obey him. This verse is part of what is called the Shema, which Jews still recite today. Afterward, Moses asks that they teach this to their children every day.

For today: loving God is not only a feeling. You can choose a daily moment, such as when you wake up, to give thanks to him, read a passage of the Bible, and ask him how to live that day with honesty and love toward others.
exp.3:24:
It says that after the people have had children and grandchildren and have lived in the land for a long time, there is a risk that they will act corruptly. "Make an idol of any form" refers to idols made by hand. "Provoking Him to anger" means stirring up His displeasure through that kind of conduct.

Moses speaks to Israel before they cross the Jordan. He warns them that God is faithful to His covenant, but also that He is a consuming fire and jealous, meaning He does not share the exclusive love of His people. After several generations, the danger would be forgetting what God has done.

For today: comfort and the passing of time can cool our faith. It is wise to remember often what God has done and not to put anything, whether money or success, in His place.
exp.28:12:
This verse says that God wants to make Israel his people and to be their God, just as he had promised and as he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. To "establish" you means to make you firm and secure. The word "swore" points to a solemn promise.

Moses is speaking to the people on the plains of Moab, before they enter the promised land. He asks them to renew their covenant with God. Everyone was there: children, women, foreigners, and workers. No one was left out of this invitation, and Moses reminds them that everything rests on God's faithfulness to his ancient promises.

For today: our relationship with God does not rest on our own strength, but on his faithfulness. Today you can respond to him with confidence and obedience, remembering that he keeps what he promises. Take a moment to thank him for this.
exp.25:18:
It says that God promises to set Israel high above all the nations he has made, so that it receives praise, a good name, and honor. Also, Israel is to be a holy people, that is, set apart for the LORD their God, just as he has promised. The word "praise" here means what people say in admiration, and "good name" refers to a reputation that is respected.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of his teaching, when they are about to enter the promised land. They have just been reminded of how God rescued them, and now the passage speaks of a covenant relationship: they choose God and God chooses them. That "height" does not speak of pride, but of being a witness to God before the nations, and it depends on obeying him.

For today: if we say we belong to God, let us live with humility and obedience, so that our honest and kind conduct shows others what he is like.
exp.17:15:
This verse recalls what the people asked of God at Horeb (another name for Sinai). On that day, when they gathered, they were afraid and said: "Let us not hear the voice of the LORD our God again or see this great fire anymore, or we will die." The phrase "This is what you asked" means the request was exactly what they had asked for.

Moses speaks near the end of his life to the new generation about to enter the promised land. He reminds them that God accepted their request and promised to raise up a prophet like Moses who would speak in his name. In this way they would not need to seek out fortune-tellers or sorcerers like the neighboring nations. Christians see in this a sign that points to Jesus, though others also understand it as a line of prophets.

Today, instead of looking for answers in horoscopes or superstitions, we can listen to God in his Word, with respect and trust.
exp.10:10:
This verse says that the land the Israelites were about to cross into has mountains and valleys, and that it soaks up rain from the sky. The verse's own wording, "crossing the Jordan to possess," shows where the people are headed, so nothing more needs to be said about it.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the land. He explains that it will not be like Egypt, where they watered their crops with their own effort, drawing water by hand. In this land they would depend on the rain, that is, on God's provision. For this reason he asks them to obey and love the Lord.

For today: we often want to control everything, as if we could water our own fields by our own strength. This text invites us to work with responsibility, but also to trust that God sustains our lives. Today you can offer a simple prayer of thanks for what does not depend on you.
exp.11:22:
He says the people had to take care not to eat blood. The reason he gives is that blood is life, and the life was not to be eaten together with the meat of the animal. "Life" here is the word the verse uses, and "be sure" means that you stay careful about it.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He explains that, if they lived far from the place of worship, they could kill animals to eat at home. But he reminds them that the blood was poured out on the ground, not eaten. This showed that life belongs to God. Christians understand that later this points to the blood of Christ, though interpreters differ on how to apply this dietary rule today.

For today: value life as a gift from God. When you eat, give thanks and remember that everything that sustains your life comes from Him.
exp.0:12:
Moses asks the people to choose wise, understanding, and respected men from each of their tribes. He will appoint them as leaders. Those who are understanding are the ones who reason with good judgment, and those who are respected are people with experience who are esteemed for their good character. "Leaders" means those who guide and have authority.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of the forty years in the wilderness, recalling what happened earlier. He felt he could not carry the problems, burdens, and disputes of such a large nation alone. So he proposed sharing the leadership, and the people took part by choosing the individuals, something the verses that follow confirm.

For today: no leader should have to carry everything alone. In the family, the church, or the workplace, it is wise to share responsibilities with people who are wise and of good character, and also to encourage others to serve. In this way the work is cared for, and so are those who carry it.
exp.22:17:
This verse forbids bringing to the temple money earned through prostitution to fulfill a promise made to God. The "wages of a prostitute" are the payment received for that sinful work, and the verse now says "whether female or male," so it covers both. The "vow" is a solemn promise made to God. The verse calls these things "detestable," meaning that God strongly rejects them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. In these chapters he gives them laws to live as a people set apart from the pagan practices of their neighbors, where prostitution was mixed with worship. God wanted pure worship.

For today: God is not pleased with offerings that come from injustice or deceit. What we give to God should be the fruit of honest work, offered with a sincere heart.
exp.15:19:
This verse says that the people must pursue justice with earnestness. The repetition of the word "justice" in the verse, "Pursue justice, and justice alone," stresses that it is something very important. "Pursue" means to go after it with effort, to chase it actively. "So that you may live" shows that the life and the inheritance of the land are tied to this pursuit. "Possess the land that the LORD your God is giving you" refers to receiving the land as God's gift.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just commanded that they appoint honest judges in every city, without favoritism or bribes. Then he warns against imitating the worship practices of the neighboring peoples. In this way he joins justice with loyalty to God.

For today: practice justice in small things, such as your work, your family, or your business. Do not lie to come out ahead, do not favor anyone out of sympathy, and treat everyone with the same honesty.
exp.26:4:
This verse says that the people were to build an altar to God on Mount Ebal, using stones just as they were found, without carving them. The word "iron" refers to metal tools, such as chisels or picks; the verse says "any iron tool," so the term here means the same thing. The phrase "build there an altar to the LORD your God" means "there you are to build an altar for the LORD your God."

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they cross the Jordan into the promised land. He gives them instructions to renew their covenant with God as soon as they arrive. The altar would be a place of offerings and gratitude. As to why iron was not to be used, the text does not fully explain it; many think the aim was simplicity, and that the altar should not be the product of human ingenuity.

For today: draw near to God with simplicity and sincerity. You do not need to impress him with ornaments or human effort; he looks for a grateful and obedient heart.
exp.17:14:
Moses tells the people that the LORD your God will raise up for them a prophet from among their own brothers, one of their fellow Israelites, who will be like Moses. The instruction to "listen" to him means to pay attention and obey. "LORD" is the name of God.

Moses speaks near the end of his life, before Israel enters the promised land. The neighboring peoples sought guidance from diviners and sorcerers, but God promises to speak to them through prophets. This answers the fear the people felt at Horeb, when they did not want to hear God's voice directly. Some see here a promise of a line of prophets; the New Testament (Acts 3:22) applies it to Jesus.

For today: before seeking direction from horoscopes or popular opinions, take time to listen to God in His Word and in Christ, and put into practice what He tells you.
exp.29:14:
Moses tells the people to look carefully: God sets two paths before them. One brings life and prosperity; the other brings death and disaster. This is not a hidden threat but a clear invitation to choose. The word "see" is like saying "pay close attention, this is serious."

Moses speaks to the new generation of Israel, just before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that God's law is not far away or impossible, but is close, within their reach, in their mouth and in their heart. The verses that follow explain that life consists in loving God, walking with Him, and obeying Him.

For today: our daily decisions, even the small ones, lead us toward one path or the other. Today you can choose one concrete step of obedience and trust in God, knowing that His word is near you and that He helps you to follow it.
exp.3:17:
This verse continues a list of things Israel was not to make as an image for worship. Here it names two more: any creature that crawls on the ground, such as reptiles and insects, and fish that live in the waters. The phrase "in the waters below" refers to the seas and rivers.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that at Horeb they heard the voice of God but saw no form. For this reason he warns them not to corrupt themselves by making idols, as other peoples did.

For today: God cannot be contained in anything we make. Examine whether something created, such as money, success or a person, has taken the place that belongs only to God, and return to worshiping Him.
exp.32:3:
It says that Moses gave the people of Israel a law, and that this law is a possession belonging to the whole assembly of Jacob, that is, the people of Israel. The word "possession" means something received and passed down to one's children. The "assembly" is the gathering or community of the people.

Moses speaks just before he dies, as he blesses the tribes of Israel. He has just recalled how God revealed himself at Sinai, where he gave his law. Here the people respond, and Moses implies that the law is not a distant burden but a treasure God gave them. Some understand that he speaks on behalf of the whole people.

For today: value the Word of God as a possession you have received, not as a mere obligation. Spend a few minutes each day reading it with gratitude, and think about how you can share it with your children, your family, or your friends.
exp.23:19:
When someone beats the branches of an olive tree to knock the olives loose, they must not go back over those branches to pick up what was left behind. What remained was meant for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. The instruction about not going over the branches again is simply about not doing a second sweep, branch by branch, to collect every last olive.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they were slaves in Egypt and that God set them free. For that reason he tells them to treat with kindness those who have no land and no one to protect them. He gives the same instruction about the harvest of grain and grapes.

For today: you do not have to squeeze every gain down to the last penny. You can leave a margin of generosity, such as sharing part of your time, food, or money with someone in need, remembering how much God has given you.
exp.8:24:
Moses reminds the people that he fell down before the Lord for forty days and forty nights. "Fell down" means bowing low to the ground in humble prayer. He did this because the Lord had said he would destroy Israel for their sin.

Moses speaks to the new generation, now close to the promised land. He reminds them that Israel had been rebellious from Kadesh-barnea, where they did not believe God. Many understand that here he is recalling what happened after the golden calf, and that he tells it so they will not think of themselves as righteous on their own. His prayer that follows appeals to God's mercy and to his promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Today we can learn to pray persistently for others, even when they fail. Intercede for someone you love, without accusing them, trusting in God's mercy.
exp.14:10:
He says there will always be people in need in the land, and that is why God commands generosity with an open hand. The needy are those who are poor or in want. "Open your hand" means giving willingly, without holding tightly to what you have. The command includes your brother, the poor person, and the person in need who lives in your land.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. Shortly before, he warned them not to refuse to lend simply because the seventh year was approaching, when debts were canceled. God wanted a generous heart, not a calculating one. This verse probably does not say that poverty is unavoidable, but that it is a constant reality that calls for a response.

For today: think of a person in need close to you, such as a neighbor, a relative, or someone in your church. Ask God how you can help them, and do it this week with joy and without excuses.
exp.27:32:
It says that a people unknown to Israel would eat the produce of the land and everything gained through their hard work. "Crushed" means broken down, worn down both outwardly and inwardly. "Oppressed" means treated harshly and unfairly. And this would be the case every day, with no rest or relief.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He sets before them blessings if they obey God, and curses, or serious consequences, if they turn away from him. This verse is part of a serious warning about losing the fruits of their work under the rule of enemies.

For today: God warns us out of love because he wants to see us well. Today you can examine whether there is something in your life where you have stopped listening to him, and return to him with humility, trusting that his forgiveness and his guidance are still available.
exp.6:5:
The verse calls Israel a people holy to the LORD, meaning set apart for God and belonging to him. God chose them to be his own prized possession out of all the peoples on the face of the earth. "Prized possession" means a treasure that is especially his. "Chosen" speaks of a choice made by God himself.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter the land of Canaan. He warns them not to mix with the nations living there or adopt their gods. That is why they must destroy the altars of those nations. He reminds them that their identity comes from God. The verses that follow make clear that they were not chosen for being great, but because of God's love and his promise to their ancestors.

Today we can remember that our worth does not depend on our achievements, but on the love of God. That love invites us to live set apart for him, with faithfulness and gratitude, and to remove from our lives whatever competes with him.
exp.10:8:
This verse says that if the people obey God's commands, they will live many years in the land God promised. The phrase "live long in the land" means staying there for a long time. The word "swore" means that God made a solemn promise. "Descendants" means children and grandchildren. "A land flowing with milk and honey" is a way of saying the land is fertile and good.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel near the end of his life, before they enter Canaan. He reminds them of what God has done for them and encourages them to obey, so that they will be strong and not lose the blessing promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

For today: God keeps his promises, and obedience grows out of remembering his faithfulness. Think today about something God has done for you, and respond with one concrete step of trust and obedience.
exp.27:16:
