It says that if the people turn away from God, even the most everyday part of their food would suffer. The "basket" was the container where bread or the harvest was kept. The "kneading bowl" is the vessel where dough was prepared. In other words, what is stored and what is prepared to eat would fall under a curse, that is, without blessing or benefit.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them of the covenant with God: obeying him would bring blessing, and rejecting him would bring painful consequences. These are warnings about a specific covenant with Israel, given to call them to faithfulness.

For today: don't take for granted what you have on your table. Thank God for your food each day, and seek to live with honesty and trust in him, without assuming that every suffering is a punishment.
exp.31:10:
God cares for his people the way an eagle cares for its young. The phrase "stirs up its nest" describes how the eagle shakes the nest to encourage the chicks to come out. "Hovers over its young" means she flies gently above them. Then he spreads his wings to catch them and carries them on his pinions, holding them up when they are still not able to fly well.

Moses speaks at the end of his life, in the song he teaches to Israel. He reminds them how God found them in the wilderness, guided them, and protected them. He wants them not to forget his faithfulness or to go after other gods.

For today: sometimes God shakes our "nest" with changes or uncomfortable trials. Even when they hurt, you can trust that he does not let you go. When you feel insecure, remember how he has sustained you before, and take a step of faith today.
exp.10:25:
It says that God, through Moses, sets two paths before the people: the blessing and the curse. The word "See" in the verse, used to draw attention, is what the verse addresses. It is not a hidden threat, but a clear choice placed in full view of everyone.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. He has just reminded them of the victories God will give them. Now he prepares them to live there, showing them that enjoying that land would depend on hearing and following the Lord's commands, as the verses that follow explain.

For today: God invites us to choose, and our daily decisions lead us in one direction. Today you can pick one concrete decision, such as speaking the truth or forgiving, and ask God for help to obey him in that, trusting that his way is good.
exp.19:14:
This verse says that the rules of war in the verses before this one applied to the cities that were far away, that is, those outside the land God was giving to Israel. The phrase "these nations" refers to the peoples of Canaan. The Berean wording describes the cities as "far away" and as not belonging to the nations nearby, so the distinction is between distant cities and the nearby nations of Canaan. Where an older text uses a word for what is taken in war, the plunder seized in battle is meant.

Moses speaks to the people before they enter Canaan. He distinguishes two cases: distant cities, which first had to be offered terms of peace (verses 10-11), and the Canaanite cities, treated as a special judgment. It is a difficult text. Some read it as a limited and unique historical command; others note the exaggerated language typical of ancient warfare. Scholars discuss how it should be understood.

Today it does not authorize us to use violence in God's name. It invites us to approach these passages with humility, reading them in the light of Christ, and to seek peace and justice with those with whom we have differences.
exp.29:16:
This verse describes the opposite of what God asked for. It speaks of a heart that turns away, that stops listening, and that is drawn away until it bows down to other gods and worships them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel in Moab, just before they enter the promised land. He renews the covenant with God and sets two paths before them: life and blessing if they love and obey the Lord, or death and loss if they turn away from him. He wants them to choose well.

For today: the problem begins in the heart, before the actions. Today other gods can be anything that takes the place of God, such as money, success, or comfort. Ask yourself honestly what is holding your attention, and give God first place again.
exp.10:7:
It says that Israel must keep every commandment Moses gives them that day. The purpose is that they have the strength to go in and possess the land they are about to cross the Jordan River to take. The wording here is simple: the commandments are things being given to them today, and the land is one they are crossing over to possess.

Moses speaks to the people at the end of the forty years in the wilderness, just before they enter Canaan. He reminds them of what they saw with their own eyes: God's discipline, as in the case of Dathan and Abiram, and his great works. He wants their memory to produce obedience.

For today: the strength to face new challenges does not come only from our own courage, but from remembering what God has done and walking in what He teaches us. Today you can write down one occasion when God helped you and choose one concrete step of obedience.
exp.14:12:
The verse says that when you release your servant, do not send him away empty-handed. This verse says that when a Hebrew servant completes his six years of service and is set free, his master must not let him leave with nothing. The phrase "release him" means to let him go or grant his freedom. "Empty-handed" means without anything, without provisions.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. A poor Hebrew could sell himself to serve another person in order to pay his debts. God commands that in the seventh year he be released and receive generous help to start over. The verses that follow remind Israel that they too were slaves in Egypt and God rescued them.

For today: if God has given you blessing, think about whom you can help get back on their feet, such as an employee, a relative or a neighbor. Give generously and without resentment, remembering how much you yourself have received.
exp.9:1:
God tells Moses that he himself will write on new stone tablets the same words that were on the first tablets, the ones Moses broke. Afterward Moses is to place them in the ark.

Here Moses speaks to the people of Israel and reminds them of what happened after the sin of the golden calf. Moses had broken the first tablets when he saw the people's rebellion. Even so, God decided to give them another chance and to renew his covenant with them. This shows his mercy.

For today: God does not give up on us when we fail. If we have gone wrong, we can come to him with sincerity, and he offers us forgiveness and a fresh start. His word remains the same, and we can keep it in our hearts.
exp.31:26:
God says that he would not punish Israel to the point of destroying them, because he takes into account what their enemies would say. His concern about how the adversary would react is a concern about how the enemy would respond. Being puffed up with pride means being filled with arrogance. "Our own hand has prevailed" means the enemies would credit their own strength and power. They would boast: "Our own hand did it, not the LORD."

God speaks in the Song of Moses, near the end of Deuteronomy. Israel has rebelled, and God announces severe discipline. But he holds back, because his name and his honor are at stake before the nations. Interpreters understand the idea of God dreading or fearing as a human way of speaking about God, not as real fear.

For today: God guards his honor and continues to work even when we fail. May his patience not lead us to take advantage of it, but to return to him and give him the glory, not claim credit for ourselves.
exp.18:8:
Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. If they carefully keep all the commandments he gives them that day, loving the Lord their God and walking in his ways at all times, they are to add three more cities of refuge to the three already set apart.

The cities of refuge protected those who had killed someone without meaning to, so that they would not be put to death in revenge. God promises to enlarge the territory, and then more cities would be needed. The text joins obedience with justice and with care for innocent life.

For today: loving God should show in how we protect and treat others. We can seek justice and mercy, and not let anger or revenge take control of us.
exp.10:9:
This verse compares the promised land with Egypt. It says that Canaan is not like Egypt, where the people sowed their seed and irrigated it on foot, like a vegetable garden. That phrase probably refers to moving some kind of irrigation system with the foot, although some scholars think it could mean opening the water channels between the furrows with the foot.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that in Egypt everything depended on human effort to bring water to the crops. In Canaan, by contrast, they would depend on the rain from heaven, that is, on God's provision. For this reason he asks them to obey his commandments with confidence.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we live relying only on our own effort. Work is good, but we can do it with gratitude and prayer, remembering that everything we need ultimately comes from the hand of God.
exp.27:60:
It says that if the people are disobedient, the LORD will bring sicknesses and plagues even beyond those recorded in this Book of the Law. The verse closes by saying the consequences would continue until the people are destroyed, meaning brought to ruin. The point is that turning away from God would have serious results, with no set limit placed on them.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land. He presents to them the blessings that come with obedience and the curses that come with breaking the covenant. These warnings are part of an agreement between God and Israel, and they were meant to lead the people to take their faithfulness seriously.

For today: we should not read every illness as a punishment, since the Bible itself denies this in other passages, such as in Job and in John 9. But we can learn to take God's voice seriously and turn back to Him with humility, trusting in His mercy in Christ.
exp.12:4:
It says that the prophet or dreamer who advocates rebellion against the LORD and tries to turn the people from the way God has commanded must be put to death. The reason given is that this person has set himself against the LORD your God, who brought them out of Egypt and redeemed them from the house of slavery. He wanted to draw them away from the path God had told them to walk. With that, the text says, the evil is purged from among the people.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter the promised land. God allowed a false prophet to appear, even with signs, to test whether the people truly loved him. This was a law for the nation of Israel under the covenant of that time, where idolatry was treated as treason against their King.

Today we do not apply this penalty, but we do apply the principle: let us examine every teaching in the light of what God has already revealed. If anyone, however impressive he may seem, draws us away from Christ and the Bible, we should not follow him.
exp.4:1:
This verse says that God, whom Moses calls "the LORD our God," made a covenant with his people at Horeb. Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai. A covenant is a solemn commitment between two parties: God binds himself to his people, and the people promise to respond to him.

Moses speaks to all Israel before they enter the promised land. Almost all the adults who were at Horeb had already died, so he addresses the new generation. He tells them that the covenant is not only a thing of the past: it is theirs too. That is why he calls them to hear, learn, and obey.

For today: do not live your faith only on what others have told you. Make it your own. Set aside a moment this week to read the Word and to answer God with a concrete decision of obedience.
exp.23:10:
This verse says that the lender must stay outside, while the man who borrowed goes into his house and brings out the security that was given for the loan. A security is an object left as a guarantee for a loan. The word "lend" is used here for lending money or goods to someone. The lender is not allowed to go into the house to collect it on his own.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land, and reminds them of God's law. This rule protected the dignity and privacy of the one who owed money, especially the poor. The verse before it mentions Miriam and what God did to her; scholars understand this as a reminder of how serious it is to obey God, though not all of them explain the connection in the same way.

For today: if someone owes you something, look after them and treat them with respect. Ask for what is fair, but never humiliate or intrude on the privacy of someone who is in a difficult situation.
exp.19:6:
A man who has become pledged to a woman but has not yet married her may go back home and not go to war. The word "pledged" means engaged, and "married her" means marrying her and bringing her into his home. The reason is that he might die in the battle and another man would marry her.

These words are instructions from Moses to the people of Israel before they entered the promised land. The officers were to repeat them before each battle. Together with the new house and the vineyard, the text shows that God cared that no one would lose what was just beginning to live. Some scholars think it also protected the morale of the army.

For today: God values the important moments of life, such as an engagement or a home that is just beginning. We can care for those stages and support those who are going through them, without demanding more from them than they can give.
exp.12:0:
This verse speaks of someone who may arise among the people and claim to be a prophet, or to receive messages from God through dreams. That person proclaims a sign or a wonder, that is, something amazing or out of the ordinary.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He warns them that a miracle is not enough to prove that someone speaks on behalf of God. According to the verses that follow, if that prophet invites them to follow other gods, they must not listen to him. God allows that test to see whether they love him with all their heart.

Today we can learn to measure every spiritual message by what God has already revealed in his Word. Even if something seems impressive, if it draws us away from God, it does not come from him.
exp.2:11:
This verse says that Moses gave out the land that Israel had taken east of the Jordan River. From Aroer, beside the Arnon Valley, and half of the hill country of Gilead, along with its cities, he gave it to the tribes of Reuben and Gad.

The phrase "took possession" means that Israel actually took control of that land.

Moses speaks to the people in Moab, near the end of his life, and reminds them of what God did. After defeating powerful kings like Og, the land was divided. Later, the other half of Gilead and Bashan passed to the half-tribe of Manasseh.

For today: God keeps his promises, and it is good to remember with gratitude what he has already given us. When we recognize his past blessings, we trust him more for what is to come.
exp.32:7:
God gave the tribe of Levi the Thummim and the Urim, objects the priests used to seek God's will. The verse calls the faithful man God's "godly one," the person God tested at Massah and contested with at the waters of Meribah. Here "tested" means "put to the test." "Contested" means argued or disputed.

Moses speaks just before his death and blesses each tribe. To Levi he recalls their priestly service. Scholars do not agree on who the "godly one" is: it could be Moses, Aaron, or the whole tribe. The episodes at Massah and Meribah show moments of testing in the wilderness, and Levi appears as a tribe that was tried and found faithful.

For today: God uses trials to reveal and strengthen our faithfulness. When you go through a difficult season, ask him to help you respond with trust and obedience, not with complaint.
exp.11:17:
This verse says that the people were to eat their tithes, firstfruits, vows, and offerings in the place God would choose, not in their own towns. There the whole family, the servants, and the Levite would eat together. "Towns" means cities or villages, and "Levite" refers to a member of the tribe of Levi, who served in worship and had no land of his own. All of this was to be done with joy before God, from the fruit of their labor.

Moses speaks to Israel before they enter Canaan. He teaches them that worship must center on the place God chooses, not on just any location. He also reminds them to care for the Levite, who depended on the generosity of the people.

For today: give with gratitude and do it in community. Enjoy with others what God has given you, and do not forget to support those who serve others or are in need.
exp.13:2:
It says that God's people were not to eat any "detestable" thing, that is, anything God regarded as unclean or repugnant for his people. It is a short phrase that opens the list of permitted and forbidden animals.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel before they enter the promised land. He reminds them that they are children of God, a holy people, set apart and special. For that reason, even the way they ate distinguished them from other nations. Some believe these rules had health reasons, others had to do with identity; the text emphasizes above all holiness and obedience.

Today, as Christians, we do not follow those dietary rules, but we do learn that belonging to God touches everyday life. We can ask ourselves which habits, words, or customs reflect that we belong to Him.
exp.20:21:
If a person commits a crime so serious that it deserves death, and after the execution the body is hung on a pole or a tree, that body must be treated with care. The Spanish phrase quoted in the source, "Hubiere pecado de sentencia de muerte," refers to the same idea: the person has committed a crime punishable by death. The verse that follows makes clear that the body was not to be left hanging overnight.

Moses speaks to the people of Israel shortly before they enter the promised land, going over God's laws. These rules governed the justice of that people. It is believed that the hanging happened after death, although some understand it in a different way. The emphasis is on respecting human dignity and keeping the land clean.

For today: even someone who has failed gravely deserves to be treated with dignity. This invites us to reject mockery and cruelty, and to seek justice with humility and respect.

sum.1: After years of wandering in the desert, God tells Israel not to attack Edom, Moab, or Ammon, because he has given those lands to their relatives, and to buy the food they need as they pass through. When the rebellious generation had died off, God gave them victory over King Sihon, whom they destroyed.
sum.18: God commands that three cities of refuge be set apart, where a person who has killed someone unintentionally can flee to be protected from the avenger of blood. But a murderer who acted out of hatred must be handed over and put to death. The chapter also orders people not to move their neighbors' boundary markers, and it requires at least two or three witnesses before a charge can be upheld. A false witness is to receive the same punishment he had intended for the person he accused.
sum.21: Moses gave Israel laws for living with care and justice: helping one's neighbor with lost animals and lost belongings, protecting life by putting a railing on the roof, and respecting creation. He also set rules about marriage and sexual purity, defending a woman who had been falsely accused and punishing adultery and abuse.
sum.2: Moses recalls how God gave Israel victory over Og, king of Bashan, and how the land east of the Jordan was divided among the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. He asks them to help their brothers conquer the rest, and he encourages Joshua to trust that God fights for them. Moses begs to enter the land, but God tells him that he will only see it from the top of Mount Pisgah.
sum.31: Moses sings a song in which he praises God as the faithful and just Rock. He recalls how God cared for Israel, and how Israel forgot Him and turned to other gods. God announces punishment, but also that He will judge His enemies and have compassion on His people. At the end, Moses urges the people to obey the law, and God tells him that he will see the promised land but will not enter it.
sum.9: Moses recounts that God gave him new tablets of the law, which were kept in the ark, and that God listened and did not destroy the people. He then explains that God asks for reverence, love, obedience, and service with all one's heart. God is great and just, and He loves the orphan, the widow, and the foreigner, and for that reason His people must love them too.
sum.24: God teaches Israel to be just and humane. Punishments have a limit (no more than forty lashes), the name of a deceased man's family is to be cared for, and false weights are forbidden. The passage also commands Israel to remember what Amalek did when he attacked the weak, and that his memory is to be blotted out once Israel has rest.
sum.20: Deuteronomy 21 gives laws so that Israel can live justly: a purification ritual when a dead body is found and no guilty person is known, and protections for the captive woman, for the firstborn son of the less-loved wife, and for the body of someone who has been executed. It also commands that a rebellious and stubborn son be punished.
sum.15: Moses reminds the people that they must celebrate three festivals each year before God: Passover, Weeks, and Booths, with joy and with offerings according to how God has blessed them, and including servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows. He also commands that fair judges be appointed who do not accept bribes, and he forbids setting up sacred trees or statues beside the altar.
sum.28: Moses gathers all of Israel in Moab to renew the covenant with God. He reminds them of what God has done for them and warns that if anyone turns away from the LORD to serve other gods, judgment will fall on that person and on the land. He concludes by saying that the secret things belong to God, but the things revealed are for us to obey.
sum.22: God gives laws to keep his people set apart and clean: who was allowed to enter the assembly, how to take care of the camp during war, and not to return a slave who has run away. It also teaches not to charge interest to a fellow Israelite, to keep the promises made to God, and to be fair to one's neighbor.
sum.16: God asks that sacrifices offered to him be without defect, and he commands that idolatry be punished only after a careful investigation and on the testimony of at least two or three witnesses. Difficult cases are brought to the Levitical priests and the judge, and their ruling must be obeyed. In addition, the future king must be chosen by God, must be an Israelite, must not accumulate horses, wives, or wealth, and must read the law every day so that he remains humble.
sum.5: Moses tells Israel to listen: the LORD is the only God, and they must love him with all their heart, soul, and strength. His words are to be taught to their children every day and kept constantly in mind. When they enter the promised land, they must not forget God or follow other gods, but remember how he delivered them from Egypt.
sum.13: Moses reminds Israel that they are children of God and a holy people, so they must live differently from others, including rules about which animals they may eat and which they may not. He also commands them to give a tithe so they can eat it with joy before God, and every three years to share it with the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow.
sum.17: God takes care of the Levites, who have no land of their own because the LORD is their inheritance, and the people give them offerings for their support. God forbids divination, sorcery, and consulting the dead, and promises to raise up a prophet like Moses, whom the people must listen to. A false prophet, whose words do not come true, should not cause fear.
sum.12: Moses warns Israel not to follow anyone who invites them to worship other gods, whether it is a prophet who performs signs, a close family member, or an entire city. God tests them to see whether they love him with all their heart. For this reason he commands them to follow him alone and to remove this evil with severity.
sum.14: Deuteronomy 15 commands that debts between fellow Israelites be canceled every seven years. It instructs people to give generously to the poor without hesitating because of the approaching year of release. It also says that a Hebrew servant is to be set free in the seventh year and sent off with provisions, with the reminder that Israel was redeemed from Egypt. In addition, it orders that firstborn animals without defect be set apart for God, and that the blood must not be eaten.
sum.23: The chapter gives laws about divorce, the care of newlyweds, and respect for loans, for the poor, and for the worker. It commands that wages be paid on the same day, and that each person answers for their own sin. It also calls for justice for the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow, reminding the people that Israel was enslaved in Egypt.
sum.29: Moses says that even if the people are scattered because of their disobedience, if they turn back to God with all their heart, God will have compassion, gather them together, and bring them back to their land. His word is not far away but near, in the mouth and in the heart. For this reason Moses sets before the people life and death, and asks them to choose life by loving God.
sum.7: Moses asks the people to remember how God cared for them and tested them in the wilderness for forty years, teaching them to depend on his word and not on bread alone. Soon they will enter a good and fertile land. He warns them not to forget God or become proud of their wealth, because forgetting him would bring ruin.
sum.19: God tells Israel not to be afraid in battle, because He goes with His people and fights for them. Rules for war are also given: first offer peace, let certain men return home, and take care of the fruit trees. It also commands that the peoples of Canaan be completely destroyed, something that many scholars explain in different ways.
sum.10: Moses urges Israel to love God and obey Him, reminding them of what He did in Egypt, at the sea, and in the wilderness. The promised land depends on rain and God's care, so there is blessing if they obey and curse if they follow other gods. They must teach these words to their children and choose the path of blessing.
sum.3: Moses asks Israel to obey God's law without adding anything to it or taking anything away from it, and not to make idols, because at Horeb they heard only his voice and saw no form at all. He warns them of punishment if they turn away, but promises that God, who is merciful, will receive them back if they seek him with all their heart. Three cities of refuge are also set apart.
sum.27: Moses tells Israel that if they obey God, they will be blessed in every area of life: in their homes, their fields, their harvests, and against their enemies. But if they turn away from God, terrible curses will come, such as disease, famine, defeat, and exile. The central teaching is that serving God with joy and obedience brings life, and abandoning him brings ruin.
sum.0: Moses reminds the people how God told them to leave Horeb and head toward the promised land, and how he appointed leaders to help him guide them. At Kadesh, the people were afraid and refused to obey, so that generation did not enter the land. The lesson is to trust God and obey him.
sum.32: Before he dies, Moses blesses the tribes of Israel, recalling how God came with his law and became their king. To each tribe he asks for protection, strength, teaching, or abundance, according to its place. He ends by saying that there is no one like the God of Israel, his eternal refuge, who gives victory to his people.
sum.30: Moses, now 120 years old, encourages Israel and Joshua not to be afraid, because God will go with them into the promised land. He puts the law in writing so it can be read every seven years, and God warns him that the people will turn away, so he is commanded to teach them a song to serve as a witness.
sum.11: Moses commands that the places of worship and altars of the nations living in Canaan be destroyed, and that God be worshiped only at the place he chooses. There, people are to bring their offerings and rejoice together with their families, not forgetting the Levite. He allows them to eat meat at home, but not the blood. He warns them not to imitate the gods of those nations or to add to or take away from the law.
sum.4: Moses gathers Israel and reminds them that God made a covenant with them at Horeb. He repeats the Ten Commandments to them, which speak of loving only God, keeping the Sabbath day of rest, honoring parents, and respecting one's neighbor. The people, filled with fear, ask that Moses be the one who listens to God, and God commands them to obey so that things will go well for them.
sum.6: Moses tells Israel that, when they enter the promised land, they must not make treaties or intermarry with the nations living there, and that they must destroy their altars and idols so they will not turn away from God. God chose them not because they were great, but out of love and faithfulness to his promise, and he asks them to trust in him and obey him.
sum.8: Moses tells Israel that God himself will go ahead of them to defeat strong nations, but they must not think they are receiving the land because they are righteous. He reminds them of their rebellion, such as the golden calf at Horeb, and of how he prayed that God would not destroy them. Everything shows that the land is a gift from God and a result of his promise.
sum.25: When Israel enters the promised land, they must bring the firstfruits to the sanctuary and remember with gratitude how God delivered them from Egypt. They must also share the tithe of the third year with the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow. God calls his people to obey him wholeheartedly and to be his holy people.
sum.26: Moses and the elders gave Israel this command: when you cross the Jordan, set up large stones with the law written on them, and build an altar on Mount Ebal, and worship with joy before God. Six tribes would stand on Mount Gerizim to pronounce blessings, and six on Mount Ebal to pronounce curses. The Levites would read twelve curses against idolatry, injustice, and secret sin, and the people would respond, "Amen."
sum.33: Moses climbs Mount Nebo, and God shows him the promised land, but he will not be allowed to enter it. There he dies at the age of 120, with his eyesight still good and his strength intact, and God buries him in a place no one knows. Israel mourns him for thirty days, and Joshua, who is full of wisdom, takes his place.
